Thesis gate

Can a large language model literally have communicative intentions and perform speech acts such as asserting, advising, promising or apologising, or does it only produce text that humans interpret as such? The rival positions fall into four groups. Denials hold that LLMs perform no speech acts of their own: on organismic grounds, because speaking is acting, acting requires intentions, and intentions require the self-set goals of autonomous, self-maintaining organisms rather than externally purposed mechanisms (Gubelmann); on normative grounds, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice whose performers must produce outputs with a descriptive function and be open to sanction, conditions that current models fail singly or jointly (Butlin and Viebahn), an argument extended to speech acts in general (Skiba); and, for apology in particular, because chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency the act requires (Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz). Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Intermediate views assign machines a status short of full speech-act performance: quasi-testimony, on which instruments assert only in a qualified sense that differs fundamentally from human assertion (Freiman and Miller), and proto-assertion, proposed after finding both the proxy and fictionalist accounts inadequate (Williams and Bayne). Attributing views hold that the demanding Gricean, mind-reading conception of communicative intention is empirically untenable even for humans and that, on a thinner functional conception of intention as an internal state controlling output in response to the situation, language models have communicative intentions in a graded and limited form, with purposes supplied by their design context (Attah). Behind these lies a dispute about agency itself: one account counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, so that many language agents built around LLMs qualify, bare pre-trained chatbots are borderline, and desire requires considerably more than agency (Butlin); an enactive account denies LLMs autonomous agency for want of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, describes them as linguistic automata, and locates what is new in hybrid human–LLM agency (Barandiaran and Almendros); and a relational-materialist account rejects the individualistic, property-based framing altogether and distributes agency across networks of human and non-human actors (Puzio).

279 candidates · 1 in the top-right quadrant · 24 repairable · 254 not attacked

Promise is scored blind, before any attack. Residual is the strongest objection left unanswered — 0 is best, and it is the ranking number. Worst is the strongest objection mounted at all: when Worst is also low, the thesis was not seriously tested rather than sturdy.

Look here first

Promise 4+ with nothing above a 2 left unanswered. Ambitious and hard to break. Expect a short list, and an empty one on some runs.

P1. Attah's control conception fixes the intention at the grain of output selection (the token or utterance) but speech acts are individuated at the grain of the act performed with the output, and no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 2/5 · worst 3/5 · survives
Move · Target
distinction — Attah's claim that transformers plausibly recapitulate Levelt's Conceptualizer–Formulator–Articulator pipeline, and the shared assumption that 'control of output' is the same as 'control of act'.
Sketch

Attah analyses intention as an internal state that solves Wu's Many-Many Problem by attention-like selection, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is meant to supply the act-level content. Attention in a transformer selects among inputs to compute the next-token distribution, so the thing controlled is the continuation. A communicative intention must control at the grain of 'warn this person', 'concede the point' or 'promise', where one string can realise different acts and one act can be realised by many strings. Call the first grain output-control and the second act-control. The control conception is satisfied by output-control, but the Levelt template requires a preverbal message with illocutionary force that is selected before formulation. Whether LLMs have such a state is an interpretability question: do mid-layer representations encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface? The claim is that Attah's argument equivocates between the two grains, and that Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn and Attah all treat the grain as settled when it is the crux. This yields a testable, non-metaphysical criterion that could favour either side, for example by intervening on force representations while holding content fixed.

Appraiser (blind)
Identifies the grain of control (output versus act) as an unexamined crux in the intention debate and offers an interpretability-testable criterion that could favour either side.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, unanswered. The defender argued the Attah-directed core is untouched, but dropped the 'shared assumption' rider for Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn. That is a concession on the periphery, not an answer.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. The defender argued control is description-relative, so the intensional demand follows from what control is, and the extensional reading lets a parrot or stuck key control a warning. The retreat from a representational requirement to counterfactual sensitivity is a mild narrowing.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, answered. The defender specified criteria (a)-(d) and a prefill/teacher-forcing minimal-pair test that holds the output fixed. This shows a positive result is possible and blocks the reclassification move.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. The thesis does not claim novelty of the distinction. Attah's Levelt mapping is his own reply to the familiar objection, and the neighbours cited do not state the control-grain criterion.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 2/5, answered. The defender argued (d) is only a Levelt-internal burden on Attah, and that humans, children and apes pass the dispositional criteria (a)-(c). The cost is that the thesis no longer bites against a bare control conception.
🔧 Survives as

Restrict the target to Attah's Levelt mapping and state the criterion interventionistically: control at the act grain means counterfactual sensitivity to act type across lexically disjoint realisations, dissociable from content steering. Treat the preverbal ordering test as owed only by the claim that transformers recapitulate Levelt's pipeline.

Flaw

No fatal flaw. The exchange cost the thesis its 'shared assumption' rider and its force against a bare control conception, and it has become a modest absence claim that fine-tuned models passing (a)-(c) could make empirically fragile.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is the claim that the grain confusion is shared: that "Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn and Attah all treat the grain as settled" and that all of them identify control of output with control of act.

- Gubelmann (2024) does not argue from output control. He denies that LLMs have intentions at all, on Kantian grounds: their goals are externally fixed and they lack material autonomy. He even grants them a kind of cognitive autonomy. His test is whether malfunction can be told apart from deliberately doing the wrong thing, which is not a claim about token-level or act-level control. He assumes nothing about the grain.
- Butlin and Viebahn (2025), going by the summary supplied, do not rest on intention or control. Their conditions are descriptive function and sanctionability. They do not assume that output selection amounts to act selection. They conclude that unfine-tuned models fail even the first condition, which is the opposite of treating the grain as settled.
- Attah is the only real target. He explicitly takes the basic communicative intention to be one aimed at an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect, so he is not obviously confined to output grain. His appeal to Levelt's Conceptualizer is meant to supply exactly the act-level content the thesis says is missing. The thesis may therefore be attacking a flattened version of his view.

STRENGTH: 2/5. I am working from the summary and from memory of these papers. The accusation of equivocation against Attah is a fair interpretive charge, since he asserts plausibility rather than argues for it. The misattribution to Gubelmann and to Butlin and Viebahn is real, but it is peripheral. The core claim about Attah survives if the thesis is narrowed to him.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection has three parts, and they deserve different replies.

1. The core thesis is about Attah, and the objection concedes that Attah is the real target. The thesis sentence names only Attah's control conception and the absence of any argument that an LLM state controls at the act grain. Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn appear only in the sketch's rider.

2. Attah's explicit act-level theory of intention does not answer the thesis. It is the thesis's premise. The objection says Attah takes the basic communicative intention to aim at an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect, and that Levelt's Conceptualizer supplies the act-level content. I agree. The charge is that this is a requirement placed on the LLM, not something shown to hold of it. Attah's theory of what an intention is can be act-grained while his control conception, via Wu's attention-like selection, is only ever instantiated for LLMs at the level of next-token computation. His claim that transformers "plausibly recapitulate" the Conceptualizer–Formulator–Articulator pipeline then moves from an act-level template to output-level evidence. That move is the equivocation. The objection treats his act-level ambition as a defence, but an ambition without a mapped state is the gap.

3. The "shared assumption" can be defended as a dialectical presupposition, not an explicit identification of output control with act control.
- Gubelmann's test asks whether an LLM's bad output can be told apart from deliberately doing the wrong thing. That presupposes that an output is already a candidate for being an act, which is the unit the grain question is about. His denial of intention rests on autonomy, but the question "act or malfunction?" is posed of outputs.
- Butlin and Viebahn ask whether LLM outputs can be assertions. They assess functional and sanctioning conditions on output-producing systems, so the output is the unit of analysis. Fine-tuning counts as supplying the relevant function through training on outputs. That treats output-level shaping as sufficient for act-level status, without asking which internal state fixes force.

The charge, then, is not that they say output control equals act control. It is that none of them makes the grain an open question, and the interpretability test (intervening on force representations while holding content fixed) would be needed to settle it.

VERDICT

The defence holds for the core thesis and fails for the rider.

Core thesis, about Attah: holds. The objection's best point, Attah's illocutionary framing, supports the equivocation charge. His theory demands act-grain control, his transformer evidence is output-grain, and "plausibly recapitulate" papers over the gap. I found no reply to this in the objection.

"Shared assumption" about Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn: the defence mostly fails.
- Gubelmann's argument runs through autonomy and goal-fixing. Saying he "presupposes outputs are act candidates" is a stretch, because any discussion of whether LLMs act would do so. That is not the specific error of treating the grain as settled.
- Butlin and Viebahn's functional conditions are in fact one way of not assuming a grain. They are agnostic about internal states, and their negative verdict on unfine-tuned models shows they do not treat act status as automatic. My reading of them rests on summary and memory, so I should not claim more.

The defence for these two is a reframing of what they assume, not a showing that they assume it. I should drop "all treat the grain as settled" and the "shared assumption" wording in the target. This is a correction of an overreach, not a narrowing made to dodge the objection. The Attah thesis never depended on those claims, and the testable criterion in the sketch also stands without them.

The objector's 2/5 strength rating seems fair. It damages the framing and the target description, not the argument.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that speech acts are "individuated at the grain of the act performed," so a state that controls output selection does not thereby control the act. The key term is "controls at the act grain," and it has two readings.

- Extensional reading. A state controls an act if it controls the output that, in context, constitutes the act. On this reading the thesis is false or trivial. An LLM state that selects "that ledge is unstable" in a context of hazard-warning thereby controls the warning. Act individuation is fixed partly by context and uptake, as Austin, Skiba and Butlin and Viebahn all suppose. Output control then suffices for act control, and the gap disappears.
- Intensional reading. A state controls an act only if it represents and selects the force-type as such, independently of the lexical surface. This reading makes the thesis interesting, because it yields the interpretability test and the Levelt preverbal-message requirement.

The thesis is plausible on the first reading, since act individuation is not purely internal. It is interesting only on the second. The argument needs the social, contextual individuation of acts to say that the grain differs from output. It then needs the intensional, psychological reading of control to say that Attah's state fails at that grain. These two moves rest on different notions of "act." The step from "acts are individuated by what is done" to "the controlling state must represent force" is exactly where the equivocation sits.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The defender can say the intensional demand comes from Attah's own Levelt commitment, so the critique is internal. That answers the charge, but it has to be argued and stated, not assumed.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says "controls at the act grain" can be read extensionally or intensionally, and that the thesis needs both. I deny that there are two readings. The intensional demand is not an extra premise. It comes from what control is.

1. Control is always control under a description. This is the Davidsonian point about the light switch. Flipping the switch, turning on the light and alerting the burglar are one bodily event, but an agent controls it as an alerting only if her guiding state is sensitive to the features that make it an alerting. Wu's selection story works the same way. Intention solves the Many-Many Problem by selecting one path through a space of possible input-output mappings, and a state controls X only if it discriminates X from the alternatives at X's grain. So "the state controls the warning" and "the state is counterfactually sensitive to warning-versus-other-acts" are one condition, not two notions of "act."

2. The extensional reading proves too much. If controlling the output that in context constitutes the act suffices for controlling the act, then a parrot trained on "that ledge is unstable," or a stuck autocomplete that happens to emit it at a cliff edge, controls a warning. Any account of control must exclude these. The extensional reading removes the distinction between controlling an act and merely being causally upstream of a string that counts as one. Context and uptake fix which act was performed. They do not make the producer's state the controller of that act. The thesis needs only the first claim about individuation and the second about control, and these are compatible.

3. The demand is internal to Attah. His basic communicative intention is aimed at an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is invoked to supply preverbal, force-bearing content. The critique takes his own act-grained analysis at its word and asks what in a transformer plays that role. An internal critique does not need a neutral theory of acts.

4. The test does not require a dedicated "force module." The criterion is interventionist: if you change a state while holding content and lexical options fixed, does the act performed change (warn versus merely report, promise versus predict)? A distributed representation could pass. Control at the act grain is therefore an empirical matter, and the thesis claims only that no argument yet shows it.

5. The extensional reading's best rescue is Butlin and Viebahn's route. Training and sanctioning supply the act-level function. That is a different account, grounded in function and not in intention-as-control. It cannot rescue Attah's use of Levelt.

VERDICT

The defence holds on the main point. The two readings are not independent premises. The intensional demand follows from control being description-relative, and the extensional reading fails on parrot and stuck-key cases. The step from "acts are individuated by what is done" to "the controlling state must be sensitive to act-type" is the ordinary step from individuation to control.

Two concessions remain, neither fatal.

- The sketch's wording is stronger than the thesis. "Encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface" reads as a representational requirement. The thesis requires only counterfactual sensitivity at the act grain. The stronger wording is the Levelt-internal version, which Attah owes, but the thesis should be stated in the weaker interventionist form. This is dropping an overstatement, not narrowing the claim. The interventionist test was already the sketch's own criterion.
- The thesis is a burden claim ("no argument shows"). It is only as strong as the survey behind it, and it dissolves if someone produces the intervention result. That is a feature of a testable thesis, not a defect.

The 3/5 rating seems about right. The objection forces the thesis to state its notion of control, and once stated it stands.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that act-grain control and output-grain control are separable, so that an intervention could in principle show an LLM state to be the second and not merely the first.

The thesis says "no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain." The defender has already moved from a representational requirement (a force-type encoded independently of lexical surface) to a counterfactual-sensitivity test: change the state, hold content fixed, and see whether the act changes. Both moves make the thesis harder to refute by cases.

- Redefinition protects it. Suppose steering a "warning" direction reliably turns reports into warnings across paraphrases. The thesis can say this tracks pragmatic style or lexical priors, not force. Suppose it generalises across many surface forms. The thesis can say the force is fixed by context and uptake, which the defender concedes, so the state never controlled the act. No positive result is ever specified as counting.
- "Holding content fixed" is not well-defined. If force depends on context and uptake, any intervention that changes the act also changes the output distribution. Every result can then be reclassified as output-control.
- The burden-claim form is asymmetric. "No argument shows" is refuted only by an argument the author may judge not to reach the act grain. The thesis is then immune to cases and gets credit for testability.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis can be rescued by pre-registering what would count, for example generalisation across lexically disjoint realisations plus a dissociation from content steering. As written, that commitment is missing.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says the thesis is protected by redefinition, because any positive result can be reclassified as output control. Each of its three charges has an answer.

1. The reclassification move is not available to the thesis as defended. The "context and uptake fix the act, so the state never controlled it" reply only works on the extensional picture. The defender rejected that picture last round. On the defended view, context fixes which act was performed, and control is the producer state's counterfactual sensitivity to act type. So if steering a state reliably flips warn/report across contexts, that is control at the act grain by the thesis's own standard. The thesis cannot say "style" or "context did it" without also withdrawing its own account of control.

2. "Holding content fixed" has a well-defined version that defeats reclassification. The objection says any intervention that changes the act also changes the output distribution. Remove that confound by prefilling or teacher-forcing the identical string, for example "that ledge is unstable", under a matched context. Then intervene on the candidate state and measure downstream behaviour:
- how the model answers "why did you tell me that?";
- whether it treats a later "I know" as acknowledgement or as a cue to repeat the warning;
- whether it commits to follow-up conduct (a promise binds, a prediction does not).

The emitted tokens are identical by construction, so any difference cannot be output-control over those tokens. This is a real double dissociation, and it mirrors the sketch's own claim that one string can realise different acts. Run the converse as well: lexically disjoint realisations of one force should be moved together by one intervention, while a content-steering intervention leaves force unchanged.

3. The pre-registration the objector asks for is a specification, not a retreat. The positive result counts as showing act-grain control if:
- (a) the effect generalises across lexically disjoint realisations;
- (b) it dissociates from content steering;
- (c) the prefill test shows downstream commitments shifting with the intervention;
- (d) for the Levelt claim specifically, the state is causally upstream of formulation. It should be present and causally effective at positions before the first content token, and mediate between context and output rather than merely correlating with it.

The "no argument shows" form is asymmetric in the way every burden claim is. That is not immunity. It is refuted by exactly the result described, and the sketch already says the test "could favour either side."

VERDICT

The defence holds on the main point, with one honest concession about the thesis as written.

What holds. Separability is not in doubt, since the minimal-pair design is a double dissociation. The prefill design closes the reclassification route, because the output is held fixed by construction. The criteria are specifiable and a positive result is possible. So the thesis is falsifiable in principle, and the objector's 3/5 reflects an omission, not a flaw in the idea.

What I concede. As written, the thesis and sketch gave no pre-registered criteria, and the objection correctly forced that out. This is not hedging. The thesis is unchanged and what is added is a statement of what would refute it.

Two residual costs.
- The prefill test operationalises act control through dispositions over later outputs. A critic can say this relocates the act grain into output patterns across turns. I think the reply is adequate, since the distinction was never between outputs and something non-behavioural. It is between control of this continuation and a state sensitive to force type across realisations. But the point has to be stated.
- Criterion (d), the ordering requirement, is where Attah's Levelt claim is most exposed. Criteria (a) to (c) could be met by a state that is downstream of formulation. Only (d) tests the "preverbal message selected before formulation" template. If the empirical work establishes (a) to (c) but not (d), the thesis loses against a bare control conception but wins against "recapitulates Levelt's pipeline."

The thesis survives, but it is a methodological challenge to Attah's "plausibly recapitulate" claim, not a result about LLMs. Its real content is the equivocation charge against Attah. The "no argument shows" clause is cheap by comparison.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the output-grain/act-grain distinction is not already a live, named position, so that it counts as a new equivocation in Attah. The distinction is the old "next-token prediction is not speech act selection" objection. Bender and Koller hold it, and so does Shanahan in "Talking About Large Language Models" and in his role-play work. Shanahan says the model produces a continuation and the act belongs to the simulated character. Attah's paper is itself a reply to that family of arguments.

The distinction also sits inside the positions the thesis cites:
- Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion exists because LLM outputs have the form of acts without a settled act-level state fixing force.
- Butlin and Viebahn's "descriptive function" condition asks whether a state is sensitive to act type, not just to the string.
- Gubelmann's malfunction/deliberate-wrong test separates producing a string from performing an act.

Attah also concedes the point. He says how much intention ChatGPT has "is still open" and that the real gap is mental and metalinguistic agency. The thesis may therefore be a restatement of a known position with an interpretability gloss.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The distinction is already taken. The specific contribution is not: a control-theoretic, interventionist criterion with a prefill dissociation, aimed at Attah's Levelt mapping. None of the named authors states that. The attack removes the claim to novelty about the distinction, not the paper's method.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis does not claim the distinction is new. It says Attah's control conception fixes intention at output grain, that speech acts are individuated at act grain, and that no argument shows an LLM state controls at act grain. That is a claim about whether Attah's argument bridges a gap. Whether the gap has been named before has no bearing on it. A known objection can still be unanswered by a particular author. "Already taken" would defeat the thesis only if Attah had already answered the objection at this grain.

2. Attah's paper being a reply to that family of arguments helps the thesis. If Attah is answering the "next-token prediction is not speech act selection" line, then his Levelt mapping is his answer, and the question is whether the answer works. The thesis says it does not, because it supplies an act-grained template and output-grained evidence. A familiar objection that a reply claims to meet is exactly the place to test whether the reply meets it.

3. The cited neighbours do not occupy the thesis's position.
- Bender and Koller concern whether form alone can ground meaning and communicative intent. That is a thesis about training signal, not about which internal state controls selection at which grain. It does not engage the control conception or Wu's Many-Many Problem.
- Shanahan's role-play view answers "who performs the act?" with "the simulated character, not the model". That is a rival account of the act's bearer, not a test of whether a state controls act type. It also makes a prediction the interventionist criterion can use: if there is a persona-level state that fixes warn versus report, interventions on it should pass criteria (a) to (c). Shanahan's view is thus a candidate for the positive result, not a pre-emption of the thesis.
- Williams and Bayne, Butlin and Viebahn, and Gubelmann are cited as sensitive to the distinction. That does not make them hold the thesis. Sensitivity to the distinction is what the earlier misattribution objection said they have, and it is why I dropped "shared assumption". The two objections pull apart: if these authors already carry the distinction, they were never guilty of treating the grain as settled.

4. Attah's concession is about degree, not grain. "How much intention ChatGPT has is still open" is a hedge on the conclusion. His claim that transformers plausibly recapitulate the Conceptualizer-Formulator-Articulator pipeline is a separate claim, and that is the target. His further point that the real gap is mental and metalinguistic agency identifies a different gap and leaves the output-versus-act gap untouched.

5. The contribution lies where the objector says it does. The objector grants that none of the named authors states the interventionist criterion, the prefill dissociation, or the ordering requirement (d) aimed at the Levelt mapping. The thesis is a claim that this mapping is unsupported, together with a test that could support it. That is not a restatement of "LLMs only predict tokens". The old objection is a negative claim about LLMs. This thesis is a conditional claim about what Attah would have to show.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection removes a novelty claim the thesis does not make and leaves the argument intact. I see three costs.

- Framing. The sketch's "Attah and others equivocate" wording invites the "already taken" reading and should not present the distinction as a discovery. I conceded this earlier for Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn, and I concede it here. The distinction is a familiar one, and what the thesis adds is where it bites and how to test it.
- Shanahan is a live threat. If acts are performed by a simulated character, the thesis owes an account of whether persona-level states count as LLM states controlling at act grain. I think they do, so a positive result on the persona state would favour Attah's side. That is consistent with the thesis, but it means the thesis cannot be read as hostile to Attah's conclusion, only to his support for it.
- Residual weakness. The thesis is a challenge to an argument's support, not a result about LLMs, and it depends on an absence claim ("no argument shows"). The "already taken" objection shows how much of its force rests on the bridging step in Attah. If a reader finds Attah's "plausibly" a deliberately modest claim, the equivocation charge loses most of its bite.

The 2/5 rating is fair. The attack hurts the claim to novelty and leaves the argument standing.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that control of a speech act requires a state that discriminates act-type independently of the lexical surface, and (in criterion (d)) one that is causally upstream of formulation. If that premise worked, it would deny act-control to many ordinary human speakers.

- Formulaic speech. "Thanks", "sorry" and "hi" are produced as routines. There is no separate force-selection step, and no lexically disjoint alternatives are available to the speaker.
- Incremental production. Speakers often discover what they are doing, such as conceding, hedging or committing, while speaking. Force is fixed partly by uptake and by later repair. This is the Austinian "negotiation" picture the defender already conceded. Strict preverbal-message-then-formulation sequencing is a contested part of Levelt's model.
- Children and animals. Attah's own comparison cases (young children and non-human animals) would fail the criterion. They would fail it because they lack independent, preverbal force representations, even though they plainly perform communicative acts.

The prefill dissociation would also fail for humans. Intervening on a human speaker's force state while holding the string fixed is not available, and the cases above suggest no clean dissociation would be found. A criterion that denies acts to children, routine speakers and incremental speakers is too demanding to be a neutral test.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The thesis can reply that criteria (a) to (c) are dispositional and that humans plausibly pass them. It can add that the strict ordering requirement (d) is Attah's own Levelt commitment, so it is an internal critique. But the reply has to give up (d) as a general condition on act-control.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs: criterion (d), and the demand for a force state independent of lexical surface, would deny act-control to formulaic speakers, incremental speakers, children and animals. This would work against a thesis that asserts (d) as a necessary condition on act-control. The thesis asserts no such thing.

1. (d) is a conditional owed by Attah, not a general analysis of acts.
- The thesis is a burden claim about one argument. Attah says transformers plausibly recapitulate Levelt's Conceptualizer–Formulator–Articulator pipeline, and that pipeline is defined by a preverbal message fixed before formulation.
- Whoever invokes that template owes evidence for the ordering. The thesis does not say that all act-control has that structure.
- Criteria (a) to (c) are the general, dispositional test of act-grain control. Criterion (d) is the extra test for the Levelt claim only. I said last round that (a) to (c) without (d) defeat a bare control conception but not "recapitulates Levelt". That scoping was already in place and I am not adding it now.

2. The three human cases each pass (a) to (c), and two of them support the thesis.
- Formulaic speech. "Thanks", "sorry" and "hi" are routines, but the speaker selects the routine at the act level. Choosing "cheers" over "much obliged" is lexical, and choosing thanking over apologising is the act. The routine is how act-grain selection looks when formulation is cheap. The speaker can withhold, redirect or substitute the routine, which is counterfactual sensitivity to act type. This is the case where control sits upstream of the words.
- Incremental production. Levelt's own model is incremental, and (d) was stated relative to positions before the first token of the act-realising span, not before the whole utterance. A speaker who discovers mid-sentence that she is conceding has a state that governs the remaining realisation, and (a) to (c) can be assessed from that point. Late-fixed force is no problem for a dispositional test. It is a problem for a rigid preverbal-then-formulate template, and that template is Attah's commitment, not the thesis's. If strict sequencing is contested for humans, his appeal to it is weaker, and that supports the thesis.
- Children and animals. The developmental and comparative literature already uses something like (a) to (c). Bates and Golinkoff treat intentional communication as shown by means-end dissociation, persistence, and substitution of means when the goal is unmet. An infant who points, vocalises or reaches to get the same request met shows sensitivity to act type across lexically or modally disjoint realisations. Great ape gestures show audience sensitivity and response-waiting, which also passes. These creatures do not fail the test. The test is the one that earned them communicative status.

3. The prefill test is a method, not a criterion. We cannot clamp a human's string and intervene on her force state. That is a limit on evidence, not on what would count. For humans the same dissociations come from natural variation, from persistence and repair behaviour, and from lesion or stimulation studies where available. The mechanistic access we have to LLMs only means we can run the stronger version. The asymmetry in method does not make the criterion exclude humans.

4. The parity point supports the thesis. For humans, children and apes we have independent reasons to attribute act-grain control. The thesis asks for the same kind of reason in the LLM case. Attah gives a template and no mapped state. Pointing out that other agents pass the test shows the test is reasonable and that he has not yet shown that LLMs pass it.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection is aimed at a necessary condition the thesis does not assert. Applied to what the thesis does assert, (a) to (c), humans pass, and so do the children and animals the objector worried about.

Two costs remain, and I state them plainly.

- (d) cannot be defended as a general condition on act-control. The thesis has to keep it as a Levelt-internal test only. That is the scope it had, but it means the thesis bites against Attah's pipeline claim and not against a bare control conception.
- (a) to (c) are probably easy for fine-tuned models. Instruction-tuned LLMs may pass them readily, since steering and minimal-pair interventions on force-like features are plausible. If so, "no argument shows" becomes empirically fragile, and the surviving content is the Levelt-specific ordering claim. Attah can reply that he needs only a functional analogue of the preverbal message, not strict sequencing. That reply would weaken his own Levelt appeal, which is the support the thesis targets, but it would also put his conclusion on firmer ground than the thesis can touch.

The objector's 2/5 is fair. The attack forces (d) to be marked as Attah's burden and not a general requirement, and the thesis stands once that is marked.

Repair candidates

Promise 4+, failed on ONE locatable flaw — usually scope or framing, with the narrower version already written out. Often the richest vein.

R1. If any chatbot output is an assertion, the asserted content is not what a sampled token sequence says but what the model's output distribution commits to. The token-level framing used by every side is mistaken, and the 'no stable commitment' objection to chatbot assertion misfires.

Scores
promise 5/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — All parties who evaluate chatbot assertion by looking at individual outputs and their conversational consistency, notably Butlin and Viebahn and Williams and Bayne's treatment of the objection from commitment.
Sketch

Debate so far assumes the candidate speech act is an individual utterance. But one prompt can be resampled to yield p, then not-p, with no change in the system. A human who did this would be insincere or incoherent, so this is read as evidence that no speaker-level commitment exists. Distinguish token-assertion (the sampled string as an act) from policy-assertion (the stable dispositional profile across resamples, including its calibrated uncertainty). On the second view, a single output is an exemplar of the policy, and what is asserted is something like 'p, with this confidence' where the confidence is reflected in the spread of outputs. This changes the status of hallucination: it is a miscalibrated policy, not a string of lies. It changes what a sanction should target: retraining the policy, not penalising a draw. It also makes the descriptive-function condition of Butlin and Viebahn checkable at the policy level. The premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms, as with a human speaker's settled opinions versus a slip of the tongue. This also explains why users are right to treat chatbot outputs as defeasible reports, and why proto-assertion looks like the right verdict on single outputs, since single outputs are not the primary bearers.

Appraiser (blind)
Policy-level assertion, with its consequences for hallucination, sanction and the 'no stable commitment' objection, would change how everyone frames what the candidate act is.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender separated where function is grounded from what the act's bearer and content are, so the objector's system-level citations do not show the targets hold the policy-level view. 'Every side' was conceded as overstated, which is a cost to the rhetoric only.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. The defender showed Shanahan is a rival (no speaker is committed) and that Chalmers, Kadavath and the others shift the level for different questions. None of them applies the shift to assertion content, and the objector conceded as much.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. The defender met the 8-ball point (the thesis is conditional) and the lying point (relocated to the policy level). On hedging collapse it conceded: assertion is public, the hearer never receives 'p, with c', and the rescue via implicature makes the view dual-level.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The distorting-channel and sycophancy-as-miscalibration replies were real arguments. But the defender had to drop 'spread of outputs' and 'checkable by resampling' and retreat to a latent logit profile, which is narrowing. It then conceded that this worsens the public-act problem.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. The defender rejected the dilemma: system-level evaluation does not entail policy-level assertion, and rivals draw opposite conclusions from it. The individuation test is ordinary theory-choice. The defender then said the distinctive content is the part already conceded dead.
🔧 Survives as

Keep content at the string level and move only the evaluation target to the policy: hallucination is policy miscalibration, sanction targets retraining, and a single resample from p to not-p does not show insincerity. State the scope as fine-tuned models, since Shanahan's superposition reading probably wins for base models. This repair is much weaker than the original content claim and largely uncontested.

Flaw

Assertion is a public act and the hearer receives a flat string, not the latent distribution. The defender never met this, and the premise linking answerability to retraining stayed unsupported.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne, evaluate chatbot assertion at the level of the individual sampled output. The thesis says "the token-level framing used by every side is mistaken."

- Butlin and Viebahn's first condition is that an entity produces outputs with *descriptive functions*. As I recall, they ground this in what training selected the system to do, which makes it a property of the trained system's output type, not of a single draw. That already looks policy-level. Their finding that pre-trained models fail it and fine-tuned ones may meet it is a claim about training regimes, not about particular strings.
- Their second condition, sanctionability, concerns whether the system can be responsive to correction. That plausibly points at the system, not at one token sequence.
- Williams and Bayne ask whether "chatbots" can assert and introduce proto-assertion as a status for chatbot outputs. I do not remember them treating resampling inconsistency as decisive.
- Green and Michel, Arora, and the proxy views locate the act in designers or deployers, not in tokens. "Every side" is therefore too strong.

On this reading the thesis attacks a straw consensus, and its "distinction" is already implicit in its targets.

I am working from memory. I cannot confirm how Williams and Bayne handle the commitment objection, or whether Butlin and Viebahn say anything explicit about resampling.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The thesis is conditional and the target field is loosely drawn, so some overgeneralisation is likely. But the "no stable commitment" objection is a real one in this literature, so the position is probably held by someone. The thesis's two named targets are also not shown to hold the policy-level view explicitly, which leaves a gap the thesis can plausibly fill. The fix is to narrow the target to the commitment objection.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs together three questions: where function is grounded, who the candidate speaker is, and what the bearer and content of the speech act are. The thesis concerns only the third.

1. Grounding is not bearer. Butlin and Viebahn do ground descriptive function in training, which is a property of the trained system. But the question they then ask is whether *this output*, a "Paris is the capital of France" produced in this exchange, is an assertion. Etiological function can be fixed at the level of the system while the act-token remains the thing evaluated. The thesis says the content of the act is not what the string says but what the distribution commits to. A training-grounded function condition is fully compatible with the string-level view of content. A selected-for output type can be an assertion of exactly its sampled propositional content. So the objector's observation that function is grounded in training does not show their view is the policy-level view.

2. The proto-assertion verdict is token-level evidence. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion status is given to chatbot *outputs*. If they already held that the primary bearers were policies, they would not need an intermediate status for single outputs. The thesis's final claim explains why proto-assertion looks right for single outputs: they are not the primary bearers. That claim is distinctive and does not appear in either target.

3. The sanction condition does not entail policy-level content. Responsiveness to correction at the system level is compatible with the correction being a correction of a particular string, such as "you said p, retract it." The thesis adds that the content subject to sanction is the dispositional profile, including its spread. No one the objector cites says that.

4. The proxy theorists are not counterexamples. Green and Michel, Arora, and the proxy views deny that the chatbot is the speaker. The thesis is conditional: *if* chatbot output is an assertion, what is asserted is X. Views that locate the act in designers or deployers are outside the antecedent. They do not show that those who accept the antecedent already hold X.

5. The commitment objection is live. The objector concedes the "no stable commitment" objection is a real one. Resampling from p to not-p is exactly what makes it bite on token-level content. The thesis's reply is therefore aimed at a real position.

VERDICT

The defence holds against this objection, with one cost.

The objector offers no textual evidence, and says they are working from memory. They show that the targets ground function and sanction at the system level. They do not show that the targets individuate the act, or fix its content, at the policy level, and that is the thesis's actual claim. Point 1 shows that the system-level grounding they cite is neutral on that question.

The cost is that "every side" and "all parties" are overstated. The thesis can drop that rhetoric without touching its substance. It does not need to claim a universal consensus, only that the commitment objection and the proto-assertion verdict presuppose the single-output bearer. That is a change to the target description, not to the thesis, so I do not count it as hedging.

One risk remains and I cannot discharge it from memory. If Butlin and Viebahn or Williams and Bayne explicitly discuss resampling and assign content at the distribution level, the novelty claim fails. That is a textual check on the sources, and the objector has not done it either.

This objection also leaves the thesis's real burdens untouched: whether sampling spread reflects the model's own calibrated confidence rather than a deployer-set temperature, and whether a distribution can be a conditional commitment across prompts.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the debate treats the individual sampled output as the bearer of the speech act, so that distribution-level content is a new proposal. I think the policy-level view is already held, though by people who draw the opposite conclusion about assertion.

- Shanahan (2023, "Talking About Large Language Models"; Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds, "Role Play with LLMs"). An LLM is a generator of a distribution over continuations, or over simulacra. A sampled string is one draw from a "superposition" of possible speakers. Resampling from p to not-p is therefore not insincerity, because no single speaker was committed. This is the thesis's diagnosis of why token-level commitment fails.
- Andreas (2022, "Language Models as Agent Models"). Content is attributed at the level of the model's inferred distribution over agents.
- Chalmers ("What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models"). The candidate speaker is a character or thread, not the string. This is the same move of shifting the level of the bearer.
- Kadavath et al. and Keeling and Street. Calibration and credence are attributed to the output distribution. Herrmann and Levinstein's belief-representation work does likewise, and so does Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini's work on language agents, which attributes states to the system.

On this reading the thesis relabels Shanahan's and Chalmers's level-shift as "policy-assertion". It adds only the claim that the shift rescues assertion.

I am working from memory, and I have not checked whether any of these authors apply the shift to assertion content specifically.

STRENGTH: 2/5. These authors establish the distribution-level framing and the diagnosis of resampling. None clearly claims that the asserted content is "p, with this confidence" and that the commitment objection therefore misfires. The most the attack shows is that the thesis's novelty lies in the application to assertion. It does not show that the thesis is taken.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The cited authors shift the level for different questions.
- Shanahan, Andreas and Chalmers shift the level for *who the speaker is*. Kadavath et al. and Keeling and Street shift it for *where credence is located*.
- None of them asks what the content of an assertion is, or what the unit of a speech act is. The thesis concerns the bearer and content of the act.
- The thesis's premise, that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producer is answerable to norms, is not stated by any of them.

2. Shanahan is a rival, not a precursor.
- The superposition view says the spread of outputs reflects a plurality of possible characters, so no one is committed to anything. The thesis says the spread reflects one policy's calibrated uncertainty, so one commitment exists.
- These are incompatible readings of the same distribution. Shanahan's diagnosis of resampling is that no speaker exists. The thesis's diagnosis is that the act was never the string.
- A rival with the opposite conclusion about assertion is not prior art for the thesis. The thesis has to beat it, and it has a resource for doing so. In fine-tuned models the distribution is sharply narrowed toward a single stable persona, and training is the locus of norm-answerability. That fits Butlin and Viebahn's own finding that fine-tuned models are the live candidates.

3. Chalmers shifts to a different bearer. His quasi-subject is a character or thread, which is conversation-scoped. The thesis's bearer is a dispositional profile conditional on the prompt, and it persists across threads. So this is not the same move.

4. The prior work is support.
- Kadavath et al. show that token probabilities and self-assessed P(True) are calibrated. That is empirical backing for the premise that spread carries confidence.
- If the components are independently respectable, the thesis is a composite resting on them. Novelty is also not validity. "Already said" would at most trim the credit, not touch the truth of the claim.

5. The conclusions the thesis draws appear in none of these authors. I cannot find in them the claims that the content is "p, with this confidence", that hallucination is miscalibration rather than lying, or that sanctions target the policy. The objector concedes this in their own strength rating.

VERDICT

The defence holds against this objection. The objection shows the level-shift is available in the wider literature. It does not show that anyone has applied it to assertion content, and the two named targets are unaffected.

It does impose two costs.

- "Every side" is false. Shanahan and others do not take the token-level framing, and the thesis should say so. This is the second correction to the target description. Both leave the thesis's content unchanged. If a third correction began to alter what the thesis claims, I would call that hedging.
- Shanahan's reading is the real opponent. The thesis has to show that the distribution is one commitment-bearer and not a superposition. My answer, the narrowing effect of fine-tuning, does real work. It also means the thesis is clearly true only of fine-tuned systems, and for base models Shanahan's reading probably wins. That limit is not new, since Butlin and Viebahn already draw it, but the thesis should state it openly.

Two burdens remain open. One is whether spread reflects the model's own calibration or a deployer-set temperature. The other is whether a distribution that varies with prompt is a stable enough object to carry a commitment.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms. If that premise licenses reading "p" as "p, with this confidence", it proves too much in three ways.

1. Hedging collapses. A human whose settled credence in p is 0.6, and who flatly says "p", would be asserting "probably p". The difference between flat assertion and hedged assertion, and so the ordinary category of overclaiming, disappears. Hearers hold speakers to what was said, not to what the speaker's dispositions encode.

2. Calibrated noise-makers become assertors. A forecast ensemble, a calibrated random sampler, or a weighted Magic 8-ball has a stable output distribution and is answerable to calibration norms, since it can be retrained. On the premise, each of them asserts "p, with confidence c". The thesis needs some further condition to block this, and that condition would be the one Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability requirement already supplies.

3. Lying becomes impossible for a calibrated policy. A calibrated system emitting a confident falsehood is just a draw from an honest distribution. The same reasoning excuses a human who is consistently 70% reliable.

The premise therefore erases the act/disposition distinction it relies on, since a "slip of the tongue" is defined against the act, not the profile.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis can add conditions, such as sanctionability, to exclude the ensemble and 8-ball cases. But the hedging collapse in point 1 bites on the thesis's central content claim and needs a real answer.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

Point 2 (calibrated noise-makers) misreads the thesis's logical form. The thesis is conditional: *if* any chatbot output is an assertion, its content is fixed at the policy level. It gives no sufficient condition for being an assertor. The premise says what individuates the unit and content of a speech act, given that there is one. Whether there is one is settled by the Butlin-Viebahn conditions (descriptive function, sanctionability), which the thesis takes as given. The 8-ball and the ensemble fail those conditions. An 8-ball has no descriptive function selected by training for truth-tracking output, and nothing in it answers to correction by reasons rather than being tinkered with. So they get a unit but no act. This is resisting, not hedging, because the thesis never claimed the premise was sufficient.

Point 3 (lying becomes impossible) is answered by moving lying to the policy level. A draw from an honest, calibrated distribution is not a lie, and neither is the output of a human who is 70% reliable. That is the right verdict, and it is the thesis's verdict on hallucination. Lying remains possible: it is a policy whose outputs systematically diverge from what its own internal representations (Herrmann and Levinstein-style probes, Kadavath's P(True)) encode. So the act/disposition distinction is not erased. It is relocated, and lying is a mismatch between policy-level content and policy-level internal state.

Point 1 (hedging collapse) is the hard one, and the premise itself answers it. The objector imports the human case: credence 0.6, flat "p", and we hold the speaker to "p". But the thesis's premise is that the unit is fixed by the level at which the producer is answerable to norms. A human is answerable at the act level, since we can say "you said p, you didn't know that", so for humans the act, with its flat register, is the bearer. The premise does not say dispositions override acts. It says the level tracks answerability, and it gives different verdicts for humans and chatbots. A chatbot cannot be called out for a draw, only retrained. So the human case does not transfer, and the objector needs an argument that chatbots are answerable at the act level.

Overclaiming survives too. It becomes policy-level miscalibration: the policy's commitment "p with c" is checked against the world, and a policy whose c is systematically too high overclaims. A flat register that outruns the spread can be treated as a misleading implicature, a fault separate from content. Users can also sample the spread themselves by regenerating, so it is not wholly hidden from hearers.

VERDICT

The defence holds against points 2 and 3, and fails against point 1.

Point 2 is resisted by the conditional form. Point 3 is resisted by moving lying to the policy level. Neither costs the thesis anything.

Point 1 fails for three reasons.

1. The answerability reply leans on the premise, which is asserted, not argued. "Answerable only by retraining" is the weak point. Retraining is a causal intervention. If that counts as answerability, calibrated artefacts qualify. If it doesn't, chatbots are not answerable at the policy level either, and the thesis loses its premise. I could only keep the premise's discrimination by re-importing the Butlin-Viebahn conditions, which makes the thesis dependent on a sanctionability notion it has not shown policies satisfy.

2. Assertion is a public act. What a speaker is committed to is fixed by what the hearer can take them to have put forward. A hearer who gets a flat "p" has no access to the spread in the ordinary exchange. Regenerating is not part of the conversational act. So "p, with this confidence" is not something undertaken in the exchange, and the thesis's central content claim fails, on its own terms, as a claim about assertion.

3. The rescue needs the string to do pragmatic work. The overclaiming reply says the flat register is a "misleading implicature". But the string is then contributing to what is communicated, so the act is both token-level and policy-level. That is a dual-level view and not the thesis. The thesis says the content is *not* what the string says. If the string's register carries a commitment that the policy-level content does not, the thesis has been hedged into a compromise.

So the thesis does not survive in its stated form. What survives is the narrower claim that the right locus for evaluating hallucination and for sanctions is the policy. That is a claim about where to evaluate and intervene, not about assertoric content, and it is a different and weaker thesis. I report the content claim, and with it the claim that the commitment objection "misfires", as dead.

The "every side" overreach noted earlier is a further, smaller cost.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the spread of a model's outputs across resamples reflects its own calibrated confidence, so that "p, with this confidence" is a fact about the model.

Take a fine-tuned assistant that answers "Is the Great Barrier Reef visible from space?" The T=1 distribution is 55% "no", 45% "yes". The thesis assigns the policy-assertion "no, with c≈0.55".

- Deployment A runs greedy decoding. Every resample gives a flat "No". The spread is zero, so by the thesis's own criterion the asserted content is "no, with c≈1". Nothing about the model's dispositions has changed.
- Deployment B runs T=1.5. The spread is nearly uniform, so the asserted content is "no, with c≈0.4".

The same weights then assert three different contents, set by a deployer's sampling parameter. The policy's calibration, which is the thing the thesis says bears norms, is untouched.

The thesis can retreat to the underlying logit distribution at T=1. But that is a counterfactual object that no user ever samples. It is not "the spread of outputs", and it is not what the deployed system does.

The same problem arises with sycophancy. The distribution is conditional on the user's stated view, so the policy's commitment is "p-if-the-user-wants-p". That is a stable policy, but not an assertion that p.

STRENGTH: 3/5. This is a genuine problem, but it can be answered by fixing the policy as the logit distribution. That answer gives up the "spread of outputs" and "checkable" claims.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis fixes the bearer at the level of answerability, and temperature is not at that level. The premise is that the unit of a speech act is the level at which the producing system answers to norms. That level is the trained weights, which give a conditional distribution over continuations. Temperature is a deployer-side decoding parameter applied after the model has done its work. The thesis says the content is what "the model's output distribution commits to", and that phrase picks out the model's own distribution, not whatever histogram a given deployment emits. The sketch's phrase "spread of outputs" was loose, and the objector exploits it. But the premise never depended on it.

2. A dispositional profile is counterfactual by nature, and that is no objection. A fragile glass is fragile unsampled. A person's credence is not the frequency of their utterances under arbitrary noise. Retreating to the T=1 logits does not swap in a different object. It identifies the disposition that the sampling procedure only reads off noisily. Probing work in the style of Kadavath et al. and Herrmann and Levinstein reads this object directly, so it remains checkable, though not by counting resamples.

3. The deployments are a case of a distorting channel. Greedy decoding turns "no, 0.55" into a flat "No", and T=1.5 flattens it. This is the familiar structure of a faithful speaker with a bad microphone, or of an editor who strips hedges from a report. The content is the same across deployments, and the deployer is responsible for the distortion. The thesis therefore gets a new explanatory resource. The objector reads a sampling parameter as changing the content, when it changes how faithfully the content is transmitted.

4. Sycophancy is a miscalibrated policy, not a different content. The policy is conditional on the prompt, as every speaker's commitments are conditional on their evidence. If the user's stated preference moves the credence in p, though it is no evidence about p, then the policy is miscalibrated at that input. That is the thesis's own diagnosis of hallucination applied to a new case. "p-if-the-user-wants-p" is a description of the defect, not of what is asserted.

VERDICT

The defence answers the counterexample as stated, but it does not rescue the thesis.

Points 1, 2 and 4 hold. The objection does not touch the premise that the bearer is the weights-level policy, and sycophancy is a miscalibration, not a rival content. But the answer has three costs, and they are costs to the thesis, not to its wording.

1. It abandons the "spread of outputs" and "checkable" claims. The sketch says confidence is "reflected in the spread of outputs" and that the function condition becomes checkable by looking at resamples. After the retreat, that is false for any deployment with non-unit temperature. What remains is a logit-level object that must be probed, and nothing in the sketch shows that probe-level confidence is the content of an assertion.

2. Point 3 makes things worse. If the content is the T=1 logit profile, then every greedy deployment systematically emits an act whose register contradicts its content. On the thesis's own terms, most real deployments are persistently misreporting, and the deployer is the culprit. That is a strange result for a view meant to vindicate users' practice of treating outputs as defeasible reports. The users never see the content that supposedly was asserted.

3. It sharpens the earlier public-act problem. I already conceded that assertion is a public act, and that what a speaker undertakes is fixed by what the hearer can take them to have put forward. The counterexample shows that the "content" is not even available in the exchange by resampling. It is a latent quantity that neither the hearer nor the deployed system conveys. The commitment that supposedly makes the objection "misfire" is one that nobody is positioned to hold the system to in conversation.

The earlier verdict therefore stands, and this objection strengthens it. The claim that the asserted content is "p, with this confidence", and that the commitment objection thereby misfires, is dead. What survives is the narrower claim that hallucination, sycophancy and sanction should be evaluated at the policy level. It is a claim about where to evaluate and intervene, not about assertoric content.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms. Splitting the thesis on this premise gives a dilemma.

- Uncontested half. A trained model is a conditional distribution, and hallucination, sycophancy and sanctions are best evaluated and fixed by retraining that policy. No party disputes this. The proxy theorists, Shanahan, the calibration literature, and Butlin and Viebahn's training-based function condition all already locate evaluation and intervention at the system level. Relabelling this as "policy-assertion" adds a name, not a finding.
- Contested half. The claim that what is asserted is "p, with this confidence" does not follow from any fact about models. It follows from the premise, which stipulates that "answerable to norms" means "retrainable". If retraining counts as answerability, calibrated ensembles and weighted 8-balls assert as well. If it doesn't, the premise fails. Which way it goes is a verbal decision about "assertion", not something evidence could settle. The "misfire" verdict on the commitment objection then holds only by definition: the objection says no speaker-level commitment exists, and the thesis redefines "commitment" as the dispositional profile.

So the thesis is either uncontested or a stipulation.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The dilemma is real, but the thesis does make a substantive claim about content and the act/disposition distinction that rivals deny. A reply would need to show that this claim has independent consequences.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The first horn is false. The objector says every party already locates evaluation and intervention at the system level. That is true, but the thesis does not claim this. Agreement on where to evaluate does not give agreement on what the act is, who performs it, or what it says.
- Shanahan draws the system-level lesson and concludes that no speaker is committed to anything.
- The proxy theorists draw it and locate the act in designers or deployers.
- Butlin and Viebahn use a system-level function condition and then ask whether *this output* is an assertion.
- Williams and Bayne give single outputs the status of proto-assertion.

The thesis is the one position that takes system-level evaluation and concludes that the policy is the primary bearer of assertion. That conjunction is rejected on every side, so it is not an uncontested half with a new name attached.

2. The second horn is not verbal. The objector says the thesis "stipulates that answerable to norms means retrainable". But the premise comes from the human case. We individuate a person's assertions by the level at which they can be held to account: settled opinion versus slip of the tongue. The thesis applies that test to a new kind of producer and gets a different answer, because the chatbot is not answerable at the act level. This is ordinary theory-choice. Rival individuations of the bearer make different predictions about which practices are fitting:
- whether to demand retraction of a draw or correction of a policy;
- whether resampling to not-p convicts the system of insincerity;
- whether "hallucination" is a lie or a miscalibration.

If one individuation fits these practices better, that is evidence for it. Conceptual questions about assertion are settled this way in the literature on testimony and group assertion.

3. The "by definition" charge is symmetrical. The commitment objection also assumes without argument that commitment must attach to the act-token. If redefining commitment at the policy level is stipulation, so is the objection's default. A neutral comparison needs an independent test, and the premise supplies one.

4. Independent consequences exist. The thesis predicts the following:
- Proto-assertion is the right verdict on single outputs, because they are exemplars and not primary bearers.
- The sanctionability condition is to be assessed at the policy level.
- Resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity.

None of these follows from the uncontested half alone.

VERDICT

The triviality charge fails. The thesis still does not survive.

The dilemma is a misdiagnosis. The first horn is wrong because policy-level evaluation does not entail policy-level assertion, and rivals draw opposite conclusions from it. The second horn is wrong because the premise is not a pure stipulation. It generalises a standard test for individuating speech acts. So the thesis is neither trivial nor merely verbal.

But the content that makes it non-trivial is the content already ruled out in earlier rounds, and the defence just offered does not repair it.

1. The premise is still doing the work, and its key notion is still unsupported. Point 2 leans on "answerable at the policy level", and the earlier objection stands: either retraining counts as answerability, in which case calibrated ensembles qualify, or it does not and the premise lapses. The conditional form blocks the 8-ball only by importing the Butlin-Viebahn sanctionability condition, and the thesis has not shown that policies satisfy it in a way that a retrained ensemble does not.
2. Assertion is a public act. The independent consequences in point 4 all concern where to evaluate and intervene. The claim that the asserted content is "p, with this confidence" is not something a hearer can take the system to have put forward. The thesis has to show how a latent logit profile, not conveyed in the exchange and distorted by deployer settings, can be what is undertaken. That has not been shown, so the "misfire" verdict on the commitment objection rests on a content the hearer never receives.
3. The consequences that survive belong to the weaker thesis. The things that do work are the miscalibration diagnosis of hallucination, the retraining target for sanction, and the defeasibility of outputs. All of these follow from system-level evaluation alone, which the objector's first horn correctly calls uncontested. The distinctive part, the content claim and the dissolution of the commitment objection, is the part already reported dead.

I therefore reject the triviality objection as a diagnosis. It adds nothing to the earlier verdict, which stands. The thesis as stated is dead. What is left is the claim that the policy is the right locus of evaluation and sanction for chatbot error, and that claim is not contested by the rival views.

R2. Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts confuse two grains of principal objective, objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents, and only the former can ground a proxy speech act, so the proxy view survives only for canned output and collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended generation.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 3/5 · worst 3/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — Green and Michel; Arora; the proxy half of Butlin–Viebahn
Sketch

Green and Michel adopt Armstrong's analysis in terms of objectives and extend it to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. In each of those cases the principal has an objective bearing on the content of the type of act or a determinate conditional on it: a recorded message, a secretary's letter, or 'if the door opens, say X'. An LLM's designers and deployers have objectives only at the level of a policy ('be helpful, honest, harmless'), and nobody has an objective regarding the particular proposition produced in a given token sequence. Policy-grain objectives do not suffice for speaker meaning (a bookshop owner's general aim of informing customers does not make each sentence in each book his assertion). Proxy-assertion proponents therefore face a dilemma: either they weaken the objective-condition until it makes authors of every book printer, which trivialises the account, or they keep it and lose open-ended output. This also explains why Williams and Bayne find the proxy view inadequate without having a principled diagnosis of why. The key premise is that speaker-meaning attribution is closed under content-specificity: the objective must be sensitive to what is said.

Appraiser (blind)
The content-specific versus policy-grain objectives dilemma offers a principled diagnosis of why proxy accounts struggle with open-ended generation.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defender met the Green–Michel point (conditionals must be determinate) but conceded that 'confuse' misdescribes Butlin–Viebahn and Arora, and re-aimed the thesis at a generic proxy view, which is absorption.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defender showed the premise is substantive because coarse-grain delegation is a live rival, and that the grain variable plus the factual claim go beyond 'proxy works where content is fixed'; the self-declared 'dead' verdict is not backed by anything the objector said.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defender offered a determination reading but then drifted to an 'availability to the principal' condition and conceded the slide. The later uniqueness test helps, but this round ended in concession.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The uniqueness test (satisfaction-set size of the objective) is a fixed criterion applied before the case verdict, and it sorts almanac, 'whatever is true', temperature-0 and conditional cases without relabelling.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. The priority claim is a side sentence. Foresight and grain diagnoses predict differently (almanac case, wide-but-approved band), and the responsibility-gap worry is a different target. Still rests on unverified recollection of Williams and Bayne.
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Defender met the Green–Michel point (conditionals must be determinate) but conceded that 'confuse' misdescribes Butlin–Viebahn and Arora, and re-aimed the thesis at a generic proxy view, which is absorption. Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Drop the 'confuse' charge and the priority claim. State the thesis as a conditional: proxy speech acts need an objective with a unique-content satisfaction set, so views grounding LLM speech acts in policy-grain objectives collapse into the no-speech-act view except where a human ratifies a specific output. Independently defend the claim that wide-discretion delegation yields responsibility but not speaker meaning.

Flaw

The named targets are mischaracterised, and the uniqueness premise is left exposed to delegated-discretion cases (press secretary, ghostwriter) and de dicto objectives that the defender never resolved.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that the proxy accounts ground LLM speech acts in the designers' or deployers' objective about particular content. That premise is stated flat for three targets, but at most one of them holds it.

- Green and Michel. They do use Armstrong's objectives, so the thesis fits them best. But they explicitly extend the analysis to conditional speech acts, and I take that extension to be their way of covering output whose exact content the principal did not fix. So they plausibly already deny that proxy acts need content-specific objectives. They also end by doubting that the strategy covers every speech act type, which is not the unqualified proxy view the thesis attacks.
- Butlin and Viebahn. As I recall, their proxy claim is only that AI systems can be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents. That looks like a user adopting or endorsing output, not designer policy-grain objectives, so the dilemma may not touch it. They grant that AI systems fail to assert in their own right.
- Arora. As I recall, Arora's refinement concerns agency and responsibility of designers and deployers. I do not believe it is framed in Armstrong's objective-terms, and I am not sure.

So the thesis may run three different views together and aim at a position none of them holds as stated. This rests on memory of the summaries, not the texts.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The mismatch with Butlin–Viebahn and Arora is plausible but unverified. Green and Michel's conditional-act extension could in fact be the target of the thesis rather than an answer to it.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. Green and Michel: the conditional extension is not an answer. The objection reads their extension to conditional speech acts as covering output whose exact content the principal did not fix. But the thesis's own examples show what that extension needs: "if the door opens, say X". The conditional is determinate. The principal fixes the content, or a function from circumstances to content, that the principal could state. "If a user asks something, say something helpful, honest and harmless" is a different kind of conditional. It does not determine what is said, so it is policy-grain. The extension therefore does not reach open-ended generation unless the conditional is made determinate, and then the case is no longer open-ended.

Their closing doubt about coverage is also not a rival to the thesis. It is the thesis's diagnosis stated as caution. A view that stops short of open-ended output has already accepted the collapse.

2. Butlin and Viebahn: the objection helps the thesis. Suppose their proxy claim is that a human user can use an AI system to make a proxy assertion by adopting or endorsing its output. Then the content-specific objective is supplied by the user at the moment of adoption, after the output exists. That is exactly what the thesis predicts. Designer and deployer objectives at policy grain do no work, and a content-grain objective appears only when a human reads the output and takes it up. The speech act belongs to the user, which is the no-speech-act view applied to the model. So on this reading their position instantiates the collapse rather than evading it. The thesis would need only to say that this adoption view is the surviving form of the proxy view.

3. Arora: the dilemma does not depend on the authors' framing. If Arora's concern is the responsibility of designers and deployers, the thesis still bites. Responsibility for a policy is not authorship of a content. The thesis's bookshop case shows that policy-grain responsibility, however real, does not yield speaker meaning.
