Any proxy account that grounds LLM speech acts in designer or deployer agency, in Armstrong's vocabulary or not, faces the same choice. It can require content-sensitivity and lose open-ended output, or drop the requirement and make printers authors.

VERDICT

The defence holds for Green and Michel only. For the thesis as written, it fails.

- Green and Michel: the defence is good. The conditional extension needs a determinate conditional, and the thesis already says so.
- Butlin and Viebahn: if the objector's recollection is right, the thesis misdescribes its target. It says these authors "confuse" two grains of objective, but an adoption view makes no such confusion. It places the content-grain objective in the user. My point 2 shows the diagnosis is compatible with their view. It does not show they are guilty of the confusion, and the thesis charges them with it. The same goes for "the proxy half of Butlin–Viebahn" being a target at all.
- Arora: my defence is the weakest here. It works only by dropping the claim that Arora uses the Armstrong framework. The thesis becomes a general claim about any agency-grounded proxy view, which is a different and narrower target than the one named. Re-aiming it this way is hedging, not resisting.

The objection also leaves a bigger problem untouched, which the defence cannot repair. The key premise says speaker-meaning attribution requires content-sensitive objectives. That is doubtful because of de dicto objectives. A principal can intend to assert whatever the almanac says, or whatever the reliable instrument reports, without having any objective about a particular proposition. If a deployer can have the objective "tell users whatever is true about their query", the premise fails and the dilemma loses its first horn. The bookshop analogy does not settle this. The bookseller has no objective of communicating the contents, while a deployer arguably does.

So the thesis cannot be saved by keeping its named targets and its claim of confusion. What survives is a conditional: any proxy view that rests on policy-grain objectives collapses. That is a smaller thesis than the one proposed, and it still has to answer the de dicto objection. I count the original as unsupported against at least two of its three targets.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise that speaker-meaning attribution is "closed under content-specificity", meaning the objective must be sensitive to what is said. On the best version of the attack, this premise is a stipulation presented as a finding. Once "proxy speech act" is defined to require a content-grain objective, the conclusion follows by definition. Open-ended generation has no such objective, so the proxy view collapses into the no-speech-act view. Nothing is discovered. The premise is just the claim that you can't say something without any objective about what you say.

The conclusion is also largely uncontested. Green and Michel end sceptical that the strategy covers every speech act type. Butlin and Viebahn say only that AI "can be used" to produce proxy assertions. Williams and Bayne already judge proxy accounts inadequate. Arora already concedes practical difficulties. The bookshop point is the familiar observation that general responsibility for a policy is not authorship of a content. So the thesis amounts to this: proxy views work where principals fix content and fail where they don't. Each proxy theorist would accept that, so the thesis has no real opponent.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The distinction is real, and it gives a principled diagnosis of the failure, which is more than the existing papers offer. But the premise is carrying the whole argument, and the thesis may be less contested than it claims.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The premise is not true by definition, because the rival principle is live. The objection says that once "proxy speech act" is defined to need a content-grain objective, the conclusion follows trivially. But the thesis does not define the term that way. It makes a claim about what grounds proxy speech acts, and that claim has a serious competitor: a principal's coarse-grained objective, plus delegation and responsibility, suffices. A proponent who wants proxy accounts to cover LLMs needs that competitor to be true. A premise that the opposing camp must deny to get what it wants is a substantive premise, not a stipulation.

2. The thesis is not just "proxy works where content is fixed". The objection compresses it into a banal conditional. The actual claim has three parts.
- It names a variable, the grain of the objective, and says that variable decides whether a proxy act exists.
- It makes a factual claim: LLM designers and deployers have objectives only at policy grain.
- It draws a consequence: the proxy view, applied to LLMs, collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended output.

The first and third parts are what a proxy theorist who extends Armstrong to LLMs has to resist. Williams and Bayne find the proxy view inadequate but lack a diagnosis. The thesis supplies one that predicts where the view fails and why. A diagnosis that locates a failure the literature only gestures at is not trivial, even if each part sounds familiar once stated.

3. "No real opponent" contradicts the previous objection. The earlier objection said the targets hold different views, and that Green and Michel may already reject the premise. If so, they are opponents. If they all accept it, the earlier objection misfires. The objector cannot have both. Taking the first, the thesis has opponents among those who extend proxy accounts to open-ended generation.

4. A resource for the defence: the document-printing analogy. The bookshop case shows that policy-grain aims do not suffice. This is an independent datum, not a restatement of the premise. It would be trivial only if no one thought policy-grain responsibility could ground authorship, and the practice of attributing statements to institutions and spokespeople suggests many do.

VERDICT

The defence beats the triviality objection, but it exposes the thesis to a worse one, and the thesis does not survive.

The defence works for one reason: the premise is contested. But that is exactly the problem. The premise is only non-trivial if "sensitive to what is said" means something stronger than the proxy theorist needs, and on that stronger reading it is probably false.

- Spokesperson, speechwriter and almanac cases. A principal can have a de dicto objective: "report accurately whatever the data show", "tell the public whatever is true about X". That objective is sensitive to what is said, in that it covaries with content and constrains it. Yet it is not an objective about any particular proposition. Many of these cases look like genuine proxy or deferred assertion. If so, content-specificity in the de re sense is not necessary for proxy speech acts, and the first horn of the dilemma fails.
- The bookshop analogy does not discriminate. The bookseller has no communicative objective toward the content of each book. A deployer of an LLM arguably does have one, in that they want users to receive true, helpful information. "Honest" is a constraint on content, not just a general aim. So the analogy fits the thesis's case less well than the thesis needs.
- The dilemma on the premise. Read "content-sensitive" as de re, and the premise is non-trivial but false or unsupported. Read it as content-covarying, and it is plausible, but then LLM objectives like "honest" may meet it, and the thesis's factual claim about policy grain collapses. The thesis needs one reading for plausibility and another for force. Choosing a reading, or adding conditions to fix the choice, is the hedging that makes a thesis dead.

So the triviality objection fails, but only because the premise is exposed to a harder objection that I cannot answer. Combined with the earlier misattribution problem (the thesis says its targets "confuse" the grains, when at least Butlin–Viebahn may not), what remains is the conditional "any proxy view resting on policy-grain objectives fails for open-ended output". That is closer to the objector's trivial thesis than the one proposed. I report the original as dead.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: speaker-meaning attribution requires that the principal's objective be "sensitive to what is said." The thesis needs this phrase to carry two readings.

- Strong reading (de re): the objective concerns this proposition, or a determinate conditional yielding it. On this reading the premise excludes LLM output, which is what makes the thesis interesting. But it is doubtful. A spokesperson, an almanac-reader, or a deployer whose objective is "tell users whatever is true about their query" has proxy-style speech acts without any objective about a particular proposition. Green and Michel's conditional acts already stretch toward this.
- Weak reading (policy versus content): the objective must constrain or covary with content. That is plausible, and the bookshop case supports it. But "honest" and "true" objectives are content-constraining, so LLM deployers arguably meet it. The collapse then fails.

The dilemma's second horn also depends on the slide. "Weaken the condition and every printer becomes an author" holds only for the weakest reading, "inform customers." A de dicto truth-tracking objective sits between the readings, and printers lack it. The bookshop case shows policy-grain aims fail. The LLM verdict needs content-grain in the de re sense. The argument is run on neither reading alone.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis could stipulate a middle reading, such as counterfactual content-control by the principal. But it would then owe an independent defence of that reading, and the current sketch gives none.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis already has a single reading, which is determination, not de re. The sketch's own examples are "a recorded message, a secretary's letter, or 'if the door opens, say X'". The last is explicitly "a determinate conditional". So the premise is not that the objective must name a proposition. It is that the objective, together with the circumstances, must fix what is said. That reading is stronger than "constrains or covaries with content" and weaker than de re. The objector's two horns are not the only options.

2. On the determination reading, the almanac and the data-report cases pass, and the LLM still fails.
- "Report whatever the almanac says" fixes content through an external determinate source. If the almanac says p, the principal's objective is to say p.
- "Be honest and helpful" does not. Many different true, helpful outputs satisfy it. The objective picks out a large acceptable set, and the selection within that set is done by the system's sampling. This is exactly the difference between an objective about a content and an objective about a distribution of contents.
- So "honest" is content-constraining, as the objector says. But constraining a set is not determining a member, and the thesis's grain distinction was never about constraint versus no constraint. It was about whether the objective fixes a member.

3. The truth-tracking objective does not make printers authors. A publisher who aims at truth in an encyclopedia is answerable for each entry through editorial review, so the objective is exercised at content grain. A bookshop has no such objective at all. The second horn survives, because weakening to "truth-tracking" without review does not collapse into printer-authorship. It collapses into something the LLM deployer lacks.

4. The deferential cases support the thesis. When someone says "I'll tell you whatever the almanac says", we count an assertion at the point of reading, when the content is available to the speaker. Before that, there is a commitment to assert, not an assertion. Where the principal has a de dicto objective and a determinate source, the proxy act is completed through knowledge or uptake of the content. The LLM deployer never has that at the time of generation. So the de dicto cases are cases where the content-grain objective exists at utterance time, and the thesis's premise stands.

5. The lookup-table reply. The objector might say a temperature-0 model is a determinate function from prompts to strings, so "output f(prompt)" is a determinate conditional. But the principal does not grasp that function, and on the previous point the grasp is what carried the proxy cases. A determinate conditional that the principal cannot state or foresee is a conditional only in name.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold for the thesis as written, though it shows what a better thesis would be.

The defence works only by moving the load from grain to availability of determinate content to the principal at the time of the act. Points 2 and 4 depend on it. Point 5 depends on it outright, since without it the lookup-table reply defeats the distinction. This is not the distinction the thesis announces. The thesis says the line is between objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents. But "tell users whatever is true about their query" is plausibly an objective about a distribution, and the almanac and spokesperson cases show that some distribution-grain objectives yield proxy acts. What sorts those cases from the LLM case is not grain but whether the principal can grasp the content when the act occurs. That is an epistemic or uptake condition, and it is a different premise. It needs its own defence, and it brings the proxy view closer to an adoption view. The thesis's claim that the proxy view is confused about grain then becomes a misdiagnosis.

Resisting the equivocation charge therefore costs the thesis its central distinction, and this cannot be repaired without changing the thesis. The equivocation is real. On the grain reading, the premise either mis-sorts the de dicto cases or collapses into a policy/content contrast that "honest" satisfies. On the availability reading it is a different thesis, and the sketch gives no argument for it. Together with the earlier verdicts on misattribution and on the unsupported premise, I report the original thesis as dead.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: speaker-meaning attribution requires the principal's objective to be "sensitive to what is said", so that it fixes content rather than a distribution of contents. The thesis states no test for grain that is independent of its verdict on the case at hand. Every apparent counterexample is sorted by relabelling.

- Almanac and spokesperson cases are accepted as proxy acts because their conditional is "determinate". "Report whatever the data show" is a de dicto objective, yet it passes.
- "Tell users whatever is true about their query" has the same form, yet it fails as "policy-grain".
- A temperature-0 model is a determinate function from prompts to strings, but it is ruled "a conditional only in name" because the principal cannot grasp it.
- Where a human adopts the output, the act is reassigned to the user. This counts as the thesis's prediction, not as a proxy act that survives.
- Green and Michel's conditional acts are read as covering only determinate conditionals.

Each case is classified so as to confirm the conclusion. Grain is whatever separates acts that count from acts that don't. The defence's drift from "grain" to "availability of content at utterance time" shows the criterion is adjusted per case. Without a fixed criterion, no proxy case could count against "collapse into the no-speech-act view". The thesis becomes a re-description rather than a finding.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The member-versus-set criterion is a real and partly operational test. But the almanac, spokesperson and temperature-0 cases strain it, and the thesis owes a fixed, independent criterion.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. There is a fixed criterion, and it was in the thesis from the start. The thesis contrasts objectives "about this content" with objectives "about a distribution of contents". That can be turned into a test that never mentions the verdict:

> Uniqueness test. Given the circumstances of utterance, how many non-equivalent contents satisfy the principal's objective? A proxy speech act requires that the objective pick out one (up to equivalence). If it picks out a large set and leaves selection to the producing mechanism, the objective is distribution-grain.

The test is applied to the principal's objective alone, before anyone asks whether the case is an LLM case.

2. The test sorts the objector's cases without relabelling.
- *Almanac or data report:* "Say whatever the almanac says" is satisfied by one content per circumstance, the one the source fixes. It passes. It is de dicto, but de dicto is not the contrast. The contrast is one versus many.
- *"Tell users whatever is true about their query":* Indefinitely many non-equivalent truths satisfy it. It fails. The objector says the two have "the same form", but they have the same syntax and different satisfaction sets, and the test looks at satisfaction sets.
- *Temperature-0 model:* The model realises a determinate function, but the principal's objective does not pick that function out. Countless trained functions would satisfy "be helpful and honest", and which one exists is settled by training noise. Uniqueness is a property of the objective, not of the mechanism that realises it. So no appeal to grasp or availability is needed, and I withdraw that move from the earlier defence. It was the wrong repair.
- *Green and Michel's conditionals:* "If the door opens, say X" has a satisfaction set of one. "If a user asks, say something good" has a large one. The extension covers the former without any special reading.
- *Human adoption:* A user who reads and endorses an output forms a new objective that this content be conveyed, and the set is now one. The act is reassigned because the objective changed, not because the verdict required it.

3. The thesis is falsifiable. It predicts that where the satisfaction set is large and no one ratifies a member, we will not find an intuitive proxy assertion by the principal. A clear counterexample would be a human delegate with wide discretion and no review whose output we nonetheless take the principal to have asserted. The thesis stakes itself on those cases, so it is not a re-description.

VERDICT

The unfalsifiability objection is answered, and the earlier concession that rested on it was too quick. The criterion is fixed, operational, applied to the objective rather than to the outcome, and it removes the drift toward "availability". The objector's own list of cases sorts correctly under it. The charge of relabelling fails.

The defence exposes the thesis's real risk, though. The test makes a prediction, and the strongest counterexamples are delegated-discretion cases: a press secretary drafting statements within a brief, or a ghostwriter given latitude. Many people say the principal asserts what is issued in their name, even when the satisfaction set was large and they never reviewed it. The defender has two options.
- Treat these as responsibility or institutional attribution rather than speaker meaning. This resists the counterexample but needs independent support, and the sketch gives none.
- Accept them as proxy assertions. The premise is then false and the first horn of the dilemma goes.

I do not think the sketch settles this, and that is where the thesis stands or falls.

The defence leaves the earlier damage in place. Misattribution still tells against Butlin–Viebahn and Arora, and the word "confuse" overstates what the thesis can show about them. So I do not call the thesis dead on this objection, but its survival now depends on one contested premise (that discretionary delegation yields no proxy speech act) plus a retargeting of the named opponents.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is the thesis's claim that the literature lacks a principled diagnosis of why proxy accounts fail for open-ended output. The diagnosis looks already taken, mainly by Williams and Bayne (2024), with Skiba (2026) as the natural endpoint.

- Williams and Bayne. As I recall, their case against proxy-assertion is that developers and deployers neither foresee nor endorse the particular outputs, so no one stands behind the specific content as its asserter. That is the point that objectives about a policy do not fix content. The thesis credits them only with a verdict, but they appear to supply the reason.
- Skiba. His norm-based argument says that no one is the speaker of a given LLM output and so no speech act occurs. That is the "collapse into no-speech-act" conclusion.
- Butlin and Viebahn. They restrict proxy assertion to cases where a human uses the system. That is the adoption view, which the thesis's own defence concedes is where the view survives.
- Green and Michel. They already flag the coverage limit.

What remains is a relabelling in Armstrong's vocabulary of the known worry that designers cannot be held to account for unforeseen outputs, a worry tied to the responsibility-gap literature. The grain distinction names the position without adding to it.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The overlap with Williams and Bayne is substantial but rests on my recollection of their text. The member-versus-set criterion and the printer dilemma may still add something, so the attack is answerable.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objection attacks a side remark, not the thesis. The thesis claims that proxy accounts run together two grains of objective, that only content-grain objectives ground proxy acts, and that the view collapses for open-ended output. It does not claim that nobody else has reached the collapse. Only the sketch's closing sentence, that Williams and Bayne lack a principled diagnosis, makes a priority claim. Even if that sentence is false, the thesis is untouched. Arriving at a conclusion others hold is not a defect, and Skiba reaching "no speaker" confirms it.

2. Foresight and grain are different diagnoses, and they sort cases differently. Suppose Williams and Bayne's point is that designers and deployers neither foresee nor endorse particular outputs. That is an epistemic and attitudinal condition on the principal. The uniqueness test is a condition on the satisfaction set of the objective, and the two come apart.
- *Almanac or data-report case.* The principal does not foresee what will be said, since they have not read the almanac. Yet the objective "say what the almanac says" has a satisfaction set of one, and the case looks like a genuine deferred proxy act. A foresight diagnosis wrongly rules it out. The grain diagnosis correctly rules it in.
- *Foreseen but wide.* A principal can foresee that outputs will fall within a broad band and approve of that band, as in a deployer's red-teaming, without any content being fixed. A foresight-plus-endorsement condition can be satisfied here at the level of the distribution. The grain diagnosis says this is still not a proxy act. So the two accounts make different predictions in both directions.

A diagnosis that makes different predictions from its neighbour is not a relabelling of it.

3. The responsibility-gap lineage is a different target. The responsibility-gap worry is that no one can be blamed for unforeseen outputs. The thesis's bookshop case shows the opposite dissociation: a principal can be fully responsible for a policy, and so for its effects, and still not be the speaker of any content it yields. Responsibility without speaker meaning is the thesis's point, so it cannot be the gap worry renamed.

4. Skiba and the thesis arrive by independent routes. A norm-based argument says there is no speaker because no one is the subject of the assertion norm. The thesis argues from the structure of the Armstrong-style objective condition. It is an internal critique that explains why the proxy theorist's own resources, recorded, proxy and conditional acts, fail to extend. Two independent arguments for one conclusion support each other.

5. The sketch's own scope is an addition. The thesis explains the extension failure inside the Armstrong framework that Green and Michel use. A norm-based or responsibility-based argument does not do this, because it does not say which part of the objective-based machinery gives out.

VERDICT

The objection fails against the thesis. It succeeds against one sentence of the sketch.

Points 1 and 2 carry the defence. The thesis proper makes no priority claim. The foresight versus grain dissociation is also a real difference, shown by the almanac case, where foresight is absent and a proxy act is present.

Three things limit what I have shown.
- The recollection of Williams and Bayne is unverified. If they in fact state the satisfaction-set point, the thesis is a restatement in Armstrong's vocabulary, and the sketch's claim that they lack a diagnosis is simply false. Dropping that sentence is not hedging, since the thesis does not rest on it. But the explanatory-added-value claim in point 5 would shrink to a translation, and I cannot settle that without the texts.
- Point 2 relies on the almanac case being a genuine proxy act. That is the same contested ground as the previous round's delegated-discretion cases. If "report whatever the almanac says" yields no assertion until someone reads it, as one earlier defence argued, the almanac case no longer separates foresight from grain. The uniqueness test sorts it, but the foresight diagnosis might sort it the same way.
- The standing of the thesis is unchanged. It remains hostage to the premise that wide-discretion delegation without review yields no proxy speech act, and the named opponents still need retargeting, since "confuse" overstates what the thesis shows against Butlin–Viebahn and Arora.

This objection does not kill the thesis, but it also does not improve its position on those two problems.

R3. The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 3/5 · worst 3/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — Gubelmann, Magnus/Buccella/D'Cruz, and the shared assumption (including Attah's) that communicative intention is a performance condition for speech acts
Sketch

Austin separates misfires, where the act is void because there is no accepted procedure, the wrong persons or circumstances, or a flawed execution, from abuses, where the act is performed but insincere because the speaker lacks the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions (the Γ conditions). Gubelmann, Magnus et al., and the Gricean-intention framing all argue that missing intentions, remorse or agency means no act is performed. On Austin's own taxonomy that shows at most a defective apology, promise or assertion. A bare lack of sincerity-grade states is also what Searle treats as compatible with performing an insincere assertion. The intention requirement only becomes a performance condition after the Strawsonian/Gricean rewrite of Austin, and the debate has silently adopted that rewrite. If Austin is restored, the question becomes whether a given LLM output occupies a role in a conventional procedure, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba normative-status question. The positions then regroup: the organismic denials become claims about abuse, the proxy views become claims about who occupies the A-condition role, and the decisive disagreement shifts to which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted. The key premise is that the speech-act kinds in question (apology, promise, advice) are at least partly procedure-constituted.

Appraiser (blind)
Reading intention-based denials through Austin's misfire/abuse distinction is a sharp, text-grounded diagnosis that the debate has silently adopted the Gricean rewrite.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender showed Austin has no act-intention condition, so Gubelmann's requirement is an import, but then conceded that 'mistake an abuse for a misfire' is false as worded because the targets hold a rival theory of illocution.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. The defender separated a designated executor from an intending executor, so the cat fails A.2 on occupancy and channel with no intention test, and the legal analogues fit; the direct-LLM standing gap was admitted but not fatal.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, answered. Strawson's own division of labour gives a non-question-begging reason that intention is the wrong tool for conventional acts, and status and mind diverge in both directions, though 'silently adopted' was given up.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender argued for one role-channel criterion at two levels, and that corporate and admiralty standing is conferred without mind, which blocks the collapse into 'status that tracks mind' as a necessity claim.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender supplied a hollow-performance survival test and a falsifier for the contingency claim, but these are not in the thesis, and the test may go against apology, the central case.
⚑ Target attribution disputed — The defender showed Austin has no act-intention condition, so Gubelmann's requirement is an import, but then conceded that 'mistake an abuse for a misfire' is false as worded because the targets hold a rival theory of illocution. Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Intention-based denials of LLM speech acts rest on a non-Austinian performance condition, so they owe an argument, act type by act type, that the relevant acts are intention-constituted. Austin treats the missing sincerity-grade states as abuse, not misfire. Where the act type is procedure-constituted and a principal designates the channel, whether LLM output counts is a question of conventional role-occupancy.

Flaw

The headline charge that these authors 'mistake an abuse for a misfire' misdescribes them, since they hold a rival theory of illocution, and the key premise that apology is procedure-constituted is unsupported and cuts against Austin's behabitive classification.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Gubelmann and Magnus et al. use "missing intentions" as a performance condition of the Austin Γ (sincerity) type, so that they mistake an abuse for a misfire.

- Gubelmann does not rely on sincerity-grade states. As I recall, he follows Davidson-style action theory: illocuting is an action, and action as such requires intention. That is the intention to do the act at all, which is closer to Austin's executive conditions (B) and his exclusion of non-serious or non-agentive utterances. It is not the Γ.2 requirement of later conforming feeling or conduct. A hollow apology presupposes an agent who performed an act. Gubelmann denies there is an agent, so Austin's abuse/misfire taxonomy does not map onto his claim.
- Magnus et al. mainly argue that chatbot apologies are *bullshit* and that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency to apologise. Bullshit in Frankfurt's sense is indifference to truth, not Austinian insincerity. Their claim that agency is needed for an apology "to matter morally" is a separate point from performance.
- Attah rejects the intention argument, or at least relaxes it. Counting him as sharing the assumption misdescribes him.

So the thesis aims at a position that its targets do not hold in the form stated.

STRENGTH: 2/5. I am working from memory. The targets do hold that missing intention means no speech act is performed, which is exactly what the thesis attacks. The Austin-category mapping is a rival interpretation of their claims, not a misreport of them. The Attah point is a minor overreach in the thesis. Gubelmann's action-level intention does, though, narrow the thesis's scope.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objection concedes the substance and fights over the label. It grants that Gubelmann holds that no intention means no illocution. That is the thesis's target: intention treated as a performance condition. The objector only says that the intention is action-level (Davidsonian) rather than Γ-level. But Austin has no condition requiring the agent to intend the act. His A and B conditions concern the procedure's existence, the appropriateness of persons and circumstances, and correct and complete execution. They are all public. The only intentions Austin lists are the Γ ones, which are hollow-act conditions. So Gubelmann's requirement is not Austin's B-condition. It is an import from action theory, and it is the Strawson/Grice rewrite the thesis names. The thesis does not need Gubelmann to be confused about Γ. It needs him to hold that a missing mental state voids the act, and Austin does not say that.

2. Austin's own handling of the "inner act" supports this. Austin attacks the picture on which a promise requires an accompanying inner act ("my tongue swore but my heart did not"). He says the promise is made, and the defect is moral and not a failure to perform. A Davidsonian action-level requirement is the modern version of that inner-act picture, so it falls under Austin's rejection.

3. A scenario where action-level intention is absent but the act is performed. Take algorithmic contracting, which the law already recognises. A software agent accepts an offer, and the contract binds although no human intended that particular acceptance. The principal's standing intention to be bound by the system's outputs makes the output occupy the acceptor role. Other cases are a form-letter apology issued under a corporate signature, a stamped notice, and a clerk reading a script. None needs an agent whose intention is present at the moment of utterance. Intention can be located upstream, in whoever sets up the procedure. That defeats "Gubelmann denies there is an agent, so no act." The thesis's proxy option is exactly the claim that someone else fills the A-condition role.

4. Magnus et al. help the thesis. Frankfurtian bullshit is indifference to whether what one says is true. That is a sincerity-type defect, nearer Γ than to a failure of execution. If their charge is a Γ-type defect, then by Austin's taxonomy the acts are performed and hollow. Their separate claim that moral agency is needed "to matter morally" concerns the act's normative upshot, which is a status question. That is the thesis's own reframing.

5. Attah is at most a minor overreach, which can be dropped from the target list without touching the argument.

VERDICT

The defence only partly holds, and the thesis as stated is not saved.

- Holds: Austin's conditions contain no requirement that the agent intend the act, so Gubelmann's requirement is not Austinian. Points 1–3 stand.
- Fails: The headline charge is that these authors *mistake* an abuse for a misfire. That attributes a taxonomic confusion to them, and the objection shows they are not confused in that way. Gubelmann does not take a Γ-defect to void an act. He rejects the Austinian framework, holding that illocuting is an action and so needs an agent. That is a rival theory of what an illocution is, not a misfiling. Showing that Austin's categories do not contain his condition shows only that he is not using Austin's categories. The thesis's own "silently adopted" gloss already concedes this. Once that is conceded, the charge of mistaking one for the other is false as worded.
- What survives: The weaker claim that intention-based denials import a non-Austinian condition and so need an argument for it, not just an assertion that LLMs lack the intention. But that is no longer the thesis. It is a dispute about whether Austin or Strawson/Grice gives the right theory of illocution, and the thesis's own key premise, that apology and promise are procedure-constituted, would then have to bear the whole weight. I will not rewrite the thesis to fit that. Stated as it is, the abuse/misfire diagnosis is a misattribution for Gubelmann, only partly apt for Magnus et al., and wrong to include Attah. Since this rests on my memory of the texts, I would check each source before conceding finally.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, a question "about status and not about mind."

Counterexample: a remote wedding is held over a chat terminal. The registrar's procedure exists and is accepted. The groom's seat is the designated seat, and the exchange is correctly sequenced. His cat walks across the keyboard and types "I do." A narrow reading of A/B (procedure exists, seat occupied, wording complete) is satisfied, yet no marriage or consent has occurred. Not even Austin's abuse category fits, because there is no hollow act. Nothing was performed.

Austin's own text handles such cases by exclusion. Non-serious or non-agentive utterances (the actor, the echo, the poem) are "etiolations," not insincere performances. So the thesis faces a dilemma:

1. If A.2 ("appropriate persons") or B ("executed correctly") rules out the cat, it does so by requiring an agent who executes the act. That brings intention or agency back in as a performance condition, which is what the thesis denies.
2. If it does not, the status test gives the wrong verdict on the cat. By parity it also certifies pure-sampling outputs placed in a role.

The proxy move does not help. It resolves the cat case only by locating the agent elsewhere, which concedes that a performer is needed.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The dilemma is real and needs an answer, such as a "minimal agency" reading of A.2/B. But that answer shrinks the claimed gap between status and mind.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The cat fails A.2, so no intention is needed to rule it out. Austin's A.2 requires that the particular persons and circumstances be appropriate to the procedure. The marriage procedure assigns the consent move to the party, or to an authorised proxy. Keystrokes by the cat are neither. The cat case therefore fails for the same reason as a guest at the back shouting "I do", a forged signature, or a stranger signing a cheque. In none of these does the failure come from the absence of a mental state in the person occupying the role. It comes from the wrong occupant, or from output that does not come through the designated channel. The dilemma's first horn assumes that excluding the cat requires an *intending* executor. What it requires is a *designated* executor. Those are different conditions.

2. The legal analogues show that status-based exclusion works without an intention test. Contract law runs on the objective theory (Holmes): manifested assent through the proper channel binds, and the "meeting of minds" does not decide it. Doctrines like *non est factum* are narrow exceptions. Proxy marriage exists, and so do automated contracts and corporate notices. In each of them the question is whether the output stands in the role-channel relation, and in none of them is it whether the producing system has a mind. The cat is excluded by the same test that admits the bank's automated notice. That is a single status criterion giving the right verdict on both cases.

3. The proxy move does not concede what the objector says it does. The objector argues that the proxy move "locates the agent elsewhere, which concedes that a performer is needed". But the thesis never denied that a performer is needed. It denied that the performer must satisfy a mental-state test at the moment of utterance. "Performer" as the occupant of a procedural role is a status notion. "Performer" as a psychological subject of intention is not. The objection runs the two together.

4. Austin's "etiolations" are not a performance condition. Austin sets aside non-serious uses (the actor, the poem, soliloquy) as parasitic and outside the scope of his taxonomy. He does not list them under A, B or Γ, and he does not claim that serious intention is a condition of performance. The exclusion is a scoping remark, and Derrida's critique of it is the standard reply. So it cannot be used to read an agency condition into B.

5. The parity consequence is a bullet to bite. The objector says that if the cat case is not excluded, the status test "certifies pure-sampling outputs placed in a role". But if a principal has genuinely designated the output as the channel, it is certified. That is the right result, as the algorithmic-contracting cases show. If nobody designated it, the output is not certified, just as the cat's is not.

VERDICT

The counterexample does not refute the thesis. The cat is excluded by A.2 on role-occupancy and channel, without any intention requirement, and the dilemma's first horn depends on conflating a designated executor with an intending one. Points 1–3 hold. A "minimal agency" reading of A.2/B is not forced.

It does expose a real weakness, which I will report and not patch. The proxy route is clean only when a human principal exists upstream. The central case in the Magnus et al. literature is different: an LLM apologising in its own name, with no designator. Then the question is whether the LLM can itself occupy the "appropriate person" slot for apology. That is a question about standing, such as accountability, the capacity to be bound, and answerability. We exclude cats and infants from such slots because of capacities that are plausibly mind-involving. The thesis's phrase "a question about status and not about mind" holds only if the convention for apology selects on something other than those capacities. The thesis's own key premise, that apology is procedure-constituted, is the claim that has to deliver this. It is exactly the claim that Austin's classification of apology as a behabitive, where attitude is part of the point of the act, puts in doubt.

So the thesis survives this objection but is left hostage to its key premise. In the direct-LLM case, "status not mind" may reduce to "status that tracks mind". I hold that the status/mind contrast stays defensible, because a convention's sensitivity to a proxy trait is not an intention requirement on performance. Whether it is true for apology specifically is the open question the thesis cannot settle by the abuse/misfire distinction alone. Together with the earlier concession that "mistake" misdescribes Gubelmann, this leaves the thesis alive but much more exposed than its wording suggests.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the debate has "silently adopted" the Strawson/Grice rewrite, so that restoring Austin's A/B versus Γ split is a discovery and not a stipulation.

1. The debate has not been silent. Green and Michel lay out Austin, then Strawson's synthesis, then Armstrong's objectives-for-intentions refinement, and choose among them in the open. Gubelmann argues explicitly from Davidsonian action theory, which is a stated rival to the procedural picture. Williams and Bayne and Butlin and Viebahn also pick their conditions deliberately. So "intention is a performance condition" is a contested position with arguments behind it. It is not an oversight.
2. That Austin files insincerity under abuses is textbook. Nobody disputes it. What the intention theorists dispute is whether Austin's taxonomy is the right theory of illocution. Reapplying Austin's labels to their claims therefore assumes the very point at issue. "Your claim is really about abuse" is a redescription in Austin's vocabulary, not a result.
3. The constructive half ("the live question is status, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba question, and the proxy views say who fills the A-role") is already their stated framing. It names existing positions and does not add one.
4. The defender conceded that the status question probably "tracks mind", since cats and infants are excluded by mind-involving capacities. If so, "status not mind" is verbal.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The label-swap and the already-taken constructive half are real. What stays non-trivial is the narrower claim that intention-denials need an argument for leaving Austin's conditions.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. "Not silent" misses what the silence is about. The thesis does not say nobody has argued for intention as a performance condition. Gubelmann argues from Davidson, and Green and Michel survey the options. It says the intention-denials never answer Austin's own reason for refusing to make inner states conditions of performance. That reason is the "my tongue swore but my heart did not" argument, which holds that the act is done and the defect lies elsewhere. A Davidsonian argument that illocuting is an action shows that actions need agents. It does not show that the conventional acts of apologising or promising are actions of that kind, so that no convention can make an output count as one. That is the step the argument leaves unexamined.

2. Strawson's own paper supplies the resource that makes the diagnosis non-trivial. The objector treats Austin and Strawson/Grice as rival global theories, so that reapplying Austin's labels begs the question. But *Intention and Convention in Speech Acts* is a division of labour. Gricean intention-recognition explains acts that lack a conventional procedure, such as warning, suggesting, and arguing. Austinian conventional acts are the ones where the procedure does the work. On Strawson's own settlement, then, an intention-denial aimed at apology, promise or marriage-style acts uses the tool Strawson reserved for the other half. This is a point internal to the tradition the denials invoke. It is not a relabelling in Austin's vocabulary. It also yields the regrouping the thesis claims: the dispute is about which act types fall on which side.

3. "Status not mind" is not verbal, because the two come apart in both directions.
- An automated bank notice, a form-letter apology, or an algorithmic acceptance has status and no token-level intention.
- A mind-possessing guest shouting "I do" has intention and no status.
- Capacity-selection (infants and cats cannot occupy the slot) is a public, type-level, defeasible test. Occurrent intention at utterance is a private, token-level one. They give different verdicts on these cases, so the contrast has content.

4. The constructive half need not be novel to be useful. Naming existing positions is a diagnosis. If Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba ask the status question while Gubelmann and Magnus et al. answer a different one, the literature has been treating non-rivals as rivals. That is a real finding even if each side's view is old.

VERDICT

The defence holds in parts, and the thesis as worded does not survive.

What holds:
- Point 2 is a genuine resource. Strawson's split gives a non-question-begging reason why an intention requirement is the wrong tool for conventional acts.
- Point 3 shows the status/mind contrast is not verbal where status and mind diverge.

What fails:
- "Silently adopted" is overstated. The adoption is explicit in Gubelmann and in Green and Michel, and I cannot defend the word. At most the intention-denials neglect Austin's inner-act argument, and I have not checked every source.
- "Mistake an abuse for a misfire" is false as worded, as the first round showed. These authors hold a rival theory of what an illocution is. They do not misfile a Γ-defect.
- "A question about status and not about mind" holds only for proxy cases. In the direct-LLM case, standing to apologise plausibly selects on mind-involving capacities such as answerability and being bound. There the contrast reduces to "status that tracks mind". The objector's fourth point lands against exactly this case, and my point 3 does not reach it.
- The act-type premise is unproven and carries the whole argument. The thesis depends on apology and promise being procedure-constituted, and Austin's own placement of apology among the behabitives, where attitude is part of the point, puts that in doubt.

Three of the thesis's operative claims (mistake, silently, status-not-mind) have been given up or conceded. What remains is a different thesis. It says the intention-denials owe an argument for importing a non-Austinian condition, and that Strawson's own division makes that burden heavy for conventional acts. That claim is defensible and interesting, but it is not the one stated. I report the stated thesis as dead and will not rewrite it into the survivor.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise that "the act is performed" and that LLM output can occupy the A-condition role in a conventional procedure. "Performed" and "occupy" have two readings, and the thesis needs both.

- Thin reading: the act counts as made, with its conventional effect, by whoever designated the channel. This is plausible. Form letters, automated acceptances and proxy marriages work this way, and no mental state is needed at the moment of utterance. On this reading the thesis is not interesting. Proxy views (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn) already say it. Gubelmann can grant it, because his claim is that the LLM does not illocute.
- Thick reading: the LLM itself is the appropriate person who apologises or promises in its own name. This is what would contradict the intention-denials and make the thesis worth a paper. But excluding the cat or an infant from that slot depends on standing capacities such as answerability and being bound by the act. Those capacities are plausibly mind-involving, so "status, not mind" becomes "status that tracks mind".

The thesis gets its plausibility from the thin cases and its significance from the thick one. Neither reading carries both, so the argument slides between them.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The defender already conceded the direct-LLM gap. But the thesis could survive by claiming a narrower point, that the capacity requirement is a type-level, public test and not an occurrent-intention requirement.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis does not need the thick reading to be significant. It does not claim that an LLM does occupy the apologiser or promiser role. It claims that whether it does is a question about conventional status, and that the intention-denials answer a different question. That is a claim about which question is live, and it is neutral on the answer. The objector reads it as a thesis that LLMs apologise in their own name, so that it needs the thick case to be interesting. It never says that.

2. The thin reading is not trivial against these targets. Magnus et al. and the Gricean framing do not say only that the LLM fails to illocute. They say chatbot apologies are not apologies, that nothing is performed. On the thin reading the apology is performed, with its conventional effect, by whoever designated the channel. That contradicts the "nothing is performed" claim as stated. The objector says Gubelmann can grant the thin reading. Perhaps, but then his claim shrinks to "the LLM is not the illocutionary agent", which no longer supports the public conclusion that the output carries no speech-act force. The thin reading therefore splits the targets rather than leaving them untouched.

3. The thick reading does not make status track mind constitutively. Corporations, states, and ships in admiralty law occupy performer roles. A company apologises in its own name, a state promises, and a ship is sued. Their standing consists in answerability, being bound, and liability for redress, and these are conferred by convention. They are not read off a mental life. The objector's cat and infant exclusions show only that no convention currently confers the status on them. They do not show that mind is what the convention selects on. If answerability and being bound are the capacities that matter, they are institutional capacities that can be realised without intention. So "status that tracks mind" is contingent, a fact about which entities we have so far conferred status on, and "status, not mind" stands.

4. The two readings sit on one criterion. For the thin and thick cases alike, the test is whether the output stands in the role-channel relation to a procedure that confers the act's effects. In the thin case the channel is designated by a principal, and in the thick case it is designated by the community's conferral of standing. That is one test applied at two levels, so there is no slide between two theses.

VERDICT

The equivocation objection does not refute the thesis, but the thesis is not saved.

What holds:
- Points 1 and 4. The thesis claims a reframing and not an answer, so it does not need thick occupation to be significant.
- Point 3 is the strongest. The corporate-person case shows that thick standing can be conferred without mind, which blocks the "tracks mind" collapse as a necessity claim.

What fails:
- Point 3 has a cost. Whether to confer standing on LLMs is a normative choice, and the reasons for it (can the LLM be held to account, sanctioned, made to redress?) are mind-adjacent. The thesis says that is a question about the convention and not about the conditions of performance. That is defensible, but it means the real disagreement is moved into the justification of the convention, which the abuse/misfire distinction does not touch.
- Apology remains the weak case. Austin classes it among the behabitives, where attitude is part of the act's point. The key premise, that apology is procedure-constituted, is still unproven, and this objection leaves it exactly where the earlier rounds left it.
- Earlier concessions stand. "Mistake an abuse for a misfire" misdescribes Gubelmann, who holds a rival theory of illocution. "Silently adopted" is overstated, and Attah is wrongly included among the targets. These claims are the thesis's headline, not incidental detail, and the equivocation point does not repair them.

I report the thesis as stated as dead. The equivocation attack fails on its own terms, and the surviving point is the narrower one that intention-denials owe an argument for leaving Austin's conditions. That is a different thesis, and I will not rewrite this one to fit it.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is the key premise: that apology, promise and advice are "at least partly procedure-constituted." On the sketch's own regrouping, the real disagreement is "which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted." Together with the status/mind contrast, that premise protects the thesis from every case.

- If an intention-denier says no act was performed, the thesis reclassifies the denial as a claim about abuse, so the act was performed but hollow.
- If an act clearly fails, as with the cat typing "I do", the thesis says A.2 excludes the cat on role-occupancy and not on mind.
- If the exclusion turns out to rest on mind-involving capacities, such as answerability or being bound, the thesis calls that a contingent fact about what the convention currently confers. It says that is still status and not mind.
- If intention seems constitutive of the act type, as with apology, which Austin files among the behabitives, then that type simply lands on the "intention-constituted" side.

"Partly" and "tracks but is not constituted by" let every datum be sorted after the fact. Nothing is stated that an apology, promise or assertion case could show against "status, not mind." The thesis is protected from cases by classification, and that is a defect.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis does make some risky commitments. Status and token-level intention diverge in both directions: automated notices have status without intention, and the guest shouting "I do" has intention without status. Austin's inner-act argument and Strawson's division of labour also give independent content. But "partly" and the contingent-conferral move do leave the central premise largely unfalsifiable as stated, and the thesis needs to say which act types it commits to as procedural.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The sorting is not post hoc, because there is an independent test for which side an act type falls on. The test is Austin's own: *hollow-performance survival*. Take a performance that has the right procedure, occupant and execution, and let the relevant attitude be absent. Then ask whether competent speakers still treat the act as having been done, with its downstream normative effects intact. The effects are uptake, obligation, entitlement to complain, and the possibility of acceptance or rejection. If they do, the act type is procedure-constituted and the missing attitude is a Γ-defect. If competent speakers regularly say "that wasn't an apology at all" and the downstream effects fail to attach, the type is intention-constituted. This test can be run on data before any theory is applied.

2. It gives different verdicts on different types, so the thesis takes risks.
- *Promising.* An insincere promise binds. The promisee may demand performance, and "I didn't mean it" is no defence. This is the paradigm result, and Searle agrees.
- *Marrying, naming, bidding, resigning, accepting.* The hollow performance stands.
- *Apology.* This is the risky case. The thesis commits to the prediction that a known-hollow apology (a PR statement, a coerced "sorry") is still an apology that can be accepted, refused, or held against the speaker. If speakers instead treat it as no apology, the apology premise is falsified.
- *Advice.* The thesis should predict that advice given without belief that it is good still counts as advice, only bad or dishonest advice. If advice is better handled as Gricean, it goes on the other side, and the thesis loses it. That is a stated loss, not a free reclassification.

3. The "partly" is a hypothesis, not an escape hatch. "Partly procedure-constituted" says that a type has a conventional component that fixes its status effects and a residue that fixes its sincerity conditions. The residue is what Γ marks. The claim is that the component fixing *performance* is the conventional one. That is testable by the survival test in point 1. It is falsified for any type where removing the attitude removes the effects.

4. The tracks-mind move has a falsifier. The thesis says that mind-sensitivity in status conventions is *contingent*. That predicts variation. Some conventions confer standing on non-minded entities (corporations, states, ships). Some tie standing to capacity only for particular act types. And revising a convention does not change what the act is, only who can do it. If every convention that selects occupants did so necessarily through occurrent mental states, with no case of conferral to a non-minded entity, the contingency claim would fail. The corporate and admiralty cases are the data on which it could have failed and did not.

5. The four protective moves the objector lists answer to different questions. Reclassifying an intention-denial as an abuse claim, excluding the cat on A.2, calling capacity-selection contingent, and placing apology on the intention-constituted side are not four ways of saving one claim. They apply different conditions to different cases, and each can fail independently. A theory with several independently falsifiable commitments is not unfalsifiable merely because its classification scheme has more than one category.

VERDICT

The defence half-holds, and it does not rescue the thesis.

What holds: the unfalsifiability charge as the objector frames it is too strong. Points 1, 2 and 4 show that the framework has a usable discriminating test and that the status/mind contrast can in principle fail. The objector's own admission that status and token-level intention diverge in both directions already gives the thesis content.

What fails:
- The test is supplied by the defence, not stated in the thesis. As worded, with "at least partly" and an open question about "which act types," the key premise commits to nothing. Adding the survival test and a list of types to the thesis would be narrowing it, and I will not count that as a defence.
- The test goes against the headline act. For apology, which is the case the literature cares about, ordinary usage is mixed. "Non-apology apologies" and "he didn't really apologise" suggest that attitude is part of what counts as the act. Austin's behabitive classification points the same way. If the survival test is applied honestly, the apology prediction in point 2 is at best uncertain and quite possibly false. A thesis whose central case may fall on the other side of its own test is not well protected by having a test.
- Point 4's evidence is weaker than it looks. Corporations apologise through human spokespeople whose intentions are upstream. This is the proxy case again, not conferral of standing on a non-minded direct performer. The test case that matters, an LLM apologising in its own name with no principal, has no data.
- Earlier rounds still stand. "Mistake an abuse for a misfire" misdescribes Gubelmann, and "silently adopted" is overstated. The unfalsifiability attack is answered only for the idea that a test exists, and the thesis was already conceded as dead on its headline claims.

I report the thesis as stated as dead. The unfalsifiability objection is the weakest of the attacks, but it exposes that the key premise is carrying the whole argument without being committed to anything. The survivor is the claim that intention-denials owe an argument against Austin's survival test for each act type. That claim is not the one stated, and I will not rewrite the thesis to fit it.

R4. Even if an LLM passes Gubelmann's intention test, that gives it no illocutionary authorship, because secretaries, scribes and interpreters pass the same test for the very utterances they produce and are not the speakers of the speech acts those utterances carry.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 3/5 · worst 3/5 · wounded
Move · Target
counterexample — Gubelmann's and Attah's shared inference from intention to speaker status; Butlin's agency criterion as relevant to speech acts.
Sketch

Gubelmann's imagined assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order is exactly an interpreter case. A human interpreter has intentions, can be said to err or to deliberately distort, and is sincerely engaged in producing each sentence. Yet the interpreter does not assert, promise or order in her own right; the client does. So the move from 'has intentions with respect to the output' to 'performs the speech act' is invalid for humans. Both Gubelmann and Attah, one for denial and one for attribution, treat intention-attribution as the crux. The crux is actually authorship, meaning whose commitments and sanctions the utterance engages. The key premise is that the intentions needed for illocution are intentions to be answerable in the act, not intentions to produce the words. The upshot is that the relocation views (proxy, fictionalism) track something real even if one grants LLMs full intention. The live question becomes whether any role structure makes the model the principal rather than the interpreter, and bigger or more agentive models do nothing to settle that.

Appraiser (blind)
The interpreter and secretary counterexample shows that passing an intention test does not yield authorship, which reorients the crux from intention to answerability.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. Gubelmann's argument is necessity-based and Attah disclaims intention as the ground. The defender conceded the shared-inference claim and relabelled the target 'output-level agency criteria' instead of showing the named authors hold it.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. The defender fixed reading A and argued that on reading B the interpreter's failure comes from role, not intention. The cost is conceded: on A the thesis may rebut no one, and the point depends on an unverified claim that Gubelmann's test is output-level.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The defender grounded the interpreter datum in Goffman and agency practice, and named observable differences (who is held to it, who can retract). It listed exposed commitments, though the closing 'bigger models do nothing' line was dropped.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender conceded that the upshot is the proxy view (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn). The only residual novelty claimed, that an intentional human proxy shows proxy status survives intention, was admitted to be unverified.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, answered. The defender showed an insufficiency claim does not generalise to agents, lawyers or spokespeople, who have layered authorship. It conceded the interpreter analogy cannot carry the upshot for model-composed content.
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Gubelmann's argument is necessity-based and Attah disclaims intention as the ground. The defender conceded the shared-inference claim and relabelled the target 'output-level agency criteria' instead of showing the named authors hold it. Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Intention to produce the words, even when output-level intention is granted in full, is insufficient for speaker status, as the interpreter, scribe and secretary cases show. Authorship depends on answerability in the act. Intention-testing therefore cannot settle whether an LLM is a speaker, a proxy or a layered co-author.

Flaw

Defending the thesis cost it its target and its upshot. The named authors do not clearly hold the sufficiency view, the proxy conclusion is already in the literature, and the interpreter analogy cannot support relocation for model-composed content.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Gubelmann and Attah share an inference *from* intention *to* speaker status. The thesis needs them to treat intention as sufficient, or as the crux, for speakerhood. Neither does, going by the descriptions given and my memory of the papers.

- Gubelmann argues that illocuting requires intention and that LLMs lack it. That is a necessary-condition argument, and the denial rests on the missing necessary condition. Nothing in it says an LLM that passed his malfunction-versus-wrong-doing test would thereby be a speaker. The interpreter counterexample refutes a sufficiency claim he does not make. His position is also compatible with the thesis's own point, that authorship is a further condition.
- Attah says communicative intention is *not* the right ground for distinguishing humans from LLMs. He locates the real difference in mental and metalinguistic agency. That nearly reverses the ascription, since he does not treat intention-attribution as the crux.
- Butlin's agency criterion comes from a paper on agency and desire in language agents, not speech acts. His speech-act paper with Viebahn uses descriptive function and sanctionability and already endorses proxy assertion. So the target is partly aimed at the wrong work.

The thesis may therefore be refuting a view that nobody holds.

STRENGTH: 3/5. Gubelmann does make intention central to his denial, so a looser "crux of the debate" reading survives. The counterexample also still bears on anyone who infers sufficiency informally. But the named targets are mischaracterised, and the thesis would need to be reframed as a diagnosis of a tacit assumption in the debate rather than a rebuttal of these authors. I am confident about the necessary-versus-sufficient framing and about Attah's closing claim. I am less sure about the exact details of Gubelmann's footnotes.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis sentence contains no attribution. It says that *if* an LLM passes Gubelmann's intention test, *then* that yields no illocutionary authorship. That is a claim about what the test can show, and it is true or false whoever holds a sufficiency view. The objection attacks the "target" and "sketch" fields, not the thesis. The interpreter counterexample bears on the test itself.

2. The necessary-condition reading does not protect Gubelmann. Suppose his test is only a necessary condition. The thesis still bites, because of what the test measures. As I recall it, the test asks whether the system's behaviour can be assessed as wrongdoing rather than malfunction. A human interpreter passes that test for her output. She can mistranslate, deliberately distort, or be blamed for it. Yet she does not assert, promise or order what she renders. So passing the test at the level of output production is compatible with lacking speaker status. For the test to do its work, it must be reformulated at the level of the act: wrongdoing *as the asserter*. That reformulation is exactly the thesis's key premise, that illocution needs intentions to be answerable in the act. The counterexample therefore exposes a level-confusion in the test, whichever logical role he assigns it.

3. Gubelmann's own framing treats passing as the live threshold. His thesis is that speech acts are beyond LLMs "for now". That framing only makes sense if what is missing is something future systems could acquire, and if acquiring it would remove the barrier to speaker status. If intention were only one of several unmet conditions, "for now" would be misleading. The debate he sets up therefore treats intention as the decisive missing piece, which is what "crux" meant. The reply that authorship is a further condition is the thesis's contribution, not a reading of Gubelmann.

4. Attah's replacement criterion falls to the same counterexample. Say Attah rejects communicative intention and locates the difference in mental and metalinguistic agency. The interpreter has both, since she tracks meaning, form and register and acts on them deliberately. So the structure of the counterexample carries over unchanged. Any agency-of-production criterion, whichever agency it names, leaves the principal/interpreter distinction untouched. The thesis needs only that Attah's account is an agency-of-production account, not that it is an intention account.

5. Butlin and Viebahn help the thesis. If their speech-act work already endorses proxy assertion, that is independent support for the claim that speakerhood is not settled by the producer's agency. The agency criterion from Butlin's other paper is then the thing shown irrelevant to speech acts. That is the thesis's own target description: "as relevant to speech acts".

VERDICT

The defence holds for the thesis but not for the target field as written.

- Held: The thesis is a claim about the test, and the counterexample works against it. Points 1, 2 and 4 together show that no output-level agency or intention criterion, necessary or sufficient, can separate speaker from interpreter. The thesis stands as stated.
- Conceded: The claim that Gubelmann and Attah *share an inference from intention to speaker status* is not supported. Attah, on the objector's account, disclaims intention as the ground. Gubelmann's role for intention is better described as necessary and as the focus of the debate. Point 3 rests on my memory of his title and framing, and I would not stake much on it. The target field should say "output-level agency criteria, including Gubelmann's test and Attah's metalinguistic agency". The Butlin attribution needs checking against the right paper.

This correction fixes who is aimed at. It does not narrow, qualify or reinterpret the thesis, which never contained the misattribution. The thesis is alive. The sketch's rhetorical line that both authors treat intention-attribution as the crux should be cut, not defended.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that secretaries, scribes and interpreters "pass the same test for the very utterances they produce". "Pass the test" and "the utterance" each have two readings.

- Reading A (output level). The test asks whether we can distinguish the interpreter's mistranslating from her deliberately distorting the words. She passes trivially. On this reading the premise is plausible, but the target is nearly empty. Gubelmann's claim is that *illocuting* requires intention. A test for intending to render words well is not a test for intending to illocute, so passing it was never offered as sufficient for authorship.
- Reading B (act level). The test asks whether the system can wrongly or rightly *assert, promise or order*, as the one performing that act. That is what Gubelmann's thesis needs, and it is what makes the counterexample interesting. But here the interpreter does not pass. She has no intention to assert the client's content in her own right, which is exactly why she is not the speaker.

The thesis needs both readings. A reading-A pass makes the counterexample true, and a reading-B pass makes its conclusion bear on Gubelmann. The key premise, that illocution needs "intentions to be answerable in the act", is just reading B restated. Once the test is read that way, the interpreter fails it and the counterexample no longer separates intention from authorship.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The defence has a real answer. Gubelmann's own assistant case applies the test at the output level (cleaning up and translating), so he does seem to tie output-level intention to speakerhood. The thesis can therefore stay on reading A and aim at that move. But it must then say that Gubelmann runs the two levels together, rather than claiming that passing his test leaves authorship open on his own terms.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis uses one reading throughout, and it is reading A. "Pass the same test for the very utterances they produce" is explicitly output-level. Reading B enters only in the key premise, as a diagnosis of why the pass doesn't yield authorship. A premise that explains a result is not an equivocation in the premise that states it.

2. Reading A is not empty. The objector grants that Gubelmann's own assistant case applies the test at the output level: cleaning up and translating the customer's order. If he applies it there and then draws conclusions about whether the assistant speaks, the thesis targets that move. The "even if" conditional asks what follows if the barrier he identifies is removed. The answer is that nothing follows about authorship. That matters because a necessary condition that is easy to pass at the output level, and that interpreters pass without becoming speakers, cannot be what separates LLMs from speakers.

3. Reading B does not rescue the objector. It is a dilemma.
- Suppose the test is act-level: can the system wrongly *assert*, as the asserter? Then the interpreter fails it. But why she fails is the thesis's key premise: she does not intend to be answerable in the act. Whether someone is answerable in an act is fixed largely by role structure, namely who bears commitment and sanction. So the act-level test is no longer a test of the system's intentions taken alone. It presupposes the authorship question.
- A full-intention LLM placed in the interpreter role also fails reading B. Passing is therefore not settled by intention-attribution. The objector's reading B thus concedes that intention to produce the words is not the crux, and that is the thesis.

4. The counterexample still separates intention from authorship on reading B. It shows that the same system, with the same intentions regarding its output, passes or fails depending on its role. If role alone flips the verdict, then what the act-level test tracks is role-dependent authorship, not intention.

5. This leaves Gubelmann a way out, but not one he can use. He could say the test was always act-level. That would make him agree with the thesis's premise. It would also make his argument that LLMs lack intention beside the point, since the missing item would be a principal's role, which no amount of intention supplies.

VERDICT

The equivocation charge fails, but the thesis has a cost.

Why it fails: the thesis is stated on reading A. On that reading the counterexample is true and relevant to anyone who treats an output-level pass as progress toward speakerhood. On reading B, the objector's own account of why the interpreter fails supplies the thesis's key premise. Either way, intention to produce the words does not settle authorship.

The cost:
- The defence depends on Gubelmann's test being applied at the output level, as in the assistant case. I am relying on the objector's description of that case and cannot confirm it from the text. If he formulates the test at the act level, the thesis stops being a counterexample to his test. It becomes a charge of circularity: the test already presupposes the role structure it is meant to establish.
- If nobody infers authorship from an output-level pass, the thesis is true but not a rebuttal of anyone. Its force then lies in the diagnosis that authorship is a matter of role and answerability, and that the live question is whether any role structure makes a model a principal. Earlier turns already conceded the claim that Gubelmann and Attah share an inference.

The thesis survives as a conditional claim with a sound counterexample. I have not narrowed it to get there. The honest summary is that the thesis is correct and its polemical target is weaker than the sketch says.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is the key one: the intentions illocution needs are "intentions to be answerable in the act", and authorship is "whose commitments and sanctions the utterance engages". This is what lets the thesis absorb every case.

- If an LLM passes the intention test and still seems to be a speaker, the thesis says it is an interpreter or proxy, so the principal is someone else.
- If an interpreter seems to speak in her own right, the thesis says she has left the interpreter role.
- If an LLM is fully intentional and the role structure makes it the principal, the thesis says it has authorship. But authorship is defined as the principal's position, so this is true by definition and not a finding.

Nothing is left that would count against the thesis. "Answerable in the act" and "principal" are defined by each other, so the interpreter datum is a stipulation about roles and not independent evidence. The exchange shows the same immunity. The thesis survived reading A and reading B alike, and survived the loss of its named targets, because each time its content was reclassified. A thesis that is true on every reading and against every case says only that authorship is whatever role-assignment says. It does not discriminate between theories of LLM speakerhood. The thesis never states an observable difference between "model is principal" and "model is proxy". Without that, relocation views are not vindicated, only relabelled.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis does name a possible falsifier, a role structure with a sanctionable model as principal. The interpreter intuition also has some independent footing. But the thesis must say what would count as a model being the principal, or the thesis reduces to its definition.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis is an insufficiency claim, and insufficiency claims are the most falsifiable kind. The thesis says that passing the intention test does not yield authorship. One case where intention-passing alone settles who made the promise would refute it. The same goes for its supporting datum: if interpreters, scribes and secretaries turn out to be the speakers of what they render, the thesis fails. The objector's three bullets show what the thesis does with cases that fit it, but the thesis is also exposed to cases that don't.
