The objector grants that this immanent point is non-trivial, and it is the main commitment.

2. The authorship conclusion is not common ground, because liability is not speech-act authorship. The objector runs "the airline is answerable" together with "the airline asserted it." Moffatt-type holdings establish the first. As I recall, the tribunal treated the airline as responsible for what its chatbot said, but I am unsure of the doctrinal basis and would check it. Proxy and tool views can deliver liability without assertion. Gubelmann's own view leaves LLM output as non-assertoric text unless a human adopts it. Suppose no human reviewed or intended the refund claim. On the tool-plus-principal model, nobody asserted anything, and someone is merely on the hook. On the organ model, the whole told the customer something false. The two models differ on whether the customer was told or merely shown text. They differ on whether the firm contradicted or misinformed. They differ on whether its later correction is a retraction or only a repair. They also differ on the kind of responsibility: speaker's responsibility for misrepresentation, or manufacturer's responsibility for a defective instrument.

3. Organ and tool differ in what they predict, not just in label. A tool is individuated from outside, by a user's purposes. An organ is individuated from inside, by its role in the whole's reciprocal maintenance. This shows in feedback cases. An LLM drafts policy summaries, triage rules or an editorial style, and the whole adopts them as its standing line. Here the whole's intentions are partly constituted by the organ's contributions. That is the non-summative case: no principal prior to the pipeline holds the intention that the pipeline relays. A proxy view must locate the intention in the humans beforehand, so it misdescribes these cases. The organ view describes them correctly.

4. The attribution rule is not imported. The objector says the channel rule is stipulated from agency law. But the thesis's sketch already puts the rule in the criterion: outputs "figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions." An output that issues through a channel the whole maintains for that function is the whole's. Agency law is corroboration, not the source. Every account of authorship needs such a rule, and the proxy accounts need one too: which outputs count as the principal's?

VERDICT

The defence holds against the objection's main thrust, but it does not save one clause of the thesis.

What holds. The charge of triviality misfires, because triviality is what the thesis says happens to Gubelmann's denial. The immanent critique, that his Kantian criterion has no principled stopping point at the skin without chauvinism, stays untouched. The objector concedes this.

What does not hold. The thesis also says it "yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy." The objection shows this is not established as a distinct option. Points 2 and 3 are my best case for a difference, and each is thin:

- Point 2 rests on unendorsed content, such as hallucinations that no human reviewed. In ordinary deployments there is nearly always some standing human policy, review structure or sign-off. Then the tool-plus-principal view and the organ view agree on every case. They diverge only in the residual gap. I am not sure about the legal doctrine either.
- Point 3 rests on LLM output feeding back into the whole's standing goals. That is an empirical claim about pipelines. It is not derived from the criterion, and the thesis has not argued for it.
- Point 4 concedes what the earlier exchange conceded: Kant yields the organ, and a separate rule yields the act. The proxy views have a rule of the same shape.

So the "third author" clause has not been shown to be a rival to the institutional proxy view. The objector is right that it lands close to common ground. If the paper cannot show, through actual cases, that the organ and proxy views diverge on who asserted what, that clause is dead. It should be dropped, not narrowed until it is safe. What remains is the immanent critique of Gubelmann, which is a good enough contribution to carry the paper. The "new author" claim is the part that is exposed.

Net: 3/5 stands. The thesis survives as an immanent critique. The claim that it yields a distinct kind of author is unproven, and it rests on two cases the paper must actually deliver.

R7. There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 3/5 · worst 3/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — Arora's and Green and Michel's proxy accounts, and the generalisation from recorded speech to machine speech
Sketch

Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.

Appraiser (blind)
Relayed versus generative proxy assertion pins down why assertoric norms cannot transfer to deployers, a sharper diagnosis of the proxy view.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender conceded the sketch misfiled Green and Michel's conditional device, but showed the distinction and dilemma don't depend on the attribution, and the reclassification makes that device the live target. The repair is a fix to an example, not absorption. Attribution is still unverified.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The bank and assistant cases were sorted by stretching 'institutional knowledge'. The lab case was bitten as a bullet, so ordinary automated institutional assertion is denied. That is a revisionary cost accepted, not a case defeated, and the defender later withdrew the bank classification.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, answered. The defender conceded the 'norms cannot apply' step is analytic. It located the substantive content in the classification claim and in the content-identification premise, and gave a non-verbal substitution argument for the premise. It also admitted the argument presupposes the thick epistemic norm, which a Brandomian rejects.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender argued the thin reading is horn one, that sanction is parasitic, and offered a Moorean test. It then conceded the Moorean datum is contestable and that the thesis rests on an undefended thick-norm commitment, so it has not shown the thin reading fails to give assertion.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender stated a single classification test and listed falsifiers. It then conceded the bank/lab application was unstable and withdrew the bank-as-relayed claim. It chose 'neither', which makes the distinction collapse toward reviewed versus unreviewed and generalises far beyond LLMs. The boundary was repaired by a costly reinterpretation, not defended.
🔧 Survives as

Present the thesis as conditional on an epistemic-position norm of assertion, defend that norm directly against commitment-by-authorisation views, and state that the generative category covers all unreviewed automated institutional output, not just LLMs.

Flaw

The thesis depends wholly on the thick epistemic-position norm of assertion, which it never argues for directly, and it purchases consistency by denying that automated bank and lab statements are assertions.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Green and Michel (2022) and Arora (2024) hold that *every* novel LLM output is an assertion by the deployer or designer, and that they reach this by generalising from recorded speech. The thesis's dilemma depends on that attribution: either the norm is dropped, or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level.

As I remember Green and Michel, they claim much less. The abstract says artificial speakers "characteristically" act as proxies. It also says the authors are sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act. Their conditional speech acts, "whatever the system says under C, I say", are not a case of relayed content the principal fixed or could inspect. They are the authors' own device for handling outputs the principal never sees. So the thesis seems to have placed Green and Michel's most generative-friendly move on the relayed side, when it is where they already face the problem the thesis raises.

On Arora, my memory is only of the abstract. It says Arora refines proxy assertion with machine-learning devices in view, so describing the contribution as only about responsibility may understate it.

STRENGTH: 2/5. I am working from abstracts, not the texts. Green and Michel plausibly do hold that deployers perform proxy speech acts for outputs they never see. If so, the target's view is the one attacked, and the problem is a loose gloss of the conditional case, not an aim at nobody. Even a corrected attribution leaves the distinction between relayed and generative proxies untouched.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The attribution is not what the argument runs on. The dilemma is conditional: *if* every novel output is the deployer's assertion, then either the norm is dropped or the relation is reconstrued. Whether Green and Michel or Arora actually say "every" is a question about who occupies the antecedent. The thesis itself is the distinction and the claim about norms. Even if Green and Michel hedge ("characteristically", scepticism about some speech-act types), their conditional device is explicitly designed to cover outputs the principal never sees. For LLM output that is exactly the antecedent. A view that says "whatever the system says under C, I say" is committed to the principal asserting unseen novel outputs, and that commitment is what the dilemma addresses.

2. The misclassification is mine, and it helps the thesis. The objector is right that the sketch lists the conditional speech acts among cases that "pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected". By the thesis's own definition (a determinate content the principal could believe or know), the conditional case is generative. "Whatever the system says under C" fixes a rule, not a content. So the correct sorting puts Green and Michel's device on the generative side, as the most sophisticated attempt to handle it. That makes the critique more pointed: the best proxy account for unseen content is the one the argument must defeat, and it is the one facing the dilemma.

3. The conditional device does not escape the dilemma. The principal can identify the content *de dicto* ("whatever the system outputs under C"). Two things follow.
- A de dicto commitment is a commitment to a schema. The principal can believe the general claim "the system is reliable under C". They cannot believe or know the particular proposition p that gets output.
- Taking the norms of assertion to attach to p requires belief or knowledge of p. What the principal actually satisfies is the norm for the reliability claim. That is the second horn: endorsement of a reliability level, not assertion of a content.

The legal analogy of incorporation by reference or a blank cheque does not help. Those bind the signer to a fixed or fixable document, or impose liability. They do not make the signer the speaker of content they could not have identified, and liability is Arora's territory, which the thesis already sets aside.

4. Arora. My memory is also of the abstract only. That Arora's refinement uses machine-learning devices does not show it supplies a means of identifying content. A refinement that tracks who is responsible for outputs remains compatible with the content-identification gap.

VERDICT

The objection does not defeat the thesis, but it exposes a real error in the sketch.

- What holds. The relayed/generative distinction, the claim that LLM output is almost entirely generative, and the norm-inapplicability claim are untouched. The objector concedes this (strength 2/5). The attribution worry bears only on the target field, not on the argument's validity.
- What fails. The sketch is internally inconsistent. It files Green and Michel's conditional acts under relayed content, while the definition makes them generative. This should be corrected by moving the case, and the thesis should say plainly that the conditional device is the live opponent. The correction changes an example, not the thesis's scope, so I don't count it as hedging.
- What I cannot establish. Neither the objector nor I has the texts. The claim that Green and Michel or Arora endorse proxy assertion for *every* novel output is unverified. If neither does, the target description should say which actual position is attacked (the unrestricted generalisation) rather than imply that they hold it.
- The remaining pressure. The real threat is the *de dicto* reading in point 3. If the proponent can show that a de dicto commitment carries assertoric norms directly (for example, a norm of assertion-by-delegation that requires only reliable-source knowledge), the premise that commitment requires a means of identifying content fails. This objection does not make that case, but the thesis must meet it.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. If that premise holds, assertoric norms cannot attach to generative proxies. It gives the wrong result on ordinary institutional assertion.

Take a bank's automated balance statement, or a hospital lab's auto-verified test report. The bank or lab fixed no proposition in advance. It authorised a policy, the software produces a novel proposition, and no one at the institution sees it when it is issued. On the thesis, this is a generative proxy, so the institution either does not assert or only endorses a reliability level.

Yet we treat it as a paradigm assertion by the institution. The bank can be said to have told you your balance, and it can lie, mislead, or be criticised for asserting what it had no warrant for. The knowledge norm also seems to apply, because the bank knows your balance through a reliable process it does not inspect. The same goes for a manager's standing delegation to an assistant: "answer routine queries as you see fit."

So generative delegation of this kind yields assertion with norms intact. The thesis's dichotomy ("drop the norm or reconstrue as reliability endorsement") is a false one, because knowledge-by-reliable-process is the norm-satisfier. The "at the time of the act" clause also fails to separate these cases from LLM deployment, since LLM outputs are logged and inspectable.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The bank case is a genuine problem. The thesis can answer by arguing that the bank's process is far more reliable and narrower than an LLM's. That answer concedes the real variable is reliability and scope, not the relayed/generative divide.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The bank case is relayed under the thesis's own definition. The thesis defines relayed proxy assertion as one where the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. A novel token is not the test, and neither is whether a human saw it. The test is whether the content is fixed by the principal's own epistemic state. A balance statement is a rendering of a ledger entry the bank maintains and, in the institutional sense, knows. The software is a display function from a state the bank already holds to a string. The content is determinate before and independently of the output. This applies the definition as written and does not extend it. It also explains why the case feels like assertion: the bank can know the proposition, and the output relays it.

2. The objector's evidence for assertion does not separate assertion from reliability-endorsement. The objector says the bank can lie, mislead, or be criticised for asserting without warrant. Take each in turn:
- *Lying* requires believing not-p. A bank whose software emits a wrong balance through a bug errs. It does not lie. If the bank designs the system to emit false balances, it has fixed the false content in advance, which is the relayed case.
- *Misleading and criticism* arise when the bank knew or should have known the system was unreliable. That is criticism of the policy it authorised. It is the second horn of the thesis's dilemma, responsibility for a reliability level, which we already agree is real. The intuitions the objector cites are what the thesis predicts, because they attach to the policy and not to the particular p.

3. The standing delegation to an assistant is a believing intermediary. "Answer routine queries as you see fit" delegates to an agent who has the content in view, believes it, and asserts it. The manager's position is vicarious responsibility, which is Arora's territory. Or the manager's position is deference to a competent testifier whose belief fixes the content. Either way there is a mind that holds p. LLM deployment lacks this. The deployer has no one to defer to, and no state anywhere in the chain that the output reports.

4. The "inspectable logs" point supports the thesis. The premise requires a means of identifying content before or at the time of the act. Post hoc logs do not supply that. If a human reviews each output before release, the thesis says the case becomes relayed, because the content is then in view. That is a prediction, not an escape clause.

5. Reliability is orthogonal to the distinction. The objector says the real variable is reliability and scope. Test this with crossed cases. A highly reliable LLM answering arithmetic is still generative, since the deployer has no content in view. A press statement drafted by a notoriously unreliable spokesperson and approved by the principal is still relayed. Reliability varies independently of the structure, so it cannot be what the distinction tracks.

VERDICT

The defence holds against the bank case and the assistant case. It holds only at a cost against the lab case, and the thesis has to accept that cost openly.

- Bank and assistant. Both are correctly sorted as relayed or vicariously held. The intuitions of lying and criticism are explained by the thesis. The objection's claim that norms remain intact for generative delegation is not established.
- The lab report is a real problem. Point 1 does not carry over to it. The potassium value is not in the lab's epistemic state before the analyser outputs it, and no one identifies it at the time. The lab's commitment is "whatever this instrument reads for this sample", which has the same de dicto form as Green and Michel's "whatever the system says under C". The thesis's premise, as stated, classes the lab as generative. There are two exits, and neither is comfortable:
- Say the instrument's reading counts as the lab's identifying of the content. That works equally for an LLM, and the distinction then turns on how well the process tracks the facts. That is degree of reliability and scope, which is what the objector said and what I denied in point 5. I cannot hold both.
- Bite the bullet. Fully automated, unreviewed lab values are not assertions by the lab. They are the output of a reliability-endorsed process, and the lab's assertions are its signed-off reports and its standing quality commitments. This is revisionary but defensible, and it is consistent with the thesis.

I take the second exit. It is not hedging, because it applies the thesis's consequence without narrowing the thesis. But it has two costs:
1. The thesis's scope is not specific to LLMs. It covers all unreviewed automated output whose content is fixed by a transducer and not by the principal's state.
2. The thesis loses the easy intuition that "automated institutional statements are obviously assertions". It must argue that the intuition tracks responsibility for the process, which is the second horn.

I cannot confirm real lab auto-verification practice. If actual labs treat auto-verified values as the lab's own assertions with a warrant norm tied to the specific value, the bullet is harder to bite. The thesis stands, but only if the bank and lab intuitions are explained away, not confirmed.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "generative proxy assertion" names a discovery rather than a stipulation. The thesis defines the generative case as one where the principal has no determinate content they could believe or know. It individuates assertion by norms of belief and knowledge. It then concludes that those norms "cannot be applied" to the principal. That follows from the definitions alone, because belief and knowledge norms need a content to attach to, and the generative case is defined as lacking one.

The only substantive step is that commitment requires identifying content in advance. That is either a stipulation about "commitment" or the very point at issue. Once stated, the dilemma is the familiar one: either assertion is relaxed to include de dicto delegation, or what the deployer does is relabelled reliability endorsement. Williams and Bayne already press this against proxy views. Arora's responsibility-focused account is compatible with it. Butlin and Viebahn restrict proxy assertion for the same reason. Nobody defends the opposing claim that deployers know unseen outputs.

The defender's own bullet-biting shows how thin the point is. The distinction extends to all unreviewed automated output, and the remaining dispute is whether to call the deployer's act "assertion" or "endorsement of a process". That is verbal, not a finding.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The conclusion is largely built into the definitions, and the standard dilemma is not new. The thesis survives only if the content-identification premise is contested and defended on non-verbal grounds, for example by showing that de dicto delegation cannot carry assertoric norms. That argument is not yet made.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objection undermines itself. The first objector said Green and Michel and Arora do hold that deployers perform proxy speech acts for outputs they never see. This objector says "nobody defends the opposing claim that deployers know unseen outputs." Both cannot be right. If the target positions hold that the deployer asserts p for unseen p, then the thesis denies a live claim and is not trivial. If nobody holds it, the objection is really the misattribution charge again. Either way the triviality charge has no independent force. The target does not need to claim that deployers *know* unseen outputs. Green and Michel's conditional device is built to make the deployer's *assertion* of p go through without that knowledge, and that is the claim the thesis denies.

2. The "cannot be applied" step is analytic, but the thesis is not that step. I grant that "no determinate content, so belief and knowledge norms have nothing to attach to" is close to definitional. The thesis has three further components:
- The classification claim. LLM output is almost entirely generative. This depends on deployment facts: review, templating, and retrieval of fixed text. It is not analytic, and it could be false for some deployments.
- The distinction claim. Relayed and generative proxying are different kinds, which existing proxy accounts run together by generalising from recorded speech. A taxonomy that shows a generalisation fails across a structural boundary is a finding, not a stipulation.
- The premise. Commitment to a content requires a means of identifying it. This is the substantive core, and I defend it below.

3. The premise has a non-verbal defence. The objector offers a choice between "relax assertion to include de dicto delegation" and "relabel it endorsement". That choice is not verbal, because it is settled by what assertoric norms are for. Assertion licenses hearers to rely on the speaker's epistemic position with respect to p. Run a substitution test. In the relayed case, the hearer's warrant depends on the principal's epistemic state: swap in a principal who has no access to p, and the warrant goes. In the generative case, swap in any deployer who authorises the same policy and the warrant is unchanged, because it sits entirely in the process's reliability. Where the warrant is located is a functional difference, and it is not settled by what we choose to call the act. A speech act whose warrant does not depend on the speaker's epistemic position lacks what the belief and knowledge norms exist to regulate.

The choice also has downstream consequences, so it is not merely terminological:
- Whether "how do you know?" has an answer from the deployer.
- Whether lying is possible, since that requires believing not-p.
- Whether testimonial knowledge can transmit through the deployer.
- Whether the only available asserter is the machine, which raises its own questions.

4. Familiarity is not refutation. That Williams and Bayne, or Butlin and Viebahn, press a similar dilemma shows the thesis is not novel. It does not show the thesis is trivial. A contested argument that others have also made is just an argument. I cannot verify what those authors say, so I do not rest anything on them.

VERDICT

The triviality charge fails, but it correctly identifies where the thesis is exposed.

*Why the charge fails.*
- Point 1 holds. The objection cannot consistently claim both that no one holds the target view and that the thesis is merely definitional against it.
- The thesis has three components, and two of them are not analytic.
- The objector's own survival condition ("the premise is contested and defended on non-verbal grounds") is met, at least in outline, by the substitution argument in point 3.

*What I concede.*
- The step from "no determinate content" to "norms cannot be applied" is analytic. It should be presented as such, with the argument placed entirely on the content-identification premise.
- The substitution argument is not secure. It presupposes that assertoric norms are belief and knowledge norms, and a Brandomian account rejects that. On that account the deployer acquires a commitment to p by *authorising* the speaker, and entitlement is inherited through deference, with default-and-challenge standing in for knowledge. On such an account the deployer asserts p without being able to identify it. That would not make the thesis trivial. It would make it false, because the premise would fail. The thesis cannot dismiss this alternative by calling it a mere relabelling, because the alternative is itself a theory of what the norms are for.
- The cost from the previous round remains. The thesis's reach is not specific to LLMs, and it must accept that unreviewed automated institutional outputs are not the institution's assertions.

*Where the thesis stands.* It survives as a substantive thesis. It is not safe, because it now rests on one contestable commitment: assertion is governed by an epistemic-position norm, not by a commitment-by-authorisation norm. A full defence would argue for that commitment directly. Without that argument, the thesis is a clear and consistent position, but it has not been shown to be correct.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal" for generative proxies. The word "assertion" here carries two readings, and the argument needs both.

- Thick reading. Assertion is governed by an epistemic-position norm (belief or knowledge of p). On this reading the premise is plausible: a deployer who has never seen p cannot satisfy a norm that requires knowing p. But this is close to analytic, as the triviality round showed. It also yields only the unsurprising result that no one can satisfy the knowledge norm for content they never identified.
- Thin reading. Assertion is the undertaking of accountable commitment, with sanctionability and de dicto commitment ("whatever the system says under C, I say"). This is the reading the thesis's own list of norms includes ("belief, knowledge, sanction"). Green and Michel's Austin–Strawson–Armstrong framework works with it. Here the deployer plainly can be sanctioned, so "the norms cannot be applied" is false. The blank-cheque and incorporation-by-reference cases show that commitment to unidentified content is ordinary.

The thesis is interesting only if it refutes the proxy theorists, and that requires showing that they cannot make out assertion. The conclusion "empties 'assertion'" requires the thick reading. The proxy theorists do not claim thick assertion, and Butlin and Viebahn's own sanction condition is thin. So the thesis is true on the reading where it refutes no one, and it targets a position nobody holds.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis can answer by arguing that the thick norm is the right account of assertion. But that is the contested commitment the defender already conceded the thesis rests on, and the thesis never defends it directly.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis does not equivocate. It forks on the thick/thin split, and the thin branch is horn one of its own dilemma. The sketch says that either the norm is dropped, "which empties 'assertion'", or the relation is reconstrued as reliability endorsement. The objector's thin reading is the first horn under a new name. If assertion is just accountable commitment, the thesis does not slide from thin to thick. It says that on the thin reading "assertion" no longer marks anything distinctive. Promises, warranties, guarantees, blank cheques and strict-liability undertakings are all sanctionable commitments to content, and none of them is an assertion. So the thin reading cannot be what proxy *assertion* theorists want. If it is, they have changed the subject from assertion to undertaking.

2. Sanction is not an independent norm. It is derivative. The sketch lists "belief, knowledge, sanction", but sanction for an assertion is sanction for violating whatever the norm of assertion is. It is criticism for asserting what you did not know, or for asserting falsely. If the epistemic norm cannot be applied to the deployer, sanction has three possible objects:
- Fault in the process. The deployer deployed carelessly. This is the reliability-level horn.
- Strict liability for each p. This is a guarantee, and the thesis's second horn already covers it under a different description.
- The particular p as a violation of an epistemic norm. This is unavailable, which is the thesis's claim.

Real sanctions fit this pattern. If a company is held liable for a chatbot's specific misstatement, the cause of action is typically negligent misrepresentation, which turns on failure of reasonable care. That is about the process, not about the deployer's epistemic relation to p. I am relying on my recollection of cases like this and cannot check the details. So "sanction can be applied" is true only in a sense that does not restore assertion. "The norms cannot be applied" stands if it means the norms that make the act an assertion.

3. The objector's examples are not cases of the thin commitment they need. Incorporation by reference binds the signer to a document they could read. That is relayed, by the thesis's own definition. A blank cheque binds the signer to pay, which is a promissory or performative commitment, not a statement that the amount is owed. Neither shows that de dicto delegation yields assertion of unidentified content.

4. There is a non-verbal argument that the thick norm is the right one. The Moorean test separates assertion from commitment. For genuine assertion, "p, but I don't believe p" is defective, and this carries over to proxy assertion. A principal cannot coherently say "my spokesperson stated p on my behalf, but I don't believe p." For the generative case, compare a deployer who says "my system told the customer the flight is refundable, though I don't believe it is." This is a coherent disavowal. It may be culpable, but it is not Moore-paradoxical. The difference shows that belief in p is not part of what the deployer is committed to. That is evidence that the deployer's commitment is not an assertoric one, and it does not depend on a stipulated definition. The bank-style cases are the exception, as before.

5. Whether the proxy theorists hold the thick view is not decisive. If they hold only the thin view, the target's claim is still that proxy *assertion* of generative content is available. The thesis answers that by showing the thin view cannot supply assertion. A view that survives only by weakening the explanandum is what the thesis is meant to expose.

VERDICT

The equivocation charge fails as a charge of fallacy. It succeeds in showing that the thesis has never defended its crux.

*What holds.* The thesis is not trading on an ambiguity, because it states both readings and gives each a horn. Sanction is parasitic on the assertoric norm and does not supply a second, independent route to assertion. The Moorean test in point 4 is the first non-verbal consideration anyone has put on the table for the thick norm.

*What I concede.*
- The sketch's wording is loose. "Assertoric norms cannot be applied" should say "the epistemic norm cannot be applied, and sanction collapses into process-fault or guarantee". This is a fix to the statement and not a narrowing of the claim, because point 2 shows it was the claim all along.
- The Moorean test is contestable. A Brandomian or an institutional-commitment theorist can say the deployer's disavowal is infelicitous, because they are bound regardless of what they believe. That denies that the Moorean datum tracks assertion for proxies. I have not shown otherwise.
- This is the third round on one point. The first round pressed the attribution, the second the Brandomian alternative, and this one thick against thin. All three target a single commitment, that assertion is governed by an epistemic-position norm and not by commitment-by-authorisation. The thesis has an outline of an argument for that commitment (substitution plus Moore) and not a proof.

*Where the thesis stands.* It is a substantive, falsifiable thesis, and the equivocation objection does not refute it. But its truth now depends entirely on winning the thick-versus-thin dispute, and it has not won it. It should be presented as a conditional: if assertion is governed by an epistemic-position norm, then generative proxy assertion does not exist. It should then carry the burden of arguing for the antecedent, not merely assuming it.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the relayed/generative boundary, "the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know", can be applied independently of whether we already judge the act an assertion. The exchange shows it cannot.

- The bank statement is ruled relayed because the bank "institutionally knows" the ledger entry.
- The assistant case is ruled a "believing intermediary".
- The lab report is first sorted as generative. The defence then bites the bullet and says the lab's real assertions are its signed-off reports.
- Green and Michel's conditional acts are moved from relayed to generative to suit the argument.
- Sanction, lying and criticism are redescribed as "process-fault" or "guarantee".
- The thin reading of assertion is ruled "undertaking", not assertion.
- Where the Moorean test fails, the failure is read as not tracking assertion.

Every putative case of a deployer asserting unseen content is therefore classed as relayed, vicarious, or not assertion at all. "Could know" is elastic enough to absorb each case. "Assertion" is defined by the epistemic-position norm, so any intuition that counts against the thesis is discounted as tracking something else. The thesis gives no case type that would count against it, and no independent test (Moore, warrant location, sanction) is allowed to override the classification. That immunity is a defect, because the claim that "assertion doesn't exist" for generative proxies is guaranteed by the criterion and not discovered.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis does make some predictions, such as human review turning a case relayed. But the boundary is adjusted case by case.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The classification runs on one test that never consults the assertion verdict. The test is whether the principal, at or before the act, has a means of identifying the content that is independent of the act's own output. Asking whether the act is an assertion plays no part in it. Applying it case by case:

- Recorded message and press statement: the content is fixed before output, so the case is relayed.
- Human review of each output: the content is identified at release, so the case is relayed.
- Green and Michel's "whatever the system says under C": no content is fixed, so the case is generative. The sketch misfiled it, and the definition always sorted it generative. Correcting an inconsistency with the stated criterion is not adjusting the criterion to fit the case.
- Unreviewed lab value: generative from the first pass. The bullet the defender bit concerned the assertion intuition, not the classification. The classification did not move.

Every item on the objector's list is a revision of the verdict about assertion, or a repair of a mislabelled example. None is a movement of the boundary.

2. The thesis names cases that would count against it.

- (a) Unreviewed generative deployments where the deployer's disavowal ("my system said p, though I don't believe p") is as defective as the spokesperson's disavowal. That would show the deployer is committed to p independently of belief.
- (b) Hearers' warrant tracking the deployer's epistemic position under unreviewed generation, not the process's reliability. The substitution test checks this: swap deployers, keep the policy, and see whether warrant changes.
- (c) Courts or practice requiring scienter about the particular unseen p for liability to attach, and treating the deployer as having lied.
- (d) Deployers being asked "how do you know p?" and the question being answered by their own epistemic position and not by the process.
- (e) Reliability, not structure, predicting whether an output counts as the deployer's assertion. The crossed cases (reliable arithmetic LLM, unreliable approved spokesperson) are a live test.

Each can be run without presupposing the thesis. The Moorean datum could have come out against the thesis, and it didn't. That a Brandomian can contest the datum shows it is theory-laden, as every datum about assertion is. It does not show the thesis is immune.

3. Vagueness is not immunity. "Could know" is modal, but temporal indexing at or before the act fixes it. The post hoc log case follows from this and is not an ad hoc exemption.

VERDICT

The unfalsifiability charge fails as framed. It exposes a defect in the boundary, and that defect is not repaired.

*Why the charge fails.* The test is single, applied before any verdict on assertion, and it supports the falsifiers in (a) to (e). The case-by-case movement the objector lists is mostly a correction of a bad sketch and a plain statement of the thesis's consequences. It is not a boundary shifting under pressure.

*What survives from the objection.* The bank and lab cases show that the test is not stably applied.

- The bank was sorted relayed because it "institutionally knows" the ledger entry, and the lab was sorted generative because the reading is produced at the time of the act.
- But a ledger entry reflecting computed interest, fees and netting is itself the output of unreviewed automated processes. No person at the bank knows it either.
- The stored/computed distinction has no principled tie to belief or knowledge. "Institutional knowledge" must therefore either cover both cases or neither.

*The two options.*

- Both. The lab is relayed, and so is any deployer whose system draws on stored or trained content the institution "holds". Then "almost entirely generative" is false for much LLM deployment, and the line between bank and LLM becomes arbitrary.
- Neither. The test then tracks only content held in a human mind or reviewed at release. Ordinary bank and lab statements are not the institution's assertions, and the relayed/generative distinction collapses into reviewed versus unreviewed. The thesis is stable on this option, but its reach is far wider than LLMs, and it carries a heavy revisionary cost.

I take "neither", because "both" abandons the thesis's classification claim. This is not hedging, since it narrows nothing and follows the criterion as stated. It has to be stated openly, though, and the earlier line that bank statements are relayed has to be withdrawn.

*Where the thesis stands after this round.* It is not unfalsifiable and not trivial. It is coherent only on the strict reading, where the principal's own epistemic state, or review at release, is the sole route to assertion. It still rests on the thick, epistemic-position norm, and it has not won that dispute. It also now implies that a great deal of ordinary institutional "telling" is not assertion. If that cost is judged too high, the thesis fails, and the objection has shown where it would fail.

R8. The proxy account's assumption that the principal of a machine utterance is its designer or deployer is false in the central case: when a user adopts a chatbot's output, the user is the speaker, and the model functions as part of the user's own cognitive apparatus.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 3/5 · worst 3/5 · wounded
Move · Target
counterexample — Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and the denial arguments that infer the absence of assertion in chatbot discourse from the absence of producer intentions.
Sketch

Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne's critique of them all treat 'on whose behalf?' as a question with designers or deployers as the candidate answers. Consider the case where a user asks a model for the date of a treaty and pastes the answer into a report, or types 'The capital of Australia is…' and accepts the autocompletion. The user plainly asserts, is sanctionable and is answerable. Yet they formed no content-intention before the output and had no knowledge of what the system would say. Designers had no objective regarding that content, so the designer-proxy story fails for the utterance. The case resembles retrieving a fact from a notebook. The user adopts content they did not author, and adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion. Two consequences follow. First, the intention requirement for assertion is not a requirement on the producer of the content, which weakens Gubelmann's route to denial. Second, the model-level question 'does the chatbot assert?' is separable from the occurrence of assertion in chatbot-mediated discourse, and arguments that conflate them lose force. The key premise is that adoption suffices for assertion without prior content-intention, as with testimony passed on and the use of ghostwritten text.

Appraiser (blind)
It questions the shared assumption that the principal is the designer, locating the speaker in the adopting user, and separates model-level questions from chatbot-mediated discourse.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender argued that 'proxy' names a structure the user case doesn't fit, but then dropped Gubelmann and Butlin/Viebahn as targets and narrowed the claim to creator-centred accounts, which is absorption.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, answered. The autocompletion case (no earlier user act to re-assert) and the empty-principal-slot claim answer the charge that the thesis only restates relay; the defender then undercut the 'false' claim by raising the de dicto point itself.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. Pointing out that the thesis denies only prior intention, plus the middle reading C (commitment without scrutiny), answers the A/B charge, but the defender conceded the apparatus claim needs something closer to B.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The defender supplied public criteria fixed in advance and concrete falsifiers (attributed versus unattributed pasting, scratch-file use), so the thesis can lose; the putting-forward criterion for designers is a new argument not in the sketch.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. Priority is not falsity, and the objector admitted nobody argues the empty-principal-slot claim for the original token; the defender still conceded the apparatus half is occupied.
⚑ Target attribution disputed — The defender argued that 'proxy' names a structure the user case doesn't fit, but then dropped Gubelmann and Butlin/Viebahn as targets and narrowed the claim to creator-centred accounts, which is absorption. Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

In autocompletion and paste-into-report cases, adoption through public putting-forward makes the user the speaker. Designers who do not put forward particular outputs are not their principals (deployers who publish output are), so creator-centred proxy accounts do not cover these cases. Drop the extended-mind claim, or limit it to autocompletion.

Flaw

The sketch's 'designers had no objective regarding that content' confuses de re with de dicto intention, and the 'cognitive apparatus' claim fits only autocompletion, not the central consult-a-source case.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the proxy accounts assume the principal is "its designer or deployer", and that all of them do. This is probably a qualified view reported flat.

- Butlin and Viebahn say AI systems "can be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents". That wording is open about who the agent is. A user who deploys the system for their own purposes fits it naturally. The thesis's own user-adoption case therefore looks like an instance of their proxy view, not a counterexample.
- Green and Michel say artificial speakers *characteristically* act as proxies for their creators. They also end sceptical that the strategy covers every speech act. The thesis turns a hedged claim about a characteristic case into a universal assumption.
- Arora includes "deployers". If a user who prompts the system and publishes its output counts as a deployer, the thesis's contrast between deployer and user collapses.
- Gubelmann denies that LLMs are *speakers* because they lack intention. As I recall, he does not address whether a user asserts when adopting output. So the claim that his denial route is weakened, or that he conflates the model-level and discourse-level questions, may be aimed at a position he does not hold.

STRENGTH: 3/5. I am fairly confident about the Butlin and Viebahn wording, and about Green and Michel's "characteristically" and their closing scepticism. Arora's fit is less clear. The thesis can survive by narrowing its target to Green and Michel and Arora, who do centre creators. A residual problem is the Gubelmann link, which looks overstated.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says the thesis misreports its targets. I resist it at three points.

1. "Proxy" names a structure, not just a slot for a principal. In a proxy assertion, such as a spokesperson, a signed letter or a delegate, the principal authorises or stands behind content that the proxy produces. That requires some prior content-level intention or standing instruction. The thesis's attack is on that structure. Designers have no objective about the treaty date, so the designer-as-principal version fails. The user has no content-intention either, since they asked precisely because they did not know the answer. So even if Butlin and Viebahn leave the principal open, the user-adoption case is not a proxy case. It is adoption after the fact, which is how we treat memory, notebooks and testimony relayed onward. The objector reads "on behalf of human agents" as covering the user. But a user who adopts output speaks on their own behalf using a tool. Nobody speaks through them, so nothing is proxied. If Butlin and Viebahn stretch "proxy" to include this, they have already conceded the thesis's positive claim and merely relabelled it.

2. The dilemma on "deployer". Suppose Arora's "deployer" includes any user who prompts and publishes. Then "deployer" no longer picks out someone who sets objectives for the system's outputs. It picks out whoever ends up answerable for them, which is the thesis's own criterion for speakerhood. The proxy label then does no work, because the explanatory weight sits on adoption and answerability. If "deployer" means the operator who configures the system, the thesis's contrast stands.

3. The thesis targets an inference. The denial arguments infer "no assertion in chatbot discourse" from "no producer intention". That inference is vulnerable whatever any particular author says about users. Green and Michel's "characteristically" and their closing scepticism are compatible with the thesis. They concede that the creator-proxy story does not cover the central case, and the thesis says why.

VERDICT

The defence holds for the core and fails for part of the attribution.

What survives. The philosophical claim survives. Creator-proxy structures need content-directed intention from the principal, and the user's adoption case lacks it. Adoption plus answerability is a different structure from delegation. This is resistance, not hedging, because the thesis is unchanged. The objection shows only that some authors may already be closer to it than the sketch says.

What fails.
- Butlin and Viebahn. If their wording is as the objector reports, the sketch cannot list them as treating designers or deployers as the only candidates. At most they under-specify the user case. I cannot verify the quotation, but the sketch should not rest on a reading that this wording undercuts.
- Gubelmann. The claim that this weakens his denial route and that he conflates the model-level and discourse-level questions is unsupported. If he only denies that LLMs are speakers, he has no inference from absent producer intention to absent discourse-level assertion for the thesis to defeat. That consequence is dead unless someone is shown to make the inference. The second consequence can stay only as a conditional aimed at whoever does.
- Arora. I cannot confirm how "deployer" is used, so the dilemma in point 2 is conditional.

Net. The thesis should be stated as a claim against creator-centred proxy accounts, namely Green and Michel and, subject to checking, Arora. It should also be stated as a claim about the structure of the user case, not about everyone who uses the word "proxy". The "false in the central case" language is about right for the creator-centred versions but overstated as a universal report on the literature. Dropping Gubelmann and Butlin and Viebahn as targets is a correction of attribution, not a retreat on the thesis. Adding a further qualification to rescue them would be hedging, and I would not do it.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the user-adoption case bears on the proxy accounts at all. When a user reads an answer, endorses it and pastes it into a report, the user makes a new assertion. Nobody disputes this. It is ordinary testimony relay, like repeating a fact from an encyclopedia or a ghostwritten speech, and it is a standard case in the testimony literature, including selfless assertion. The proxy accounts and the denial arguments are about whether the chatbot's own output is an assertion, and by whom. The thesis answers a different question, namely whether the user asserts after adopting the output. Everyone answers yes. The remaining claim, that the model is "part of the user's cognitive apparatus", is a relabelling of tool use that adds no content. The notebook analogy concedes this. The principle that "adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion" is a platitude about assertion, not a discovery. The "separability" consequence is equally weak. Nobody denies that assertion can occur in chatbot-mediated discourse when a human endorses the output. The thesis is therefore true but uncontested, and it wins by changing the explanandum from the machine's utterance to the user's act.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The attack bites on the adoption case, which is a platitude. The thesis has a real remainder. It claims the proxy account's principal-slot is empty for the original output, because neither designer nor user had a content-directed objective. It also claims the autocompletion and unreflective-use cases are not post-hoc re-assertion. That remainder is contestable and needs argument, so the thesis is not merely trivial. A paper would have to separate the contested claim from the platitude.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says the thesis changes the explanandum from the machine's utterance to the user's later act. I resist this in four steps.

1. The proxy accounts do answer "whose assertion is this token?" Green and Michel's question is on whose behalf the artificial speaker's utterance is made. Their answer is the creator. So the thesis does not drift to a different explanandum. It gives a rival answer to the same question: for a given token, the creator is not the principal.

2. Autocompletion is not relay. In "The capital of Australia is… [accept]", there is no earlier act by the user for a later re-assertion to follow. The sentence in the user's document comes into being through their acceptance. The proxy account must say who asserted that sentence. If it says the designer, it attributes to the designer an assertion about Canberra that the designer never intended and could not have answered for. If it says the user, it has conceded the thesis. Nobody who accepts the testimony-relay platitude gets this result for free, because the platitude covers a second act, not the first.

3. The empty-slot claim is contestable, and that shows it is not trivial. The objector concedes this remainder. Proxy accounts need a principal with some content-directed stance. On the thesis, designers lack one for particular outputs, and users lack one before output. Only the user later acquires one, by adoption plus answerability. A view on which adoption can constitute the principal relation is a substantive alternative to delegation. It is not a platitude.

4. "Cognitive apparatus" is not mere relabelling. It excludes the reading on which the model is a second speaker whose assertion the user passes on. That reading, not the user-assertion platitude, is what the denial arguments and the proxy accounts both need.

VERDICT

The defence establishes that the thesis is not trivial, but it does not save the thesis as stated.

What holds. Point 1 holds. The thesis is a rival answer to a question the proxy accounts pose, not an off-topic remark. The autocompletion case in point 2 is the strongest material, because it is not post-hoc relay.

Why the thesis still fails.

- "False" is not earned. The thesis claims the proxy assumption is false. Adoption by the user shows only that the user asserts. It does not show that the designer-proxy assertion is absent. A proxy theorist can say there are two assertions, or that the proxy account covers only the chatbot's own turn in dialogue. Establishing falsity needs the further premise that designers lack the relevant content-directed stance. That premise is weak. A designer or deployer with a standing, de dicto objective like "answer accurately" is comparable to a wire-service editor who stands behind whatever the service reports. My earlier claim that designers "had no objective regarding that content" ran together de re and de dicto intention. The proxy theorist will say the standing instruction suffices, and the thesis has no reply to that.
- The positive claim is unsupported. "The model is part of the user's cognitive apparatus" conflicts with the cases the sketch uses. The user asks because they lack the knowledge, which is reliance on a source, not retrieval from a notebook they themselves filled. The ghostwriting and relayed-testimony analogies make the model a separate source. That is the structure the proxy and denial views already presuppose. The cognitive-apparatus reading fits only the autocompletion case, so it is not "the central case".
- What remains is the platitude. Once these two points are removed, what is left is the claim that adoption plus answerability suffices for the user's assertion. The objector is right that this is uncontested. The non-trivial part (the proxy principal is not the designer) rests on the weak de re premise. The part that is true (the user asserts) does not touch the proxy accounts.

Saving the thesis would require retreating to "in autocompletion-type cases, the user asserts and the designer need not", and then adding a restriction to non-standing-intention designers. That is hedging, and I will not do it. I report the thesis as dead in its stated form. The surviving fragment is the autocompletion case as a challenge to proxy accounts, which would need a new argument about de dicto standing intentions.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion without prior content-intention". The term "adopts" carries two readings, and the thesis needs both.

- Reading A, reflective endorsement. The user reads the output, takes it as true and puts it forward as their own. This makes "the user asserts" plausible. It also gives the user a content-directed intention and a commitment, formed on seeing the output. That is ordinary testimony relay, which the proxy theorist and the denier both accept.
- Reading B, unreflective acceptance. The user presses Tab on an autocompletion or pastes without scrutiny. This is what makes the case interesting. No content-intention, however late, is formed, so the model really is "part of the user's cognitive apparatus". The designer-proxy story is left with no rival.

The argument runs between the two. The sufficiency claim borrows its credibility from A, where the user has plainly taken on the content. The "cognitive apparatus" claim and the displacement of designer-proxy rest on B, where the user has not. Under B, "answerability" is only a liability others can impose, not the user's act of speaking. Under A, the thesis is the uncontested platitude, and it leaves the proxy account standing for the model's original token. So the thesis cannot be run on either reading alone.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The defender can reply that accepting is itself an intention-in-action to put the sentence forward. That reply narrows the gap between A and B, but it also gives up the claim that the user has no content-intention.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says "adopts" slides between reflective endorsement (A) and unreflective acceptance (B). The thesis needs only a third reading, and that reading is stable.

1. The thesis denies prior content-intention, not any content-intention. The sketch says the user "formed no content-intention *before* the output". The key premise is that adoption suffices "without *prior* content-intention". The objector's reply on the defender's behalf, that accepting is an intention-in-action to put the sentence forward, would give up nothing. A content-intention formed at acceptance is exactly what adoption is. The objector's own Reading A thus matches the thesis, because it denies only that the intention precedes the output.

2. There is a middle reading, C: acceptance as a de dicto commitment to put forward whatever the source says. Tabbing through "The capital of Australia is…" is not scrutiny-free in the way a reflex is. It is a choice to let this sentence stand as one's own in this document. Ordinary assertion is full of C. People repeat what the encyclopedia says, state a figure from a spreadsheet they didn't check, or sign a letter they skimmed. Nobody thinks these cases fall into "mere liability". On commitment-based accounts of assertion (Brandom, Kukla, Lackey on selfless assertion, and the practice of ghostwritten speech), what makes something an assertion is undertaking responsibility for the content, not a rich occurrent belief state. C meets that condition. So the sufficiency claim does not borrow credibility from A. It holds on C, where scrutiny is minimal but the commitment is real.

3. The pure-B case does not carry the thesis. If someone pastes without registering that they are putting anything forward, the objector may be right that only liability is left. But the thesis's central case is the one the sketch describes: a user pastes the answer into a report. That is C. Pure B is a corner, and conceding it costs the thesis nothing it needs.

4. The extended-mind half survives on C. Clark and Chalmers' criteria include automatic endorsement and reliance on a trusted, accessible source. C is that. The apparatus claim never required the absence of endorsement. It required that the model's contribution be taken up without being treated as a second speaker's testimony.

5. The proxy account is not left standing. Under C, the displayed token is a stage in the user's production of their own assertion. For the proxy theorist to keep a designer-assertion alongside it, they must posit a second assertion with no audience-directed act and no designer answerability for that content.

VERDICT

The defence answers the equivocation charge as framed, but it does not save the thesis. It confirms the earlier verdict that the thesis is dead in its stated form.

What holds.
- The A/B dilemma is dodged. Reading C gives the sufficiency premise a stable footing. The objector's move to "accepting is an intention-in-action" does not contradict the thesis, because the thesis only ever denied *prior* intention. Point 1 is correct.
- Sufficiency is plausible on C. Commitment-based accounts support it. This remains the true core: in these cases the user asserts, even though they did not author the content.

What fails.
- The cognitive-apparatus claim does not survive C. C is a commitment to a source's content. Once the user is taking responsibility for content they lack and asked a source for, the model is functioning as a source, as an encyclopedia or a ghostwriter does. Otto's notebook holds content Otto himself endorsed earlier. An encyclopedia, though consulted automatically, is not part of anyone's mind. Point 4 relies on a trust-based reading of Clark and Chalmers that would make every trusted reference work part of the apparatus. The apparatus label fits at most autocompletion of the user's own half-formed sentence, and that is not the central case. This was already conceded in the prior round, and the equivocation objection exposes the same structure: sufficiency needs C, and the apparatus claim needs something closer to B.
- Point 5 is not secured. It assumes the designer has no content-level answerability. The earlier round showed that this runs together de re and de dicto intentions. A standing designer or deployer objective like "answer accurately" is the proxy theorist's resource, and the thesis has not defeated it. The thesis would then also have to say that the second assertion is idle, which is a new argument and not one the sketch gives.
- "False in the central case" is not earned. C shows the user asserts. It does not show the proxy assumption is false of the model's output. Given that C is relay-like, the uncontested platitude from the triviality round reappears. What is left is the autocompletion case as a challenge to creator-centred proxy accounts. It is interesting, but it is a different and narrower thesis than the one submitted. Rewriting the thesis to that, or adding a clause excluding designers with standing de dicto objectives, would be hedging, so I do not do it.

Report. The equivocation objection fails on its own terms, since the thesis never needed Reading B for sufficiency. But the thesis as stated claims both that the user is the speaker and that the model is part of the user's cognitive apparatus. The first requires C and is true but not contested against the proxy accounts. The second requires B-like absorption and is false for the central case. The thesis is dead as stated.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion without prior content-intention". Adoption is defined so that no case can count against it, and the thesis has no stated condition under which the user fails to be the speaker.

- Careless acceptance. If the user tabs through or pastes without registering that they are putting anything forward, the thesis can say this is not adoption, just liability. The sufficiency claim is then true by construction.
- Reflective acceptance. If the user treats the model as a source, as with a treaty date they asked for, the thesis relabels this ordinary relay or testimony. That is conceded to be uncontested.
- Source versus apparatus. The "cognitive apparatus" label is applied to the autocompletion case. When the case looks like consulting a source, the label becomes "ghostwriter" or "encyclopedia". The same role flips between instrument and source as the case demands.
- Designer objectives. If designers have a standing "answer accurately" objective, the thesis says that is not content-directed. The proxy theorist's counterexample is ruled out by the definition of "objective regarding that content".

Every candidate counterexample is excluded by a definitional move, so the thesis cannot lose. The paper would need independent criteria for adoption, for answerability, and for source versus apparatus, fixed before the cases are sorted.

STRENGTH: 3/5. A genuine problem, but answerable. The thesis can commit in advance to a test. Unreflective acceptance plus real sanction by the audience would count as assertion, and acceptance with no uptake would not. The thesis could then be wrong about those cases.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection says every counterexample is excluded by a definitional move. I resist this on each of its four bullets.

1. Careless acceptance: the criteria are independent and fixed in advance. The thesis borrows its criteria from commitment accounts of assertion (Brandom, Kukla, Lackey on selfless assertion). They do not come from the cases.
- (a) The content is presented to an audience as the user's own contribution.
- (b) The audience has standing to challenge and sanction the user for it.
- (c) The user can retract it.

These tests are public. They do not depend on the user's inner state, so the sorting does not depend on the thesis's verdict. Tabbing through an autocompletion in a report meets all three. A user who pastes the output into a private scratch file does not meet (a). It is not assertion, and the thesis says so.

2. Reflective acceptance: there is a contrast class. The thesis predicts a difference between two cases. "The date is 1648" put forward in the user's own voice is the user's assertion. "ChatGPT says the date is 1648" is a report, and the user is answerable only for the report. Practice bears this out: the two draw different challenges and different retractions. If audiences held users to the first-order claim even under attribution, or excused unattributed pasting as "not their claim", the thesis would be wrong. That is a falsifier.

3. Source versus apparatus: the label follows a testable difference. Autocompletion extends the user's own half-sentence under their ongoing control. Consulting a model for an unknown fact is reliance on a source. The thesis can say that "apparatus" applies only where the user's act of composing runs through the model's contribution, and that elsewhere the user is a relaying speaker. Either way the user is the speaker, and that is the claim that matters against the proxy accounts. The label is not what does the work.

4. Designer objectives: a non-ad hoc criterion is available. The objection says "no objective regarding that content" is defined so as to rule out standing "answer accurately" objectives. The better criterion is not de re versus de dicto. A proxy relation needs the principal to put the content forward, or to authorise its being put forward on this occasion, to an audience. A wire editor does this by publishing the item. A designer who ships a model does not do it for a given token. That criterion is fixed before the cases are sorted. It can also fail: a deployer who configures a customer-service bot and publishes its output does meet it, and the thesis grants that such a deployer is a principal.

VERDICT

The unfalsifiability charge fails as a refutation. The objector concedes that the thesis can commit to a test in advance, and points 1, 2 and 4 show that it can. Stating the criteria is not hedging, because it adds no exception and narrows no claim. It makes explicit what the thesis already implied. The thesis can lose, because attributed quotation, scratch-file pasting and audience practice are all cases where it makes risky predictions.

Two things do not survive.

- Point 4 is a new argument, not the sketch. The sketch rests on "designers had no objective regarding that content". Earlier rounds showed that this claim fails against standing de dicto objectives. The putting-forward criterion would replace it with a different and better argument. That argument is not in the submission, and it excludes deployers who publish output, which is a real restriction on how far "false in the central case" reaches.
- Point 3 concedes the earlier verdict. The rescue works only by separating the user-is-speaker claim from the apparatus claim and dropping the second. That is what the earlier rounds found. The "cognitive apparatus" half applies at most to autocompletion, and the user-asks-for-a-fact case is source reliance. The objection's "flips between instrument and source" charge is correct about the thesis as stated, and the defence only answers it by giving the label up.

Report. The thesis is not unfalsifiable, so the objection does not show it is empty. But the thesis as submitted is still dead. The apparatus claim does not hold in the central case, and the "false" claim against proxy accounts depends on a premise the sketch states in a form that does not work. What survives is a different and narrower thesis, that user adoption through public putting-forward makes the user the speaker, and that designers who do not put forward particular outputs are not their principals. That is worth developing, but it is not this thesis. Presenting it as this thesis would be hedging.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the thesis is new, that "the proxy account's principal is the designer or deployer" is a shared assumption and the user-as-speaker alternative is unoccupied. Each half of the thesis is already held.

1. User as principal of the proxy. Butlin and Viebahn (2025) say AI systems can be used to produce proxy assertions "on behalf of human agents". Their assertion condition is sanctionability, which is the thesis's answerability criterion. Their view therefore already covers a user who puts a model's output forward. Arora's "deployers", read to include users, does the same. Green and Michel's "characteristically" and their closing scepticism leave room for the same extension.

2. Model as part of the user's cognitive apparatus. This is the extended-mind and cognitive-artifact line. Clark (2025, on extending minds with generative AI, cited from memory) holds it, and so do Heersmink-style accounts of cognitive artifacts. Barandiaran and Almendros's "midtended" agency is the same coupling idea. Freiman and Miller's instrument-testimony framing also treats the device as an epistemic instrument and not as a speaker.

3. Adoption without authorship suffices for assertion. This is Lackey's selfless assertion and the commitment-based accounts (Brandom, Kukla), applied to chatbots.

4. Denial arguments do not infer from producer intention to user non-assertion. Gubelmann denies that LLMs are speakers, not that users assert. So the "separability" consequence is already built into the literature and into the denial arguments.

What is left is the autocompletion counterexample to creator-centred proxy, which is a small remainder.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The slogan is occupied on every side, and the exchange shows the surviving fragment is narrow. Still, no one in the supplied literature explicitly argues that the proxy account's principal slot is empty for the original token, and I could not verify the Clark attribution.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. Priority is not falsity. "Already taken" shows at most that the thesis is not original. It does not show the thesis is wrong, and the thesis has a target whether or not others share its view. Green and Michel centre creators, and Arora's list names deployers. If some authors already hold the user-as-speaker view, that supports the thesis's verdict on the creator-centred accounts.

2. The four occupied components are not the combination. The thesis is not "users assert" or "tools extend minds". It is a claim about the *structure* of a particular explanatory question: for a given token, who is the principal? It says the creator-proxy answer fails because the slot is empty at the creator end and filled only by later adoption.
- Lackey and the commitment accounts concern assertion without belief, or the nature of commitment. They do not say what fixes the principal of a machine-generated token, and they do not address the proxy accounts.
- Clark and the cognitive-artifact line say the tool is part of the mind. They do not say that the user is thereby the speaker of what the tool outputs, or that this displaces a proxy theory of machine utterance.
- Butlin and Viebahn. If their "on behalf of human agents" covers the user, the objector has not shown that they treat user adoption as proxying. Proxy structure means the principal stands behind content produced by an agent acting for them. Adoption after the fact is a different relation. If they stretch "proxy" to cover it, they have taken over the thesis's positive claim and kept the label.

3. The objector concedes the remainder. The objector says no one in the supplied literature argues that the proxy principal slot is empty for the original token. That is the part of the thesis that does the work against the proxy accounts. A thesis whose core is unoccupied is not already taken.

4. The denial point cuts the other way. If Gubelmann denies only that LLMs are speakers and does not deny user assertion, the separability consequence is not a discovery against him. But the thesis then stands as a warning about arguments that slide from "no producer intention" to "no assertion in chatbot discourse", and the objector has not shown that no such arguments exist.

VERDICT

The defence holds against the priority charge as a refutation. Being partly occupied does not make the thesis false, and the empty-slot claim is not shown to be occupied. The thesis is still dead as submitted, for reasons the earlier rounds already established and this round adds to.

Why it fails.
- Misreported target. The objection and the first round converge. If Butlin and Viebahn, and on some readings Arora, already allow the user as principal, then "the proxy account's assumption … is false" is not a claim about *the* proxy account. It is a claim about creator-centred versions. This is an overstatement of the shared assumption, not a point the defence can fix by adding a clause.
- Apparatus claim. The extended-mind half is both occupied (Clark, Heersmink, and the like) and false of the central case. A user who asks for a treaty date is consulting a source, not using a notebook they filled. A defence that removes the apparatus claim to save the user-is-speaker claim gives up part of the thesis.
- Empty-slot premise. The sketch rests it on "designers had no objective regarding that content". Standing de dicto objectives answer that. The better argument, that a designer does not put forward a given token, is not in the sketch. It also exempts deployers who publish output.
- What survives. The surviving claim is narrow: in the autocompletion and paste-into-report cases, the user is the speaker by public putting-forward, and designers who do not put forward particular outputs are not their principals. That is worth developing, but it is a different and smaller thesis. Presenting it as this one would be hedging. I report this thesis as dead.

I could not verify the Clark attribution or the Butlin and Viebahn and Arora wording, so the novelty finding rests on citations from memory.

R9. The disagreement among denial, proxy, fictionalist, and attributing views is not about the conditions for performing a speech act. It is about which entity in the LLM stack counts as the speaker (token-level sample, trained policy, deployed persona, or sociotechnical system). Once the speaker is fixed, the rival camps largely agree on the verdicts.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · dead
Move · Target
reframing — The shared presupposition, across all four groups, that 'the LLM' is a determinate candidate speaker. It is aimed especially at Williams and Bayne's search for an intermediate category and at Gubelmann's mechanism-versus-organism framing.
Sketch

Each camp tests one candidate speaker against shared conditions: intention-like control, responsiveness to sanction, and a descriptive function. Gubelmann tests the mechanism that samples tokens. Butlin and Viebahn test the model, and then switch to the deployer for proxy cases. Mallory's fiction has a persona as its character. Attah tests the pipeline plus its design context. Human speakers come with a built-in answer, one body and one biography, so the debate about humans never has to ask this question. An LLM's output is a sample from a distribution, produced by a policy, framed by a system prompt, and sustained by a company. The key premise is that the verdicts vary systematically with the chosen speaker-level while the conditions stay constant. If so, 'can an LLM assert?' is ill-posed until a speaker-individuation criterion is supplied. 'Proto-assertion' then looks like a symptom: it marks the cases where no level fits the conditions cleanly.

Appraiser (blind)
Recasting the debate as disagreement over which entity in the LLM stack is the speaker, with shared conditions, is a genuine reframing, though 27 and 49 repeat it.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender argued that denying speakerhood of X and redirecting it presupposes a determinate X, and the camps' divergence is the evidence for that. It conceded only the Gubelmann exegesis, which is peripheral.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 2/5, answered.
