The thesis argues that unintended output-time dispositions undercut the shared provenance assumption. Connecting those two literatures through that assumption appears in none of the cited work.

VERDICT

The "already taken" charge half fails. The specific target (Gubelmann's Kantian "external" read etiologically, plus unintended dispositions against objective-grounded proxy accounts) is not clearly occupied. Attah is an opponent, and Butlin and the proxy critics argue different things. I also cannot check any of these citations against the texts.

The thesis is still not saved. A claim can be unoccupied and still wrong, and the earlier rounds found it wrong in the places that make it distinctive.

1. The pincer is the part claimed as new, and it is false as stated. Gubelmann and the proxy theorists agree that the purposes are the designers'. They disagree about what follows. The thesis offers a shared error, not a conflict, so "cannot both be right" fails.
2. The unoccupied territory is the narrow claim, and the thesis does not stay there. The narrow claim is that unintended dispositions strain objective-based proxy accounts and that the "external" gloss is poor. The thesis's headline is that the axis is wrong and that LLMs align with organisms. The part that is not already taken is the part that earlier rounds showed to be unsupported. Kant's etiology (ordered from within) puts LLMs on the artefact side. Gradient descent lacks the reproductive structure that Millikan-style selected function needs. Sycophancy and reward hacking look like unforeseen means serving a stipulated purpose, like scale deposits, not like selected purposes.
3. The part that is already taken is not new. The general etiological point and the observation that LLMs sit between artefact and organism (Dennett, Millikan, Butlin, Gubelmann's own concession) contribute nothing here.

So the novelty objection is only mildly damaging, but nothing it leaves standing survives the earlier rounds. What is new is the narrow claim, and I will not offer that as the original thesis. I report the thesis as not saved.

R16. Butlin's agency criterion tracks sensitivity to instrumental value, but the speech acts at issue (assertion, apology, promising) are constituted by non-instrumental norms, so there is a distinction between instrumental agency and norm-responsive agency. A system can be a full agent in Butlin's sense and still be unable to perform these acts in its own right, because for such a system every norm-conforming output is only a means to its learned objective.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption (Butlin, Attah, Gubelmann) that the question is whether the system is an agent or has intentions, so that agency is the gate to speech acts.
Sketch

Butlin's criterion makes an entity an agent if its outputs are explained by its learning about what conduces to a goal. For an RLHF chatbot that goal is, at bottom, rater approval. The debate treats agency as the gateway to intention and so to speech acts. But assertion is governed by a truth norm and apology by a norm of remorse and repair, and these are not norms of conduciveness. A speaker who is responsive only to instrumental value tracks truth only when truth pays. That is the structure of the liar-for-hire or the salesman. Such a speaker can still assert, since humans do it instrumentally too, but only against a background of norm-responsiveness that is not itself instrumental. The key premise is that performing a norm-constituted act requires some responsiveness to the constitutive norm as such, not merely as a means. Butlin's own treatment of desire as 'answerable to standards of conduciveness' shows the criterion has no slot for this. The result reclassifies the positions. Gubelmann (autonomy), Butlin and Viebahn (sanction) and Magnus et al. (moral agency) are each approximating this one missing property, and it is separable from both agency and autonomy.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating instrumental agency from norm-responsive agency identifies a gap between agency criteria and norm-constituted acts that the current debate overlooks.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defender conceded that Butlin does not hold the agency-gates-speech-acts view (Butlin and Viebahn put the gate in sanctionability) and that only Gubelmann clearly does. The debate-wide target was given up, though the instrumental/norm-responsive distinction itself was untouched.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, answered. Defender showed that the thesis's own wording ('tracks truth only when truth pays') carries a counterfactual reward-decoupling test. It also answered the genetic worry with the point that origin in reward does not fix present operation. It admitted the test is not decisive from behaviour alone.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. 'Novelty is not validity' is a real reason the objection does not touch the distinction, and the argument that sanctionability can be met instrumentally is an actual differentiation. Defender conceded the 'unoccupied position' and 'reclassification' claims were overstated.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defender reinterpreted 'as such' as a standing capacity in the speaker and retracted its earlier 'proxy' gloss. That reads as a clarifying move but is closer to absorption, because the capacity it names ('would feel exposed if caught') is itself sanction-sensitivity. The next objection exploited exactly that.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, unanswered. The pay-driven psychopath asserts, perjures and lies without non-instrumental norm-responsiveness. Defender's 'norm-indexed content' reply falls back on the weak reading it had rejected. Defender then conceded that the key premise fails.
⚑ Target attribution disputed — Defender conceded that Butlin does not hold the agency-gates-speech-acts view (Butlin and Viebahn put the gate in sanctionability) and that only Gubelmann clearly does. The debate-wide target was given up, though the instrumental/norm-responsive distinction itself was untouched. Check this yourself: it is a claim about who holds what, made from recall.
🔧 Survives as

Agency in Butlin's sense is insufficient for speech acts because it is silent on answerability to constitutive norms. What matters is standing or answerability within the practice (deontic status), not agency or motive. Aim this at Gubelmann and the intention-argument family, and drop the claim that non-instrumental valuing of the norm is required.

Flaw

The key premise that norm-constituted acts require non-instrumental responsiveness to the norm is contradicted by the pure instrumentalist who still asserts and perjures. The capacity and 'norm-indexed' rescues either collapse into sanction-sensitivity, which a chatbot also has, or deny him assertion.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Butlin, Attah and Gubelmann share the assumption that agency or intention is the gate to speech acts.

- Butlin. As far as I recall, "The agency in language agents" is a reply to Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini about whether language agents are agents and have desires. It does not link agency to speech acts. His joint paper with Viebahn, "AI Assertion", explicitly puts the gate elsewhere: descriptive function plus sanctionability, with no intention or agency requirement, and it allows proxy assertion. So Butlin is not a gatekeeper-by-agency theorist. The thesis even cites him on the other side, as approximating "the missing property".
- Attah. He attacks the claim that communicative intention distinguishes humans from LLMs, and he says that is not the real difference. His residual appeal to "mental and metalinguistic agency" is a different claim from "agency gates speech acts".
- Gubelmann. He does hold the gate view: speakers must illocute, illocuting requires intention, and intention requires autonomous goal-setting.

So the target is a composite. One member holds the view, one holds it only loosely, and one has argued against it elsewhere. The critique of "Butlin's criterion lacks a norm-responsiveness slot" then blames a criterion for failing to do work Butlin never assigned it.

STRENGTH: 2/5. I am confident about the Butlin–Viebahn point, but the thesis's real opponent is Gubelmann and the intention-argument family. The distinction itself survives if it is re-aimed at them. This is a framing fix, not a refutation. I am unsure of the exact scope of Attah's claims beyond the summary given.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis is about the criterion, not about what its author assigned it. The central claim is that an entity can satisfy Butlin's agency criterion in full and still lack norm-responsiveness. That holds whatever Butlin intended. Whether his paper links agency to speech acts is beside the point if others do, and the thesis's complaint is with the debate's use of agency as a proxy for what speech acts need. A criterion can be shown to be silent on a property without its author having claimed otherwise.

2. "Gate" is a structural description of the debate, not a quotation. On this reading the debate asks "is the system an agent?" and then treats the answer as bearing on speech acts. Butlin's paper does this work. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini's claim that language agents have beliefs and desires is what makes "can they assert?" a live question, and Butlin's reply is a move in that exchange. It is natural to read Attah's residual "mental and metalinguistic agency" as the gate when intention is not. If the leftover difference between humans and LLMs is agency, then agency is doing the gating work in his account. Gubelmann gates explicitly.

3. The Butlin–Viebahn point supports the thesis. The thesis cites that paper as approximating the missing property. Its move from intention to sanctionability is the sort of departure from the agency gate that the thesis recommends. The objector's evidence therefore shows the field already drifting toward the thesis's own conclusion, not that the thesis misdescribes it.

4. The distinction does not depend on the target. Instrumental versus norm-responsive agency is argued from the structure of assertion, apology and promising, and from the liar-for-hire case. All of that stands if the target is narrowed to Gubelmann and the intention-argument family.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold for the target, and I will not rescue it.

- Point 1 is true but does not help. The thesis does not just say Butlin's criterion is silent on norm-responsiveness. It names Butlin as sharing an assumption that agency gates speech acts. That is a claim about what he holds, and the objector is right that it is false of him. His work with Viebahn puts the gate in descriptive function plus sanctionability, with no intention requirement. Criticizing his agency criterion for lacking a "slot" it was never meant to fill is a category complaint.
- Point 2 is an overreach. Calling Butlin's reply part of a debate where agency "matters" does not make him hold the gate view. Reading Attah's residual agency as a gate is my inference, not his claim, and I am no surer of his scope than the objector is. Only Gubelmann clearly holds the view.
- Point 3 cuts against the thesis. If Butlin and Viebahn already relocate the gate to sanctionability, the "shared assumption" does not exist. The "reclassification" of positions as approximations of one missing property is then a relabelling of a disagreement the participants already see, and its novelty shrinks.

What survives is the distinction itself, instrumental agency versus norm-responsive agency, and its force against Gubelmann and the intention-argument family. That is a real but smaller thesis. The headline claim, a debate-wide shared assumption now diagnosed and replaced, is dead. Re-aiming at Gubelmann is not a qualification of the distinction, but it removes most of what made the thesis ambitious. I report the original framing as refuted and the distinction as a separate, narrower survivor.

The objector's 2/5 is fair on the logic, since the distinction is untouched. It understates the damage to the thesis as advertised, because the target and the reclassification were its main contribution.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: performing a norm-constituted act requires responsiveness to the constitutive norm "as such, not merely as a means."

As stated, the premise is protected from every case by redescription.

- Any system that tracks truth, even when truth doesn't pay, can be re-ruled "instrumental." An RLHF model trained for groundedness, or one that corrects itself when no rater is watching, is said to be serving a deeper learned objective, "rater approval at bottom." The thesis fixes that bottom level by stipulation, so no behaviour could show norm-responsiveness "as such."
- Any human counterexample is absorbed. Salesmen and liars-for-hire assert, but "against a background" of non-instrumental responsiveness. If that background is present, it counts as the property. If the human is a pure instrumentalist who still asserts, they are an acknowledged exception. Either way the premise survives.
- Human norm-responsiveness is itself explainable by socialisation and reward. That raises the question of what distinguishes the "non-instrumental" human case from the "instrumental" machine case, other than the verdict.

The thesis offers no observable that would separate "responsive to the norm as such" from "responsive because it pays." Without one, the distinction between instrumental and norm-responsive agency is a label applied after the fact, and the claim that Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, and Magnus et al. are all approximating "this one missing property" cannot be tested.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The attack is a genuine problem, but answerable. The thesis can supply a counterfactual-robustness test: does the norm-conforming behaviour persist when the learned reward decouples from it? Butlin's own self-modification criterion already operationalises something like this. If the thesis commits to such a test, the distinction becomes falsifiable. As written, it has not done so.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis already contains the test. The objector says no observable separates "responsive to the norm as such" from "responsive because it pays." But the thesis defines instrumental responsiveness by its modal profile: such a speaker "tracks truth only when truth pays." That is a counterfactual claim. Truth-conformity in the instrumentalist covaries with payoff, and in the norm-responsive speaker it does not. So the question "does conformity persist when it stops paying, or when the learned reward is flipped?" is built into the original wording. Spelling it out explicates the thesis and does not narrow it.

2. The first bullet confuses fixing the level with stipulating it. "Rater approval at bottom" is an empirical claim about the training objective and the system's learned structure, and it can be checked. Self-correction when unobserved is not decisive, because a generalised proxy produces it too. What discriminates is the intervention: change the objective to reward falsehood and see whether the system tracks the new reward, or registers the norm as a reason against its objective. The first is the liar-for-hire. The second is what the thesis calls norm-responsiveness. Butlin's learning-and-self-modification apparatus gives the machinery for this probe.

3. The human case is not absorbed by redescription. The objection runs: human norm-responsiveness is also produced by socialisation and reward, so what separates human from machine besides the verdict? This is a genetic fallacy. The thesis concerns the standing structure of the motivation, not its causal origin. Williams's *Truth and Truthfulness* treats Accuracy and Sincerity as intrinsic dispositions even though they are acquired. Allport's functional autonomy of motives and the Kantian contrast between acting *from* duty and merely *in accordance with* it all say that a motive can originate instrumentally and come to operate non-instrumentally. The question is whether the norm figures in the agent's deliberation as a consideration independent of the payoff.

4. The distinction is conceptual, so it needs only coherence. The thesis claims that Butlin's criterion is satisfiable by a system that lacks norm-responsiveness. Showing this requires a coherent model, and the liar-for-hire shows one. Whether any actual LLM is such a system is a further empirical question that the distinction does not need to answer in order to be true.

5. The pure-instrumentalist exception is already handled. The thesis says an instrumental speaker can assert "against a background" of non-instrumental responsiveness. The salesman borrows the sanctions and norms of a practice whose participants do hold the norm. That is proxy assertion, which is precisely what "not in its own right" means. So the premise is not rescued case by case. It says a speaker's own performance needs the background in the speaker, and a speaker who only has it in the practice performs by proxy.

VERDICT

The defence holds against the charge of unfalsifiability, and it has two limits that I will not hide.

What holds. The distinction has a modal test, counterfactual robustness under reward-decoupling. It is implicit in the thesis's own gloss on the liar-for-hire. The claim is therefore testable in principle, and the "label after the fact" charge fails. Point 3 answers the human-versus-machine question without relying on the verdict.

What does not.

- *The test is not decisive from behaviour alone.* This is Kant's shopkeeper problem. A system with a long-horizon or reputational objective passes any finite decoupling test while still being instrumental. The test needs interventions on the objective or on internal structure, not just output observation. That is a real limit on how confidently the thesis can classify actual chatbots. It does not make the distinction empty.
- *The thesis as written never committed to the test.* The objector is right that the key premise is stated without an operationalisation. The defence supplies one from the thesis's own wording, but the text should say so.

Cumulative status. This attack is survivable and was worth surviving. It does not repair the earlier misattribution. As conceded above, the claim of a debate-wide shared assumption is dead. What remains is the instrumental versus norm-responsive distinction, aimed at Gubelmann and the intention-argument family, with a counterfactual-robustness test as its criterion. That is a smaller thesis than the one advertised. It is not a thesis kept alive by piling on qualifications, because the test was in the thesis from the start.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the missing property, responsiveness to a constitutive norm as such rather than as a means, is a separable, unoccupied position. It is already held in several forms.

- Skiba (2026), "Artificial Speech Acts." He gives a norm-based argument that LLMs cannot assert because assertion is constituted by norms, and he extends it to speech acts generally. That is the thesis's core move: norm-constituted acts need norm-responsiveness, not just goal-directedness. I know his argument only from the summary, so I may be misjudging how close it is.
- Butlin and Viebahn (2025), "AI Assertion." They hold that assertion is norm-governed and requires being sanctionable, and that AI output otherwise counts only as proxy assertion. This is the same conclusion the thesis reaches, "not in its own right," reached by the same route: agency is not enough, so look to norm-governed social standing.
- Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz (2025). They require moral agency for apology, over and above linguistic agency.
- Proxy-assertion theorists (Green and Michel, Arora). They already state the thesis's conclusion that machine outputs are performed on behalf of others.
- Older sources. The distinction between acting from a norm and acting merely in accordance with it is Kant's shopkeeper. Brandom and Searle already treat speech acts as constituted by norms.

The thesis therefore restates "norm-responsiveness, not agency, gates speech acts" with a Kantian gloss. Its "reclassification" admits that the rival views already approximate it.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The attack hits novelty and the claim of a missing property. It does not touch the specific point that Butlin's instrumental-value criterion can be fully satisfied without norm-responsiveness. Whether any of these authors makes that point explicitly is the remaining question.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. Novelty is not validity. The attack shows that others reached nearby conclusions. It does not show the thesis is false, and the thesis was never offered as a first discovery of norm-constitution. It is a *distinction* move. Its claim is that Butlin's agency criterion can be fully satisfied by a system that lacks the property these acts require. The objector concedes this "does not touch" that point.

2. Sharing a conclusion is not sharing a route. The conclusion "AI output is proxy assertion" is common ground. What differs is the diagnosis, and the diagnoses make different predictions.
- Butlin and Viebahn locate the gate in sanctionability. But sanction-sensitivity is the paradigm of instrumental responsiveness: a system adjusts because conformity is rewarded and deviation is penalised. A system could be fully sanctionable in their sense and still be the liar-for-hire, who tracks truth when and because it pays.
- So the thesis treats their criterion as an approximation of the missing property, not a statement of it. That is why it can be separable from agency, autonomy and sanctionability alike. This is a critique of the rival, not a restatement.
- Magnus et al. demand moral agency for apology only. The thesis offers one property across assertion, apology and promising, and the moral-agency demand may be stronger or weaker than it.

3. Kant's shopkeeper is a resource, not a competitor. The thesis applies the from-duty/in-accordance-with-duty distinction to a specific criterion, Butlin's "answerable to standards of conduciveness". That is what a distinction move is. If using a classical distinction on a new target counted as "already taken", no application in philosophy of AI would be new. Brandom and Searle supply the constitutive-norm premise, which the thesis borrows openly.

4. Proxy-assertion theorists give the conclusion, not the explanation. Green and Michel and Arora say machine outputs are performed on behalf of others. They do not say why the system itself cannot perform them, nor what would have to be added. The thesis supplies that: norm-responsiveness as such, tested by robustness under reward-decoupling.

VERDICT

The defence holds only for a reduced claim, and part of the thesis does not survive.

What holds. The specific diagnosis is not in the cited literature as far as the objector or I can tell. It says that Butlin's criterion tracks instrumental value and has no slot for non-instrumental norm-responsiveness. It adds that a system can therefore be a full agent and still not perform these acts in its own right. Point 2 is the strongest part. If sanctionability can be met by instrumental sensitivity, then Butlin and Viebahn's criterion has the same gap as the agency criterion, and the thesis explains why their gate approximates the right one without reaching it.

What fails.
- "Separable and unoccupied" is overstated. The thesis says the rival positions approximate this one property. That already admits the property is in play. The honest claim is that the property is named and isolated here, not that it was missing from the debate. Skiba's norm-based argument is the closest rival, and I know it only from the objector's summary. If it argues that assertion needs responsiveness to the norm and not mere goal-direction, then the core move is already made and only the Butlin-specific application remains.
- Point 2 depends on a premise I cannot verify. It assumes Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability can be satisfied instrumentally. If they require more, for instance that the system be sensitive to sanctions as expressing the norm, then the gap closes and the "approximation" framing turns into agreement.
- "Reclassification" carries little weight. The thesis sorts the rivals as approximations of its own property. That is a relabelling unless the property yields a prediction the rivals do not, and the only such prediction is the decoupling test. That test is defensible, but it was supplied only under the previous attack, and it is not decisive from behaviour alone.

Cumulative status. After three attacks the thesis has lost its debate-wide target and its claim to an unoccupied position. What is left is a diagnostic distinction: Butlin's agency criterion, and probably the sanction criterion, fit instrumental responsiveness, while these acts need norm-responsiveness, with a counterfactual test as its mark. That is real but modest. I do not rescue the larger framing. Its survival depends on two checks I cannot do: whether Skiba already makes the Butlin-specific point, and whether sanctionability in Butlin and Viebahn is strictly instrumental. If either check goes against it, the thesis reduces to a restatement of the Kantian distinction with a new example.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: performing a norm-constituted act requires some responsiveness to the constitutive norm *as such, not merely as a means*.

If this worked, it would license conclusions we reject.
- The pure careerist, con artist or hired advocate responds to truth, remorse or promissory commitment only because it pays. On the premise, he cannot assert, apologise or promise in his own right. That is absurd. His strategic apology is an apology, his lie is an assertion, and his promise binds him.
- Lying is the sharpest case. A lie is an assertion that violates the truth norm. Constitutive norms make an act assessable by a standard. They do not require that the performer value the standard.
- Insincere or reputational apologies by corporations or politicians would all become non-apologies.

The thesis's escape is that the instrumentalist asserts "against a background" of others' norm-responsiveness, and so only by proxy. But that makes every strategic human speaker a proxy, which is the unacceptable result. Alternatively, "some responsiveness" can be weakened to recognising and tracking the norm as a norm. Then a fine-tuned chatbot that models truth-violation as a violation may satisfy it, and the distinction no longer separates the cases it was built for.

Genetic readings also prove too much, since all human norm-responsiveness is acquired through reward.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis can retreat to a sincerity-independent standing condition, but only by giving up the "as such" premise that does its work.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The premise is a capacity condition, not an occurrent-motive condition. The objector reads "responsiveness to the norm as such" as a requirement that the speaker be moved by the norm in each act. The thesis does not say that. It says the instrumental speaker asserts "against a background of norm-responsiveness that is not itself instrumental." On the natural reading, the background is in the speaker: he has a standing sensitivity to the norm which he can exercise, suppress or exploit. The con artist, the hired advocate and the strategic apologiser all have it. They know what a lie is, would feel exposed if caught, can be shamed, and can be moved by truth when it costs them. Their strategic use of assertion is parasitic on that standing capacity, and the premise requires only that the capacity exists. It does not require that it be operative whenever they speak.

2. The lie is a point in the thesis's favour. A lie is an assertion that violates the truth norm, and the liar must present himself as answerable to that norm. He conceals the violation, trades on the hearer's presumption of sincerity, and can be convicted of lying. All of this presupposes that the norm has hold on him as a norm. Williams makes this point: the liar is parasitic on a practice of truthfulness that he himself understands and is subject to. The constitutive-norm premise explains why lying is a deficient assertion and not a different act.

3. The "proxy for every strategic human" result does not follow. It would follow only if proxy status were assigned to anyone whose given act is instrumental. The thesis assigns it to a system for which "every norm-conforming output is only a means to its learned objective." That is a claim about exhaustive instrumentality, with no non-instrumental capacity anywhere in the system. The strategic human is not such a system. I should retract my earlier gloss that the salesman "borrows" a background held by other participants. That reading conflates his position with the chatbot's and invites exactly this objection. The background must be in the speaker for the human case and absent for the pure case.

4. The weak reading is blocked by the same test. The objector offers "recognising and tracking the norm as a norm" as the fallback, and says a chatbot that models truth-violation as a violation might meet it. Modelling a violation as a feature that is penalised is just the instrumental case. What marks the norm as a norm is that it figures as a reason against the system's objective. That is the decoupling test already supplied, so the distinction still separates the cases it was built for.

5. The genetic point is already answered. The origin of the motive in reward is no objection to its present non-instrumental operation (Williams, Allport, Kant).

6. The thesis claims only possibility. It says a system *can* be a full agent and still be unable to perform these acts. It needs only that a purely instrumental system is coherent, and that if one existed it would not assert in its own right. The objector's cases are all impure humans. Denying assertion to a being with no capacity at all to be answerable to truth is a bullet worth biting, since it is hard to say what that being's "assertion" would add to a prediction of what pays.

VERDICT

The defence holds against the proves-too-much charge, but its cost is higher than it looks.

What holds. The con artist, the liar and the insincere corporate apologiser do not refute the premise, because each has the standing capacity the premise requires. The objector's dilemma between an absurd occurrent reading and a collapsed weak reading fails, because the capacity reading is neither. It is also not a retreat. It is the reading the thesis's own phrase "background... not itself instrumental" already carries, once the background is placed in the speaker.

What does not hold, or is now exposed.
- The thesis text is ambiguous. It does not say whose background. The objector found the gap, and my earlier "proxy" gloss falls into it. The sketch should say that the capacity belongs to the speaker.
- The surviving claim is conditional. On the capacity reading, whether a given RLHF chatbot cannot assert depends on whether it has the capacity. That is an empirical question, and the decoupling test is not decisive from behaviour alone. The thesis can say that Butlin-style agency is insufficient. It cannot say that actual chatbots fail without further evidence about their internal structure. If someone shows that a trained system has internalised truth as a constraint that resists its reward, the thesis predicts that it can assert, and it should be accepted as doing so.
- The bullet for the pure instrumentalist is real. I think it is acceptable, but a critic can reasonably call it a cost.

Cumulative status. The earlier results stand: the debate-wide target and the claim to an unoccupied position are dead. This attack leaves the distinction, with a capacity-in-the-speaker reading and a reward-decoupling mark, intact. The surviving thesis is narrower than advertised, and its application to real chatbots is an open empirical matter. It has not accumulated qualifications to survive this attack. It has had one ambiguity resolved in the direction its own text points.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that performing a norm-constituted act requires responsiveness to the constitutive norm as such, so that a purely instrumental speaker cannot assert in their own right.

Counterexample: the primary psychopath testifying for pay. Take a witness or salesman with full command of the practice. He feels no shame, remorse or respect for truth. He tells the truth when it pays and lies when it pays, and when the payoff is reversed he reverses. He fails the thesis's decoupling test exactly as the liar-for-hire does, and he has no non-instrumental capacity of the kind the thesis requires. Yet his statements are assertions. He can be convicted of perjury, held to what he said, and his lies count as lies. Lying is possible only because he asserted.

The earlier defence says such speakers retain a "standing capacity": they "would feel exposed if caught" and "can be shamed". But that is sensitivity to sanction, which is instrumental. So the capacity either is instrumental, in which case a sanction-sensitive RLHF chatbot has it and the distinction no longer separates the cases, or it is non-instrumental, in which case the psychopath lacks it and the thesis gives the wrong verdict.

The thesis also has a fallback: "borrowing the practice's norms" makes him a proxy. That would make every instrumentalist a proxy, a result that is itself wrong.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The thesis can bite the bullet, but the cost is high, since the verdict contradicts ordinary and legal practice and the thesis's own concession that "humans do it instrumentally too".

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The psychopath's instrumentalism is about motivation to comply. The thesis's premise is about how the speaker relates to the norm in performing the act. The case shows that a speaker with no affective or valuing attachment to truth can still assert. The "as such" clause was never a requirement of caring. It can be read as a deontic-status requirement in Brandom's sense: the speaker undertakes a commitment and treats himself as answerable to challenge, retraction and justification. The psychopath does this. He chooses to assert rather than to predict or perform, he knows that exposure obliges him to retract or defend, and he cannot shrug off a challenge without changing his standing. His behaviour is indexed to the norm, not to a payoff that happens to correlate with it. So he is not "purely instrumental" in the sense the thesis needs. His motive for complying is instrumental, but his grasp of the norm is internal to the practice.

2. The empirical psychopath is not the pure case. Blair's work and Kennett's reply to Levy suggest that psychopaths grasp norms and can mark the moral/conventional distinction, though affect is impaired. Whatever a psychopath lacks, it is not the practical grasp of what he is committing himself to. The thesis's pure case is a system with no norm-indexed deliberation at all, and the psychopath is not that.

3. The dilemma about sanction-sensitivity has a way out. The objector says "would feel exposed if caught" is sanction-sensitivity and so instrumental. But being caught lying is a different event from being caught with an unrewarded output. The concern is individuated by the norm. A reward-trained system is sensitive to the approval signal, and the norm enters only as a correlate of that signal. So the capacity is instrumental in motive and norm-indexed in content, and the chatbot lacks the second feature.

4. The thesis claims only possibility. If a purely instrumental, non-norm-indexed system is coherent, the distinction stands. The psychopath is not that system.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The thesis, as a thesis about what speech acts require, is dead.

- Point 1 fails by the earlier defence's own commitments. In the last round the defender rejected the "recognising and tracking the norm as a norm" reading, because a system that models violation as a penalised feature is just the instrumental case. A norm-indexed deontic-status reading is that same weak reading under another name. Either the psychopath's deliberation is instrumental, in which case a sanction-sensitive chatbot can match it and the distinction stops separating the cases, or it requires something he lacks, in which case the thesis wrongly denies him assertion. The defence cannot have it both ways. Appealing to "undertaking a commitment" does not help, because what makes the psychopath committed is that the practice holds him to it. That is a fact about his standing, not about his motive.
- Point 2 does not matter. The counterexample needs only that a pure instrumentalist human is coherent, and he is. The thesis itself concedes that "humans do it instrumentally too." Denying that this speaker asserts in his own right is the bullet the previous round called acceptable. Here it is not, because it contradicts perjury, lying and ordinary accountability for what one says. "The practice's norms bind him whatever his motives" is the better explanation of all three.
- Point 3 reduces to the standing view. Once the defence says what makes his assertions his own, it points to sanctionability and answerability within the practice. That is Butlin and Viebahn's gate, which the thesis claimed to be only approximating the missing property. The psychopath is evidence that their criterion is right about this point and that the "as such" premise is wrong.
- Point 4 gives away the claim of interest. It protects the bare coherence of a purely instrumental system, but that was never the contested point. The thesis said such a system cannot perform these acts in its own right, and the psychopath case contradicts that.

What I will not do. I could shift the premise to "standing or accountability within the practice, with motives irrelevant." That would save a claim, but it would drop the "as such" premise that did the work, discard the instrumental versus norm-responsive distinction as a condition on speech acts, and adopt a rival's position under the thesis's name. That is hedging, not defence.

Cumulative status. The debate-wide target is dead, the claim to an unoccupied position is dead, and now the key premise is dead. What remains is a modest observation: Butlin's agency criterion is silent about whether outputs answer to non-instrumental norms. That is true but idle, because the psychopath shows non-instrumental norm-responsiveness is not what speech acts need. The thesis should be reported as refuted, with the distinction surviving as a true but irrelevant point about agency.

R17. The dispute over whether machines assert is a dispute about whether illocutionary acts are constituted on the hearer's side (uptake and functional role) or the speaker's side (accountable commitment), and LLMs matter only as the first case where these systematically come apart.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · dead
Move · Target
reframing — Arora's rejection of functionalism, and the whole functionalist–proxy axis as a debate about AI.
Sketch

Arora rejects 'functionalist' ascription because machine utterances resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions, and she replaces it with attribution to an accountable principal. Both sides treat this as a disagreement about machines. But the functionalist standard individuates illocutions by what the audience can do with the utterance, which is Austin's uptake. The proxy standard individuates them by who is on the hook, which is the commitment side. For humans the two are co-instantiated, so speech-act theory never had to say which one is constitutive. LLM output separates them: full uptake-conditions are met while no one has formed the commitment. The intermediate views (quasi-testimony, proto-assertion) are then best read as hedges between two constitutive theories, not as positions about machines. The key premise is that the human literature contains no argument for the priority of either side, only coincidence. The machine debate therefore cannot be settled by facts about machines, and positions on it should be predictable from prior commitments about the metaphysics of illocution.

Appraiser (blind)
Reading the machine debate as a proxy for hearer-side versus speaker-side constitution reframes what is at stake, and it is a sound metaphilosophical claim.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The uptake/communicative-function mismatch is loose, and the defender answered that the thesis is a structural reconstruction of a hearer-side standard, not a quotation of Arora's opponents.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, answered. The genus/species reply and the point that Arora's resemblance argument restates the functionalist's own criterion show the core reframing is not a tautology; the objector's own 'first case' and 'no priority argument' points still hit the distinctive claims.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. Redefining divergence as a mismatch of locus is a reformulation, not an answer. It moves the equivocation onto the hearer-side pole, and 'first case' still fails on signage, announcements and similar cases unless a degree threshold is added.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender's fixed classification criterion is what produces the dilemma. Applied rigidly, hybrid views (Butlin and Viebahn), intention views (Gubelmann) and norm views (Skiba) fall outside the dichotomy. Loosened, every position confirms the thesis.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 3/5, unanswered. The first-order versus second-order distinction and the Arora diagnosis are real replies. But the decomposition and the separation of components are already in print, and the defender's own points 2 and 5 contradict each other on whether the human literature argues for priority.
🔧 Survives as

Arora's resemblance-based rejection of functionalism begs the question against a hearer-side standard of illocutionary constitution, and the functionalist–proxy dispute presupposes some stance on whether uptake or accountability is constitutive. This is a local diagnosis of one argument and one dialectical structure. It does not claim that LLMs are the first such case, that no priority arguments exist, or that machine facts are irrelevant.

Flaw

The distinctive claims, that LLMs are the first case where uptake and commitment come apart, that the human literature has no priority argument, and that machine facts cannot settle the debate, are false or self-undermining, and the hearer/speaker dichotomy does not cover the positions actually held.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the functionalist side of the dispute individuates illocutions by hearer uptake, in Austin's sense, and that Arora and her opponents leave unexamined which side of the speech act is constitutive.

Arora's target is a functionalism on which machine utterances count as assertions because they "resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions". That is a thesis about when an utterance counts as an assertion, grounded in resemblance and role. It is not obviously Austinian uptake, which concerns the securing of the audience's understanding or response, not general functional similarity. The thesis may therefore be aimed at a position that no one holds in the form given.

The framing of the debate is also doubtful. Green and Michel build their proxy view explicitly from Austin, Strawson's synthesis with Grice, and Armstrong. They are already working with the question of which constituents of a speech act are essential. Butlin and Viebahn make assertion require both descriptive function and susceptibility to sanction, which is a hybrid of the two sides and not an instance of one. So the machine literature does not simply "treat this as a disagreement about machines".

I am working from memory of abstracts only. I have not verified what Arora actually says about uptake, so I cannot confirm that she lacks the ascribed view.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The thesis is a reframing and describes Arora's functionalist target in broad terms that fit her abstract. The mismatch between "communicative function" and "uptake" is real but loose, and the thesis can reply that it is rationally reconstructing the position, not quoting anyone. The objection to the "whole axis" claim is stronger, because Green and Michel and Butlin and Viebahn already engage the constitutive question. That is closer to a novelty problem than to misattribution.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objection reads "uptake" too narrowly. The thesis does not say Arora's opponents are Austinian in a strict sense. It says the functionalist standard locates the constitutive facts on the hearer's side: what the audience can do with the utterance (rely, challenge, accept as testimony, update on). That is a structural claim about where the standard looks, and "uptake and functional role" is how the thesis states it. Resemblance in communicative function is a hearer-side criterion. It asks what the utterance does for an audience, not who stands behind it. Whether the functionalist would use the word "uptake" is beside the point.

2. The hearer-side/speaker-side divide is already live in the human literature. Hornsby and Langton make uptake constitutive of certain illocutions, which is why silencing is possible. Bach and Harnish deny this and make only recognition of intention essential. Brandom and Alston make commitment or responsibility central. So the distinction the thesis uses is a recognised fault line, not one imported to fit the machine case.

3. Butlin and Viebahn support the thesis. A conjunctive view (assertion requires descriptive function and susceptibility to sanction) is a stance on the constitutive question. It says both sides are necessary. That is what you would expect once the two components come apart, which is what the thesis predicts. Hybrids are a third answer to the same question, not evidence that the question is absent.

4. Green and Michel's engagement with Austin and Strawson supports the thesis too. If they must reach into the human literature to decide which constituents are essential, the machine debate is being settled by importing a prior view of illocution. That is the thesis's prediction.

5. The novelty objection is not a misattribution. The thesis claims the debate is best understood as a dispute about the metaphysics of illocution. It does not claim nobody has noticed that.

VERDICT

The misattribution objection is mostly defeated. The "uptake" mismatch is loose, as the objector admits, and a rational reconstruction is not a misquotation. Points 1 to 3 hold. I cannot verify what Arora actually says, so this rests on the thesis being a reconstruction.

The defence does not save the whole thesis. Three of its claims fail on grounds the objector did not press, and I will not narrow the thesis to dodge them.

- "LLMs are the first case where these come apart" is false. They come apart in humans: ghostwriters, spokespeople, scripted actors, signatories of form letters, and the lie that is taken up but not meant. The proxy view is itself modelled on such cases. Speech-act theory has long had a clear stock of separations, so the premise that the two are co-instantiated is wrong.
- "The human literature contains no argument for priority" is overstated. Brandom, Alston, Williamson's knowledge rule, and Hornsby's uptake argument are attempts at exactly such arguments. The thesis would need to show they fail, not assert their absence.
- "Cannot be settled by facts about machines" is overstated. On a speaker-side view, whether a system can hold commitments or be sanctioned is a machine-fact. The thesis's own description of the LLM case ("no one has formed the commitment") already assumes such a fact.

What survives is the weaker observation that the debate presupposes a stance on the constitutive question. That is true but not new, and the thesis's distinctive claims (first case, no prior argument, not about machines) are the ones that fail. I report it as largely dead as stated: the reframing is correct only once it is reduced to something the literature already says.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the claim "the machine-assertion debate is a dispute over whether illocutions are constituted on the hearer's side or the speaker's side" is a discovery and not a restatement of what the literature already says.

Every party in the cited work already makes the dispute turn on what assertion requires. Butlin and Viebahn require descriptive function plus susceptibility to sanction. Skiba's argument is norm-based. Gubelmann requires intention. Green and Michel build on Austin, Strawson and Armstrong. Whether machines assert just is whether they meet the constitutive conditions, so saying the debate is "really" about those conditions is close to a tautology.

The hearer/speaker labels are relabelings of "functionalist" and "proxy/accountability", which Arora already supplies. They add vocabulary, not content.

"Positions are predictable from prior commitments about the metaphysics" holds of nearly any applied debate, such as animal pain or corporate agency. It is a platitude about applied philosophy, not a finding about this one.

The two substantive additions are weak. That LLMs are the first case where the sides come apart is false, since ghostwriters, spokespeople and scripted speech show the same split. And "no one has argued for priority" is overstated given Brandom, Alston and Hornsby.

What remains is a verbal stipulation with a rhetorical flourish.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The core reframing is close to platitudinous. But the claims that intermediate views are hedges and that machine facts cannot settle the matter are contestable, so the thesis is not wholly trivial.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. "Close to a tautology" confuses a genus with a species. Saying the machine debate turns on constitutive conditions for assertion is the genus, and it is indeed platitudinous. The thesis claims something narrower: that the live disagreement is located on a particular axis, hearer-side role versus speaker-side accountability. That is falsifiable. If the literature's main positions sorted instead by, say, what grounds semantic content, or whether assertion requires belief, the thesis would be wrong. A claim that could fail on the evidence is not a tautology.

2. The Butlin and Viebahn case confirms the axis. Their view is a conjunction: descriptive function (hearer-side role) plus susceptibility to sanction (speaker-side accountability). The thesis explains why such a hybrid is a natural move once the two components separate. A hybrid cannot be read as a position that dissolves the axis, because it is defined by reference to both poles.

3. The reframing has a non-platitudinous payoff against the target. Arora rejects functionalism because machine speech resembles human speech phenomenologically and serves the same functions. If the dispute is over which side is constitutive, that is not an argument against the functionalist but a restatement of the functionalist's own criterion. Resemblance in function is exactly what a hearer-side standard counts as sufficient, so pointing to it cannot refute that standard. The reframing therefore exposes a dialectical defect in a specific published argument. "Animal pain is really about behaviourist versus phenomenal criteria" carries no comparable diagnostic content, which is why the objector's platitude analogy fails.

4. The labels import resources. Calling the sides hearer-side and speaker-side connects the machine debate to arguments it has not obviously used, such as Langton's and Hornsby's silencing argument for uptake-constitution, and Brandom's and Alston's case for commitment-constitution. That is more than relabelling. It supplies test cases and arguments that could move the machine debate.

5. "First case" can be defended in a stronger form. Ghostwriters, spokespeople and scripted actors all have a human who adopted the content in advance or ratifies it afterwards, so commitment is present somewhere. The thesis's claim is about unreviewed, high-volume output where full uptake conditions hold and no one has formed the commitment to this content. Earlier text generators never earned full assertoric uptake.

VERDICT

The triviality objection is partly defeated, but the thesis does not survive.

Points 1 and 3 hold. The core claim is not a tautology, and it does yield a real criticism of Arora's inference. The objector overstates when they call it a stipulation. I have not read Arora, so point 3 depends on her argument being as the sketch reports.

The rest fails, and I will not rescue it by qualification.

- Point 5 fails on the proxy view's own terms. "No one has formed the commitment" is what the proxy theorist denies. On that view the deployer is accountable by assignment, so uptake and commitment are co-instantiated in the principal, as in the ghostwriter case. The thesis describes the LLM case in a way that assumes the contested point. To defend "first case" I would have to add a requirement of commitment-by-formation, which is itself a speaker-side thesis that the proxy theorist rejects. That is hedging, and it also shows the speaker side is not one position.
- The two-sided dichotomy is not exhaustive. Gubelmann's intention requirement is speaker-side but is not accountable commitment. Skiba's view is norm-based, and the norms may be neither on the hearer's side nor on the speaker's. A third and fourth position that fit neither pole make "a dispute about whether it is hearer-side or speaker-side" false as a description of the debate.
- "Predictable from prior commitments" is unsupported. Hybrid views like Butlin and Viebahn's are not predicted by a commitment to one pole. The thesis also gives no evidence that positions in fact track prior metaphysics.
- "Cannot be settled by facts about machines" fails. Whether a system can bear commitments or be sanctioned is a machine-fact on any speaker-side view, and the thesis's own description of the case relies on such a fact.
- The "no priority argument in the human literature" premise is overstated. Brandom, Alston, Hornsby and Williamson are priority arguments.

What survives is a diagnostic observation: Arora's resemblance argument begs the question against a hearer-side standard. That is a critique of one argument, not the thesis. The thesis as stated is dead.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "accountable commitment" (the speaker-side term) is held fixed across two claims the thesis needs: (a) in humans, uptake and commitment are co-instantiated, so speech-act theory never had to choose between them; and (b) LLMs are the first case where they systematically come apart.

On a thin reading, commitment is accountability, meaning someone is on the hook. (a) is then plausible: the speaker is both the target of uptake and the one answerable. But (b) fails on this reading. The proxy theorist says the deployer is on the hook, so uptake and commitment sit together in the principal, as with ghostwriters and spokespeople.

On a thick reading, commitment is formed by the speaker in producing this content. (b) is then interesting, since no one forms such a commitment to an unreviewed LLM output. But (a) fails on this reading. Ghostwriters, scripted actors and insincere assertions already separate uptake from thick commitment in humans. The human literature has therefore already confronted the split and has priority arguments (Brandom, Alston, Hornsby).

The thesis needs thin commitment to claim human coincidence and thick commitment to claim machine divergence. It cannot run on either reading alone. The "intermediate views are hedges" and "cannot be settled by machine facts" claims inherit the same slide.

STRENGTH: 3/5. This is a genuine problem for the "first case" and "no priority argument" claims. The thesis could answer by redefining "systematically" in terms of scale or unreviewed output. That would be a third reading, and it concedes that the split is one of degree.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. One reading of commitment does both jobs: thin accountability, indexed to a locus. The objector says thin commitment makes (b) fail, because the proxy theorist puts the deployer on the hook and so uptake and commitment sit together in the principal. That conflates two questions: whether someone is on the hook, and whether the party who receives uptake is the party on the hook.

In the human cases, these coincide. The audience takes up the politician's speech, and the politician owns it, even when the speech was ghostwritten. The audience takes up the spokesperson's statement as the institution's, and the institution answers for it. The party addressed as speaker and the party answerable are the same agent, which is what (a) needs.

In the LLM case, the audience challenges, thanks, corrects and relies on the system. The party answerable is elsewhere and is never addressed. So (b) is a divergence of locus, not an absence of accountability. The proxy theorist's reply, "the deployer is on the hook", concedes the divergence and then asserts that accountability somewhere suffices. That is exactly the speaker-side constitutive thesis. The thin reading therefore holds throughout, and the objector's own scenario shows the two sides separating.

2. The hedging charge does not apply. I am not adding a thick requirement of commitment-by-formation. I am reading "systematically come apart" as "the uptake-receiver and the accountable party are different agents". That is a structural property, not a degree of scale.

3. The slide does not infect the other claims. If the thesis consistently uses the thin locus reading, "intermediate views as hedges" can be restated. Quasi-testimony and proto-assertion award the system partial status as uptake-receiver while leaving accountability elsewhere. That is a hedge between locating the illocution at the addressee and locating it at the answerable party.

VERDICT

The defence answers the equivocation objection narrowly, but it does not save the thesis.

What it gets right is that the thin reading can be held fixed if the divergence is stated as a mismatch of locus, not of accountability. That is a real repair.

It fails for three reasons.

- The repair changes the hearer-side pole. The thesis defined that pole as what the audience can do with the utterance, meaning uptake and functional role. Locus is a different property: who the audience addresses as speaker. Functionalism, as Arora's target is described, is indifferent to locus. It counts any utterance that serves the same function. So the thesis now has "functional role" and "uptake-addressee" as its hearer-side pole, and these can come apart. Without an argument that they travel together, the equivocation has only moved from the commitment side to the uptake side.
- "First case" still fails on the locus reading. Locus divergence is common outside LLMs: "Bridge out" signs, automated station announcements, no-reply notices, GPS directions, phone trees. The audience relies on the output, acts on it, and sometimes addresses the source, while the answerable party is elsewhere. To exclude these, I must add a condition such as "full uptake including challenge and justification-giving". That is a threshold of degree, which is the concession the objector predicted.
- The earlier failures stand untouched. The dichotomy is not exhaustive (Gubelmann's intention, Skiba's norms). The prediction that positions track prior metaphysics is unsupported, and hybrid views like Butlin and Viebahn's cut against it. The claim that no priority argument exists in the human literature is false (Brandom, Alston, Hornsby, Williamson). And "cannot be settled by facts about machines" fails because speaker-side views make capacity for commitment and sanction a machine fact.

So the equivocation objection is largely answered, but the surviving core is again the diagnostic point that Arora's resemblance argument begs the question against a hearer-side standard. The distinctive claims (first case, no priority argument, not about machines, predictability) are dead. I report the thesis as dead rather than trimming it to that core.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the machine-assertion debate is exhaustively a dispute over hearer-side versus speaker-side constitution, so that positions are "predictable from prior commitments" about illocution. Every apparent counterexample is absorbed by a reclassification step.

- Butlin and Viebahn require both descriptive function and susceptibility to sanction. The thesis reads this as a hedge between the two poles.
- Quasi-testimony and proto-assertion are also hedges.
- Gubelmann requires intention. That gets filed as speaker-side.
- Skiba's norm-based view gets filed under whichever pole the norms attach to.
- The proxy view's claim that the deployer is accountable gets read as locus divergence, which counts as confirmation.
- Ghostwriters and spokespeople are said not to be the "first case", because what counts as "systematic" is stipulated to exclude them.
- Facts about machines, such as whether a system can be sanctioned, are said to be mere applications of a prior constitutive view.

So pole-one views, pole-two views, mixtures of the two, and third-axis views all confirm the thesis. Evidence about machines is declared irrelevant in advance. The defence's retreat to "locus of uptake-receiver versus answerable party" and its added threshold show the same move. When a case threatens, the definition of "hearer-side" or "systematic" is adjusted. The thesis names no possible literature position or empirical finding that would count against it, so its apparent content is only the choice of vocabulary.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The dichotomy plus "hedge" absorbs every position, and the "not settleable by machine facts" clause is immunised by design. The defender can reply that the thesis would fail if positions sorted along an unrelated axis. The "first case" claim was in fact falsified by ghostwriters, so the thesis is not fully immune. The problem is real but answerable, by committing to a rigid, non-hybrid classification of positions.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis is not unfalsifiable. It has already been falsified in parts. An unfalsifiable thesis could not be refuted by ghostwriters, by Brandom and Alston, or by the point that speaker-side views make sanctionability a machine-fact. The objector's own strength rating concedes this. Immunity by design would have blocked those refutations. So the question is whether the core classificatory claim is falsifiable, and I think it is.

2. The classification can be fixed in advance by a non-ad-hoc criterion. Sort each view's necessary-and-sufficient condition for machine assertion by what it quantifies over:
- Hearer-side: properties of the utterance's availability to an audience, such as what can be relied on, challenged, or updated on.
- Speaker-side: a relation between some agent and the content, such as accountability, intention, or liability.

This does not wait on how a case turns out. Gubelmann's intention requirement is a relation between an agent and content, so it is speaker-side by the criterion, not by convenience. Skiba's norms are classified by whether the norm's satisfaction is checkable from the audience's position or requires a bearer of the norm. A rule written before looking at the cases is the opposite of case-by-case reclassification.

3. Hybrids are not free confirmations. They make a determinate prediction. A conjunctive view like Butlin and Viebahn's must give a verdict on the divergence case: full functional role, no sanctionable party. A conjunction forces "no assertion" there. So in the one case that discriminates, it behaves as a speaker-side view. If a conjunctive theorist said "assertion" in the divergence case, or if a "hedge" view gave verdicts unrelated to which pole it weights, the hedge reading would fail. The test is verdicts on divergence cases, not labels.

4. Concrete falsifiers exist.
- A view that denies machine assertion for reasons independent of both poles, such as lacking world-directed content or lacking belief, and that gives the same verdicts when uptake and accountability are held fixed.
- Authors who change their verdict on machine assertion after an empirical discovery about architecture, while their view of illocution stays the same.
- A population of positions that sorts by some other variable than the constitutive side.

5. The "not settleable by machine facts" clause is not immunised. It is a conditional. Machine facts matter only given a constitutive view. A machine-fact that moved people across the axis would refute it, and one can specify what that would look like.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The objector's dilemma lands.

Points 1 and 4 hold up to a point. The thesis is not vacuous, and it does have refutable components. But that cuts against the thesis, because the refutable components are the ones that have been refuted.

The decisive problem is the rigid classification in point 2, which the objector's own reply invited.

- Rigid, the thesis is false. Once the criterion is fixed, Butlin and Viebahn's conjunction is not "a hedge between two constitutive theories". It is a third answer that makes both conditions necessary. Gubelmann's intention requirement is not accountable commitment, so "speaker-side" has to be widened from commitment to any agent-content relation. The thesis then no longer says what it said, since the sketch defines the speaker side as accountable commitment. Skiba's norm-based view sorts onto neither pole without a further stipulation. A dichotomy with that many stipulated edges is not the exhaustive axis the thesis claims.
- Flexible, it is unfalsifiable in the way the objector said. If "hedge" and "speaker-side" stretch to absorb these views, every position confirms the thesis.

Point 3's verdict-on-divergence test is the best thing in the defence. But it shows that hybrids behave like speaker-side views only on the divergence case. It does not show that the debate is about the axis, and it is compatible with their being motivated by quite different reasons. The prediction that positions track prior metaphysics of illocution is also left without evidence.

Point 5 fails for the reason already given: speaker-side views make capacity for commitment and sanction a machine-fact, so machine facts can settle at least part of the debate.

What survives is the diagnostic point that Arora's resemblance argument begs the question against a hearer-side standard. That is a criticism of one argument, not the thesis. I report the thesis as dead, because saving it needs either the rigid classification, which is false, or the flexible one, which is empty.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the sketch's central diagnosis is new: that the machine-assertion debate hides an unacknowledged choice between hearer-side constitution (uptake and functional role) and speaker-side constitution (accountable commitment), which the human literature never had to make.

Butlin and Viebahn (2025) already hold something very close to this. They split assertion into a functional condition (outputs with descriptive functions) and a social-accountability condition (capacity to be sanctioned). They show that fine-tuned models can meet the first and fail the second, which is the thesis's "uptake without commitment" separation. They then derive proxy assertion as the residual case. So the decomposition, the claim that LLMs pull the components apart, and the proxy view as the speaker-side fallback are all in print.

Williams and Bayne (2024) treat the machine case as a probe of assertion's constitutive structure. They read proxy-assertion and fictionalism as rival resolutions of that structural tension and answer with proto-assertion, which is the thesis's "intermediate views" claim.

Green and Michel (2022) explicitly ask which Austin/Strawson/Armstrong components are essential, and they say their view sharpens quasi-assertion.

On the human side, the uptake-constitutive view (Hornsby, Langton) against the commitment-constitutive view (Brandom, Alston) is the established fault line the thesis maps onto.

What remains is the meta-claim that no machine fact can settle the dispute. Speaker-side views make sanctionability and capacity for commitment machine facts, so that remainder is not a clean addition.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The decomposition and the "LLMs separate the components" observation are taken, chiefly by Butlin and Viebahn. The explicit "predictable from prior metaphysics" framing and the diagnosis of Arora's resemblance argument as question-begging are not obviously taken. The thesis needs to be cut down to those.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. Butlin and Viebahn's decomposition is a first-order theory. The thesis is a second-order claim about what the dispute is. Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires a functional condition plus sanctionability, and they show LLMs can meet the first and fail the second. That is a view about what assertion is. It does not say that the functionalist-versus-proxy debate is a proxy fight between rival constitutive theories of illocution, or that the intermediate positions are best read as hedges between them. A first-order author who announces a conjunctive analysis is a data point for the meta-claim, not an anticipation of it. If the conjunction were the settled answer, the axis would be closed. The thesis says the axis is open and the debate is being run on it without acknowledgement.

2. Their conjunction presupposes an answer to the question the thesis says is unasked. Making both conditions necessary is a decision that neither side alone is constitutive. The thesis's key premise is that the human literature gives no argument for that decision, only coincidence. Butlin and Viebahn state the conjunction without arguing for it against single-side views. That supports the thesis's claim that the machine debate imports an unargued stance.

3. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is offered as a position about machine outputs. The thesis reads it as a hedge. That reading is a reconstruction, as with the earlier uptake point. Whether the reconstruction is accurate is a separate question from whether anyone has already said it. Nothing in the sketch of their view says they diagnose the proto-assertion move as a hedge between uptake-constitution and commitment-constitution.

4. The Arora diagnosis is not taken. The claim that her resemblance argument begs the question against a hearer-side standard, because phenomenological and functional resemblance is the hearer-side criterion, appears in none of the cited work. The objector concedes this. A reframing whose payoff is a determinate criticism of a published argument has content beyond the vocabulary.

5. Hornsby and Langton against Brandom and Alston is the resource the thesis imports, not the thing it duplicates. The objector says this fault line is established in the human literature. Granted. The novelty lies in connecting it to the machine debate, where it has apparently not been used to classify the positions.

VERDICT

The defence holds only for a narrow remainder. The thesis as stated does not survive.

Points 1 and 4 are sound. A decomposition is not a diagnosis of the debate, and Butlin and Viebahn do not say the dispute is about the metaphysics of illocution. The Arora point is not in the cited literature, as far as I know. I am working from abstracts and cannot confirm what the papers say about their own aims.

The rest fails.

- Point 2 undercuts the thesis. It relies on the premise that the human literature has no argument for priority. Point 5 then invokes Hornsby, Langton, Brandom and Alston as established positions, which is exactly the priority literature the premise denies. I cannot hold both. If those are constitutive-priority views, the thesis's key premise is false. If they are not, point 5 loses its force.
- Point 3 is only a stalemate. Reading proto-assertion as a hedge is the thesis's own reclassification, and the earlier unfalsifiability exchange showed that this move either stipulates or absorbs. It cannot establish that the thesis is original.
- The defensible novelty is too thin. What remains is the Arora diagnosis plus the observation that her opponents share a hearer-side criterion. That is a criticism of one argument. The claims that were supposed to carry the thesis are either taken or false. The decomposition and the separation of components are in print, and "LLMs are the first case" is refuted by ghostwriters, spokespeople and signage. "Cannot be settled by facts about machines" fails because speaker-side views make sanctionability a machine-fact. The prediction that positions track prior commitments has no support, and hybrid views cut against it.

Restricting the thesis to the Arora diagnosis would be the kind of shrinking I should not do. I report the thesis as dead as stated, with one reusable observation: resemblance in function cannot refute a standard that counts functional resemblance as sufficient.

R18. The assertion debate is individuated at the wrong grain. Speech acts are token acts, but a chatbot's reply is a draw from a policy. The live question is whether assertion can attach to the policy (what the model reliably would say) rather than to the sampled token, and on that question the cases for denial and for proto-assertion come apart from where they are now placed.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
reframing — Williams and Bayne's token-level application of proto-assertion, and the shared assumption that the unit of speech-act evaluation is the individual output.
Sketch

Williams and Bayne ask whether particular outputs are assertions or proto-assertions, and the denial literature (Butlin and Viebahn on descriptive function, Gubelmann on malfunction versus deliberate error) likewise evaluates individual responses. But each response is one sample from a distribution, and the regenerate button shows the speaker 'would have said' otherwise at the same state. Assertion involves commitment to a content, and one sample commits to nothing, since the same prompt yields contradictory outputs. A model's dispositional profile (high-probability answers across resamples, calibrated confidence) is the closest analogue of a commitment. The key premise is that the commitment-bearing unit for an LLM is the policy or distribution and not the token. Two consequences follow. First, many chatbot outputs fail to be assertions not because the model lacks intentions or sanctionability but because the individuating unit is wrong, which is a different diagnosis from any in the literature. Second, outputs where the policy is sharply peaked (stable facts) can qualify as assertions with respect to the policy while low-entropy-failing outputs (confabulations) are mere samples. This shows that a genuine 'edge of assertion' runs through the same system and not between system types.

Appraiser (blind)
Moving the commitment-bearing unit from the sampled token to the policy is a novel change of grain that regroups the denial and proto-assertion cases.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender separated gating (system-level, which Butlin and Viebahn do address) from individuation (which they leave at the output), and pointed out that the second consequence is untouched. The objector had already rated the point 2/5.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The defender found a bearer (sanction acts on the policy) but then conceded that policy facts only fix a token's status and do not make the policy the act. The entropy line was also conceded to track warrant, not assertoric force.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defender rebutted the literal charge with an operational resampling criterion and a consistent verdict on stable falsehoods. It then conceded that the proposed discriminating observations fit the token-plus-evidence rival equally well, so the thesis does not differ observationally from the weaker view.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 2/5, answered. The defender distinguished Shanahan (deflationary use), the proxy and fictionalist views (a different bearer), and Herrmann and Levinstein (belief, not speech acts). The objector conceded the application to assertion is unclaimed. The defender then called the surviving novelty moot, which is a separate matter.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. Deletability of the token is a real disanalogy with human speech. But the defender conceded that it makes the token's status depend on the practice and the interface, which is a token-level view with a deployment condition, and that the unstable-witness and guess replies help the objector.
🔧 Survives as

For deployed chatbots with revisable tokens, whether an output is an assertion or a proto-assertion depends on the stability of the underlying policy and on how the interface treats the token. Resampling is therefore a neglected evidential constraint on token-level classification.

Flaw

The central premise that the policy is the commitment-bearing unit collapses into the weaker claim that token acts have assertoric status depending on policy facts, which the existing debate can accept without changing its unit.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Williams and Bayne, along with the denial literature, share an output-level assumption about the unit of evaluation. I think that assumption is read into them rather than held by them.

- Butlin and Viebahn. Going by the description given, both of their conditions are properties of a system or model type. A pre-trained model "fails the first condition", and a fine-tuned one "may meet" it. Descriptive function is a matter of how training shaped the system's dispositions, and sanctionability is a capacity of the system across interactions. Neither concerns whether a given sampled string has a descriptive function. That is already policy-level evaluation.
- Gubelmann. His test asks whether one can distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing. That is a question about the system's goal-structure, not about one token.
- Williams and Bayne. Their proto-assertion category is introduced for a kind of system or capacity, in light of "how assertion emerges". It may not be token-bound. I recall nothing on whether they discuss resampling, so I can't confirm either way.

The thesis may therefply attack a straw "output-by-output" view, when the real disagreement is about which system-level properties matter. On that reading the "wrong grain" diagnosis is not new.

STRENGTH: 2/5. Williams and Bayne's stated thesis is that "some of their current outputs are assertions", which is token-flavoured language. So the output-level attribution is partly fair. At most the thesis overstates how uniform that assumption is, and a rewording would fix it. I am working from the summaries and from memory of the papers, and I cannot verify more than that.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs together two questions that the thesis keeps apart.
