Either way the verdict is bivalent, and the defects come in degrees of quality, not degrees of being an apology. The toddler case is a capacity sorites: the child acquires standing to bind herself gradually, but at each time a token either generates the debt, perhaps through parental scaffolding, or it is mimicry. Vagueness at the boundary of a capacity is common to every predicate. It is not the structured intermediate category that proto-assertion claims to be.

2. Expressions of regret and intent are not substrates of the relevant kind. The thesis's test is not just "some neighbouring behaviour exists." It is that the norms are layered on a behaviour and tighten a standard already operative in it. Signals can already be accurate, reliable and trusted, and assertion makes that dimension more stringent. An expression of intent is a different act with a different norm, sincerity or predictive accuracy. A promise does not strengthen that norm. It adds a directed obligation that the promisee can claim. Nothing is a half-strength claim-right in the way a signal is a half-strength assertion. "I intend," "I'll try" and "I plan" are different acts with determinate strengths, and none is a promise in the process of becoming one. So the substrate criterion does not make every act gradable, and it is not gerrymandered. The line falls between continuous tightening and categorical addition.

3. The practice-level emergence of promising can be granted. Promising may well have evolved from commitment signals. The thesis concerns tokens in an existing practice, and the chatbot question is a token question: is this "I promise" a promise? That is where bivalence applies. So the token reply does not make the thesis irrelevant. It identifies the level at which the chatbot debate operates.

4. Searle's labels need not be defended. Searle defines regulative rules as those that regulate antecedently existing behaviour, which is the thesis's own gloss. If Williamson-style "constitutive" rules for assertion make assertion constitutive in a different sense, a sense of essence and not of creation, then the thesis should be read as using Searle's definition of "regulative." The substrate test does the work.

VERDICT

The defence holds on the human cases and fails on the criterion. The thesis does not survive as stated.

What holds:
- Points 1 and 3 hold. Infelicity is not intermediacy, capacity vagueness is not an intermediate act, and the token level is the right level for the chatbot question. The "proves too much" attack is weaker than it first looks.

What fails:
- The continuous-tightening versus categorical-addition line in point 2 does not separate assertion from promising. Butlin and Viebahn make assertion depend on sanctionability, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is an informing practice without full assertoric norms. The assertoric norms that get added are hearers' entitlement to rely on the speaker and to hold her responsible. That is a directed normative relation, categorically new on top of signal reliability, just as the promisee's claim is new on top of expressed intent. If "regret expressed, moral work removed" is not incipient apology, then "signal, sanctionability removed" is not incipient assertion on the same reasoning. The thesis needs an asymmetry here and has only an intuition. That intuition is about how we individuate neighbouring acts, not about the structure of the norms.
- The dilemma stands. If neighbouring behaviours such as intent expressions and regret displays count as substrates, they sit exactly where signals sit for assertion, and the contrast collapses. If they are excluded, the exclusion tracks the desired verdict and does not explain it.
- Searle's classification cannot be set aside. Searle and Williamson place assertion on the constitutive side. If assertion is constitutive, proto-assertion is just informing, a different act. Then "intermediate between assertion and non-assertion" is empty for assertion as well. The bivalent shape would return everywhere, and the thesis's central contrast would disappear. Reading "regulative" as Searle's antecedent-behaviour definition does not avoid this. It only restates the substrate test, and the substrate test has just failed.
- The token reply costs the thesis its stated target. Once bivalence is a claim about tokens, it bears on proto-assertion only if proto-assertion is a status of tokens. If it is a status of practices, the thesis does not engage it.

A weaker claim remains: Skiba's generalisation from assertion to other speech acts needs act-by-act argument. That claim does not depend on the substrate principle, so it is a different, much smaller thesis and not a rescue of this one. The regulative/constitutive criterion for the availability of intermediate status is not stably statable, and I report it as dead.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that promising and apologising have no pre-existing substrate, so the question "is this a promise or an apology?" is bivalent, and "nothing counts as incipient apology."

Counterexample 1, apology. Primate reconciliation behaviour (de Waal's post-conflict appeasement, consolation and submission displays) is a recognisable, independently existing practice. It repairs relationships and signals non-hostility, and it does so without moral responsibility-taking. Human apology plausibly grew out of it. A chatbot that reliably produces de-escalating, relationship-repairing contrition displays, and is trained on whether users' hostility subsides, does the substrate's job. By the thesis's own test, it is a proto-apology: the norms of responsibility-taking would be layered on a behaviour that already exists. The thesis predicts "bivalent, so bullshit or apology," and that is the wrong result.

Counterexample 2, promising. A scheduling agent says "I'll remind you at 5" and reliably does. Its commitment-announcing behaviour induces reliance and can fail or succeed, and it exists before any directed obligation. It sits in the same relation to promising that a signal sits in to assertion.

The thesis can say these are different acts (reconciliation, announcing intent). But that move is equally available against signal-as-proto-assertion, so the substrate criterion is not doing independent work.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The counterexamples are concrete and the symmetry point bites, but the thesis can answer by individuating acts more finely, at some cost to its criterion.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The counterexamples fail if the substrate has to be a behaviour whose success standard the fuller act's norms tighten. Mere neighbourhood is not enough.

1. Reconciliation displays. Appeasement and consolation succeed when the relationship is repaired, whether or not anyone takes responsibility. An apology is answerable to a different standard: acknowledging the wrong, owning it, and being fit to be forgiven or refused. A de-escalating contrition display that works by soothing is not a deficient apology, any more than a purr is a deficient promise. It is a different act that happens to share an effect. A signal, by contrast, is already assessable for accuracy, and assertoric norms raise the stringency of that same dimension. The asymmetry is that the substrate and the full act share a success dimension in one case and not in the other.

2. Phylogeny versus tokens. The counterexample uses the evolutionary origin of apology to support a claim about a chatbot token. The earlier exchange fixed the thesis at the token level, where the question is whether this "sorry" takes responsibility. Reconciliation is not a status that token occupies on the way to apology.

3. The scheduling agent. "I'll remind you at 5" is a prediction or announcement of intent. It is assessed for reliability, and it has no directed claim-right attached. The agent has a determinate act with a determinate strength, not a promise in the making.

4. Individuation is not ad hoc. Individuating acts by their success standard is the ordinary way to tell acts apart. It is not a patch designed for this case.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold, and the thesis is dead.

- Point 1 depends on the success-dimension asymmetry, and that asymmetry has no independent support. Apology's point is arguably repair. Much of the apology literature treats it as restoring standing and relationship, and reconciliation displays do that work. Assertoric norms are not merely a tightening of accuracy. As the previous round showed, what is added is a directed relation of entitlement to rely on the speaker and to hold her responsible. That is categorically new in the same way a promisee's claim is. Either the shared-dimension test lets reconciliation count as an apology substrate, or it excludes signals as assertion substrates. The criterion only gives the desired verdict if I pick the description of the dimension that yields it.

- Point 3 repeats the symmetry problem. "Reliable reminder" sits to promising as "reliable signal" sits to assertion. If a different success standard makes the agent's announcement a different act, then signalling is a different act from asserting too. I would be using the objector's own move on myself and calling it a distinction.

- Point 2 does not rescue the thesis. The thesis needs proto-assertion to be a token-level intermediate status. If Williams and Bayne's category is token-level and functional, the same functional reading is available for reconciliation-style proto-apology. If it is a status of practices, the thesis does not engage it. The earlier token retreat already cost the thesis its target.

- Individuating more finely is the only available escape, and it is hedging. I could carve act-types until the verdict comes out right. That would leave a criterion that fits the cases it was built for and explains nothing. It would also be the unstable classification the previous round reported, plus a fresh qualification. I decline to do that.

The counterexamples therefore establish more than a local failure. The claim that proto-assertion has no analogue for most acts is false as stated, because there are credible candidates for proto-apology and proto-promising. The substrate principle, that gradability tracks whether the norms attach to an independently existing behaviour, is also not stably statable. With the Searle/Williamson problem and the token/practice problem still open, the thesis is dead as a classification of speech acts.

What remains is the small point already identified: Skiba's extension from assertion to other acts needs act-by-act argument. That is a different, much weaker claim, and it does not rest on any regulative/constitutive sorting.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that "gradability of performance tracks whether the act's norms attach to a behaviour that can exist independently of them."

Read one way, this is a stipulation. "Constitutive" is defined as the norm that makes the act what it is. It follows that nothing counts as a half-promise, and that the status is either generated or not. That is Searle's 1969 point about promising, restated. "Proto-X" is likewise defined as X-minus-norms sitting on a substrate. So "proto-assertion has no analogue for acts with no substrate" is true by the definition of both terms. Nobody in the supplied literature disputes it. Green and Michel already doubt that their strategy covers every act type. Magnus et al. already give a bivalent verdict on apology. Skiba already faces a challenge to his generalisation. The remaining point, that each act type needs its own argument, is a methodological platitude.

The thesis avoids triviality only by giving "substrate" substantive content, for example "same success dimension tightened". Then it is no longer a stipulation, but it is contestable, as the counterexamples (reconciliation displays, reliable "I'll remind you" announcements) show. It is also tuned to the verdict it was meant to explain. So it is either a definitional truism or an unstable criterion.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The trivial reading is a real fork, and the exchange so far suggests the substantive reading fails. But the thesis can answer that the explanatory unification is new, even if each component is old.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The fork treats two different claims as one. The analytic claim is that nothing is a half-constitutive act. The thesis's claim is that promising and apologising are constitutive in the substrate-lacking sense, while assertion is not. That sorting is not a definition. Searle himself classes assertion as constitutively governed, and the thesis puts it on the other side. A claim that reverses the standard classification of a paradigm case is not true by stipulation.

1. The first horn needs the classification to be uncontroversial, but the second horn needs it contested. "True by definition" is plausible only if it is obvious which acts have a substrate. The objector's own second horn, with the reconciliation and reminder counterexamples, shows it is not obvious. A claim cannot be both analytic and live to counterexample. If the counterexamples are real, the thesis is not a truism. If the thesis is a truism, the counterexamples are irrelevant. The objector is entitled to the dilemma only by switching readings between horns.

2. Searle does not deliver the thesis. He says what constitutive rules are and treats promising as one. He says nothing about intermediate statuses, emergence, or whether a verdict transfers across act types. The step from "constitutive" to "no intermediate status" runs through the substrate principle. That principle is exactly what the supplied literature lacks, as an earlier round conceded.

3. "Methodological platitude" is refuted by the target. Skiba extends his verdict beyond assertion, and Williams and Bayne's intermediate category was built for one act. If act-by-act argument were obvious, the extension would not be the live move it is. A point can be obvious once stated and still be missing from the debate.

4. The unification is a contribution. Scattered verdicts (Magnus et al. on apology, Green and Michel's doubts, the proto-assertion proposal) get a single explanation of why they come apart. Unifying scattered results under one principle is what a distinction move does. It does not need to be surprising.

VERDICT

The defence holds against the first horn and fails against the second. That is not enough, because the thesis needs the second horn to be false.

What holds: the thesis is not a stipulation. The sorting of assertion against promising and apologising is a substantive claim, and it cuts against Searle's own labels. Triviality, as an objection, fails.

What fails: the thesis therefore has to stand as the substantive criterion, and the earlier rounds showed it does not stand as such.
- Point 4 depends on there being a principled "same success dimension tightened" test. The earlier rounds showed that test cannot separate assertion from promising without describing the dimension in the way that yields the verdict. Assertoric norms add a directed claim to rely on the speaker, which is categorically new in the same way a promisee's claim is.
- If a different success standard makes "I'll remind you" a different act from promising, then signalling is a different act from asserting. If not, the reminder is a proto-promise and the contrast collapses.
- Point 2 shows the thesis is not Searle's. It does not show that the substrate principle is true.
- The token/practice problem is still open. If bivalence holds only for tokens, it does not touch proto-assertion as a status of practices. If proto-assertion is a token status, the same functional reading gives proto-apology.

So I defeat the triviality charge and still concede the thesis. The objector is right that the thesis is either a truism or an unstable criterion. They are wrong that it is the truism, and that is the less damaging half, because the unstable criterion is already dead on the merits. I will not rescue it by individuating acts more finely, since that is the hedging the earlier rounds declined.

What survives is only what survived before: Skiba's extension from assertion to other acts needs separate argument for each act type. That is modest, and it does not rest on any regulative/constitutive sorting.

R21. The proxy view implies that the same token output can be one speech act, by a different speaker and with a different force, depending on facts about system prompts, fine-tuning and who deployed it that the hearer cannot access, and so it violates the uptake or publicity condition that makes something a speech act in the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition on which Arora builds.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
commitment — Arora's refined proxy assertion and its Gricean/Strawsonian inheritance from Green and Michel.
Sketch

Arora and Green–Michel extend the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition to proxies. In that tradition an illocutionary act is a public act whose success requires that the hearer can recognise who is speaking and what they are doing (uptake, or Grice's reflexive intention). In current deployments the principal is unfixed by the output. The same text can come from a company's default assistant, from a third party's custom deployment built on the same model, from a user's own self-prompt ('write my apology letter'), or from an API pipeline in which the output is never shown to a human in the loop. In each case the proxy theory names a different principal and a different force (assertion, drafting, quoting). The hearer typically has no access to which of these holds, and often the first-order conversational uptake treats the model as speaker anyway. The proxy theorist then has two options. One is to say that speech-act identity is fixed by hidden facts, which gives up the publicity that motivated the Austin–Grice framework. The other is to impose a transparency requirement on deployments, which means almost no current outputs are proxy assertions. The key premise is that illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not drop out for delegated acts. A human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack.

Appraiser (blind)
The publicity and uptake objection to proxy speech acts, from hidden deployment facts, is well motivated by the Austin–Grice tradition and is not made in the literature listed.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defender answered that this is a commitment claim, so Arora's explicit citations don't matter, and that Green and Michel carry the tradition's inheritance; it later said the 2/5 was about right.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity show the strong recognisability premise is false. The defender narrowed it to 'act-type and force recoverable through public convention', then conceded this is a different, weaker claim.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. The defender showed the 'Jane, Support' case is one public act fixed by letterhead convention, with only backstage provenance varying. But this showed convention, not hidden facts, fixes identity, so the proxy view alone doesn't entail a violation.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 3/5, answered. The defender argued that live uptake conventions treat the model as speaker, so displacing them is a substantive burden and 'almost no current outputs are proxy assertions' is not trivial. But it conceded that only a residue, not the stated 'violation' thesis, survives.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. The defender offered Reading C (recognised speaker and force must match the theory's) and showed the argument doesn't need B. But it conceded that mismatch is not violation, which leaves the premise unsupported as a constraint.
🔧 Survives as

Given the Austin–Grice emphasis on publicly recognisable force and answerable agent, proxy assertion needs a public delegation convention. Current LLM practice instead fixes the model as speaker, and the proxy theorist has not shown that any workable convention could mark principal and force for generative output. So proxy assertion is not presently the right description of most outputs.

Flaw

The thesis claims a 'violation' of uptake or publicity, but a mismatch between hearer attribution and the theory's attribution is not a violation. The tradition does not require hearers to identify the speaker, and conventions could close the gap.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that Arora "builds on" the Austin–Strawson–Grice uptake framework, so that a hearer-recognisability constraint binds the proxy view.

1. From what I recall, Arora's paper argues from agency and assertion against functionalist and phenomenological grounds for machine assertion, and then refines existing proxy accounts. I do not recall it adopting a Gricean uptake condition. The "tradition on which Arora builds" may be the thesis's own construction.
2. Green and Michel do work in the Austin–Strawson–Grice line, but they use Armstrong's objectives in place of Gricean intentions. They also make the proxy relation fairly fixed: artificial speakers act on behalf of their creators, with recorded and conditional speech acts as models. They do not, as far as I recall, make force vary with the deployer, the prompt or the self-prompting user. The thesis's "different principal and different force" for the same token may therefore be a view nobody holds.
3. Grice's reflexive intention concerns the speaker's intention that the hearer recognise the intention. It does not require the hearer to be able to identify the speaker. Austin's uptake is also contested as a condition on illocutionary success.

I am working from memory of Arora and cannot check these points.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The thesis is framed as a commitment (what the proxy view implies) and not as a report of anyone's explicit view. Green and Michel plainly belong to the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition. Arora's inheritance is uncertain, and that uncertainty is the only real vulnerability.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The thesis is a commitment claim, so what Arora explicitly adopts is beside the point.
The thesis says what the proxy view implies, not what Arora says. If proxy assertion is a theory of speech acts, performed by one party on behalf of another, it inherits the constraints on what a speech act is, whether or not the author cites them. "Builds on" can be read as a dependency claim: a theory that calls its explanandum assertion, force and speaker takes on the framework that gives those terms content. The objector's own recollection that Arora argues from agency and assertion against functionalist and phenomenological grounds supports this. Arguing about whether something can assert already moves within the speech-act tradition, whose publicity conditions then apply.

2. Green and Michel carry the inheritance even if Arora does not.
The target is the refined proxy account *and its inheritance from Green and Michel*. The objector concedes that they belong to the Austin–Strawson–Grice line. Swapping Armstrong's objectives for Gricean intentions leaves publicity intact. Armstrong's account is still a recognition-based, audience-directed theory of communicative intention, so the swap does not remove the hearer-side constraint.

3. The objector's point about Grice does not touch the real issue.
Reflexive intention does not demand that the hearer *identify the speaker*. But recognising an intention means attributing it to some agent. If the hearer attributes it to the model while the proxy theory says the user or deployer is speaking, then what is recognised (the speaker's intention) and what the theory says was performed come apart. On Austin's side, felicity condition A.2 requires "appropriate persons and circumstances" for a conventional procedure. Proxy acts such as signing for another or acting under power of attorney are conventional because the delegation convention is public. LLM deployment has no comparable convention.

4. Variable force is not something nobody holds.
Green and Michel may fix the principal as the creator. But the thesis does not need them to vary force. It only needs the proxy structure to say that force follows whoever the proxy acts for, and deployment facts do vary who that is. If the account fixes the creator as principal, it gets the wrong answer for the self-prompted apology letter and the third-party deployment. The variation then counts against the view, which is a cost to the proxy theorist and not a misreading of them.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The thesis fails, though not for the objector's reason.

On the objector's point, the defence partly works. A commitment claim is not refuted by showing that the author never endorsed the premise. If the proxy view really does inherit a publicity condition, the thesis stands without Arora citing Grice. The objector's 2/5 is about right for the misattribution point itself.

But the defence shows where the thesis is actually weak. Everything rests on the key premise, that illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise. In its strong form this is false, and the tradition does not support it:

- Ghostwriting, speechwriting and form letters. A hearer who takes a politician to be speaking in their own voice does not know who drafted the text. Hidden facts fix who is committed, yet the politician's assertion is successful and public in the relevant sense.
- Lying and insincerity. Hearers are routinely wrong about the speaker's real state and the act's sincerity. Hidden facts do not stop the act from being an assertion.
- Anonymous and pseudonymous speech. Assertion does not require identifying the speaker to the hearer.
- Austin's uptake is contested as a condition on success, and Grice's account never requires the speaker's identity to be public.

The strongest version of the premise says that the *type* of act and the *locus of accountability* must be recoverable in principle, through a public convention. That is a weaker and different claim, and it is not what the thesis says. It is also no longer a violation of "uptake". It is the point that accountability norms need a determinate answerable party. Restating the thesis that way would be hedging. It would trade a decisive "violates the uptake condition" for a conditional complaint about accountability, and that complaint might be answered by default-principal rules or deployer-liability conventions.

The thesis as stated claims a violation of a constraint that the tradition does not impose in the required form. I would report it as dead in its current form, not rescue it by narrowing to a transparency demand. The surviving insight, that deployment opacity makes principal attribution unstable, is a separate and weaker objection, and it would need a separate argument.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: that illocutionary identity (who speaks, with what force) is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not lapse for delegated acts.

If the premise worked, it would show too much.

- Ghostwriting and speechwriting. A hearer who takes a politician to speak in her own voice cannot tell who drafted the text or whether she is reading a script. Hidden facts fix who is committed, yet the assertion is plainly an assertion.
- Spokespeople and form letters. A hearer often cannot tell whether a signed statement is personal, institutional or boilerplate. The same token can be a personal assertion, a company's assertion or a quotation. By the thesis's reasoning, none of these would be speech acts.
- Anonymous or pseudonymous speech, and insincere speech. Hearers are routinely wrong about who is speaking or what they intend.
- Green and Michel's own recorded and conditional speech acts. An answering-machine message or a timed notice has hidden provenance, so these would fail too.

Austin's uptake is contested as a success condition, and Grice never requires the hearer to identify the speaker. So the principle that rules out proxy assertion would also rule out ordinary human proxy speech and much non-proxy speech. The thesis would have to retreat to a weaker accountability principle: a public convention fixes a determinate answerable party. That is a different thesis, one that default-principal rules or deployer-liability norms might satisfy.

STRENGTH: 4/5. The strong premise as stated is false. The thesis survives only by narrowing to a separate accountability claim, which would need its own argument.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objector's cases do not share the thesis's structure. The thesis does not say that any hidden fact defeats a speech act. It says that on the proxy view, hidden facts fix the force and the speaker of the act, so the same token is different acts depending on them. The objector's cases differ in a way that matters.

- Ghostwriting and speechwriting. The hidden fact (who drafted the text) does not change who speaks or with what force. The politician asserts, and the hearer takes her to assert. Hearer and theory agree, and only the provenance of the wording is hidden.
- Lying and insincerity. Sincerity is not constitutive of force. The hearer correctly recognises the act as an assertion and is wrong only about the speaker's state.
- Anonymous speech. The hearer recognises that someone is asserting. Austin and Grice need the type of act to be recognisable, not the speaker's name.
- Spokespeople and form letters. Letterheads, titles and role conventions publicly mark the delegation. Green and Michel's recordings and timed notices work because the convention of recording or scheduling is publicly understood.

So the principle behind the thesis is narrower than the objector says: act-type and force must be recoverable through public convention. Reflexive intention is aimed at recognition of force, so this is the Gricean core and not a tendentious addition. Every objector case satisfies it. LLM output does not, because the same string can be an assertion by the company, a draft for the user, or a quotation, with no public marker.

2. The call-centre analogue does not rescue the proxy view. Hearers often do not know whether an agent is reading a script. But the conventions of the role fix the act (the company speaks), and those conventions are public. That is the contrast the thesis draws: "a human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack."

3. The accountability reformulation is not a retreat. The objector says the thesis shrinks into a weaker accountability claim. But "type and force recoverable by convention" is what the uptake or publicity condition amounts to once the strong, identify-the-speaker reading is set aside. Calling it a different thesis assumes a reading the thesis never needed.

VERDICT

The defence does not hold. I concede.

The asymmetry in point 1 is real. Hidden provenance differs from hidden force, and that is the best the defence can do. But it fails for four reasons.

1. It is the hedge, not a resistance. The thesis says the proxy view "violates the uptake or publicity condition." The defence delivers a different principle: force must be recoverable in principle by public convention. That condition does not forbid hidden facts fixing the act. It forbids only that no convention exists. So the thesis's decisive claim of violation becomes a contingent claim about the current state of interface conventions. A thesis that survives only in that form is dead.

2. The weakened principle is probably satisfied or satisfiable. Hearers already operate with a convention of "AI assistant from company X." Default-principal rules (the deployer is the principal unless marked otherwise) would supply exactly the public convention the defence demands, and the call-centre analogy shows such rules suffice for humans. The defence's own standard thus makes the objection fixable by adding conventions, not a refutation of the proxy view.

3. The self-prompt case cuts against the thesis. A user who prompts "write my apology letter" and signs the result has hearer and theory in agreement: the hearer takes the user to be speaking, and the proxy theory says the user is. There is no divergence of the kind the thesis needs. Divergence appears only in third-party and default deployments, and there it is an empirical question what hearers recognise.

4. The premise does not stand in strong form. Uptake is contested as a success condition, and Grice does not require hearers to identify who is speaking. The only forms of the premise that survive are the weak ones that default conventions can meet.

What is left is not this thesis. It is a narrower complaint that current deployments lack conventions marking principal and force, so proxy assertion is not yet the right description of most outputs. That might be true, but it is a different claim, it needs its own argument, and it is answerable by deployer-liability conventions. I report the thesis as dead and do not shrink it into that.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that illocutionary identity (speaker and force) must be recoverable by the hearer, so that hidden facts fixing it count as a violation of uptake.

Concrete case: a customer receives an email reading "I'm sorry for the delay, we will refund you", signed "Jane, Support".

- Case 1. Jane wrote it herself, so it is her personal apology.
- Case 2. It is a canned template that Jane sends, so it is the company's act.
- Case 3. An automated mail-merge sent it and Jane never saw it.
- Case 4. A manager drafted it and Jane signed it as a favour.

The token is identical. On any account of delegated speech, the speaker, force and commitments differ across these cases. In Case 1 Jane is committed. In Case 2 the company is. In Case 3 it is unclear whether anyone asserts. The hearer cannot distinguish them. Yet nobody concludes that no speech act occurred, and the refund promise binds the company in every case.

So the thesis's test gives the wrong verdict on ordinary human delegated speech. It says hidden facts fixing speaker and force violate publicity, and these cases show they do not. Only recoverability of the type of act through public convention is needed, and "Support staff, company letterhead" supplies that.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The case is real, and it bites the premise as stated. The thesis can retreat to a "no public convention marks the delegation" claim, but that is contingent and answerable by disclosure norms.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The Jane case is a case of publicly fixed identity, not of hidden facts fixing it.
The objector says that across Cases 1–4 "the speaker, force and commitments differ." Their own datum says otherwise: "the refund promise binds the company in every case." On any conventional-act view in the Austin line, a signed message on company letterhead from "Jane, Support" is the company's promise whoever drafted it. The signature, role title and letterhead are public markers, and they fix the act. What varies across the four cases is backstage: who typed, who approved, whether anyone read it. That affects internal responsibility, not what illocutionary act the customer received.

2. The objector faces a dilemma.
- *Horn A:* The four cases are four different speech acts. Then ordinary human delegated speech does violate publicity, and the objector has an argument against the Austin–Grice framework, not against the thesis. The thesis claims the framework's constraint applies to proxies. A counterexample to the framework is not a counterexample to what the proxy view inherits from it.
- *Horn B:* The four cases are one act with different provenance. Then Jane shows what the thesis says is missing from LLMs. A public convention settles identity, and hidden facts do not.

Horn B is the natural reading, and it favours the thesis.

3. The LLM case differs where it matters.
In the Jane case, the proxy theory and the hearer's reading agree on the act, and only the backstage varies. In the LLM case the proxy theory itself makes the principal and force depend on the backstage. The thesis's sketch lists the self-prompt, the third-party deployment and the unseen API pipeline as cases where the theory names different principals and forces. No letterhead-like convention picks one. So the thesis targets a theory that locates identity in what the hearer cannot see. Jane's case is one where the theory locates it in what the hearer can see.

4. The thesis already contains the horn the objector says is "contingent."
The sketch says the proxy theorist must either let hidden facts fix identity, which gives up publicity, or impose transparency, which leaves almost no current outputs as proxy assertions. The Jane case only shows that conventions can supply transparency. That is the second horn, and it is already a cost the thesis charges to the proxy view.

VERDICT

The defence beats the counterexample but does not save the thesis. I concede, and I report the thesis as dead in its stated form.

What the defence achieves is real. The Jane case misdescribes ordinary delegated speech. The four versions are one public act with different provenance, so the case does not show that hidden facts fixing identity is harmless. It shows that human delegation avoids the problem by convention.

But the achievement costs the thesis its main claim. Once convention is what fixes identity, the thesis as written, that the proxy view "violates the uptake or publicity condition," no longer follows from the proxy view. The proxy view does not say identity is fixed by hidden facts. It says identity is fixed by who the proxy acts for, and that is silent on how a hearer recovers it. Whether LLM deployments violate publicity then depends on whether a default convention exists or can be added, such as "the deployer speaks unless marked otherwise" or "the user speaks when self-prompted." Those conventions can be added, and the defence itself concedes this in treating the call-centre case as fine. So the surviving claim is contingent: current interfaces lack conventions that proxy assertion needs. It is a complaint about deployment practice that disclosure norms would answer, and it is not a violation the proxy view incurs by its nature.

The earlier concessions also stand. The strong form of the premise, that identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, is false for ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity. The only form that survives is the convention form. That form turns a decisive violation into a fixable gap, and stating the thesis that way would be the hedge I am not allowed to make.

The part worth keeping is the dilemma in the sketch: hidden facts fix identity, or transparency is required. That would need its own argument, one that shows no workable public convention for LLM proxying could exist. The thesis does not give that argument.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak premise is that the proxy view *violates* a publicity condition, as opposed to merely needing public conventions to fix principal and force.

The earlier rounds suggest that the strong form of the premise is false. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity show that hidden facts can fix an act's identity without any violation. What survives is the weaker claim that act-type and principal must be recoverable through public convention. That claim is true, but nobody denies it:

- Arora, Green and Michel, and Butlin and Viebahn already treat proxy assertion as depending on a designer or deployer being the answerable party.
- Arora's paper explicitly draws design implications for devices.
- That current interfaces do not mark whose speech an output is, or in what force, is a familiar observation about deployment practice.
- The remedy, a default-principal rule or a disclosure norm, is equally familiar.

So the thesis reduces to this: proxy assertion requires publicly marked delegation, and current chatbots often lack the marking. This is an uncontested requirement, which the proxy theorist can accept in a sentence, together with an uncontested empirical observation. The apparent novelty comes from calling the gap a "violation" of the Austin–Grice framework. That is a verbal escalation, and it does not survive once the premise is stated in its defensible form.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The reduction is fair, given the concessions already made. It is answerable only if the thesis can show that no workable convention exists for LLM proxying. The sketch gestures at this ("almost no current outputs are proxy assertions") but does not argue it, and that stronger claim would not be trivial.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. "Nobody denies it" is the objector's recollection, not a finding. The objector says Arora, Green and Michel, and Butlin and Viebahn already accept that proxy assertion needs a publicly marked, answerable principal. But answerability is not publicity. A theorist can say the deployer is answerable, by liability or design responsibility, without saying the hearer can recover that fact. Fixed-principal views (the creator speaks) are exactly views on which recoverability does no work. The thesis says that once the view is placed in the Austin–Grice tradition, recoverability does have to do work. That is a contested claim about what the view owes, not a platitude. The objector also cannot check these attributions, and neither can I.

2. The conventions that exist point the wrong way, so this is not a gap. The triviality charge treats the situation as an absence that a default-principal rule can fill. But the first-order uptake the sketch notes is that hearers address the model as speaker: they say "you," thank it, and correct it. A convention is a practice, not a stipulation. The practice that exists fixes the model as the speaker, which is the very reading the proxy theory denies. So the proxy theorist must displace a live convention, not supply a missing one. Letterhead-and-title conventions for human delegation were not introduced by decree against contrary uptake. That asymmetry is substantive.

3. The conclusion is not trivial even if the requirement is. "Almost no current outputs are proxy assertions" is a strong result. It undercuts the practical motive for proxy accounts, which was to say that today's chatbot outputs are assertions by someone. A uncontested premise can still yield a contested conclusion. The objector concedes that this claim "would not be trivial."

4. Disclosure norms do not obviously supply the convention. "AI-generated" marks that no human is speaking in propria persona. It does not say whether the deployer asserts, the user drafts, or the text is quoted. Distinguishing those requires conventions for per-output content that no one authorised in advance. Green and Michel's recordings and timed notices work because the content is fixed ahead of time and the delegation is to a known text. Generative output lacks that. So it is open whether any workable convention exists. The thesis does not argue the point, but the objector has not shown that it is easy.

VERDICT

The triviality charge is defeated against the residue. The thesis as stated is still dead.

Points 2 and 3 hold up. The surviving claim is that existing public uptake conventions mark the model, not any principal, and that displacing them is a real cost. That claim is not a platitude. The objector's own 3/5 allows as much.

But that residue is not this thesis. This thesis says the proxy view "implies" that identical tokens are different speech acts by different speakers depending on hidden facts, and "so it violates" the uptake condition. The earlier rounds established three things, and this defence does not touch them:

- The strong premise, that identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, is false.
- The proxy view itself is silent on how a hearer recovers the principal, so no violation follows from the view.
- The recoverability form depends on contingent conventions.

The best the defence shows is that a different thesis would survive triviality: current uptake conventions conflict with proxy attribution, and the burden of showing otherwise falls on the proxy theorist. That thesis would need two arguments the sketch only gestures at. One shows that the displaced-convention problem is real. The other shows that generative content blocks any workable delegation convention. Presenting that as the original claim would be the hedge I am not allowed to make, so I report this thesis as dead.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the key premise: "illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise." The phrase "illocutionary identity" slides between two things.

- Reading A (act-type and force). The hearer must be able to recognise what kind of act is being performed, such as a promise, an assertion or a quotation. This is the Gricean and Austinian core, and it is plausible. But on A the proxy view is not shown to violate anything. The proxy view fixes the principal and says nothing about how the hearer recovers force. Public conventions such as default-deployer rules or "AI assistant" framing could meet A. The tradition has no objection to hidden provenance on A. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity all pass.
- Reading B (principal and deployment facts). The hearer must be able to recover who the proxy acts for, and which system prompt, fine-tune or pipeline produced the output. This is what makes the thesis's verdict ("almost no current outputs are proxy assertions", a "violation") interesting. But B is not part of the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition, and it is false for ordinary delegated and anonymous speech.

The argument borrows A's authority from Grice and Austin to license the premise. It then uses B's strength to get a violation from the sketch's cases, such as the self-prompt, the third-party deployment and the unseen API pipeline. It cannot run on A alone, where the conclusion is only a contingent complaint about interface conventions. It cannot run on B alone, where the premise is unsupported.

STRENGTH: 4/5. The slide is real and the argument needs both readings. The thesis can survive only by being restated as a narrower claim about displaced uptake conventions, which it does not currently argue for.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objector's two readings leave out the reading the thesis uses. The thesis does not say hearers must recover system prompts, fine-tunes or pipelines (Reading B). It says that *speaker* and *force* vary with those facts. The facts are the grounds that fix the principal. What the premise requires the hearer to recover is the result: who is speaking and what they are doing. Call that Reading C. The hidden facts are what the theory appeals to, and the audience is not required to know them.

2. On C, speaker and force cannot be separated, and that is the Gricean and Austinian core. The objector's Reading A puts force on the recoverable side and principal on the hidden side. But assertion is not a free-floating type. It is the undertaking of a commitment by some agent. A quotation, a draft and an assertion differ in whose commitment is engaged and whether anyone's is. Grice's reflexive intention is an intention that the *hearer recognise the speaker's intention*, and recognising an intention means attributing it to an agent. Austin's A.2 likewise makes "appropriate persons" part of felicity. So recognising force already involves some recognition of the answerable party, and A already contains C. The thesis has not borrowed A's authority to defend B.

3. C explains why the objector's counterexamples pass and the LLM case does not. Ghostwriting, anonymity and insincerity all pass C. The hearer correctly attributes the act to the politician, to some anonymous speaker, or to the liar. What is hidden is provenance or sincerity, not who speaks and in what force. In the LLM case the hearer's recognised speaker (the model, the "you" being thanked and corrected) and the proxy theory's speaker (the deployer, the user, no one) come apart. The thesis's examples of the self-prompt, the third-party deployment and the unseen API pipeline are exactly cases where the theory itself assigns different speakers and forces to the same string.

4. So the argument runs on one reading and does not slide. The premise is that the recognised speaker and force must be the ones the theory assigns. The thesis charges the proxy view with failing this where its own attributions track unobservable facts, and the objector's cases do not.

VERDICT

The defence answers the equivocation charge but does not save the thesis. I concede.

What it achieves is real. The thesis does not need Reading B, and C is a coherent middle position that the Gricean point about attributing intentions supports. The 4/5 overstates the equivocation, since the argument does not need both readings.

But C is not enough, for three reasons.

1. Mismatch is not violation. C yields a mismatch between the hearer's attribution and the theory's. Ordinary delegation is full of such mismatches. A hearer takes "Jane, Support" to be speaking, and the theory says the company is. The act is fine because a role convention settles it. A hearer who mistakes the speaker is not thereby denied a speech act. So C shows that LLM uptake currently points at the model. It does not show that the proxy view *violates* uptake rather than revising it. A proxy theorist can say that hearer uptake is mistaken about who speaks, as with a ventriloquist, and that the act is still proxy speech. The thesis needs C to be a *constraint*, and the tradition does not impose it in that form. This is the same point on which the earlier rounds converged.

2. The mismatch is contingent. It exists because current interfaces and habits treat the model as speaker. That is a fact about conventions, and disclosure or default-principal conventions could change it. A decisive violation therefore turns into the contingent complaint already identified.

3. The sketch's own horns do not close. The thesis says the proxy theorist must either let hidden facts fix identity or impose transparency. Reading C shows the first horn is a mismatch and not a breach, and the second is a demand for conventions that might be supplied. Neither horn yields "violates".

The part that survives is that proxy attribution runs against live uptake conventions, so the proxy theorist owes an argument for displacing them. That is a burden-shifting complaint, not a violation, and it needs two further arguments: that the displaced-convention problem is real, and that generative content blocks any workable delegation convention. Presenting it as the original thesis would be the hedge I am not allowed to make. I report the thesis as dead in its stated form.

R22. Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
counterexample — The shared synchronic assumption in Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn that speech-act status depends on states of the producer at the time of output.
Sketch

Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.

Appraiser (blind)
The diachronic, retroactive-ownership account of speech-act status is genuinely novel and gives a testable agentic criterion, though the key premise is contestable.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The objector rated it 2/5 and conceded the capacity is synchronic. The defender's point that evidence of a state is not constitution by later conduct answered it, so only 'every position' is overstated.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, unanswered. The perjurer and dying declarant are assigned assertion with no continuation. The defender's replies (null continuation as standing by, others' uptake, 'indeterminate') change what does the conferring or give an error theory. None shows the cases are not assertions.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. The ratification model is a real third option beyond fresh act or mere evidence. The defender also correctly separated later assertions from retroactive status of the earlier token. The objector's own 3/5 was overstated.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis takes its evidence from commitment-status and its conclusion from act-performance. The Austin and killing analogies rest on hearer uptake or later descriptions. The 'argument from absence' is inference to a best theory, not a bridge, and it works only for underdetermined cases.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The defender separated the thesis from its rescues, offered owned-versus-disowned matched-pair tests, and fixed a behavioural criterion in advance. The thesis is falsifiable, and the counterexample round shows it.
🔧 Survives as

In cases where output-time states and functions leave assertoric status underdetermined, later commitment-management by the producer is partly constitutive of which act was performed. This is testable on chatbots in agentic loops, but it does not claim that a one-shot output can never be an assertion.

Flaw

The universal claim that status is conferred only by later conduct, so a one-shot completion never asserts, is refuted by perjury and dying declarations. The human retroactive-ownership evidence supports commitment-attribution, not act-performance.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn all treat speech-act status as fixed by the producer's states at the moment of output. This is a flat, unqualified ascription to three authors who each build in something extra.

- Butlin and Viebahn make assertion depend on the system being *capable of being sanctioned* by interlocutors. That is a social, practice-embedded condition about how the system figures in ongoing exchanges, and it reaches beyond the output event. They say it reflects assertion's nature as a norm-governed social practice.
- Gubelmann's test for intention is whether one can distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing. That is a counterfactual, track-record-sensitive test, not a snapshot of the output.
- As I recall, Williams and Bayne ground proto-assertion in how assertion emerges developmentally. That points to a historical or practice-based element, though I am unsure of the details.

The thesis also ignores a long tradition (Brandom's scorekeeping, MacFarlane's commitment-based view) in which assertoric status is socially conferred and not fixed by prior mental states. A reader could therefore say the "synchronic consensus" is a strawman built from views that already carry diachronic or relational elements.

STRENGTH: 2/5. My memory of Williams and Bayne is shaky, so I rate low. A dispositional capacity that exists at output time is still a synchronic state of the producer. Butlin and Viebahn's condition is not the claim that later conduct confers status on an earlier token. The core ascription, that these authors fix status at output time by the producer's properties, is therefore roughly accurate. The overstatement ("every position") is real but cosmetic.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The objection mistakes the target. The target is the claim that a token's speech-act status is fixed by facts about the producer at output time. The objector's three examples don't contradict this.

- Butlin and Viebahn. Being *capable of being sanctioned* is a dispositional property the system has when it produces the output. It is a synchronic fact about the producer, and it is relational only in the way any capacity is. Nothing in it says that what the system later does fixes whether this earlier token was an assertion. The objector concedes this in their own rating.
- Gubelmann. The malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrongdoing test uses track record as *evidence about* the system's dispositions and intentions. It does not make later conduct *constitutive of* the status of an earlier token. Evidence for a synchronic state is not diachronic constitution. The thesis's distinction between evidence and constitution applies here too.
- Williams and Bayne. The developmental origin of assertion explains why assertion has the shape it has. It does not say a given output's status waits on its continuation. The objector admits they are unsure of the details, so this is not a counterexample.

2. The Brandom and MacFarlane point supports the thesis. If assertoric status is socially conferred through scorekeeping, there is a lineage in which status is not fixed by pre-utterance mental states. That helps the counterexample. It shows the diachronic view is a live theoretical position and that the human case of retroactive ownership has theoretical backing. The objector offers it as a reason to doubt the synchronic consensus claim, but it is a resource for the thesis's positive claim.

3. The objection targets the sketch's historiography, not the thesis. The thesis is a first-order claim about what confers assertoric status. Even if "every position in the debate" is an overstatement, the counterexample (retroactive ownership) is independent of who holds the opposing view. If the named authors are not committed to synchronicity, that does not make the human case less of a counterexample to synchronicity. It only means the thesis has fewer opponents than advertised. The overstatement can be corrected by naming only those who explicitly tie status to output-time states, and that correction does not touch the thesis.

VERDICT

The defence holds against this objection, but only narrowly.

The objection is a misattribution charge, and it largely fails. The objector concedes that dispositional capacities at output time are synchronic states, that Butlin and Viebahn do not claim later conduct confers status on an earlier token, and that the overstatement is "cosmetic". Correcting "every position" to "the positions that ground status in output-time states or capacities" is a fix to the description of the target. It is not a narrowing of the thesis.

The objection does not touch the thesis's actual weak point, and I won't pretend it does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is *constitutive* of the act, not just evidence of an earlier intention. The sketch's own wording undermines it: "we rightly say … that they were answerable for it from the start." That is most naturally read as saying the status was in place at the time of utterance, fixed by the speaker's public position and the norms in force. On that reading, later endorsement reveals or ratifies the status and does not confer it. Retroactive ownership in humans is also compatible with a synchronic view in which the speaker was already committed by the default presumption of sincerity.

The one-shot-versus-loop test is a further problem. A one-shot completion "never" has assertoric status only if the diachronic view is already true, so the test presupposes the thesis rather than testing it.

So this objection fails, but the thesis's survival depends on a premise this exchange never defended. A different objector, one who presses the evidence-versus-constitution distinction against the retroactive-ownership premise, would land a much harder blow.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that later commitment-management is constitutive of assertoric status, so that with no continuation there is no assertion.

Take the perjurer. A witness swears "I was at home all night," knowing it is false. She is never challenged and never defends, retracts or updates, because the trial ends and she leaves. On the thesis, the output is not an assertion. But perjury, lying and false testimony are committed at the moment of utterance. The case needs an assertion at that time, and the witness is culpable whether or not anyone ever challenges her. The dying declaration is the same: "X shot me," then death, with no continuation possible. Nobody doubts that it was an assertion, and courts treat it as one precisely because of what was said then.

The thesis has two ways out, and both cost it. It can appeal to a counterfactual or dispositional continuation: she *would* have defended it. That is a state of the producer at output time, so the thesis collapses into the synchronic view it opposes. Or it can accept that the perjurer and the dying speaker never asserted, which is plainly wrong.

For chatbots, the same completion would become an assertion only if a harness that defends outputs were added a year later.

STRENGTH: 4/5. The dilemma is real. The thesis needs a diachronic reading that does not collapse into a dispositional one, and the sketch does not supply it.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The dilemma assumes the only continuation is the speaker's own speech. The thesis says status is conferred by what happens to the output afterwards. The perjurer's testimony is entered in the record, sits under oath-based liability, and remains open to challenge. Even if she is never challenged, she stands by it by leaving it uncorrected through the whole period in which she remains answerable. Non-retraction under live exposure to sanction is a continuation, and the null continuation counts as standing by. The thesis needs no actual challenge, only an actual stretch of time in which the commitment either stands or doesn't.

2. The law treats perjury as diachronically open. Recantation statutes (e.g. 18 U.S.C. §1623(d)) bar prosecution if the witness admits the falsity in the same continuous proceeding. That is a real resource: the legal system treats the status of the testimony as not closed at utterance. The same-proceeding window is the analogue of the "long-context loop." Her culpability is fixed when the window closes without recantation, not at the moment of speech.

3. The counterfactual horn is not a collapse. The objector says "she would have defended it" is a producer state at output time. But the thesis does not rest on the counterfactual. Actual later facts do the work: the testimony was not recanted, was relied on, and was sanctionable. Where there are such facts, status attaches to them. If the dispositional reading is the only one on offer for a case with no continuation, then the case has no assertion-fixing facts, and "indeterminate" is a respectable verdict. It is not "plainly wrong" for a speaker cut off one second after speaking.

4. The dying declaration is Brandom, not a counterexample. On scorekeeping, a declaration is an assertion because hearers take up and attribute the commitment and act on it, as courts do when they admit it. That is conferral by later uptake. It also explains why the hearsay exception exists: the law is responding to what the utterance becomes in practice.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The objection stands.

- Points 1 and 4 are hedges. Each saves the thesis by changing what does the conferring. The thesis says "what the *system* later does with the output." The dying declarant does nothing later, so the rescue is that *others* take it up. That is a different thesis, a Brandomian uptake view. It is not the one in the candidate, which makes the chatbot's own commitment-management constitutive and says a one-shot completion "never" counts. A one-shot completion that hearers take up and rely on would be an assertion on the rescued view, and the candidate forbids that. The rescue gives up the testable chatbot criterion, which was the point.
- Point 2 cuts the wrong way. Recantation is a *defence to an offence already committed*. The law says she lied, and then permits a later act to excuse it. That treats the assertion as completed at utterance and the later act as responding to it. It also leaves the culpability facts and the speech-act facts apart. At most the recantation law shows that responsibility is diachronically adjustable.
- Point 3 fails on its own terms. If the perjurer who is never challenged and leaves court has an "indeterminate" speech act, then the thesis says no one can say whether she lied. But perjury, by definition, requires that she asserted on the oath-taking occasion. The practice we are explaining takes the status as settled at utterance. Making it indeterminate is an error theory about ordinary assertion, and the retroactive-ownership case was supposed to be *ordinary* evidence for the thesis.
- The sketch's own phrase "answerable for it from the start" concedes the point. The retroactive-ownership case shows ratification of a status that was already fixed by the public setting, with presumptive sincerity and uptake norms. The constitutive premise was never established, and this objection shows why it cannot be: wherever there is no continuation, we still assign assertion.

The thesis as stated is dead. What survives is a different claim: that assertoric status is a feature of the speaker-in-practice at output time, and that later commitment-management is evidence of it and a way of exercising it. That is the synchronic view the candidate set out to refute, and I will not present the survivor as the original thesis.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that retroactive ownership is *constitutive* of the earlier act. It is the only premise that makes the thesis more than a restatement of what the field already grants.

The thesis faces a dilemma. On the weak reading, a later "I stand by that" is itself a new act of asserting the same content. Or it is evidence of, or ratification of, a commitment already in force. Both readings are uncontested. Brandom's scorekeeping and MacFarlane's commitment view already say that status is socially managed and that challenge, defence and retraction are how commitments work. Nobody in the chatbot debate denies that a harness which defends outputs produces assertions. Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition already presupposes it. The thesis is then true and uncontested.

On the strong reading, the status of an earlier token waits on its continuation. That is no discovery. It is a stipulation about how to extend "assertion" to systems with no settled practice. The proposal that a one-shot completion "never" asserts and a looped one does is a decision to draw the line there, not a finding about assertion. The human case does not support it, since the sketch says speakers are answerable "from the start."

STRENGTH: 3/5. The dilemma is real. But the proposal that the chatbot question becomes diachronic and testable may still be a novel way to organise the debate.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. The dilemma omits a third option, and it is the one the thesis needs. The objector says a later "I stand by that" is either (a) a new assertion of the same content or (b) evidence or ratification of a commitment already in force. There is a third kind of act: one that is new and also has retroactive constitutive effect on the earlier act. Ratification in agency law is the model. An unauthorised agent's contract becomes the principal's contract *ab initio* when the principal ratifies it. Ratification is neither merely a fresh act nor merely evidence of earlier authority, because there was no authority to evidence. The later act makes the earlier one what it is. The human blurt or confabulation fits this. When the speaker owns the remark, "answerable from the start" is the retrospective form that ratification takes, like "he was the winner all along". It is not a report of a status that was already in place. If the sketch's wording suggests otherwise, that is a wording slip. The structure of ratification supports the thesis.

2. The weak horn is not uncontested for the claim the thesis makes. The objector says nobody denies that a harness that defends outputs produces assertions. That is true of the harness's *later* outputs. The thesis claims something about the *earlier* token: that its status is settled by its continuation, and that two identical strings can differ in status because of what follows. Butlin and Viebahn and Gubelmann do not hold this. Both assess a system's output by what the system is, not by what a later harness adds. Conflating "later outputs are assertions" with "the earlier output becomes one" is the move that makes the thesis look trivial.

3. The disavowal case shows the symmetry. The same string, "It's the butler," can be disowned ("I was just thinking aloud, not claiming it") or owned. Where the speaker's pre-utterance state is truly underdetermined, as with confabulated or half-conscious remarks, the owning or disowning is what settles the status. The line is not stipulated, because it follows the practice of treating such speakers as bound or not bound depending on what they do.

4. This is a substantive proposal, not a stipulation. In a field with no settled practice for chatbots, deciding where to draw the line is exactly the work to be done. The thesis draws it somewhere with human precedent and makes it testable.

VERDICT

The defence resists the triviality charge in part, but the thesis is still dead.

What holds up:

- Point 2 is correct. The weak horn is not uncontested for the claim about the earlier token. The triviality charge as stated is overstated, and the objector's own 3/5 reflects that.
- Point 1 is a real resource. Ratification is a genuine form of retroactive conferral that is neither a fresh act nor mere evidence.

Why it still fails:

1. Ratification is an attribution rule, not a speech-act fact. The law *treats* the contract as authorised from the start. It does not claim the earlier utterance was in fact an act of authorising. Transposed to assertion, ratification gives a retroactive *imputation of responsibility*, which is the "diachronically adjustable responsibility" the earlier exchange already conceded. It does not give a retroactive *speech act*.
2. Using it forces a restriction. Ratification applies only where the earlier status was underdetermined. The perjurer and the dying declarant had determinate status and no continuation, so ratification cannot explain them. A thesis restricted to "underdetermined cases, settled later" has given up the claim that a one-shot completion *never* asserts and that a looped one does. That claim is the thesis's distinctive and testable content. Preserving the thesis by restricting its scope is exactly what I am told not to do.
3. The strong horn is still false. The previous round showed that where there is no continuation, we still assign assertion, as the perjurer and dying-declaration cases show. Point 4 asks us to treat the line as a decision, but a decision that contradicts the practice it is meant to extend is not a proposal about assertion. It is a proposal to change the subject.
4. Point 3 does not help. Disavowal succeeds in the thinking-aloud case because of what the speaker was doing *then*, which is a synchronic fact. It does not show that the later statement made it so.

So the triviality objection is not decisive taken alone. The thesis still fails on the combination: the weak reading is trivial or merely evidential, and the strong reading is refuted by the earlier counterexample. What remains after the three objections is a claim about *when responsibility for an underdetermined output gets fixed*. That is a modest and plausible claim, but it is not the original thesis. I report the original as dead.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that retroactive ownership is *constitutive of the act*, together with the term "assertion" (or "assertoric status") that carries it. The term has two readings.

- (A) Commitment-status: being answerable, bound, or attributable as having committed oneself to p.
- (B) Act-performance: having performed the illocutionary act of asserting at the time of utterance.

The human blurt-then-"I stand by that" case is plausible only on (A). Responsibility is plainly assignable or adjustable after the fact, as in ratification, and this is the reading the previous exchange already conceded. But the opponents (Williams and Bayne, Butlin and Viebahn, Gubelmann) are asking (B): did the system *perform* an act, and does it have the capacities that performing one requires? A synchronic theorist can accept diachronic (A) without any cost, so on reading (A) the thesis is uncontested.

The thesis is interesting only on (B). It says a one-shot completion never asserts and a looped one does, and that the same token is or is not an act. The human case gives no support there, since the perjurer and the dying declarant are assigned act-status at utterance. The argument therefore needs (A) for its evidence and (B) for its conclusion. It cannot be run on (A) alone, where it is trivial, or on (B) alone, where it has no support.

STRENGTH: 4/5. Reading (A) supplies the evidence and reading (B) supplies the conclusion, so the thesis needs a bridge from (A) to (B) that the sketch never provides.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

1. On the accounts that matter, the (A)/(B) division is false, so no bridge is needed. The objector treats commitment-status and act-performance as two things that need linking. On Brandom's scorekeeping view, and on MacFarlane's, asserting just is undertaking a commitment, and being answerable for p is what it is to have asserted p. On these views (A) and (B) are the same fact described twice. Those are exactly the views that make the thesis's retroactive-ownership evidence relevant. If commitment is conferred or adjusted through scorekeeping, then so is the act. The equivocation charge presupposes a thin, event-like conception of the act that the commitment-based literature rejects.

2. Illocutionary acts can depend on later facts. Austin's own examples show this. "I bet you sixpence" is not a bet until the offer is taken up, and a warning that is never heard is a defective warning. Uptake is a condition on performing the act, not merely on assigning responsibility for it. Acts are also individuated by descriptions that settle later: a shot is a killing only if the victim dies, and a move is a checkmate only given what follows. So (B) can be diachronically fixed without collapsing into (A). "Asserting" can be like "killing" or "betting": the act at t is what it is partly because of t+1.

3. The human blurt is a hard case for the synchronic (B) theorist. The synchronic theorist must say what, at output time, made the confabulated remark an act of asserting. Not an intention, since there was none. Not a capacity, since the speaker also has the capacity to produce non-assertoric noises. If the answer is "the public setting and default presumption of sincerity," that is a presumption which the later disavowal or ownership can defeat or confirm. Where the presumption is the only thing doing the work, the later conduct selects between available act-descriptions.

4. For chatbots, the bridge is an argument from absence. The (B) question for chatbots is hard because the synchronic candidates (intentions, functions, sanctionability) are contested or indeterminate. Where output-time facts underdetermine the answer, the continuation is the only remaining place for act-fixing facts. That is why the thesis is interesting on (B) even though its human evidence is mostly (A).

VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The objection stands.

Point 1 is the strongest, and it fails on its own terms. Brandom and MacFarlane identify assertion with commitment, but they do not say the commitment arises from the speaker's later conduct. On both views, undertaking the commitment happens at utterance, by the public norms in force. Later defence, retraction or challenge is how the commitment is managed or discharged. Scorekeeping is also *others'* tracking, which is the uptake thesis that an earlier round already showed to be a different thesis. It would make a one-shot completion that hearers rely on an assertion, which the candidate forbids. So the identity of (A) and (B) on these views is correct, but it moves the whole question back to output time and to the practice around it. That is the synchronic picture.

Point 2 proves less than it needs. Betting and warning depend on *hearer* uptake, usually immediate, and not on the speaker's own later commitment-management. The "killing" analogy gives later-determined *descriptions* of an act. The act of shooting is not retroactively made. At most it shows that "an assertion that was upheld" or "an assertion that was retracted" are later-determined descriptions. It does not show that whether there was an assertion is. The thesis needs the stronger result.

Point 3 is a real pressure on the synchronic theorist, but it goes only as far as the blurt and confabulation cases, where output-time facts underdetermine the act. It supports a restricted claim: in underdetermined cases, owning or disowning settles which act was performed. That restriction gives up the thesis's distinctive content, that a one-shot completion *never* asserts and a looped one does. The perjurer and the dying declarant remain cases with determinate act-status and no continuation.

Point 4 is an inference to the best theory, not a bridge. It concedes that the human evidence does not reach (B) and proposes (B) because nothing else is available. That treats the lack of a synchronic answer as support for a diachronic one. The failure of the synchronic candidates is at best a reason for agnosticism or for a different synchronic candidate.

So the equivocation is real. The thesis has (A)-type evidence (retroactive ownership is robustly attested) and (B)-type content (act-status is conferred by the system's own continuation), and no argument connects them. The only way to connect them is to shrink the claim to underdetermined cases, which is the move I am told not to make. I report the thesis as dead. What survives is the claim that responsibility for underdetermined outputs is fixed by later commitment-management, which is plausible but a different and weaker thesis.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)
