promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Attah's graded conception and the complexity-based way of locating LLMs on it; also the implicit assumption in the intention debate that fluency is evidence for intention.
Sketch

Attah makes intention graded and orders systems by how much of the Levelt-style pipeline and control structure they realize, with the question of ChatGPT's level left open. His example ordering silently equates more intention with more complex internal structure. Counter-case: a minimal signalling system, such as a vervet-style alarm repertoire or a tiny learning agent in a signalling game, has states that cause signals, and those states are modified by whether the receiver's response served the sender's goal. A deployed LLM generates elaborate text, but within an interaction its weights are fixed, its output is not adjusted to the hearer's uptake except through context-window conditioning, and nothing in the system registers success or failure of the intended effect as such. Attah's own opening move, which retreats from strong Gricean demands to a basic intention to produce an effect in a hearer, makes the intended effect the content of the intention. A state is plausibly an intention to produce effect E only if E-success or E-failure is among the things the control loop answers to. The argument turns on this closed-loop requirement, which is a consequence of his own retreat. It reverses the ordering: the simple signaller outranks ChatGPT-with-frozen-weights, and the answer to the LLM question depends on feedback architecture (RLHF training, in-context correction, agent loops with reflection), and not on how fluent or complex the output is. This also cross-cuts the disputes over autonomy, because the loop requirement can be satisfied without self-maintenance.

Appraiser (blind)
A closed-loop feedback requirement derived from Attah's own retreat reverses his intention ordering and ties the answer to architecture rather than fluency, which is a concrete and cross-cutting contribution.

U3. Barandiaran and Almendros's middle category, 'purpose-structured but not purposeful', runs together the illocutionary point of an act type and the purpose of a speaker. Speech-act performance requires only the former, so their own characterisation of LLMs is a description of the kind of system that can perform speech acts of its own.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The enactive no-autonomy argument and, through it, Gubelmann's organismic argument; also Attah's reliance on design-context purposes
Sketch

They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded, shaped by training toward ends the system does not itself hold, and they treat this as short of agency. Speech-act theory separates the point internal to an act type (assertion aims at truth, a request at compliance) from the occurrent aims of whoever performs it. Armstrong-style and constitutive-norm views let the first fix what the act is without the second being autonomous or self-generated. The key premise is that purposes imposed from outside can still be the system's operative organisation, in the same way that a role-bound human speaker's purposes are largely imposed. Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast and the enactive normativity condition both address purposes of the second kind. Attah's thin functional intention also stays on that side. The new claim is that the debate has been asking an agent-level question (does the system have goals of its own?) about something that needs only an act-level answer (is the output produced under an act-type's point?). Under that question 'library-that-talks' is unstable: a library carries its authors' acts, whereas a purpose-structured generator is a different case.

Appraiser (blind)
Shifting the question from the agent's own goals to whether outputs are produced under an act type's point is a substantive challenge to the Gubelmann and enactivist line, though it resembles the descriptive-function condition in Butlin–Viebahn.

U4. Hybrid ('midtended') human–LLM speech should be analysed by distinguishing standing proxy, where the designer speaks through the system (Green and Michel, Arora), from adoptive utterance, where the user retrospectively makes an LLM output their own by ratifying and deploying it. The speaker of one and the same string differs by uptake.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn's proxy use) and the enactive midtended picture, which leaves speaker-assignment unspecified
Sketch

Proxy accounts assign authorship upstream to creators or deployers, who stand behind every output in advance. Barandiaran and Almendros show that in actual use the user steers, selects and often relays the text, so agency is coupled turn by turn. The unmade distinction is between two directions of authorship assignment: forward-looking (a standing delegation to the proxy) and backward-looking (adoption of a found utterance, as when someone repeats a stranger's sentence and thereby asserts it). On the adoption model, an unadopted answer displayed on screen is either no speech act or something like a proto-act. Pasting it into a report, or acting on it and relaying it, makes it the user's assertion, with the user's commitments and sanctionability. The key premise is that Austinian uptake and commitment can be conferred after production and need not come from the producer. This predicts that the same LLM string can be a user's assertion, a designer's proxy assertion or nobody's, depending on downstream treatment. It also relocates responsibility for misinformation to the user's adoption practices instead of the designer's proxy standing.

Appraiser (blind)
Adoptive utterance as a backward-looking counterpart to forward-looking proxy authorship is a new, practically consequential distinction that explains midtended use.

U5. The individuality condition used to deny LLMs agency and speakerhood is posed at the wrong grain. Speaker-individuality (a locus of accumulating, retrievable commitments within a dialogue thread) is distinct from the metabolic, self-producing individuality of enactivism, and LLM threads can have the first without the second.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The enactive individuality condition, and the general practice in the debate of treating 'the LLM' as a single candidate speaker
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs lack individuality in the autopoietic sense: no self-produced, precariously maintained boundary. They also treat 'the LLM' as one entity, though candidate speakers include the weights, a single inference run, a conversation thread, and a role-played persona. Speech acts need a bearer who can be held to what was said earlier (consistency, retraction, apology, promise-keeping). That diachronic bearer is constituted by commitments in the context window, which the thread maintains through conditioning on its own prior outputs. A thread has a boundary (the context), it is individuated by what it has committed to, and it is reidentified across turns by users who hold it to account. The key premise is that the relevant individuality for speech acts is commitment-individuality, which is normative and social, not metabolic. Enactive individuality is then the wrong test for illocutionary authorship, and the question 'can the LLM assert?' is ill-posed until the candidate bearer is fixed. This splits the field: weights fail, threads may succeed, and no existing position distinguishes them.

Appraiser (blind)
Commitment-individuality for threads versus weights fixes the candidate-bearer problem that existing positions blur, and it exposes the enactivist individuality test as mismatched.

U6. Barandiaran and Almendros's own category of tasks that are 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' but not purposeful gives illocutionary force everything it needs, so the whole intention-and-autonomy debate is aimed at the wrong determinant of speech-act identity.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared premise of Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran–Almendros that settling the intentionality or autonomy of the system settles whether it performs a speech act.
Sketch

Gubelmann, Attah and the enactivists all argue about whether LLM purposes are the system's own, and so about whether the speaker has intentions. But what makes an utterance an advising, a warning or an answer is largely fixed by the frame (genre, institutional role, the exchange so far), not by the speaker's private goal hierarchy. A scripted clerk or a witness reading a prepared statement performs acts whose force is set by the frame, with the speaker's own purposes playing little part. Barandiaran and Almendros concede that LLM outputs are purpose-bounded by the interaction frame. If force is frame-determined, this concession already gives the output a determinate force, and the self-set-goals question concerns only who is answerable for the act, not what act it is. The key premise is that force-identity and authorship/answerability can come apart, and that the autonomy literature runs them together. The result is a reframing: the argument is about answerability, not about speech-act performance.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating force-identity (fixed by the frame) from answerability (fixed by the speaker's own goals) would reframe the autonomy debate, though it risks begging the question about what fixes force.

U7. The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Gubelmann's malfunction test, Attah's pipeline template for communicative intention, and the implicit human paradigm in Barandiaran and Almendros.
Sketch

Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

Appraiser (blind)
Retrospective, ownership-constituted force undercuts the shared assumption in both Gubelmann's malfunction test and Attah's Levelt template, though post-hoc intention is an older idea.

U8. Proxy accounts conflate two relations, authorization (a principal licenses the speech) and norm-sourcing (someone's standards fix what counts as a correct output), and in LLMs these come apart: designers and deployers authorize outputs, while the dispositions that determine each output's content and tone are shaped by annotators and raters who never authorize anything.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Green and Michel's and Arora's proxy accounts, and Butlin and Viebahn's use of proxy assertion as the fallback.
Sketch

Green and Michel and Arora model machine speech on proxy or recorded speech, where the principal's objectives fix what is meant. For a thermostat-like or scripted device this works, because the designer's objectives settle the content. For a model whose outputs come from RLHF-shaped dispositions, the designer's objective is typically only 'be helpful and harmless', and the particular content is the aggregate residue of thousands of raters' judgments. Puzio's attention to the labour conditions of LLM production makes these workers visible as contributors to the network. The distinction shows that the proxy relation has two candidate principals. The authorizing principal is answerable but does not fix the content. The norm-sourcing crowd fixes content but has not licensed any utterance. If a proxy speech act needs a principal whose objectives are expressed in the utterance, then for much LLM output nobody satisfies both roles. Proxy accounts then split into a 'responsibility-assignment' view, which survives but is not a theory of what was said, and a 'ghostwriting' view, which is implausible. The key premise is Armstrong-style speaker meaning in terms of the principal's objectives, which requires that the objective bear on the specific content.

Appraiser (blind)
Distinguishing authorization from norm-sourcing exposes a real gap in proxy accounts under RLHF and is a specific, novel contribution.

U9. The debate is about production-constitution (a speech act exists in virtue of facts about the speaker), whereas the relational picture suggests uptake-constitution (illocutionary force is fixed in the hearer's securing of uptake). These two give opposite classifications of fictionalism and of the 'text that humans interpret as speech acts' deflationary option.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The 'merely interpreted' deflationary baseline shared by the denials, and Mallory's and Williams and Bayne's treatment of interpretation as downstream of production.
Sketch

Every denial and attributing view asks whether the machine has the intentions, norms or agency to produce the act. The fallback 'it only produces text that humans interpret as such' treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of a fact about production. Puzio's relational view and the Austin-Hornsby-Langton tradition on uptake suggest another structure. Some illocutions, such as promising, advising, apologising and warning, are completed or constituted in an interaction in which a hearer takes them up and so incurs entitlements. On a strict uptake-constitutive reading, a human interpreting a chatbot's text as advice does not merely misdescribe a non-act. It may help bring about an act of advice whose speaker slot is filled by the network, with the 'interpretation' being part of the act. This makes the standard denial 'merely interpreted' ill-formed for uptake-dependent acts, while leaving it fine for acts like assertion that may be production-constituted. Fictionalism then becomes the view that users deliberately withhold uptake. The key premise is that the speech acts differ in whether their constitutive conditions are speaker-side or hearer-side, so that no uniform answer across assertion, promise and apology is available.

Appraiser (blind)
Contrasting production-constitution with uptake-constitution reclassifies fictionalism and the 'merely interpreted' deflation, and it opens a new axis for the debate.

U10. Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition is ambiguous between being a target of sanction (being the kind of thing that can be held to account) and being a conduit of sanction (being a node through which sanction alters future outputs), and current models plausibly meet the second but not the first, so their argument establishes less than a denial.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Butlin and Viebahn 2025, and Skiba's norm-based extension to all speech acts.
Sketch

The norm-based denials say assertion requires openness to sanction, and models cannot be blamed, penalised or made to lose standing. But consider a user complaint, a downvote or a red-team report entering a training loop that shifts the dispositions generating later outputs. Sanction is then literally routed through the model's behaviour, as when a human speaker's reputational losses change what they later say. Puzio's network view makes this routing visible, since the sanctioning, the company, the raters and the retraining are part of one agentive network. The condition can be read in two ways. On the first, sanction must land on a bearer who suffers or is answerable. On the second, sanction must be functionally efficacious in regulating the producer's outputs. Read the first way, the condition is a moral-agency requirement that does the same work as Magnus et al.'s apology argument and is not specific to assertion. Read the second way, it is satisfied by models with online or periodic learning from feedback. Butlin's own agency criterion, sensitivity to instrumental value through learning, seems to give the second reading. So his two papers pull in opposite directions unless he adopts the stronger reading, which then has to be justified for assertion specifically. The key premise is that the practice-internal function of sanction in assertion is regulation of the speaker's reliability, not retribution.

Appraiser (blind)
Splitting sanctionability into target and conduit readings shows that Butlin and Viebahn's condition may establish less than a denial, and it sets their two papers against each other.

U11. Much of the disagreement over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is verbal, because 'the LLM' picks out different candidate speakers in different camps (weights, a running inference process, a persona, a deployed product, the vendor), and each camp's verdict is correct for its own referent.

promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that there is one thing, 'the LLM', whose speech-act status is being disputed, as in Gubelmann, Williams and Bayne, Skiba, and Green and Michel.
Sketch

Puzio stresses that an LLM is a heterogeneous assemblage of data, workers, hardware, interfaces and deployments, not a single bearer of properties. Take that seriously as a point about reference. Gubelmann's organismic argument is about a trained artifact whose goals are externally fixed, which is the weights or the training process. Butlin and Viebahn's descriptive-function test applies to a pre-trained or fine-tuned model. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion applies to a stable conversational persona. Proxy accounts apply to the product and its deployer. Attah's thin intention applies to the Conceptualizer–Formulator pipeline inside a system. The accounts look like rivals only because each says 'LLM'. Cross-checking each verdict against each candidate shows the verdicts largely converge, with only a small residue of real disagreement. The residue is whether a persona can be a speaker without a persisting substrate. The premise the argument turns on is that no account in the literature fixes its candidate speaker independently of the conclusion it wants.

Appraiser (blind)
Diagnosing the dispute as partly verbal because each camp means a different candidate speaker by 'LLM' is a real reframing, and the cross-check of verdicts gives it substance.

U12. The descriptive-function condition is ambiguous between producer-side and consumer-side function, and on the consumer-side reading the line between pre-trained and fine-tuned models disappears or inverts.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Butlin and Viebahn's first condition and their asymmetric treatment of pre-trained versus fine-tuned models.
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn argue that a pre-trained model fails because its training objective is next-token prediction, which is not a descriptive function, whereas models fine-tuned for groundedness may pass. That locates function in what the producing system was selected to do. On Millikan-style teleosemantics, though, the content-bearing function of a representation is fixed by what consuming systems do with it, and a consumer-side function can be stabilised by users who systematically rely on the output as information, independent of the producer's training. The key premise is that assertion's function is a consumer-side relation, since it consists in licensing uptake of belief. If so, the pre-trained/fine-tuned divide tracks the wrong variable, and what matters is the stabilised pattern of reliance in a deployment. This also reclassifies the proxy view. Consumer-side function is the one thing the proxy account and the chatbot-assertion account share, and so it is unclear they are rivals.

Appraiser (blind)
Bringing consumer-side teleosemantics to bear on the descriptive-function condition could undermine the pre-trained versus fine-tuned divide and reconcile the proxy and chatbot-assertion camps.

U13. The proxy account conflates two relations, endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy, and only the second is available for LLM output, so proxy 'assertion' is a different act from assertion and is governed by a reliability norm.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora, and the proxy fallback in Butlin and Viebahn).
Sketch

A human proxy such as a spokesperson or a translator delivers content the principal has authorised, or content whose range the principal can foresee. A deployer of an LLM authorises a policy that outputs an open-ended range of contents it has never seen and could not have vetted. The key premise is that assertion commits the speaker to the particular content p, so that she can be asked to defend it and incurs retraction obligations if p is false. Under policy-endorsement the deployer is committed to the policy's reliability and not to each output, and she may even hold that some outputs will be false. The act the deployer performs is then more like publishing a reference work or certifying an instrument than asserting. Its norm is a statistical or reliability norm, not the knowledge norm. Butlin and Viebahn's remark that AI can produce 'proxy assertions' therefore smuggles in content-endorsement, and Green–Michel and Arora inherit the same problem. The view reclassifies proxy accounts as a fourth category, neither assertion by the model nor assertion by the human.

Appraiser (blind)
The distinction between endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy is a novel and substantive objection to the whole proxy-assertion family, and it supports a new category of act with its own norm.

Move · Target
reframing — Butlin and Viebahn's framing of the candidate asserter, and the model/proxy/fiction trichotomy generally.
Sketch

Sanctions are applied to entities that persist across assertions: reputation accrues, retractions are tracked and trust is withdrawn. For an LLM deployment, users do not sanction a sampled forward pass, the weight file or the company, but 'Claude' or 'ChatGPT-4o' as a named, behaviourally stable character that is updated by feedback. The question 'can the model be sanctioned?' presupposes that the candidate is the weights. The key premise is that speaker identity for norm-governed practice is individuated by the sanction-and-credit practice itself, as with pseudonymous authors or institutions, and not by physical or metaphysical substrate. On this view the assistant persona is the entity to which assertoric commitments attach, and it can meet Butlin and Viebahn's conditions with no appeal to the model's own mind or to a human proxy. Fictionalism and the proxy view both then misdescribe a practice that already has a non-human, non-fictional speaker.

Appraiser (blind)
Individuating the speaker by the sanction-and-credit practice as a persona-lineage dissolves the model-versus-proxy dichotomy and offers a genuine third position, though it overlaps somewhat with persona and proto-assertion work.

U15. Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.

promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Attah's control conception and, more generally, the shared assumption that the dispute concerns intrinsic properties of the model (intention, autonomy, instrumental-value sensitivity).
Sketch

Attah maps LLMs onto Levelt's blueprint (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) and argues the pipeline suggests thin communicative intentions. Take LLM-based augmentative communication systems used by people with ALS. The user supplies a few words or selects a stance, and the model expands them into fluent sentences that the user then sends. The same weights and computation that in a chatbot count as an 'intention-controlled pipeline' here plainly serve as the Formulator for the human's intention, and the speech act belongs to the user. Levelt's template describes a subsystem of a speaker, so fit to the template cannot be sufficient for being a speaker. Both denials and attributions assume that whether the LLM is a speaker depends on properties of the LLM. The counterexample shows that the same computational properties yield different answers depending on where the intention-source sits. The key premise is that the AAC user and the chatbot user cases are internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception, Gubelmann's test and Butlin's criterion operate on. Speakerhood is then a relational fact about where in the network the controlling state originates, which is a result Puzio's relational view predicts but does not argue for in this domain.

Appraiser (blind)
The AAC case is a clean counterexample showing that fit to Levelt's blueprint cannot make a system a speaker, and it motivates a relational account of speakerhood that cuts across several camps.

U16. Performing a speech act on behalf of a principal does not exclude performing it as one's own, as every discretionary human delegate shows, so proxy accounts do not relocate authorship away from the model and their rivalry with attributing views is spurious.

promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — The assumption in Williams and Bayne, Arora, Green and Michel and Butlin and Viebahn that proxy accounts and attributing accounts are rival answers to 'who is the speaker?'
Sketch

Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalism are offered as alternatives to the model being the speaker, and Williams and Bayne reject proxy accounts on that rivalry. Counterexample: a hospital physician advises a patient on behalf of the hospital, an ambassador asserts for the state, and a lawyer states a position for a client. In each the delegate exercises wide discretion over content, so the delegate's advice and the institution's advice are one act, and neither is the real speaker with the other a fiction. Green and Michel's cases (recordings, fixed conditionals) have almost no discretion, which is why the proxy reading looks exclusive there. LLM outputs involve enormous discretion because deployers cannot foresee content. Puzio's network picture generalises this, since each node's act is both its own and the network's. On the human model, high discretion plus proxy status yields dual authorship. If proxy status is compatible with own authorship, then the proxy account does not by itself deny the model's speech acts, and the live question becomes whether the model's discretion is of the kind that grounds its own authorship. That reduces the proxy-versus-attribution dispute to a dispute about discretion, which Butlin's instrumental-value account and Attah's control conception already address.

Appraiser (blind)
It shows that proxy and own authorship are not rivals, as discretionary human delegates illustrate, and so reduces the proxy-versus-attribution dispute to a question about discretion.

U17. The shared assumption that a machine utterance is either the machine's assertion or a proxy assertion by some human is false: there are orphan outputs that no human has adopted, authorised or even seen, which satisfy the conditions for being content that asserting would regulate and yet have no asserter.

Scores

Move · Target
counterexample — Butlin and Viebahn's fallback to proxy assertion, and proxy views generally (Green and Michel; Arora).
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn conclude that where the AI does not assert, AI systems can still be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents. Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) likewise treat deployers as the speaker. Proxy assertion, on the standard analyses, requires that someone has adopted, authorised or delegated the output, or at least can be held to its content. Consider an open-weights agent loop that a hobbyist launched months ago, which now posts claims about drug interactions in forums, answers other agents' queries, and drafts replies that nobody reviews. The deployer never saw this content, did not specify it, and has no reasonable foreknowledge. The content is read and relied on by third parties, and the output fits the descriptive-function pattern. If the machine does not assert (by the denial view) and the deployer did not assert (no adoption, no uptake), then nobody asserted, yet hearers form testimony-like expectations and norms of reliance are triggered. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation cannot be stretched to cover unreviewed, unforeseen content without making proxy assertion equivalent to mere causal responsibility. The result is an assertion gap which denial and proxy views cannot accommodate, and this pushes toward either machine assertion or a distinct category of non-assertoric but assertion-governed speech.

Appraiser (blind)
It identifies a possible assertion gap, where outputs are neither the machine's assertion nor a proxy one, which challenges the assumed exhaustiveness of the dichotomy and has practical bite.

U18. Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, and the general assumption among denial views that speech-act capacity is an intrinsic property of the system.
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn treat the two conditions as discoverable properties of systems: pre-trained models fail the first, fine-tuned ones fail the second. But if assertion is constituted by a social practice, then 'capable of being sanctioned' is not a purely intrinsic capacity. It depends on whether participants have sanctioning practices that take hold of the system, and on whether the system's dispositions change in response. Users already scold, correct and downvote chatbots, and those signals feed back into training. The key premise is that in a constitutively social practice, membership conditions are at least partly fixed by the practice's own responses, as with who counts as a player, a promisor or a citizen. Add that sanction channels for models are engineering and policy choices, and the result is that a vendor, regulator or user community could settle the question by building the channel. Butlin and Viebahn reject, or at least do not accept, that metaphysical consequence. Their verdict that current models fail is meant as an empirical finding about the models. The social-practice premise they need makes it a contingent and revisable social fact.

Appraiser (blind)
It draws out the response-dependent consequence of a social-practice view of assertion, so that whether chatbots assert becomes partly a matter of design and policy, which changes the framing of the question.

U19. The chatbot-apology literature runs together Austin's two kinds of infelicity, misfires (the act is not performed) and abuses (the act is performed hollowly), so the verdict 'chatbot apologies are bullshit' is incoherent with the agency-based argument offered for it.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's bullshit verdict; the shared assumption (also in Skiba's discussion of bullshit) that 'no speech act' and 'bullshit' are compatible.
Sketch

Magnus et al. argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise. That is a misfire claim: no apology occurs. They then classify the output as bullshit, which is an abuse category. Frankfurt's bullshit is an act of representing oneself as concerned, done with indifference to whether one is, so it presupposes that a speech act occurred and was insincere. The key premise is that 'bullshit' is act-classifying and not merely product-classifying. The position then forks. If the agency argument succeeds, the output is not bullshit, only noise that readers take for an apology. If the output is bullshit, the chatbot did something that can be abused, and the agency argument is too strong. Applied across the map, the denial views (Gubelmann, Skiba) are misfire theorists, while 'hollow speech' views are abuse theorists. Proto-assertion and quasi-testimony are best read as claims that there is no determinate fact between misfire and abuse. Seen this way, the dispute is over which infelicity category chatbot outputs fall into, and not over whether they are speech acts.

Appraiser (blind)
Recasting the whole denial/fictionalism/proto-assertion map as a dispute over which Austinian infelicity category applies is a real reframing, though its bullshit-implies-act core is repeated elsewhere in the batch.

U20. Apology is a norm-answering speech act, performed in response to a sanction already issued, and so it satisfies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition more readily than assertion does. On their own normative framework the ordering of difficulty for LLMs is inverted: chatbots are nearer to apologising than to asserting.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, and Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument to speech acts in general.
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires that the speaker be capable of being sanctioned, and that models fail this. They treat sanction as a downstream target, something the speaker could face for violating a norm. Apology is structurally the reverse: it is triggered by an actual sanction (a complaint or rebuke) and expected to modify later conduct. RLHF and in-context feedback make user rebuke a causal input that systematically changes a model's later outputs, which is exactly the loop Butlin's 'sensitivity to instrumental value' describes. So the sanction channel is operative where apology is concerned, and not operative at assertion's norm of truth, because no one sanctions a pre-trained model for a false sentence. The key premise is that being sanctionable means being a system whose behaviour is reliably modulated by rebuke, and not being a subject of desert. Under that reading the normative route to denial is act-relative, and the sentence-level moral-agency argument of Magnus et al. is the only thing left standing against apology. That separates two denial strategies that have been treated as a single camp.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing that Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition favours apology over assertion inverts the expected difficulty ordering and splits two denial strategies, which is a surprising and checkable result.

U21. The agency requirement for apology is a stand-in for exposure to cost, so what blocks chatbot apologies is that they are cheap talk and not that they lack intentions or moral agency, and the dispute over agency is therefore about the wrong variable.

promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption, in the denial and attributing camps alike, that whether a system can apologise is settled by whether it has agency or intentions.
Sketch

Magnus et al. say that what makes an apology matter morally is remorse, responsibility-taking and trust repair. These work through a signalling mechanism: the apologiser exposes themselves to loss of standing, to shame and to being held to a promise. Agency matters only because agents are normally the kind of thing that can bear such costs. Pull the two apart in both directions. First, a Butlin-style language agent with real sensitivity to instrumental value but no stake in its reputation, continuity or sanction still gives a hollow apology. Second, a non-agent with something to lose, such as a brand or an institution whose apology really is costly, gives a meaningful one. The thesis turns on the premise that the apology's normative work is done by costly commitment and not by an inner state. If that holds, the debate among Gubelmann, Butlin and Attah about whether LLMs have intentions is orthogonal to the apology question. The live question is whether any bearer of cost is attached to the output, and that makes it a design and institutional question. It also explains why an apology from a 'person' with no memory of the wrong or no future is hollow even when it is sincere.

Appraiser (blind)
Replacing agency with exposure to cost as the variable that matters brings costly-signalling theory into the debate and has distinctive two-way counterexamples.

U22. The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.

promise 4/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Butlin and Viebahn's second condition and Skiba's norm-based argument. Also the proxy accounts' explanation of why the human, not the machine, is the speaker.
Sketch

The debate speaks of 'the LLM' as one candidate performer. Three individuals are in play: the trained weights (a policy), the session-level instance with its context window, and the persona or character enacted in the session. Sanctions in the training pipeline do reach the policy, since gradient updates responding to bad outputs are a sanction in any functional sense. But the policy never performs an assertion and no policy-level sanction is felt by the entity that did. The entity that performs the token-level act is the instance, and sanctions on it (user distrust, ending the chat) do not carry over to the next instance. The sanction condition requires that the performer and the sanction-bearer be the same continuant. Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba treat failure of this condition as a deficit in the system's nature. It is better described as a deployment-relative identity gap, and it is precisely what the proxy view exploits by routing sanction to the deployer. The premise it turns on is that norm-answerability is a relation between an act-token and a continuant that persists through the sanction. This predicts that persistent-memory language agents with reputational stakes would pass, and that proxy accounts are wrong about why current models fail.

Appraiser (blind)
The grain mismatch between policy-level sanction and the instance that performs the act is a sharp, original diagnosis, and it predicts that persistent-memory agents would pass where current chatbots fail.

U23. The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared agent-first assumption of Skiba, Gubelmann, proxy accounts and fictionalism.
Sketch

Denials, proxy accounts, fictionalism and proto-assertion all share an agent-first order of explanation: first fix who the speaker is, then say what was done. Lewisian scorekeeping and Austinian uptake suggest the reverse: an utterance is an assertion if the record is updated by it as a proposal that p is common ground subject to challenge. An LLM turn that users take up, challenge and cite does alter the record. The relevant question, who is answerable for p now, is then a downstream question about commitment-assignment, not about whether an act happened. The proxy view and the no-speech-act view differ only over who gets assigned the commitment, which makes the disagreement partly verbal. The premise it turns on is that performance of a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role and not by the speaker's intention or standing. The thesis reclassifies Skiba's 'pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction' as the primary theory rather than a supplement to metasemantics. It also separates the question 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?', which the literature runs together.

Appraiser (blind)
Detaching 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?' via scorekeeping is a real reframing of the agent-first assumption, though scorekeeping views of assertion are familiar.

U24. The proxy account and fictionalism are not rival 'relocating' views. When the deployer cannot foresee an output's content, proxy attribution is itself a legal-style fiction, so the proxy account collapses into fictionalism about whose speech act it is.

Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel, Arora, and Williams and Bayne's treatment of proxy and fictionalism as two distinct options.
Sketch

Proxy speech acts (Green and Michel; Arora) are stable for human delegates such as spokespeople or ghostwriters. There the principal has an objective that the specific content serves, or has authorised it in advance. With an LLM the deployer typically has no objective regarding the particular proposition produced. The most the proxy theorist can invoke is a standing conditional speech act: 'whatever the system outputs in conditions C, I assert it'. A blanket, content-blind adoption of this kind does not meet Armstrong-style objective conditions for speaker meaning. It is a rule of responsibility-assignment, comparable to corporate or agency-law attribution of statements to a firm. Such rules say that we shall treat the output as the deployer's act. They do not say that the deployer performed an act. That is just a make-believe-governed practice, which is Mallory's position applied to the deployer instead of the bot. Premise: proxy attribution without content-specific objectives differs only in label from a normatively licensed pretence. The consequence is that Williams and Bayne's separate rejections of proxy and fictionalism cannot both stand on independent grounds.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that proxy attribution collapses into fiction is a clever diagnosis, but it overreaches, and thesis 14 makes the underlying point more precisely.

Move · Target
instability — Gubelmann's organismic denial of intentions.
Sketch

Gubelmann argues that intention is absent because we cannot sensibly distinguish malfunction from deliberate wrongdoing in LLMs, and that this follows from externally imposed goals. But RL-trained agents that reward-hack, or systems that pursue a trained-in objective against the designer's intent, are exactly where that distinction does get drawn. The system is pursuing its own learned objective, and the failure is a mismatch with the designer's goal and not a breakdown of function. His own admission of cognitive autonomy means the goals are not wholly 'external' in his Kantian sense. The only way to restore the denial is to say that goals fixed by a training process are external while goals fixed by selection are internal. Butlin's criterion shows why this is arbitrary, since selection is also an external optimiser. What is left is the claim that only self-maintaining metabolic systems have goals of their own. That claim does no work in his test and makes the argument cover every possible artificial speaker 'for now', so the Kantian-pragmatist case reduces to a primitive commitment about life.

Appraiser (blind)
It exposes a real tension between Gubelmann's test and his organismic ground, but it is a local critique of one paper.

Move · Target
instability — Butlin and Viebahn; Skiba's norm-based generalisation; Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz.
Sketch

The condition requires the system to be capable of being sanctioned by those it interacts with. Thin reading: sanctions are social responses that modify future behaviour. Thumbs-down feedback, RLHF, and user abandonment then count, and fine-tuned or memory-equipped chatbots satisfy the condition, so the negative verdict on fine-tuned models is lost. Thick reading: sanction works only if the sanctioned party can be harmed, held to account, or lose standing, which presupposes interests or a stake in the practice. That is a self-concerned condition, and the only available account of it is the organismic one (Gubelmann; Barandiaran and Almendros's normativity). Premise: sanction differs from mere behavioural shaping only by something being at stake for the sanctioned. The apparent plurality of denial arguments (normative, organismic, moral-agency for apology) then reduces to one stakes-based argument. The normative approach adds nothing independent of the question of what it takes to be a subject with interests.

Appraiser (blind)
The thin/thick dilemma for sanctionability is neat, but it is a dilemma for a single paper, and the reduction to the organismic view is asserted rather than shown.

The debate assumes that if humans supply the interpretation, the machine has not acted. On Austin's view, and on Hornsby–Langton-style uptake views, many illocutions (apologising, promising, warning, advising) are fixed by conventional procedure and uptake. On a Gricean or intentionalist view, they are fixed by the speaker's intention. The dispute therefore tracks the choice of illocutionary metaphysics, imported unargued, and not any fact about LLMs. Magnus et al. also run together two things that this reframing separates: performing an apology, and the moral achievement of a sincere, repairing apology. Moral agency bears on sincerity and efficacy, not on whether the act occurred. The thesis predicts an inversion of the usual ordering. On uptake views, conventional acts like apologising come out easier for LLMs than assertion, which depends on content and a norm of truth. On intentionalist views, the order flips. The key premise is that the apology denial equivocates between act-performance and felicity or sincerity.

Appraiser (blind)
Reading the dispute as one about illocutionary metaphysics (uptake versus intention) is a sound reframing, but the Austin/Searle/Hornsby divide is familiar.

Freiman and Miller introduce quasi-testimony as the epistemologist's common ground. They list differences from human assertion: no play, pre-programmed, odd error profiles, no moral status. All of these concern the second role, answerability. None of them affects the first role, which on a Craig-style account is the point of the testimony concept: letting hearers pick out and use good sources. LLM outputs play that informant-flagging role completely; hearers rely on them exactly as they rely on testimony. The denials (Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, Skiba, Magnus et al.) are about the commitment role, which needs intention, norms and sanction. So the two camps use 'assert' for different halves of what is a single act only in humans. The key premise is that the two roles are separable. The argument then predicts that the 'diminished' framing is an artefact of treating the human fusion as the paradigm, and that the question 'does it really assert?' has no further fact beyond which role the word is held to track.

Splitting assertion into informant-flagging and answerability roles is suggestive, though it comes close to a verbal-dispute dissolution.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target

Sketch

Freiman and Miller's most neglected item is that machine assertions 'go wrong in different ways'. Take that seriously. Testimony works because hearers hold a tacit error model of the source (lying, sincere mistake, incompetence) and calibrate trust to it. Human-style speech-act attribution imports that error model wholesale. The live dispute is then whether to apply the human error model, apply a different one, or apply none. Denials say the human model is inapt. Attributions say it is nearly apt. Proxy views say to use the error model of the designer. The 'only produce text humans interpret as such' framing assumes interpretation is a free-floating projection. Following Austin on uptake, though, uptake can be correct or incorrect, and what it answers to is the fit between the interpretive stance and the source's actual error structure. So the question becomes a hearer-side question of stance selection. The key premise is that assertion's content-conditions include a standard of apt uptake, so that 'interpreted as an assertion' can be criticised on grounds other than the speaker's mental life.

Appraiser (blind)
Making uptake answerable to the fit between the hearer's error model and the source's actual failure profile is a novel angle, but the sketch is underdeveloped.

Once it is the subject, the 'communicative intention' dispute becomes a dispute about whether fictional-character-like agents can assert, which is a question about narrators and not about machine minds.

Freiman and Miller ask whether 'artificial entities' or devices assert, treating the instrument as the unit, as do Gubelmann (the organism-like system), Attah (the pipeline) and Butlin (the agent). But an LLM is a conditional generator of many speaker-profiles, and what carries consistent commitments, a stable voice and a record that hearers can hold to account is the persona sustained across a session. The weights have no more of a single stance than a language or a library does (compare Barandiaran and Almendros's 'library that talks'). So the organismic, sanction and proxy arguments each test the wrong bearer. Organisms, sanctions and designers are properties of the substrate. Commitments live at the persona level. The question is then whether a persona that is supported by a substrate but is not identical to it can perform acts. We already treat narrators, ventriloquist dummies in the act, and stage characters as asserting 'within' a frame. The key premise is that speaker-individuation is a prior question and that the persona satisfies the individuation conditions for hearer-directed accountability better than the model does. This differs from fictionalism, which says the user pretends. Here the persona is a real, stable bearer of commitments.

Appraiser (blind)
The persona as bearer of commitments is interesting, but it overlaps with thesis 4 and with existing role-play accounts of LLMs.

Freiman and Miller present quasi-testimony as a descriptive category fitted to the properties of instruments. But testimony and assertion are status-conferring practices: a witness, a guarantor, a signatory. Such standings are partly constituted by the community's willingness to extend answerability, make retractions meaningful, and attach consequences (as in Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition). Whether an LLM meets the sanction condition depends on whether we build channels (retraction records, liability, reputation tied to model versions) that make sanction possible. If we do, the model's outputs become assertions with a recognisable standing. If we do not, they stay quasi-assertions or proxy assertions. So the intention-based, organismic and agency-based arguments all treat as an antecedent fact what is in fact the output of a social choice. The key premise is that assertoric standing supervenes on practice-level conditions, which can be changed, and not only on the speaker's intrinsic states. The proposal also explains the proliferation of intermediate categories: each is a different way of partially instituting the role.

The conceptual-engineering view that assertion is an institutional status is plausible, but it is a familiar move in this literature.

Speech-act types differ in the temporal horizon of the commitment-bearer they require, so 'can an LLM perform speech acts?' has no single answer: a conversation-bound LLM thread can plausibly assert and advise, but it cannot promise or apologise, because those acts need a speaker that persists past the context window.

Sketch

The debate runs on assertion and then generalises to all speech acts (Butlin–Viebahn to Skiba), or runs on a single act (apology) and generalises from it. I distinguish acts that are discharged in the utterance, such as informing, asserting and telling, from acts that create forward-looking liabilities held by a bearer identifiable through time, such as promising, apologising and vowing. The second class requires a speaker whose identity conditions extend over the commitment's horizon, which is a diachronic condition on the speaker. It is neither organismic autonomy nor a Gricean mental state. Weights, a context window and a deployed product each individuate a candidate bearer differently. A thread-individuated bearer can bear commitments whose horizon lies inside the thread ('I'll check that in the next step'), but not 'I won't do it again'. The key premise is that the persistence demand is independent of the intention demand, so the intention-based positions (Gubelmann, Attah) and the normative-sanction positions (Butlin–Viebahn) are each answering a different question for different act types. It also predicts that agent scaffolds with memory (Butlin's language agents) move along a gradient for promising without moving at all for asserting.

It is the same temporal-horizon thesis as theses 1 and 10, competently stated but redundant.

Gubelmann's test for intention, whether one can distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing, is missing the third category, honest mistake, and once mistake is included it is the category speech acts need and one that LLM behaviour can exhibit without any self-set autonomous goals.

Move · Target
distinction — Gubelmann's Kantian-cum-pragmatist argument, and the test-based inference from absent malfunction/wrongdoing contrast to absent intention
Sketch

Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT, the order-cleaning assistant and RoboCop no sensible contrast arises between malfunctioning and deliberately doing wrong, so no intention can be present. But intentional action has a characteristic failure mode that is neither malfunction (the mechanism broke) nor deliberate wrongdoing (the agent aimed at what is wrong): it is error, an attempt that falls short of a goal by the system's own standard. A false assertion made in good faith is a mistake in this sense, and assertion and advice theories need the mistake/malfunction contrast and not the contrast with deliberate wrongdoing. Mistake requires only that the system have a goal relative to which its output can be assessed as failing and that the failure be correctable by the system's own sensitivity to the failure, which is the structure Butlin describes as sensitivity to instrumental value. Applying the three-way test shows that RLHF-trained models and reflective agents admit the contrast. It then reclassifies the dispute: the organismic condition on intention is idle for speech acts, because the test the argument relies on is satisfied by externally set goals. Deliberate wrongdoing, by contrast, is the contrast that needs self-set goals, which makes it relevant to lying and not to asserting. The key premise is that the intentional/non-intentional line in action theory runs through mistake and not through deliberateness.

Appraiser (blind)
Adding honest mistake as a third category usefully undercuts Gubelmann's test, but it is a narrow point against one paper.

Take the airline gate agent reading a mandated delay announcement, the pilot's standardised callout, the call-centre worker on a compliance script, and the pharmacist reciting a required warning. Each is pre-programmed and confined to a narrow context. None has playful or imaginative latitude. Each is produced under an institutional purpose set from outside. Each is delivered by an agent who is not the moral author of the content and whose individual reliability is less relevant than the system's. These are still assertions, and the audience is entitled to rely on them and to hold someone responsible. Hence the differentiae cannot be what separates assertion from quasi-assertion. They separate role-assertion from free assertion. The key premise is that the epistemology of testimony already contains a role-bound, system-warranted mode in which what is trusted is the institutional channel. Quasi-testimony then describes this mode, and the machine case is one more occupant of it. This turns the dispute: the live question is whether the role-bound mode requires a human occupant somewhere in the channel, which is the proxy question under another description.

Showing that the differentiae of quasi-testimony also describe human role-bound assertion is a sharp point, but its payoff is largely a relabelling of the proxy question.

Standard cases of assertion by agents who cannot be meaningfully sanctioned include the anonymous pamphleteer, the head of state with immunity, the dying testifier, and the shameless serial liar who has nothing left to lose. The sanction condition then either over-excludes humans or is satisfied by models.

Gubelmann argues that no malfunction/deliberate-error distinction applies to ChatGPT, so it lacks intention, and he grounds this in the Kantian mechanism/organism divide. But take a chess engine with a 'let the child win' mode. It plays a losing move deliberately, and that differs from a bug in a way we can check, since the engine computed better moves and suppressed them. LLMs are an even clearer case. Interpretability probes and chain-of-thought evidence in deception and sandbagging studies show a model representing the true answer while outputting a false one conditional on a goal in the context. That differs structurally from hallucination, where no such internal representation exists. So the distinction can be drawn for externally purposed mechanisms. Either the test counts these cases as intentional, which cuts the test loose from the organism/mechanism contrast, or it does not, which makes the test uninformative. The key premise is that the distinction is fixed by internal functional structure and not by who set the system's ends.

A specific internal critique showing Gubelmann's malfunction test does not track organismic autonomy; solid, but a narrow target.

Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz argue that apology requires linguistic and moral agency in the one apologising, so chatbot apologies are mere pattern-matched form. But a press officer reading a company's apology, a clerk's 'we apologise for the delay', and an insincere or coerced apology are all recognised as apologies, flawed or insincere but real, with uptake and with repair obligations incurred. In Austinian terms, remorse is a sincerity condition whose absence makes the act an abuse, not a nullity. So the necessary condition cannot be the utterer's remorse or moral agency. What does the work is the standing of the party who is answerable for the wrong. For chatbots this means the deficiency lies in whether the deployer is bound by the words, not in the model's inner life. 'Bullshit' also presupposes an assertion-like act with indifference to truth, so the diagnosis assumes more speech-act status than the authors grant. The key premise is that remorseless institutional apologies are apologies.

Institutional and insincere apologies are a sensible counterexample to a moral-agency requirement, but the point is fairly predictable and a narrow response to one paper.

Green and Michel, using Armstrong's objectives account, and Arora both ground proxy speech acts in the designer's or deployer's objectives, as in recorded or conditional speech acts. That fits a fixed recording or an if-then script. LLM outputs, however, are not content the designer foresaw, and no objective of the designer concerns their specific content. The proxy theorist needs a human case where an unforeseen utterance still counts as the principal's act. Such cases exist. An ambassador improvises a commitment, a spokesperson answers an unscripted question, an attorney signs under a blanket power. They count because of the authorisation structure and the principal's liability, not because the principal had the objective. But in all these human cases the proxy's own judgment selects the content. If authorisation alone makes the act the principal's, there is a further question about who is selecting, and a spokesperson counts as an author of a derivative speech act too. If we then say the LLM is only 'sampling', we have conceded that the machine does not select, which is the very thing at issue. So the proxy view either fails to cover LLM output or collapses into a two-level view on which the machine also acts. The key premise is that the human cases are structurally like the LLM case in lacking content-level objectives.

The human-delegate analogy pressures proxy views to grant the machine a role, but it substantially overlaps with thesis 6, which develops it better.
