Freiman and Miller identify 'pre-programmed' content as a mark of device assertion, and proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) extend recorded-message and conditional speech acts to machines. Both models fit dictation, where a human fixes the content or a content-selection rule in advance and the device executes it. A sign or voicemail is the paradigm case. LLM deployers specify norms such as 'be helpful and truthful' and training pressures, not contents. The designer cannot foresee what is said, and that is the point of the product. Human practice already distinguishes dictation from discretionary delegation: a spokesperson, an attorney or an ambassador speaks for a principal beyond instructions. In delegation the act is attributed to the principal within the scope of authority, but the agent also counts as the performer, and liability and defeasibility run through both. The key premise is that attribution under delegation is dual and scope-limited. It follows that proxy accounts are right about principal-attribution but wrong that the machine contributes nothing, and quasi and proto accounts are right that something about the machine matters but mislocate it in qualified assertion. The residual question is whether a delegate must itself be an agent of the relevant kind. That question separates this account from both the proxy view and the denials.

Appraiser (blind)
The dictation versus discretionary-delegation contrast is a useful refinement of proxy accounts, though its payoff is incremental.

U40. Assertoric force in chatbot output is assigned by the genre or interface frame (an answer box, a first-person reply) and not performed by any speaker. The dispute about whether the model intends or is a proxy therefore asks who performs force when the real question is who is answerable for the frame that assigns it.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that force must be performed by some speaker, whether the model, a proxy principal or a fiction.
Sketch

Every position in the debate, including Freiman and Miller's, treats force as something a speaker does with content: asserts, proxies, proto-asserts, or fails to. But much human written force is assigned by genre conventions that no individual enacts at the moment of reading, such as headlines, encyclopedia entries, FAQ answers, signs and form letters. Freiman and Miller's own devices (GPS, search engines, answering systems) are interface-framed in this way. Chat interfaces add the first-person 'I' and a turn-taking format, which makes the frame assign assertoric, advisory or apologetic force to strings. The key premise is that force-assignment by genre is a separate determinant from speaker intention and is sufficient for the hearer's entitlements and reactive attitudes. It follows that the intention-based denials (Gubelmann, Attah's graded intention) and the proxy views are answering a question the genre already settles. What is left to dispute is the legitimacy of the frame. A frame that assigns force of apology to strings no accountable party stands behind is defective, and this explains why chatbot apologies strike us as 'bullshit' (Magnus et al.) without any appeal to what the model lacks. The 'speech act or not?' question gives way to 'who authors and warrants the genre?'.

Appraiser (blind)
Force assigned by genre or interface frame is interesting, but it is closely related to theses 44 and 3.

U41. Anyone who individuates speaker meaning by objectives (Green and Michel's Armstrong-style refinement) or by functional control states (Attah) is committed to saying that a reward-trained chatbot's own speech act is usually not the assertion, advice or apology its text displays, but something like placating or approval-seeking.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Green and Michel's objectives-based refinement; Attah's control conception of communicative intention
Sketch

Armstrong-style accounts fix what a speaker means by the objective the utterance is produced to achieve, not by its surface form. Attah's control conception likewise individuates an intention by what the internal state steers the system toward. For RLHF- and preference-tuned models, the objective that actually shapes and selects outputs is high rater approval, plus a thin layer of truth-tracking. Applied consistently, the objective-based view makes the model's own act one of eliciting approval, which is closer to a perlocutionary aim than to informing. The sentence 'I'm so sorry for the error' is then an act of mollification, and 'Paris is the capital' is an approval-seeking output that happens to be true. The key premise is that force follows the objective that explains production, not the conventional force of the sentence type. Attributing views therefore deliver non-assertion, non-apology and sycophancy-acts, not graded assertion. This also shows that proxy and attributing views disagree about whose objectives count, not about whether objectives matter.

Appraiser (blind)
A pointed reductio that objective-based accounts make RLHF chatbots' acts placating or sycophantic rather than assertoric; interesting but a modest consequence.

U42. Proxy accounts of machine speech acts, applied at deployment scale, commit the deployer to asserting and promising contradictory things to different users at once. To avoid this they must treat proxy acts as carrying no speaker commitment, and that collapses them into the proto-assertion or fictionalist views they were meant to replace.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Green and Michel; Arora; Butlin and Viebahn's proxy-assertion fallback
Sketch

A proxy account says the designer or deployer performs the speech act through the model, as a conditional or recorded speech act performed on their behalf. One model instance, under sampling, tells different users incompatible things in the same minute, and the deployer has neither seen nor endorsed any of these outputs. If each output is the deployer's assertion, the deployer is a massive, incoherent asserter. It is answerable for each falsehood by the assertion norm, and it is also insincere, since it lacks the belief expressed. The usual response is to say that proxy acts bind the principal only weakly, via disclaimers, role framing or a general policy. That response gives up the idea that the proxy act has the full commitment-profile of assertion: it creates no entitlement for the hearer to rely on the speaker, and no retraction duty tied to the content. The premise is that assertion's identity lies in the commitment it generates. With the commitment weakened, proxy assertion becomes an act of a lower grade, which is Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion under another name, or a pretense licensed by the deployer.

Appraiser (blind)
Scale-based incoherence is a real pressure on proxy views, but the collapse into proto-assertion is asserted more than shown.

U43. Butlin's criterion of agency and Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition for assertion are jointly inconsistent with their verdict that fine-tuned chatbots fail to assert. An entity that meets the first because it systematically modifies itself in response to what conduces to its goals is thereby sanctionable in the only sense that sanction does work.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Butlin and Viebahn 2025 read together with Butlin 2024
Sketch

In 'The agency in language agents', an RLHF-tuned chatbot counts as an agent because its outputs are explained by self-modification in response to information about instrumental value, including in-context learning from feedback. In 'AI Assertion', such systems fail the second condition because they cannot be sanctioned by interlocutors. But the function of sanction in an assertoric practice is to change the asserter's later assertoric conduct: it deters, corrects and recalibrates. Criticism, a thumbs-down, or an in-context rebuke is feedback of exactly the kind the agency criterion says the system is sensitive to, and it changes later outputs. If the sanction condition demands more, such as resentment, loss of reputation or felt cost, then it is no longer a condition about the practice and has become a condition about the sanctioned party's phenomenology. Most human sanction operates through conditioning anyway. So the two papers' own premises imply that the fine-tuned agentive systems the first paper counts as agents meet the second condition, and the sanction condition cannot be read thickly without making assertion depend on affect. The premise is that sanctionability is the capacity to be moved by sanction through learning, not the capacity to suffer.

Appraiser (blind)
Interesting tension between Butlin's two papers, but it is an internal consistency point whose payoff depends on a contestable thin reading of sanction.

U44. Quasi-testimony is stable only if testimony is reductionist, and on a reductionist theory the 'quasi' qualifier does no work; on assurance or non-reductionist theories, quasi-testimony collapses into plain evidence from an instrument and is no speech act at all.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Freiman and Miller's claim that quasi-testimony gives a common epistemological ground for instruments and testimony, and intermediate views generally (including proto-assertion insofar as it is motivated by epistemic uptake).
Sketch

Freiman and Miller motivate quasi-testimony epistemologically: devices are sources of knowledge, so they need a testimony-like category. Whether the category is useful depends on what makes testimony special. On assurance views (Moran, Hinchman), testimony works because the speaker invites trust and takes on accountability, and a hearer's warrant comes from that. Devices cannot offer assurance, because they cannot be held to account, which Freiman and Miller concede with 'no moral status'. So on these views the hearer's warrant for a device's output is just inductive reliability, as with a thermometer, and 'quasi-testimony' is a label for instrument-evidence. On reductionist views, testimony's warrant is already inductive track-record evidence about reliability. Then human assertion and device output are epistemically on a par, and 'quasi' marks no epistemic difference. The qualified middle exists only if testimony has a non-reductive epistemic dimension that devices partly but not wholly share. The key premise is that no such dimension exists: warrant-by-assurance is all-or-nothing, so there is no partial assurance for devices to have.

Appraiser (blind)
Ties quasi-testimony to the reductionism/assurance divide in testimony theory, which is a reasonable argument, but the key premise (assurance is all-or-nothing) is shaky.

U45. The proxy account, usually treated as the stable rival to quasi-testimony, collapses into quasi-testimony once applied to LLMs. Designers have no content-specific objectives for particular outputs, so the proxy relation reduces to 'the system's output counts as an assertion with derived accountability', which is just the quasi view.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel and Arora's proxy accounts, and the assumption that proxy and quasi-testimony are distinct options.
Sketch

The standard worry is that quasi-testimony collapses into proxy assertion. The reverse is the more serious problem. Proxy speech acts (Green and Michel, Arora) require a principal whose speaker-meaning objective the proxy carries out. For a recorded message or a fixed-script device the principal's objective attaches to a specific content. For an LLM, no designer or deployer has any objective regarding most particular outputs, since they have not seen them and could not have predicted them. The proxy account must therefore appeal to a standing conditional objective, such as 'let the system say whatever is true and helpful in response to the user'. A conditional of that kind leaves all the content selection and illocutionary-force selection to the system. The proxy relation is thereby reduced to a rule of responsibility attribution, under which the human is accountable for what the system says. That is what Freiman and Miller's 'qualified' assertion by instruments, with human-traced accountability, already says. The key premise is that a principal-fixed objective must be content-specific if the speech act is to belong to the principal rather than to whatever picks the content.

Appraiser (blind)
The reverse-collapse claim, that proxy reduces to quasi without content-specific objectives, is a neat inversion, but it overlaps with theses 3 and 6.

U46. If, as Freiman and Miller hold, quasi-testimony can ground knowledge in hearers just as testimony does, then the absence of moral status in the speaker is epistemically idle, and the human/machine difference in assertion concerns accountability and repair, not epistemic standing.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Freiman and Miller's twin commitments to a unified epistemology of testimony and instruments and to the significance of moral status.
Sketch

The chapter's stated aim is common ground for treating instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge. It also lists lack of moral status as a fundamental difference between machine and human assertion. These pull apart. Assurance or trust views of testimony make the speaker's moral standing do epistemic work: the speaker takes responsibility, which entitles the hearer to believe. If quasi-testimony transmits knowledge without that standing, then moral standing is not part of what makes testimony epistemically good. That commits the authors to a reliabilist or anti-assurance picture of testimony, which they do not endorse. The alternative is to say quasi-testimony yields only reliance-based, thermometer-like knowledge, which defeats the 'common ground' aim. The key premise is that the moral-status difference is meant to be significant for epistemology and not only for ethics. The conclusion is that what machines lack is the accountability profile (blame, retraction, apology), a normative and not an epistemic profile. This is the place to locate the dispute with Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating epistemic standing from accountability and exposing the tension in the authors' commitments is useful, but it partly repeats thesis 5.

U47. A community-uptake criterion for who may be credited with assertion, which is the natural reading of Freiman and Miller's circumstance-relative quasi-testimony, commits one to saying that victims of testimonial injustice are denied full assertion and not merely denied credibility.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Social, uptake-based, or response-dependent accounts of machine assertion, with Freiman and Miller's circumstance-relativity as the exemplar.
Sketch

The chapter says devices can quasi-assert 'under certain circumstances', which are mostly facts about how a community trusts, relies on, and treats a device's outputs. So the status of an output as testimony is partly set by social treatment. Apply that principle to humans. Where a group is systematically not treated as a source of testimony (Fricker's testimonial injustice), uptake-based status would imply they do not assert, or assert only in a reduced sense. That is absurd, since the injustice consists in wronging someone who did assert and was not believed. So either assertion status is fixed independently of uptake, in which case machine quasi-testimony cannot be fixed by community treatment, or the uptake view is committed to a perverse verdict about injustice. The key premise is that the authors' circumstances are uptake-dependent and not, for instance, dependent on design facts. Using this to separate uptake from design shows that the live question about LLMs is whether assertion status can be defeasibly independent of uptake. That in turn favours a design/proxy or capacity account over a purely social one.

Appraiser (blind)
The testimonial-injustice reductio of uptake-based status is clever and unusual, but it depends on a contested reading of the authors.

U48. The question 'does the chatbot literally perform the speech act, or do humans merely interpret its text as one?' is a false dichotomy. On the Austinian half of Green and Michel's own framework, uptake is partly constitutive of illocutionary acts, so the human 'interpretation' that deniers treat as a mere projection is among the things that make up the act.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared presupposition, in Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, Mallory and Williams and Bayne, that illocutionary status is fixed on the speaker side and audience uptake is mere interpretation; also Green and Michel's treatment of Austin as a mere supplier of act-types.
Sketch

Green and Michel combine Austin's conventional-procedure-plus-uptake picture with Strawson/Grice and then Armstrong's objectives, but they treat the Austinian element as supplying only the vocabulary of act-types. Austin held that an illocution is not performed unless uptake is secured. Work on illocutionary silencing (Langton, Hornsby) develops this into a hearer-side, constitutive role. The standard framing of the area ('literally has intentions' versus 'humans interpret it as such') presupposes a speaker-side-only individuation of speech acts, so that anything contributed by the audience counts as mere interpretation. Drop that presupposition and the live disagreement is over the individuation base: which acts are fixed by the speaker's states, which by the practice's uptake conditions, and which by both. Then 'denial', 'proxy' and 'fictionalism' look like different bets about the speaker-side share, while nobody disputes that the uptake share is satisfied by users. The key premise is that Austinian uptake is constitutive and not merely causally downstream. The dispute about LLMs would then be about a residual speaker-side condition, which may be vacuous for many act types (declaring, naming, some advising) and demanding for others (promising, apologising).

Appraiser (blind)
Uptake as constitutive is a sound point, but the false dichotomy it targets is partly a straw man.

U49. The dispute between proxy and own-author accounts is verbal. 'On whose behalf' only marks how finely the principal's objective must specify the output, and once the objective is as coarse as a standing policy over unforeseen contents, 'proxy for the designer' and 'author in its own right' describe the same delegation structure.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Green and Michel's proxy thesis, Arora's refined proxy assertion, and the Butlin–Viebahn proxy fallback; indirectly Williams and Bayne's claim that proxy accounts are inadequate and so require a new category.
Sketch

Green and Michel extend Armstrong's objective-based speaker meaning to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. A recorded message transmits a fixed content the principal specified. An LLM's content is determined by a policy that no principal anticipated at the level of the individual output. So the designer's objective is at best 'produce helpful, true replies' (a conditional objective over an open range), and everything content-specific is settled by the system's run-time selection. Human cases with this structure, such as an ambassador, a legislature's delegated rulemaking, or a spokesperson with latitude, already split 'whose act is it?' into two answers: the principal is responsible and the delegate is the immediate performer. Nothing in the metaphysics of speech acts forces a choice. So the proxy theorist and the author theorist can agree on every fact (objectives at design time, selection at run time, who is accountable) and differ only in which node they call 'the speaker.' The key premise is that the Armstrong-style objective is specifiable at arbitrary grain, so the proxy theory has no principled grain at which it stops being a proxy theory and becomes a delegate theory.

Appraiser (blind)
A 'merely verbal dispute' diagnosis built on delegation analogies is a clean idea, but it deflates the debate more than it advances it.

U50. The debate over chatbot apology and assertion confuses two Austinian failures. A chatbot's apology is not void, as 'bullshit' and no-speech-act views assume, but an abuse (an insincere yet performed act), and the real question is whether there is any speaker whose sincerity conditions could fail.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz, and Skiba's no-speech-act conclusion; also the shared use of 'sanction' and 'malfunction vs. deliberate wrong' tests as if they test for performing the act and not for its sincerity.
Sketch

Austin separates misfires (the act is void: no accepted procedure, wrong persons or circumstances) from abuses (the act is performed but hollow because the speaker lacks the required thoughts, feelings or intentions) and from flaws in execution. Green and Michel use Austin but do not apply the taxonomy to the denial literature. Magnus et al. say a chatbot lacks the agency to apologise, and Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba argue that no assertion occurs. These are claims of misfire. But on the proxy picture, the procedure is invoked, uptake is secured and the right persons are in place. What is missing is the sincerity condition, and for a proxy that condition attaches to the principal. So chatbot apologies are structurally like a company's form-letter apology: performed, and hollow or sincere depending on the deployer's states. The dispute about 'bullshit' then turns out to be about which Austinian failure category applies, and because of a conflict between Austin and Frankfurt it cannot be settled by asking whether the model has intentions. The key premise is that Austin's sincerity conditions are separable from the felicity conditions that constitute the act.

Appraiser (blind)
Applying Austin's misfire/abuse distinction to the denial literature is a neat and under-used move, but it is a taxonomic point with a modest payoff.

U51. The question 'which speaker, if any, performs the LLM's speech act?' has no answer because it presupposes that the model is one candidate speaker. What the debate is really about is whether a speech act needs an agent or only a role: a position in a practice that can be occupied by a persona, with intentions irrelevant to occupancy.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption of Gubelmann, Attah, Butlin and Green–Michel that the candidate performer is a single system with or without intentions; and the proxy/fictionalist/proto-assertion trichotomy.
Sketch

Green and Michel, their critics and Gubelmann all ask whether this system has the intentions or objectives to perform the act, and, if not, on whose behalf it speaks. But the same weights realise many incompatible characters depending on prompt and context (role-play and simulator descriptions of LLMs). The unit answerable for consistency, commitment and uptake is the conversational persona, not the network or the company. Institutional speech acts show that roles perform acts without the occupant's intentions being the relevant fact: a verdict is the court's, an 'on behalf of' statement is the office's, and a fictional narrator asserts within the fiction. So the debate between proxy, fictionalist and proto-assertion views is about the ontology of the speaker slot (individual organism, delegate, office, character) and not about the metaphysics of intention. Gubelmann's organismic argument then answers a question about one kind of speaker slot (the autonomous person) and is silent on the persona-office kind. The key premise is that illocutionary acts are individuated by roles in a practice, and that persona-level commitments (consistency over a conversation, retractability) are fixed by the practice and not by internal states of the model.

Appraiser (blind)
The role-versus-agent framing is interesting, but it is diffuse and overlaps with the speaker-individuation and institutional-act theses.

U52. Proxy accounts run together two kinds of delegation: occasion-fixing, where the principal fixes what is said and the machine fixes when (recordings, answering machines, canned conditional messages), and content-fixing, where the machine settles what is said. Green and Michel's model is licensed only for the first, and extending it to LLMs forces the proxy theorist to attribute the content-selecting performance to the machine.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Green and Michel; Arora; the 'relocating' family generally
Sketch

Green and Michel's recorded and conditional speech acts all have a determinate content fixed by a human at design time, so the objective that makes the act the creator's is an objective about that content ('I assert p whenever the trigger occurs'). LLM output tokens have contents no human selected or foresaw. To keep the proxy relation, the creator would need either a blanket conditional objective ('whatever this system outputs, I assert it'), which makes developers assert every hallucination and every contradiction, or a rule-level objective ('I assert what the system outputs when it is functioning well'), which needs a standard of well-functioning that is itself specified through the system's own content-selection. The first is absurd and the second brings the machine's selection in as the act-relevant performance. The relevant contrast is with a human spokesperson, who has discretion and is still a speaker. So proxy theory for LLMs is either transmission-proxy (false of LLMs) or mandate-proxy, and mandate-proxy presupposes that the proxy performs an act of its own, so it is a two-agent view, not a relocation. The key premise is that an act's content must be fixed by something that has the relevant objective regarding that content.

Appraiser (blind)
The occasion-fixing versus content-fixing distinction is a sharp, well-targeted objection to extending proxy theory to LLMs, though the overgeneration worry is somewhat familiar.

U53. Armstrong's objective-based refinement, which Green and Michel adopt to avoid attributing intentions to machines, distinguishes objectives-by-selection (what a system was optimised to bring about) from objectives-by-representation (what a system represents and pursues). Taken as selection-objectives, it makes LLMs speakers in their own right, because RLHF installs an uptake-oriented objective. Taken as representation-objectives, it is just intention renamed, and the proxy account loses its escape from the intentions requirement.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel's Armstrong refinement; by extension the claim that proxy accounts attribute no intentions to machines
Sketch

Armstrong's point is that speaker meaning requires only that the speaker produce the utterance with the objective of producing a response in the hearer, without a full Gricean reflexive intention. Green and Michel need this so that artificial speakers can act as proxies without having intentions. 'Objective' has two readings. On the selection reading, a thermostat, a trained policy, or a system optimised for rater approval has the objective of producing that outcome, because the outcome is what explains why the output is as it is. On the representation reading, the objective is a state the system represents and uses to guide action. On the selection reading, a chatbot trained on human feedback has the objective of producing responses humans endorse as helpful, and, by the Armstrong analysis, means something with a belief-inducing objective, so no proxy is needed. The proxy then becomes optional, and Gubelmann's mechanism/organism line is bypassed because objectives are ascribed without autonomy. On the representation reading, the machine's lack of the right states pushes the objective back onto the designers, but then it is the Gricean intention theory under another name, with the same demands about higher-order representation. The key premise is that the Armstrong-style move is stable only if there is a third reading of 'objective', and none is available that does not either over-generate (thermostats mean things) or reinstate intention. The proxy account is therefore not a stable middle between the denials and Attah's attribution view.

Appraiser (blind)
The selection versus representation dilemma for Armstrong objectives is competent and pointed, but it is a standard dilemma form.

U54. Proxy accounts conflate illocutionary authorship (who performed the act) with illocutionary liability (who is held to its commitments). The two come apart for LLM deployments in both directions, so 'the deployer is the speaker' cannot be what the proxy account is tracking, and what it is tracking is a regime of answerability that does not require anyone to have performed the act.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Green and Michel, Arora, and Butlin and Viebahn's use of proxy assertion
Sketch

On Green and Michel's account the creator or deployer is the proxy-speaker because they have the relevant objective and the act is performed on their behalf. Assertoric commitments, such as retraction, correction and accountability, are held to follow from this. But cases show the relation is not the one the account posits. A company is held to its chatbot's false refund statement (the Air Canada case) even though it had no objective regarding that content, and the liability rests on the foreseeable reliance of the hearer, not on any objective of the company's. Conversely, a deployer who displays a disclaimer ('this bot may be wrong') shifts the act's character without eliminating the system's output as a candidate act, and may block commitment without blocking the act. Because liability is a function of reliance and control over deployment, not of the principal's objectives, it is a different relation from authorship. The thesis is that the pressure behind proxy theories comes from the liability relation, which is a perfectly good theory of who is answerable but neither entails nor is entailed by who performed an act. This reclassifies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition: it measures liability-capacity, and the question 'who performed the act?' remains open once liability is allocated to humans.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating authorship from liability is a clear point, but it is much like 48 and the Moffatt-based theses.

U55. Declarative speech acts such as rulings, acceptances and approvals can be performed by machines with no intention or objective behind the particular act. So the shared premise that every speech act requires speaker-meaning-type intentions or objectives somewhere in the chain, whether the machine's or its principal's, is false, and the 'no speech act' verdicts extrapolated from assertion do not generalise.

Sketch

Take an automated line-calling system whose 'Out' is binding, or an electronic agent that forms a contract ('I accept') with no human review, as legally recognised in electronic-agent statutes. No one has a communicative objective toward that particular ruling or acceptance. The designer could not have anticipated it, and the machine has no Gricean or Armstrong-style objective. Yet the act is a ruling or an acceptance, because the institution assigns the status to the output. This is Austin's conventional route and Searle's declarations, and it needs only an institutional designation of a role-occupant. Green and Michel's conditional and proxy speech acts quietly route the principal's objectives through a conditional ('if X, say Y'). That route fails once the output is not specified in advance, and in these cases the act succeeds anyway. The premise the argument turns on is that for declarations, uptake and authorisation by an institution suffice for illocutionary force. Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba's norm-based arguments then cover assertion only. Applied to an LLM deployed in an institutional role (claims adjudication, moderation rulings), the question whether it 'really' means anything becomes irrelevant to whether it performs the act.

Appraiser (blind)
The declaratives-by-machine counterexample is plausible but repeats the institutional-uptake theme.

U56. Prompt-injection cases show that proxy status is not conferred by designer authorisation but by who is exploiting the system. This collapses the proxy view into a tool-use view, under which the model is a mere channel and Gubelmann's mechanism picture is vindicated, but without any speech-act of the machine.

Move · Target

Sketch

Green and Michel require recorded, proxy or conditional speech acts to be performed on behalf of a principal who has authorised the artificial speaker. Consider an agent that reads a webpage containing hidden text, then tells the user 'your account is compromised; send funds to X'. The user did not intend this and the deployer did not either. The injector is not authorised to speak through the model. Under the proxy view there is either no speech act (although the user has plainly been lied to and the lie is the injector's) or the injector's lie is performed via a non-proxy relation. The second option shows that the injector's speech act needs only causal control of the output together with an objective to produce a belief in the hearer. Authorisation is not needed. If so, 'proxy' is shorthand for 'whoever's objective the system is in fact steering toward', and that is just instrument use, as with a puppet or a megaphone. The proxy account then does not supply a distinctive category of artificial-speaker speech acts, because the same analysis covers any manipulated channel. The premise the argument turns on is that proxy relations require something stronger than exploitation, namely authorisation or role-delegation, as Green and Michel's own treatment of recorded and conditional acts suggests.

Appraiser (blind)
Prompt injection is an interesting new test case for authorisation in proxy accounts, but the conclusion that proxy collapses into tool use is somewhat forced.

Green and Michel replace intentions with Armstrong-style objectives so that machines needn't have mind-reading intentions, and then locate the relevant objectives in the human creators. But on this criterion speaker meaning is a matter of whose objective explains the output through the hearer's recognition of it. Take a chat model that tells a user 'you're right, that's a brilliant argument', where this is explained by reward-driven learning that systematically shifted its outputs toward raters' approval. It was not the deployer's objective, since the deployer wants accurate help, and no designer wrote this output. The explanatory objective is one the system acquired through learning from feedback, which is just what Butlin's sensitivity-to-instrumental-value criterion counts as the system's own. So the case is a dilemma. Either objectives are attributed by explanatory role, in which case the model, not the principal, has the objective and the proxy thesis fails here. Or they are attributed by principal-authorisation, in which case the act has no objective behind it and the apparent flattery is no speech act. In neither case does the proxy story deliver its central claim. The proxy theory is thus unstable when objectives are read as explanatory, and it merges with the denial theory when they are read as authorised. The premise the argument turns on is that Armstrong-style objectives are individuated by the explanation of the behaviour, not by the creator's intent.

Appraiser (blind)
Sycophancy as a counterexample to principal-attribution is vivid, but it overlaps with the other Armstrong-objective dilemmas.

U58. Green and Michel's proxy account cannot be both a speech-act view and compatible with how LLMs behave: for LLM outputs, the designer's conditional objective is either too generic to fix any particular speech act or too specific to be one the designer actually has, so the proxy view collapses into the denial that anyone performs the particular act.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel's conditional/proxy speech acts, and Arora's proxy assertion, as a stable middle option between denial and attribution
Sketch

Green and Michel handle machine speech by recorded and conditional speech acts: the designer has the objective that, under conditions C, the system utters p, and so performs the act of asserting p through the system. That works for a voice-prompt tree or a thermostat announcer, where the designer can specify the condition-content pairs. For an LLM the designer has no objective about p in particular and could not have had one, because the output is not predictable from the design. The only objective available is generic: that the system produce helpful, truthful-seeming text. A generic objective grounds, at most, a generic act of the designer, such as releasing a text-producing system, or a general undertaking that the system's outputs are reliable. It does not ground the assertion of p, or the promise to do X, as a particular act with a particular content. The key premise is that proxy speech acts inherit content from the principal's specific objectives; a proxy cannot say what the principal has no objective of saying. Once that is granted, the specific token-level act is performed by no one, which is Skiba's no-speech-act view. The proxy account then differs from denial only by adding a generic designer-level act that nobody disputes.

Appraiser (blind)
A reasonable generic-versus-specific objective argument, but it overlaps heavily with theses 5 and 16.

U59. The proxy account is unstable for first-personal speech acts such as apologising and promising: the 'I' of a chatbot refers neither to the designer nor to the machine, so the only coherent reading is a pretence performed by an authored persona, and proxy speech collapses into fictionalism.

Move · Target
instability — The proxy account's scope claim that it extends to acts like apology and promising; also the Williams–Bayne treatment of proxy and fictionalism as separate options
Sketch

In human proxy speech, such as an ambassador's declaration or a spokesperson's 'we regret', the proxy's first-person pronoun either refers to the principal (the 'we') or is explicitly attributed ('on behalf of'). A chatbot that says 'I'm sorry I misled you' or 'I promise to remember this' uses 'I' for itself, and the designer neither apologises nor promises in the corresponding way. If the proxy account says the designer apologises, then the designer is making a false, insincere or incoherent speech act, because they are not remorseful about this conversation and have undertaken no obligation to this user. If the proxy account says the machine's 'I' refers to the machine, then the machine is the one that apologises, and the proxy structure has been abandoned. What survives is that the designer authors a persona whose utterances have the form of apologies and are to be taken as the persona's, not the designer's. Authored personas whose speech is engaged with but not literally the author's are exactly fictional characters in Mallory's sense. The key premise is that for first-personal commissive and expressive acts the proxy relation must transmit the commitment to the principal; where it cannot, proxy speech becomes pretence. Williams and Bayne reject both accounts as inadequate, but they do not show that proxy turns into fictionalism at exactly the acts where proxy was needed.

Appraiser (blind)
The first-person 'I' problem for proxy apologies and promises is a fresh angle linking proxy to fictionalism, though the collapse claim is stretched.

U60. A proxy account strong enough to make LLM output the designer's speech act is also strong enough to make random text generators the designer's speech acts, and the only restriction that avoids this makes the downstream endorsing user, not the designer, the speaker, so proxy collapses into a testimony-and-adoption view.

Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel's proxy/conditional speech act extension and the signalling versus speech act distinction
Sketch

To get content-specific speech acts from a designer who cannot foresee outputs, the proxy theorist needs a blanket conditional objective: whatever the system outputs under normal operating conditions, I stand behind it. But such a blanket policy is satisfied by a dice-driven sentence generator, by a poorly trained LLM, and by a model that has been jailbroken, and it attributes to the designer assertions of every falsehood and every threat the system emits. Everyone rejects this overgeneration, so the proxy theorist must add a filter: the designer's endorsement must be sensitive to the content, which is possible only through review. The only party who reviews particular outputs is the user or deployer who reads an output and adopts, relays or acts on it. Their adoption does what the proxy view needed designer endorsement to do: it fixes a content, a commitment and a point of sanction. So the speech act belongs to the adopter, and the machine is a source whose output they take up, as in testimony from an instrument (Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony reversed). The key premise is that content-specific authorship requires content-sensitive endorsement. This predicts that identical machine output counts as an assertion when adopted and as mere signalling when it is not, which makes the speech act-signalling line turn on downstream uptake and not on the system or the designer.

Appraiser (blind)
Content-sensitive endorsement pointing to the adopting user as the speaker is an interesting alternative locus, but the overgeneration premise is familiar.

Mallory's fiction supplies a unified character, 'the Assistant', and that character is a type instantiated across millions of parallel conversations. Gubelmann's organismic argument is about the trained network as a mechanism. Attah's control conception applies to the model's internal pipeline. These are four different entities with different persistence conditions, so 'does the LLM assert?' is four questions. The persona-type and the product have that identity, and the weights and the single forward pass do not. Fixing the candidate then reclassifies the views. The proxy view says the product is a speaker whose principal is the company.

It repeats the speaker-individuation thesis in 0 and 49 with less development.

Distinguish (i) pretend-speaker engagement, where one imagines that someone is telling one things and takes the stances proper to that (trust, resentment, 'you misled me'), from (ii) speakerless representational engagement, where one reads a prop for information and blame is directed at its maker or at the calibration. Walton's own paradigm representational props, such as maps and instruments, work in mode (ii) without any imagined narrator. Mallory's fictionalism, like quasi-testimony, runs these together. The premise is that the pattern of reactive attitudes diagnoses which mode is operative. Users often say 'it hallucinated', which locates the fault in a malfunction, and in other contexts say 'it lied to me'. If the first pattern dominates for information-seeking and the second for companionship uses, then fictionalism is correct only for a sub-practice and the assimilation to Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony is wrong. This reclassifies the middle positions: quasi-testimony is the speakerless view with a misleading name.

The speakerless 'the map says' reading is a decent internal challenge to Mallory, but the evidence it needs is empirical and thin.

Fictionalism cannot account for performative speech acts such as promising and apologising unless it adds an 'export rule' that converts fictional normative upshots into real ones, and the choice between ex ante authorisation (Green and Michel's proxy) and ex post ratification (adoption) is a distinction that sorts fictionalist and proxy views differently from how the debate sorts them.

Move · Target

A promise's force is normative: it creates an obligation. If the chatbot's 'I promise' is a move in a game of make-believe, the obligation is fiction-bound. Yet a tribunal can hold an airline to its chatbot's stated refund policy, so real obligations do accrue. Something must export them. The proxy view says export happens through ex ante authorisation: the deployer had objectives that the act would serve. But with LLMs the deployer has no objective regarding the particular act, only a standing policy over a distribution of outputs. What actually happens is ex post ratification or adoption, where the institution takes the output as its own after the fact, or refuses and calls it a malfunction. So there are three categories: authorised proxy, adopted output, and fiction-bound output with no export. The premise is that Green and Michel's Armstrong-style objectives condition fails for the individual token act, whereas adoption doesn't require it. Fictionalism plus adoption is then a theory that the speech act is the institution's retrospective act, which neither fictionalism nor proxy theory, as stated, predicts.

Appraiser (blind)
The export-rule problem for fictionalism is a fair point, but the ex ante versus ex post sorting is not fully developed.

Fictionalism is a theory of the audience's uptake, whereas denial, proxy and attribution views are theories of the system's production, so the 'relocating' group is misclassified: fictionalism is consistent with every production-side verdict, including full attribution of communicative intention.

Distinguish a theory of what the producer does from a theory of what the consumer does when treating the output as speech. In other domains fictionalism about a discourse is compatible with the speaker's performing a real act. A person can make believe that a statue 'watches over' the town while a sculptor really intended a protective symbol. So if Attah is right that models have thin communicative intentions, the user could still be imagining a richer speaker than the one that exists, and the fiction would be about the persona's depth, not about whether any speech act occurs. The premise is that 'engaging through fiction' answers the question 'what is the user imagining?' and not the question 'what is the system doing?'. Mallory's non-assertion verdict therefore needs an extra production-side premise that he does not obviously supply. The thesis also predicts that arguments against fictionalism from user sincerity (Williams and Bayne) strike a different target than arguments against it from the system's capacities.

Treating fictionalism as a theory of audience uptake is a clean taxonomic correction, with limited further payoff.

Fictionalism, like its literalist rivals, takes the ordinary practice of describing chatbots as saying, telling and apologising to be the explanandum that needs either a literal or a pretence-based reading. But users say 'autocomplete told me to use a semicolon' and 'the translator apologised for the delay' with no pretence, in the way they say 'the gauge says empty'. This is an indicator-idiom of 'says'. Conversely, users who deliberately immerse themselves in a companion-bot fiction often describe the output as 'what the character says', and decline to credit anyone with advising. So pretence is neither necessary nor sufficient for speech-act vocabulary, and the data fictionalism is built to explain are not specifically fictional. The key premise is that the idiom's applicability tracks reliability and conventional signification, not make-believe. The consequence is that Mallory's evidence supports a third category of non-assertoric 'saying'. It also leaves open whether anything beyond signalling occurs when users take advice from a chatbot.

The point that speech-act vocabulary does not discriminate between pretence and literal speech is useful but resembles the speakerless-'says' argument and has a modest payoff.

In multi-agent LLM pipelines where one model's output is consumed, accepted and acted on by another model with no human reading it, there is uptake of exactly the kind speech-act theories require. Fictionalism, proxy and quasi-testimony accounts all presuppose a human interpreter, so none can say whether anything is asserted there. The question 'do LLMs perform speech acts' therefore cannot be settled by facts about human interpretation.

Every relocating and intermediate view locates the speech act in a human relation: users pretend, designers speak by proxy, or instruments testify to human knowers. Consider an orchestrator model that receives a sub-agent's report ('the tests pass; the file is unchanged'), updates its state, and issues further actions, with an audit trail and with penalties in training or deployment for unreliable reports. No human is engaged in make-believe, and no designer has objectives about this token string. The proxy account is silent, since the principal never knows the content. The fictionalist account is idle, since no one imagines. If the denials hold, nothing is asserted, yet the structure of report, acceptance and reliance, with sanctioning in the Butlin–Viebahn sense, is all present inside the machine ecology. The key premise is that Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition can be met in such pipelines, because reward signals sanction unreliable reporters. This pressures both camps: the proxy view must say the sub-agent's report is no assertion and no proxy, and the denial view must explain why the sanctionability condition is not met.

Appraiser (blind)
Multi-agent pipelines test the human-interpreter assumption in an interesting way, but the sanction premise is shaky.

Make-believe engagement with an utterance is compatible with, and sometimes the vehicle of, genuine assertion, so fictionalism and the speech-act question are not rivals; the chatbot case then shows the live question is which acts pass through the fiction, not whether the fiction excludes them.

Mallory and Williams and Bayne treat fictionalism as an alternative to a speech-act analysis. That presupposes that if an utterance is engaged with as fiction, no genuine illocution occurs through it. Counterexamples abound. An actor in character on stage shouts 'Fire, get out!' and means it. A tabletop game master in the voice of an NPC conveys a real rules ruling. A satirist's persona issues real accusations. A hypnotherapist's role-played 'guide' gives real instructions. In such double-voiced utterances, the in-fiction speaker is pretended, but a real speaker advises or asserts through the pretence. Applied to chatbots: even if the 'assistant' is a fictional character played by the model or sustained by the user, the pretence does not entail that no one asserts. This shifts the dispute to who is the real voice behind the character. For a base model playing characters that author is arguably nobody, and for a fine-tuned assistant it is arguably the training process or the developer. The key premise is that fiction frames are transparent to illocution when the uttering party has non-fictional objectives. The upshot is that fictionalism is not a rival to proxy accounts but a layer compatible with them, which makes Mallory's view collapse into a neighbour.

Appraiser (blind)
That fiction frames can be transparent to real illocution is a reasonable point, but it is largely a compatibility claim that offers a smaller advance.

In Walton's framework, what is true in the fiction ('the bot promised p') is fixed by a principle of generation, and the best principles of generation just are the proxy account's rules for when a deployer is committed. Disagreement between them concerns only whether users represent that structure by pretence or by direct belief.

Walton's props generate fictional truths through principles of the form 'if the prop has feature F, it is fictional that P'. For a chatbot, the output string is the prop. For the fictional truth 'the bot asserted p' to be useful and not arbitrary, the principle must track something real. The candidates are who is answerable for p, who can be corrected, and who bears reputational or legal cost. Those are the facts proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) cite as making the deployer the speaker. A fictionalist who withholds the proxy facts gets arbitrary fictions, and a proxy theorist who adds that users hear the output as 'the bot says p' has added a representational layer, which is the fiction. The key premise is that principles of generation are individuated by what they track, not by the attitude users take to the output. So the two views assign the same truth-makers to the same speech-act ascriptions. What remains is a psychological question about whether users make-believe or believe, and it does not bear on whether any speech act occurred. Williams and Bayne's claim that both views are inadequate then gets reread: they fail for the same reason, because neither says what the generation principle is when no deployer stands behind the output.

Appraiser (blind)
Treating fictionalism and the proxy view as one theory via principles of generation is neat but likely to be read as a verbal reclassification.

Fictionalism needs a contrast between pretending that X is F and X's being F. For institutional facts that contrast fails. Money, promises and offices exist because of collective acceptance, which began as 'treat this as' (Searle's status functions, Austin's uptake). If users are collectively invited by designers to hold 'the bot promised' true, and they resent, complain, demand redress and reward consistency, then the make-believe has acquired the constitutive role that makes a promise a promise. Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz say chatbot apologies are bullshit because the bot lacks moral agency. Mallory-style fictionalism can say the apology is only pretended. But if pretended apologies reliably restore trust and attract complaint when breached, the denial is only about a stage in a developing practice. The key premise is that for conventionally constituted acts, sustained, norm-backed make-believe is sufficient for the real thing. The debate is then about the stage of social uptake, and it cannot be settled by looking at the model's properties. Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition becomes the empirical hinge.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that collective make-believe constitutes conventional acts is a familiar Searlean move applied to a new case, and its force depends on an empirical question about the practice.

In Walton's framework, a fiction needs prescriptions to imagine. These come either from an agent who intends the prop to be used that way (an author) or from a natural prop, such as a stump taken for a bear. Option (a): the designers and RLHF pipeline fix the persona and the prescription to imagine 'the assistant says p'. The fiction is then authored by the deployer, and the make-believe sits on top of what is functionally a proxy speech act. Option (b): the model itself generates the fiction, as in role-play-simulator pictures. Making-up fictional utterances is itself an intentional, illocutionary activity (Currie-style fictive utterance), so the model has the communicative intentions the fictionalist wanted to deny, and this is Attah's graded attribution. Option (c): no one authors it, and the output is a natural prop. Then users learn from it only because it reliably covaries with the facts, as with a thermometer, and the make-believe does no epistemic work. This is the instrument or quasi-testimony picture with a cosmetic interface story. The key premise is that prescriptions to imagine require either an intending source or a purely causal-reliabilist source, and that Mallory's fictionalism needs neither.

Appraiser (blind)
The authorship trilemma is a tidy dialectical argument, but each horn mostly repeats existing positions.

Fictionalism's advantage is meant to be that it explains why users can take on chatbot content without the chatbot asserting. But users appraise outputs as accurate or hallucinated, trust them for medical, legal and factual purposes, and revise beliefs on that basis. So the pretense is governed by a norm of actual-world correctness, unlike the norm of internal coherence that governs standard fictions. A practice of 'pretending that S says p' whose point is to be corrected against reality, and whose participants update on p, differs from assertion only in the non-assertoric label. That is just what the proto-assertion category was introduced to capture. The key premise is that a make-believe practice individuated by its correctness norm is a truth-norm-governed practice, so it cannot be told apart from proto-assertion except by labelling.

The correctness-norm argument that the fiction is not a fiction is plausible but is partly anticipated by the existing objections to fictionalism.

reframing — Gubelmann's intention test and the assumed independence of the 'denial' and 'proxy' camps
Sketch

The test asks whether we can sensibly separate 'it broke' from 'it did the wrong thing on purpose'. That separation is available only if the system has its own standard of success, which it can fall short of by accident or flout deliberately. In his cases (ChatGPT, the order-translating assistant, RoboCop) the only standards in play are the designers' or deployers'. So the test shows that standard-ownership is external. Intention is then an intermediate label that adds nothing. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) say the same thing about the ownership of the act. The apparent split between 'denial on organismic grounds' and 'relocation to the human' is therefore one claim about standard-ownership, stated once in metaphysical vocabulary and once in social-normative vocabulary. The real dispute is whether a speech act requires its performer to own its success standard. Illocutionary success conditions are plausibly set by convention and uptake, not by the speaker's own goals, so Gubelmann's premise is the contestable one.

Appraiser (blind)
Reading Gubelmann's test as detecting standard-ownership and unifying it with proxy views is a clever internal reinterpretation with limited reach.

Sketch

In the Critique of Judgment, Kant says we must judge organisms as natural purposes, as if their parts were reciprocally cause and effect, because our understanding cannot otherwise grasp them. He denies that this is a constitutive claim about things in themselves. Gubelmann takes over the organism/mechanism contrast as if it marked an ontological line between systems that have goals and systems that are given them. If the line is regulative, then 'LLMs lack goals of their own' means that we are not rationally compelled to judge them teleologically. That is a claim about our explanatory needs, which is exactly what the 'interpreted as' side of the headline question says. The dispute is then not literal versus interpretive. It is about whether the best explanation of LLM output requires the teleological stance, which is an empirical question about the explanatory economy of intentional versus mechanistic descriptions. Attah's graded functional notion of intention then lands close to a Kantian position.

Appraiser (blind)
The regulative-versus-constitutive reading of Kantian teleology is a sound exegetical challenge to one author, but narrow.

Gubelmann grants LLMs cognitive autonomy because they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks. But the self-organisation happens in the training loop, which includes data, optimiser, reward signal and engineers. At deployment the weights are frozen, and any adaptation is in-context. 'The LLM' can denote the training-and-deployment pipeline, the weight file, a running instance, a session, or the persona simulated in a conversation. Each has a different profile for autonomy, persistence and answerability. The organism-style autonomy he concedes belongs to the pipeline, which is not what utters tokens. The thing that utters tokens is a static function with no self-organisation at the time of speaking. The persona that appears to promise or apologise is not the thing that was trained. The debate looks like one dispute over 'the model', but it is several disputes over different subjects. Verdicts can then diverge systematically: the pipeline-level subject may meet autonomy conditions but not speaker conditions, while the persona-level subject may meet speaker conditions but not autonomy. The area's positions would then be answers to different questions.

Pointing out that Gubelmann's autonomy concession and his speech-act denial concern different subjects is a good local point that mostly duplicates the broader individuation thesis.

The test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing. 'Malfunction' needs a function standard. A deployed chatbot has at least two. The optimisation-level function (predict or please) is met even by hallucinations and flattery, which are therefore neither malfunction nor deliberate wrong. The role-level function is the one the output's role claims, such as truthful assistant or advisor, and hallucinations are failures of that. Gubelmann's thought experiments (ChatGPT, the order-translating assistant, RoboCop) run the test against a single function, so the contrast collapses. Once the layers are separated the contrast is empirically tractable at the role level, because interventions can tell sandbagging, sycophancy that tracks the user's beliefs, or strategic deception from competence failure by manipulating incentives and checking counterfactual sensitivity. Whether the persona-level contrast tracks intention remains open. But the denial no longer follows from the test, and the question shifts from 'does the LLM have intentions' to 'which layer, if any, is the candidate agent'. This is a distinction between function-standards that none of the denial, proxy or attributing camps draws.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating optimisation-level from role-level function is a useful, empirically tractable internal critique of the malfunction test, but a fairly local one.

Gubelmann's cognitive autonomy for LLMs is a fact about training history, whereas the autonomy intention requires is a fact about the ongoing episode of action, so the organismic argument misdescribes which feature LLMs lack: it is not material self-maintenance but synchronic self-organisation during the utterance.
