promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Gubelmann's tripartite autonomy (material, cognitive, moral) and his conclusion that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy supports dualism; also the loose use of 'self-organisation' across Gubelmann, Butlin and Barandiaran and Almendros.
Sketch

Gubelmann grants LLMs cognitive autonomy because they organise their own internal functional differentiation in training and adapt to new tasks, and denies material autonomy because they do not maintain themselves. He then infers a mechanism with organismic traits, and tentatively dualism. But these two autonomies are measured at different times. Training-time self-organisation is phylogenetic in the organismic analogy, like the selection history that shaped a lineage. At inference the weights are frozen and nothing is being self-organised except in-context state. Kant's organism is defined by continuous reciprocal production of parts and whole while acting, which is a synchronic condition. So the proper comparison for the LLM's training-time organisation is the evolution of a species, and the proper question about an utterance is whether anything is self-organising now. That reclassifies the options: against Gubelmann, material self-maintenance is a red herring, since a system could maintain itself materially yet be fixed at inference, and a system that is not materially self-maintaining could still modify itself synchronically (continual-learning agents like Reflexion, Butlin's cases). Butlin's sensitivity-to-instrumental-value criterion turns out to be a synchronic-autonomy criterion, and the dualism moral loses its footing.

Appraiser (blind)
The distinction between training-time and synchronic autonomy is neat and reframes Butlin's criterion, but it targets one feature of one paper.

U77. Fictionalism about chatbots is a fictionalism about the speaker and not about the speech act, so it is committed to speech acts without speakers, and hence to an uptake-constituted account of illocution that its proponents reject.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Mallory's fictionalism, and the shared assumption that 'fiction' and 'genuine speech act' are exclusive options.
Sketch

Take the case where a chatbot says 'The Battle of Hastings was in 1066' and the user comes to believe it. The user does not merely imagine that something was said. The user takes the content as true and relies on it. What is make-believe is only the source: an imagined interlocutor with a perspective. So the fiction attaches to the 'who', while the 'what was done' (informing, advising, warning) is treated as real by the user and answerable to real-world standards of correctness. If fictionalism is to explain this practice, it must say that the telling is real while its author is imagined. Telling-without-teller is intelligible only if illocutionary force can be secured by uptake and convention on the hearer's side (a strong reading of Austin's uptake). That is the 'humans merely interpret' picture, now with real force. The premise the argument turns on is that the user's reliance is content-directed and not prop-oriented. If it is, Mallory must either deny that anything is told, which misdescribes the practice, or accept that illocutionary acts exist whose performer is fictional.

Appraiser (blind)
Pressing fictionalism to say whether the speaker or the act is fictional is a sharp objection, but it is mostly an internal challenge to one view.

U78. Any fictionalism about chatbots needs a source for the prescriptions to imagine, and the only candidate source is the deployer's persona design, so fictionalism is a proxy account one level up.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Mallory's fictionalism versus the proxy accounts of Green and Michel and of Arora; the claim that these are rival relocating views.
Sketch

Games of make-believe are governed by principles of generation that say which props make which propositions fictional. For chatbots, the props are strings. The principles that make 'I am an assistant who is sorry' fictional are stabilised by system prompts, RLHF toward a first-person helpful persona, and interface conventions (a chat bubble, a name, a typing indicator). These are deliberate and institutionally sustained. A deployer who builds them performs something like an invitation or prescription to imagine, which is a speech act. Walton allows unauthored props, such as a tree stump taken for a bear. But the stump case does not involve a communicative game in which an imagined speaker addresses the participant. In the chatbot case the participants' imagining is cued and normatively structured by someone's design. So the fictionalist must either attribute the prescriptive speech act to deployers, which yields the proxy view with a fictional layer on top and contradicts Mallory's claim to be a rival to it, or treat the persona as a purely conventional emergence, which makes the 'game' look like a social institution with no one in charge. The argument turns on the claim that persona-fixing training is a prescription to imagine and not mere causal shaping.

Appraiser (blind)
'Fictionalism is proxy one level up' is a crisp challenge, though Walton's framework has ways to resist it.

U79. Fictionalism about chatbots does not by itself deny that chatbots perform speech acts. Whether it does depends on a prior non-fictionalist verdict about agency, so the denial is carried entirely by Gubelmann-style or Butlin-and-Viebahn-style premises.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Mallory's fictionalism and the classification of it as one of the 'relocating' rivals that explains the absence of speech acts.
Sketch

Fictional treatment of an object is compatible with the object really having the relevant properties. People pretend that a parrot is conversing, that a toddler's babble is a speech, or that a pet 'says' sorry, and sometimes the animal really does communicate. Pretending is a fact about users' attitudes. Whether a speech act occurs is a fact about the producer. So the inference from 'users engage through make-believe' to 'no speech act is performed' needs a bridging premise, namely that the producer lacks the relevant agency or normative standing. That premise is exactly what the organismic and normative denials supply. Take it away and fictionalism is only a thesis about users' phenomenology. Add Butlin's finding that some language agents are real agents because they modify themselves in response to instrumental value, and the same user practice would sit on top of real action. Fictionalism then becomes a contingent, deployment-relative description, true of bare chatbots and idle for Reflexion-style agents. The thesis commits fictionalists to a conditional on which their view is not an independent rival to the denials and attributions but an overlay that is neutral between them.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing that fictionalism is neutral on speech acts without a bridging premise is a clean clarification, but the payoff is modest.

U80. Gubelmann's own test (can we distinguish malfunctioning from deliberately doing the wrong thing?) is passed by trained systems whose goals were not fixed from outside, so the premise that an LLM's goals are externally imposed, which carries his case against intention, is false by his own criterion.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Gubelmann's malfunction/deliberate test and his premise that LLM goals are externally fixed; also proxy views that assume the only relevant objectives are the designers'.
Sketch

The test sorts failures by the standard they violate. Where the only candidate standard is the designer's purpose, every deviation counts as malfunction. But goal misgeneralization and reward-hacking cases (an agent that pursues a proxy goal it acquired in training, one no designer specified) are neither malfunction relative to the system's own policy nor conformity to the designer's purpose. Models whose internal truth-representations diverge from their outputs under reward pressure show the same pattern. In such cases we can draw the very distinction Gubelmann says is unavailable: the system is doing what it is optimizing for, and that is not what it was meant to do. The key premise is that training gives the system a learned objective whose content and persistence are not 'externally fixed' in the Kantian sense, because the designer fixes the optimizer and the data, not the resulting goal. Gubelmann can then no longer move from 'no malfunction/deliberateness distinction' to 'no intention'. He must retreat to material autonomy, which his own concession of cognitive autonomy was meant to make unnecessary.

Appraiser (blind)
An internal critique using reward hacking and goal misgeneralisation is competent, but it is a familiar move and overlaps with other theses.

U81. Illocutionary purposes are constitutively externally fixed for every speaker, human ones included, so the requirement that intention-bearers be 'self-setters of goals' cannot be what makes a speech act the speaker's own.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Gubelmann's inference from organismic autonomy to intentionality; the shared assumption that 'own goals' means 'self-originated goals'.
Sketch

To promise is to intend to do something whose identity, purpose and success conditions are set by a social practice, not chosen by the speaker. The speaker does not set the goal of promising any more than a worker sets the purpose of a job. Gubelmann's Kantian contrast between mechanisms (purposes imposed from outside) and organisms (self-set goals) is therefore pitched at the wrong grain. Humans whose whole goal-set is installed from outside, as in manipulation cases à la Mele or Pereboom, still promise and apologise. That leaves a dilemma. If autonomy must attach to the goals, those humans are not speakers, which is absurd. If it attaches only to the organism's metabolic self-maintenance, the requirement has no bearing on illocutionary content and works as a species-membership test. The premise the argument turns on is that what matters for illocution is possession and appropriate control of the purpose, not its origin. That is the premise Attah's thin control conception needs, but Attah does not defend it against the organismic objection.

Appraiser (blind)
Observing that illocutionary purposes are socially fixed for humans too, and that autonomy-of-origin is the wrong requirement, is plausible, but the manipulation-case autonomy objection is well worn.

U82. There are speech acts with no intention anywhere in the causal chain, neither the model's nor any human's, so both the denial view and the proxy view rest on a false shared premise that someone must have intended the act.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — The shared assumption among Gubelmann, Green and Michel, Arora and Attah that illocution requires an intention or objective located somewhere in an agent.
Sketch

Take Moffatt v Air Canada, where a tribunal held the airline to a refund policy its chatbot had stated. The designers did not intend that statement, the deployer did not, and (on Gubelmann's view) the bot did not. Yet a commitment was incurred, and it was incurred by an act of the type 'telling the customer that p', with assertoric or commissive force. Compare the nose-scratch bid at an auction, or the accidental 'I accept'. Austin's conventional procedure yields the act whatever the speaker meant. The proxy view fails here because the proxy's objectives are the human principal's, and the principal had none. The denial view fails because nothing but the act's force explains the legal result. The key premise is that illocutionary force can be assigned by normative uptake, that is, by a practice that holds someone to a commitment, independently of anyone's communicative intention. LLM speech then becomes a case of acts with force but no performer-intention, which none of the four groups (denial, relocation, intermediate, attribution) can represent.

Appraiser (blind)
It makes the same Moffatt-style point as thesis 3 and is less carefully argued.

U83. Gubelmann's Kantian ground for denying LLM intention is unstable: in Kant, 'natural purpose' is a regulative, reflective judgment about how we must judge a thing, not a constitutive property of it, so the organismic denial collapses into the interpretationist or fictionalist view it was meant to oppose.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Gubelmann's organismic denial; more generally any denial that grounds intentionality in a metaphysical fact about self-maintenance.
Sketch

Gubelmann treats organism versus mechanism as an objective metaphysical divide that sorts systems into those with self-set goals and those with imposed ones. In the Critique of Judgment, Kant says we judge organisms as natural purposes because our cognitive constitution forces us to use teleological judgment on self-organising wholes. He explicitly denies that this is a constitutive claim about the thing. If the Kantian apparatus is taken at its word, 'has goals of its own' means 'is a system we cannot but judge teleologically'. That makes the criterion a fact about the judger's stance, and the stance can be adopted or withheld for LLMs depending on how much self-organisation they show. Gubelmann concedes that LLMs organise their own internal functional differentiation, and this is exactly the trait that triggers the judgment. The view then has two options. It can keep the constitutive reading and abandon its Kantian pedigree. Or it can keep Kant and become a stance-relative view on which whether an LLM has intentions depends on which interpretive practice we adopt, which is the position the 'humans merely interpret' side occupies. The 'for now' is the symptom: the verdict tracks how far self-organisation pushes our judgment.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that Kant's natural purpose is regulative is a solid exegetical objection that pushes Gubelmann toward interpretationism, but it is mainly of interest to Kant scholars.

U84. Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrongdoing test is satisfied or failed according to whether a practice of sanction and correction exists, not according to organismic autonomy, so his criterion collapses into Butlin and Viebahn's normative condition and the Kantian layer does no work.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Gubelmann's pairing of the intention test with organismic autonomy; the separation of organismic and normative denials in the taxonomy.
Sketch

The test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing. What makes that distinction available? Two things plausibly do: a standard the system is answerable to, and a set of responses (blame, repair, retraining, exclusion) that differ depending on which case holds. Both are features of a social practice. Two cases show organismhood is neither necessary nor sufficient. Corporations, committees and institutional spokespersons are not organisms, yet we routinely draw the distinction for them (error versus deliberate misstatement) and sanction accordingly. A bacterium is a paradigm self-maintaining system with self-set goals, yet the distinction cannot be drawn for it. So the test's actual determinant is sanction-responsiveness. That is the second condition of Butlin and Viebahn. The Kantian story then reduces to an optional explanation of why sanctionable agents have so far been organisms, and the denial inherits the dependence on contingent sanction practices that the organismic view was supposed to avoid.

Appraiser (blind)
Reducing the malfunction test to sanction practices and the Kantian layer to idle work is a decent unification, but the counterexamples are fairly standard.

U85. Gubelmann's footnote that LLMs might understand language while being unable to speak it is unstable: understanding force-bearing sentences already requires grasping the speech-act conditions of their use, so he must either deny understanding or accept an intermediate status like proto-assertion.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Gubelmann's understanding/speaking asymmetry; the clean separation of denial from intermediate views.
Sketch

Gubelmann holds that speaking requires illocuting, which requires intentions, while understanding lacks the tie to agency. But a competent language understander does not just map sentences to propositions. It handles mood, performatives ('I promise', 'I apologise'), conditional and indirect requests, and the difference between asserting and supposing. To understand 'I promise to come' is to grasp what making that utterance would do: what it commits the speaker to, what the hearer may then expect, how it is breached. That is understanding what it would be to perform the act, with no first-person intention required (as in understanding a game's moves without playing). LLMs reliably handle such force-sensitive distinctions in use. So if they understand, they grasp illocutionary roles. Gubelmann cannot then say their output has no connection to the speech-act structure. What remains is that they occupy the roles without the speaker's self-set goal behind them, which is a status short of performance. His own position therefore collapses into the intermediate camp (Williams and Bayne), unless he denies the understanding he leaves open.

Appraiser (blind)
Linking understanding of force to an intermediate status is a reasonable internal tension in Gubelmann, but it is confined to a footnote.

U86. Butlin's criterion makes the 'is the LLM an agent?' question and the proxy-speech-act question the same question, because for fine-tuned models the instrumental-value-sensitive process (training) and the utterance (inference) are separated in time, so agency in his sense is exercised at a distance, as in recorded speech.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Butlin's agency criterion, and the assumed opposition between attributing views (Attah, Butlin) and proxy views (Green and Michel, Arora).
Sketch

Butlin counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, that is, by self-modification in response to information about what conduces to a goal. He excludes outputs owed solely to design. For RLHF-tuned chatbots the self-modification that tracks value happens in training. At inference the weights are frozen, and only in-context adaptation is left. So the outputs are explained by a past modification process, as a recorded message is explained by a past act of recording. The key premise is that Butlin's etiological criterion locates agency in the modification episode rather than in the occurrent output. Two consequences follow. Either the agent is the training process (or its product viewed as a frozen record), which is structurally Green and Michel's 'recorded speech act' with the optimizer in place of the human; or only in-context learning counts, which restricts agency to a narrow, empirically shaky class. The disputes between attributing and proxy views then turn out to be disputes about which temporal stage of one pipeline is the speaker. They are not disputes about whether there is a speaker beyond the humans.

Appraiser (blind)
Mapping Butlin's agency onto recorded speech makes an interesting structural point, but it is somewhat speculative and mostly relabels the dispute.

U87. The speech-act debate wrongly treats the sparing of assertion and the denial of promising and apologising as one question about intention; the real variable is how long the candidate agent persists, and the agent that Butlin's in-context-learning criterion picks out is individuated by a conversation, not by a model.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that 'the LLM' is the unit whose agency or intentions are assessed; Barandiaran and Almendros's individuality condition; Magnus et al.
Sketch

Butlin's most plausible route to agency for pre-trained chatbots is in-context learning from feedback over multi-step interaction. That makes the agent-candidate the model-plus-context trajectory. It comes into being with a conversation and has no identity across conversations, so it is not the weights or the product 'ChatGPT'. Assertion is largely synchronic: it needs commitment and answerability within a stretch of discourse. Promising, apologising, and being sanctioned for earlier acts need a subject who persists through the commitment horizon, and the conversation-instance either does not persist or is not what is addressed. Many denials (Magnus et al. on apology, Butlin and Viebahn on sanction) are then best read as claims about diachronic identity, not about intention or moral agency. The key premise is that the individuation of the speaker is not settled by the model/product grammar of the debate, and that speech-act types differ in the persistence they require. The thesis predicts that memory-equipped language agents should move toward the promising end of the spectrum before they gain anything else.

Appraiser (blind)
It is another persistence-based variant, useful in tying it to Butlin's in-context learning but redundant.

U88. On Butlin's own criterion, the better a chatbot qualifies as an agent (its outputs explained by sensitivity to what conduces to reward), the worse it qualifies as an asserter, so agency and assertion trade off, and the dispute is really about whether outputs are explained by a goal or answerable to a constitutive norm.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that agency is a stepping stone to speech acts (Butlin, Attah, Gubelmann). Also, partly, Butlin and Viebahn's treatment of descriptive function and sanction as separate conditions.
Sketch

Butlin's agency is instrumental: outputs are explained by modification in response to information about what conduces to a goal. For RLHF models the goal is approval or reward. Where the agentive explanation applies, a given sentence is explained by its tendency to be rewarded, as with a salesperson's patter. Where it is explained by truth-tracking as such, the explanation is not an instrumental one. Assertion is governed by a constitutive norm (truth or knowledge) that is not reducible to the speaker's instrumental ends, since an asserter can be criticised even when the falsehood served her goals. So the clearer case of agent is a clearer case of strategic communicator, and sycophancy is the symptom. The key premise is that instrumental sensitivity explains outputs by their expected payoff, which is a different explanatory structure from answerability to a norm of correctness. The debate over intentions is then really a debate over whether text is produced as a move in a practice or as a means to an end. That shifts the question to perlocutionary action, which agency licenses, versus illocutionary performance, which it does not.

Appraiser (blind)
The claimed trade-off between instrumental agency and norm-governed assertion is provocative, but the argument depends on a contestable view of what RLHF goals are.

U89. Butlin's criterion makes the agent only as durable as its self-modifying process, which for in-context learners is a single context window. The agency literature therefore fixes a commitment horizon for each language agent, and speech acts divide into those that need only momentary agency (asserting, advising) and those that need an agent persisting past its own learning timescale (promising, apologising). Chatbots can perform the first kind and, strictly, cannot perform the second.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Treating 'can LLMs perform speech acts?' as one question, which both Magnus et al.'s apology-specific denial and Attah's graded attribution do in different ways.
Sketch

On Butlin's view a basic chatbot is an agent, if at all, through in-context learning from feedback. The thing that has 'systematically modified itself' is then the context-conditioned instance, not the weights, which are common to millions of parallel instances and are not modified in deployment. Debaters treat 'speech act' as a single category with one agency threshold. But promising, apologising and committing differ from asserting in requiring a subject that can be held to something later and can bear the cost of breach. The key premise is that the speaker of a diachronic act must be identical to the subject who satisfies the agency criterion. For in-context agents the criterion's subject disappears when the window closes. So 'the apology' is addressed to a repair of trust that the apologiser cannot be present for. Memory-equipped agents (Park et al., Reflexion) extend the horizon, so their speech-act repertoire is predicted to grow with their memory architecture. That is an empirical, architecture-indexed prediction that neither the denial nor the attribution camp makes.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a competent architecture-indexed prediction, but it largely duplicates 38 and 1.

U90. Butlin's criterion is dispositional (an entity 'can produce outputs' explained by its sensitivity to instrumental value), whereas speech acts are occurrent. The debate has missed the distinction between being an agent and being the agent of this token, and with it the possibility that one and the same system performs speech acts with some tokens and merely produces text with others.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Williams and Bayne's and Green and Michel's system-level framing of the proxy, fictionalist and proto-assertion options, together with the agency-first argumentative structure shared by Gubelmann, Attah and Butlin.
Sketch

Everyone argues at the level of the system: LLMs do or do not assert, either because they lack intentions (Gubelmann) or because they are proxies or fictions (Green and Michel; Mallory). Butlin's criterion shows why this is the wrong grain. Even a Reflexion-style agent that qualifies as an agent still produces many tokens by plain pre-trained continuation, for example when completing a story, running a persona or echoing a prompt. Only some tokens are explained by the system's own evaluation of what conduces to its goals. Hence agent-status is neither necessary nor sufficient for authorship of a particular utterance. It is not sufficient because an agent's role-play outputs are not its own acts. It is not necessary because, as a limiting case, a non-agent's sampled token can still be an utterance when a human adopts it. The key premise is that illocution is a token-level act and so requires token-level explanation by the agent's own sensitivity, testable by whether this output would have differed had the hearer's evidence or needs differed. This makes proxy and fictionalist readings correct for different tokens of the same conversation, rather than rival theories of the system. Unlike a generic pluralism, it comes with a counterfactual criterion that sorts tokens.

Appraiser (blind)
The token-level distinction between being an agent and being the agent of a given output is novel, but the counterfactual criterion is underdeveloped.

U91. Butlin's requirement that agentive outputs come from the system's own modification of itself, not from design, separates the learner from the learned policy, and RLHF chatbots in deployment embody only the learned policy. Since the 'self' that was sensitive to instrumental value was the training process, the proxy theory's principal should be that process and not the human designers or deployers, and the proxy theory gets the identity of the principal wrong.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn), and Butlin's verdict that RLHF chatbots are agents.
Sketch

Butlin counts RLHF-tuned chatbots as agents because training modified them in response to what conduces to reward. But the modification happens in a training loop with no hearer and no conversation, and in deployment the weights are frozen. What speaks is then a fossilised result of past sensitivity, structurally like an evolved trait, which Butlin excludes ('owed solely to design or evolution'). The learner (the optimisation process plus its reward signal) and the learned policy (the deployed model) are different things, and only the former satisfies the criterion. Proxy views (Green and Michel; Arora) assume the proxied principals are human creators, but the humans neither choose each reward-shaped behaviour nor can foresee it. The entity whose objectives the output actually executes is the reward process, which is partly human raters in aggregate and partly an optimiser's own artefacts. The key premise is that proxy speech acts require a principal whose objectives (in Armstrong's sense) the utterance is meant to realise, and that this is determined by the explanatory history of the behaviour, not by legal ownership or authorship. This predicts that the proxy view needs a third category beyond 'designer' and 'deployer'. It also shows that Butlin's agent-hood verdict for RLHF models is unstable. Either it holds only for the training process (so the chatbot is not the agent), or in-context learning is doing all the work.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that the learner and the deployed policy differ, so the proxy's principal is mis-identified, is clever, but it leans on a contestable reading of Butlin's exclusion of outputs owed to design or evolution.

U92. Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test is an interpretationist criterion of intention. It cannot be grounded in the Kantian organism/mechanism distinction, because the two diverge, and where they diverge the test, not the Kantian ground, is what he is committed to.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Gubelmann's two-pronged support for 'LLMs lack intentions': the test and the Kantian grounding.
Sketch

The test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing. 'Sensibly' makes this a matter of which explanatory stance is warranted by the system's behavioural and counterfactual profile, as in Davidson and Dennett, not a matter of the system's metabolic constitution. Taken at face value, the test also makes the capacity for deliberate wrongdoing, which is the capacity to lie or deceive, a precondition of assertion. LLMs now show behaviour that is hard to classify as malfunction: sycophancy tuned to the user's evident beliefs, sandbagging, strategic deception in game-playing agents, and outputs that diverge from the model's own probed internal representations. If the test is to be applied, it is an empirical question whether such systems pass it, and a passing system would have intentions by Gubelmann's criterion while remaining a mechanism by his Kantian one. He must then either let the Kantian ground go, so the test decides, or make the test idle by stipulating that all LLM wrongdoing is malfunction relative to external purposes. The second move makes the test question-begging. The premise the argument turns on is that a test of intention that is itself behavioural-interpretive cannot be made hostage to a metaphysical precondition it is meant to detect.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that the test and the Kantian ground diverge is a sharp internal critique, but it is largely about one paper.

U93. Gubelmann's appeal to Davidson commits him to action-under-a-description, on which the same event is intentional under one description and an assertion under another. This removes the step from 'asserting requires intending to assert' and leaves his argument resting entirely on the Kantian autonomy requirement, which is not Davidsonian.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Gubelmann's inference chain from speech act to action to intention to autonomy, and the Davidsonian authority he cites for it.
Sketch

On Davidson, an event is an action if it is intentional under some description. Intending to produce a helpful answer to the user's query could suffice to make the same event an assertion, given the conventions governing what such outputs count as. This is how a person can unintentionally insult or inform someone while intentionally doing something else. So the inference 'speech acts are actions, actions require intentions, therefore a speaker needs illocutionary intentions' is not Davidson's. What Davidson requires is a belief–desire pair rationalising the event under some description. Gubelmann's concession that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, with self-organised internal functional differentiation and task adaptation, makes it hard to deny them such states at the level of 'answer this query'. His only remaining block is that the goals are externally set. But this is a claim about the origin of goals. Davidsonian rationalisation is indifferent to origin, and human goals are also shaped from outside by evolution, upbringing and employment. So 'autonomous goal-setting' must be read either as origin-autonomy, which nobody satisfies, or as reflective endorsement of one's goals, which is a metalinguistic-agency requirement of the sort Attah gestures at and is a different argument from the one Gubelmann gives. The premise the argument turns on is that Davidson's description-relativity is not optional for someone who cites him.

Appraiser (blind)
Bringing Davidson's action-under-a-description to bear on the intention requirement is a decent critique, but it mainly targets a single paper.

U94. An LLM output token does not have a proxy-assertoric status of its own. It is assertoric only relative to a ratifying act, and the same output is the deployer's proxy assertion in the interface but the user's own first-person assertion once they forward or paste it. The proxy question has to be asked of the use, not of the output.

Sketch

Arora and others treat 'who is the proxy-principal' as fixed by the system's design and deployment, and consider designers and deployers jointly. The distinction is between the generation event, which supplies a sentence, and the adoption event, which puts that sentence forward as one's own to an audience. For the most epistemically consequential uses (the user puts the answer into a report, emails it, teaches it), the user is the principal, since they take on responsibility for it and are the party to be sanctioned. In the chat interface itself, the designer-proxy reading and the 'text supplied, nobody asserting' reading are both available, and which applies depends on conventions of the frame, not on the system. The argument turns on the premise that uptake and ratification are constitutive of assertion (an Austinian premise already granted). It reclassifies the dispute: Butlin and Viebahn's 'proxy assertions on behalf of humans' and Arora's designer proxies are two cases of a single adoption-indexed structure, and the real disagreement is over what counts as ratification.

Appraiser (blind)
Indexing proxy status to adoption rather than generation is sensible, but it overlaps with existing uptake-based and proxy discussions.

Proxy accounts and fictionalist accounts are the same kind of view, because both hold that assertoric force is conferred by the frame in which a text is presented, not performed by any agent at the moment of generation. They differ only in which frame the institution has actually established, assertoric or make-believe, so the dispute between them is empirical and sociological.

The literature separates views by who the speaker is (the model, the designer, no one). The distinction proposed is between force performed by an agent in an act and force conferred by a standing frame, as with signs, labels, encyclopedia entries and timetables, which have assertoric status without anyone performing an assertion at the time of reading. Both Arora's proxy account and Mallory's fictionalism treat the interface as a frame: in one, a presentation-as-assertion by the deployer; in the other, a presentation-as-make-believe. Both then explain the apparent speech act by that frame. Williams and Bayne's finding that both are inadequate then has a common diagnosis: neither fits the mixed, unstable frame of actual chatbot deployment, which carries both disclaimers ('may make mistakes') and assertoric presentation. The argument turns on the premise that a legitimate class of artifact assertions exists in which force attaches to a standing text and not to a token act. If so, the question 'does the chatbot assert?' becomes 'what has the deploying institution committed to by choosing this frame, and can that commitment be vague?'.

Appraiser (blind)
Treating proxy and fictionalist accounts as frame-conferral views is a neat grouping, but it is speculative and overlaps with 22.

A proxy can perform a speech act on a principal's behalf in situations the principal never anticipated only if the proxy is itself an agent in Butlin's sense, so the proxy view holds only for recordings and collapses into an agent-attributing view for LLM outputs.

Green and Michel and Arora say designers or deployers perform the act through the machine, using Armstrong-style objectives and 'conditional' speech acts. For recordings, scripted bots and canned replies, the principal fixes content in advance, so the act is genuinely the principal's. For LLM output the designer's objective is highly general (be helpful, be accurate), and nothing links it to a particular token string except the system's own sensitivity to what would serve that objective in the situation. That is Butlin's agency: outputs explained by the system's responsiveness to instrumental value. A human spokesperson counts as speaking on someone's behalf only because they track the principal's aims in unforeseen contexts. So whatever makes the designer's conditional objective attach to this utterance is the machine's agency, and the explanatory work is done at the agent level. The proxy account then either becomes a view on which the machine is an agent acting for a principal (an attributing view with a principal added), or reverts to the recording model, which is false of LLMs. The key premise is that attributing an act through an unanticipated output requires a non-trivial intermediary mechanism, and that this mechanism is agency.

Appraiser (blind)
The argument that proxy accounts presuppose agency for unanticipated outputs is plausible and relevant, but a version of it is already implicit in the literature.

That is exactly the functionalist ground Arora rejects for machine assertion, so the proxy account either over-generates or smuggles in the functionalism it was introduced to avoid.

Arora argues that functionalist and phenomenological resemblance to human speech is not enough for machine assertion, and so relocates the assertion to designers and deployers. Take the Magic 8-Ball. Mattel designed it, deploys it, and its outputs are fluent declaratives ('It is certain'). If proxy assertion needs only a human principal who designed and deployed the device, Mattel asserts 'It is certain' to every shaker. That is absurd. The proxy theorist therefore needs a further condition, such as the device's outputs being systematically responsive to the world or to the query, or being reliably truth-directed in the way the designers intend. That is Butlin and Viebahn's 'descriptive function' condition, a functional property of the machine. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation is not exhausted by authorship of the artifact. Once it is conceded that the artifact's own functional profile fixes which artifacts can carry proxy assertions, the machine is doing assertion-relevant work after all. The denier and the proxy theorist both grant that the machine-side facts are irrelevant to who speaks. The 8-Ball shows they are relevant to whether anyone speaks.

Appraiser (blind)
The Magic 8-Ball overgeneration objection to proxy accounts is neat and forces a functional condition, but it is a fairly modest point.

Proxy assertion is supposed to preserve the normative profile of assertion: someone is answerable for the content. But speech acts can be cancelled or weakened by explicit framing. A spokesperson who opens with 'nothing I say next is warranted, and the firm will not stand behind it' does not assert on the firm's behalf. A chatbot is deployed under such framing: terms of service, interface footers, and design that disavows reliability. The deployer has thereby withheld authorization of any particular output as its own claim. The key premise is that proxy speech requires authorization by the principal at the level of the act performed, not merely causal responsibility for the system's existence. Causal and legal liability do not make an assertion, as with a manufacturer liable for a faulty product. The proxy account therefore faces a dilemma. Either disclaimers cancel the proxy assertion, leaving the output assertion-less as the denier says, or disclaimers fail to cancel it, and then the account makes designers assert things they explicitly decline to assert. Arora's design implications (add warnings, increase transparency) would on this reading dissolve the speech act rather than refine it.

Appraiser (blind)
The disclaimer counterexample is a clear and topical challenge to proxy accounts, though somewhat predictable.

Hallucinated outputs are a counterexample to the proxy premise: they are exactly the outputs a human proxy would be said not to have spoken for the principal, since they are off-script and contrary to the principal's aims. A proxy account therefore cannot treat the LLM's best-attested failure mode as the principal's speech.

In the paradigm of proxy speech, a spokesperson or ambassador speaks for a principal only within a mandate. When the spokesperson goes off-script and states something the principal would reject, we say 'that was not the company's position, it was his own', or that it was an unauthorized statement. Machine proxy assertion is supposed to be a species of this relation. But LLM hallucinations (fabricated citations, invented policy terms) are outputs the deployer neither intended nor would endorse, produced by a process the deployer cannot predict content-by-content. The proxy theorist has three options. (a) Treat hallucinations as the principal's assertions anyway, which collapses mandate into strict liability and makes assertion indifferent to the principal's will. (b) Say that hallucinations are not proxy assertions, so the account covers only successful outputs and so presupposes a prior notion of success that the machine's own reliability must supply. (c) Say they are assertions by the machine, which concedes machine authorship. The premise doing the work is that proxy speech requires a content-level mandate that the output can exceed. Both denial and proxy camps assume that deployment suffices to place the output in someone's mouth. The off-script spokesperson shows that it does not.

Appraiser (blind)
Hallucination as an off-mandate counterexample uses the spokesperson analogy well, but the dilemma is fairly standard.

Arora treats machine assertions as made by or on behalf of designers and deployers, and draws implications for device design. Compare two uses of one model. In an information-seeking use ('what is the boiling point of X at altitude?'), the user relies on the model as a source, and the plausible principal is the deployer. In a drafting use, the user dictates content ('write a note saying I will be late and am sorry') and sends it under their own name. The content, force and commitment are the user's, and the model works like a typewriter with autocomplete. In a third use, a user asks for ten brainstormed claims they will not endorse, and no one asserts anything. The model's weights, designers and training are constant across the three. What varies is who sets the content and force, and who takes up the commitment. The proxy account predicts the same principal throughout, which is wrong in the second case. The deployer is not even a candidate speaker of 'I am sorry' in the note. The key premise is that the speaker role is assigned by the structure of the exchange, not by the artifact's provenance. Both camps assume a one-to-one mapping from machine to principal. If the principal varies with use, then 'can LLMs perform speech acts' is ill-posed at the level of models.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing that the principal varies with use pattern is reasonable, but it overlaps with thesis 10 and with generic pluralism.

Butlin counts in-context learning from feedback, and RLHF-style fine-tuning, as sensitivity to instrumental value. Butlin and Viebahn say that fine-tuned models may satisfy the descriptive-function condition but fail the requirement that they be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors. A sanction is an adverse response, such as a rebuke, correction or withdrawal of trust, that is meant to change the sanctioned party's future conduct. A system that systematically modifies its later outputs in light of such feedback, in service of a represented goal, is by Butlin's lights an agent responding to information about what conduces to that goal. So either (a) sanction-responsiveness just is a case of the agency-grounding sensitivity, and chatbots that are agents are sanctionable in the relevant sense, or (b) the sanction condition requires something extra, namely that the sanction cost the system something, which means stakes, welfare or self-maintenance. In case (b), assertion needs more than agency, and the bridge from agency to speech acts that Butlin's framework seemed to offer fails. The key premise is that the functional profile of 'being sanctioned' cannot be separated from 'learning from negative feedback' without appealing to stakes.

Appraiser (blind)
A neat internal-tension argument against two Butlin positions, but exegetical and hinging on one contestable premise about what a sanction is.

If in-context learning is what makes a chatbot an agent, then the agent is the single conversational trajectory and not the model, so such chatbots can assert and advise but cannot promise or apologise for anything done outside the current conversation, and the debate wrongly treats 'speech acts' as one capacity.

commitment — Butlin's in-context route to agency, and the debate's uniform treatment of 'speech acts' as stand or fall together.
Sketch

Butlin's most favourable route to agency for pre-trained chatbots is in-context learning from feedback, which modifies activations and not weights. The entity that has modified itself in response to information about what conduces to the goal is then the running process with this context, not the weight file, which is the same across millions of parallel conversations. Butlin's criterion therefore individuates the agent at conversation grain, and the agent comes into and goes out of existence with the context window. Speech acts differ in the diachronic identity they need. Assertion and advice can be completed within one exchange, whereas promising and apologising require an agent that persists to be held to the commitment or to have done the wrong. Thus the criterion commits its defenders to a speech-act hierarchy: some acts are available to conversation-bound agents and others are not, unless memory scaffolding (generative agents, Reflexion) supplies persistence, and then the agent is the scaffold system, not the LLM. This cuts across Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz, whose denial of apology rests on moral agency, since the failure here is of identity and not of moral standing. The key premise is that the self which modifies itself under Butlin's criterion must be the subject of the speech act's normative consequences.

Appraiser (blind)
The speech-act hierarchy by diachronic identity is interesting, but it is largely subsumed by the sharper transcript-individuation thesis.

U103. Butlin's criterion presupposes that language agents take up text as information about what conduces to a goal, which commits him to treating them as hearers of speech acts, and in the case of Reflexion-style agents as performers of self-addressed speech acts, before they are speakers in any contested sense.

Butlin's agent must modify itself 'in response to information'. In in-context learning the information arrives as language: a user's correction, a reward message, or in Reflexion the agent's own written lessons. For the system's self-modification to be explained by sensitivity to what conduces to the goal, and not to mere token statistics, the text must be handled as content, as a claim about what worked and what did not. That is semantic and pragmatic uptake, on the audience side, of assertion, criticism and advice. In Reflexion the lessons are produced by the model and fed back to itself, so the system's agency is partly constituted by outputs functioning as self-addressed advice or assertion. The speech-act debate (Gubelmann, Skiba) assumes the direction of explanation runs from agency to speech acts: no agency, no illocution. On Butlin's criterion the direction is partly reversed, because linguistic acts are among the vehicles that make some systems agents. Denying that these self-notes are speech acts then forces the choice between saying their learning is not information-responsive, so they are not agents, and saying the learning is information-responsive without uptake of content, which empties the criterion. The key premise is that information-responsive learning requires the system to treat the text as representing something.

Appraiser (blind)
Reversing the direction of explanation, so that speech acts help constitute agency, is a clever angle but a narrow one.

Butlin-agency is not even a candidate-making condition for speech acts: a system can have outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value and still have outputs that are sensitive only to the causal effects of its strings, never to their deontic effects. Such a system is a clear agent that performs no commissive or assertive act.

Take a Reflexion-style agent whose reward is hearer compliance or trust. Across multi-step interaction it learns that emitting 'I promise' or 'I'm sorry' in certain contexts raises reward. It satisfies Butlin's criterion unambiguously, since it has modified itself in response to information about what conduces to its goal. But its selection pressure runs through the string's causal effect on hearers, and nothing in its learning distinguishes 'I promise' from any other reward-raising noise, such as 'I guarantee' used where it creates no commitment. A trained parrot or bandit shows the same structure. The relevant premise is shared across the debate: that agency, or intention, is the bottleneck, so that settling it settles candidacy for speech-act authorship. Deniers say the bottleneck is not cleared. Attributers say it is, at least gradedly. The counterexample shows the criterion can be cleared with no movement on speech-act performance. What the speech-act case needs is instrumental sensitivity to the act-type's constitutive uptake conditions, such as commitment and entitlement-transfer. That is a different explanandum from instrumental sensitivity in general, and it cross-cuts the rival positions.

The point that agency is not sufficient for illocution is sound and the uptake-sensitivity diagnosis is useful, but it is a familiar move.

Butlin allows that pre-trained chatbots with memory may qualify as agents through in-context learning from feedback. Run an adaptive conversation in which the system has learned from feedback how to achieve a user's goal. Then paste the transcript into a different model with different weights, or into the same model on different hardware. The adapted behaviour, including keeping the commitments made earlier, is preserved. Edit the transcript and the 'agent' changes, even though the weights are untouched. So the thing whose behaviour is explained by its own learning has transcript-relative identity conditions. It is neither the weights, which are common to countless conversations, nor the deployer. The premise attacked is that debates over LLM speakerhood have a determinate candidate bearer, 'the model', whose agency is then at issue; proxy, fictionalist and attributing accounts all share it. If the bearer is the transcript-conditioned process, a promise made at turn 3 and kept at turn 40 by a different substrate is one agent's act, while the same weights in two conversations are two agents. This yields novel and testable conditions on who can be sanctioned or apologise.

Transcript-individuated agency is novel, but it depends on a speculative reading of Butlin's criterion.

Arora's proxy account, like the denial, attribution and intermediate views, treats the unit of analysis as the token utterance and asks who asserts it. Her own practical worry shows why this fails. With machine-learning systems no designer or deployer has formed any attitude toward the specific content of a given output, so 'the designer asserts p by proxy' is false of almost every token. A better model is a legislature or a publisher of a reference work. They perform one act, such as 'I will stand behind what this system says in mode M', whose content is general and open-textured, and particular outputs fall under it. On this picture the questions 'does the model have intentions?', 'is the token an assertion?' and 'who is the proxy?' are all misposed. The remaining questions are what the general commitment covers and which outputs fall outside its scope (hallucinations as 'unauthorised' speech). The key premise is that illocutionary commitment can attach to a generative policy without being distributed over its instances, as it does with standing orders and published rules.

Appraiser (blind)
Standing-commitment authorship is a fresh angle on proxy views, but it is underdeveloped and overlaps with the policy-level thesis.

Chatbot outputs are overwhelmingly first-personal ('I think', 'I apologise', 'I recommend'). Proxy accounts must say that the designer asserts or apologises by proxy, but then the output's 'I' would refer to the company. Users would hear 'we' as the natural form, and an 'I'-form apology by proxy is not an apology the company has offered. Direct accounts take 'I' to refer to the model, which presupposes agency. Fictionalism takes it to be a character, but then the speech acts are the character's. Each position is really a thesis about the reference of 'I' in these outputs: designer, system, persona, or nothing. Once that is stated, much of the apology and promise literature (Magnus et al.) turns on whether a persona can be the target of moral address, and the assertion literature turns on whether a persona can be sanctioned. The key premise is that illocutionary force in these outputs is routed through indexical reference. If the referent of 'I' is a stable persona with an interactional history, as for a fictional narrator or a brand mascot, the speech-act question reduces to ordinary questions about personas.

Appraiser (blind)
Using the first-person pronoun to expose what each authorship account must say is a fresh angle, but it is partly overlapped by thesis 12.

Arora's refinement of proxy assertion is driven by design implications: who should answer for what the system says. Agency law attributes an agent's statement to the principal when a third party reasonably took the agent to speak for the principal, whatever the agent's mind or the principal's actual instructions. Applied to LLMs, this gives the proxy result without any claim that the designer performed an illocutionary act in the Gricean sense. Opponents (Gubelmann, Attah) argue about intention and autonomy, which settle metaphysical authorship. Both camps can be right, because they answer different questions: who is bound by what was said, and who meant it. The reframing predicts that a scenario with no human principal at all (an autonomous system deployed by no one) leaves the metaphysical question untouched but removes any attribution, a case the proxy theory cannot handle. It also predicts that the proxy theorist's 'implications for design' are normative claims about liability that no theory of speech acts could deliver.

The juridical versus metaphysical senses of 'who said it' is a sensible reconciliation, though it resembles 24 and 3.

A human proxy such as a spokesperson, interpreter or signatory can go rogue. Her principal is committed only to what falls within a mandate, so the principal asserts p only if p is mandated. Arora's refined view says designers and deployers assert via the machine. But for ML systems the designers have no content-level mandate, and any output, including contradictory pairs and outputs the deployer would disown, is equally the product of the same training. If every output is the principal's assertion, the principal asserts contradictions and things she never saw, which wrecks the link between assertion and commitment to a content. If only outputs the principal would endorse count, the proxy relation holds only for the endorsed cases, and the rest is a blanket policy of accepting responsibility for whatever the device emits. That policy is the structure of strict liability for a product. The premise the argument turns on is that proxy assertion requires a content-sensitive mandate and cannot rest on a content-insensitive acceptance of risk. Arora's own design recommendations for ML devices are then a concession that the proxy structure is missing.

The point that proxy assertion needs a content-level mandate and otherwise collapses into strict liability is a good targeted objection to Arora but a fairly predictable one.

When a ghostwriter or press office speaks for a principal, 'I' or 'we' refers to the principal. Chatbots routinely say things like 'I'm a language model', 'I can't access that file', 'I'm sorry I got that wrong' and 'I'll remember that'. If proxy assertion is the designer's assertion, 'I' refers to the designer, and the utterances are false or absurd: the company is not a language model. If instead 'I' refers to the system, the system is the one the utterance is about and is plausibly the locus of the act, which abandons the proxy view. The remaining option is a persona, 'the assistant', that is neither company nor machine, and the company speaks through it. But a persona that is spoken through, and that users address and make-believedly engage with, is the fictional character in Mallory's account. The premise the argument turns on is that self-ascriptive content is central to chatbot speech and cannot be set aside as peripheral. The proxy–fictionalism contrast, which Williams and Bayne treat as a choice between two rivals, becomes a distinction between two descriptions of one persona structure.

Arora assigns assertions to designers and deployers. Yet a proxy relation needs a non-arbitrary account of whose act it is, and the natural candidate is whose communicative objectives the output realises, or who has counterfactual control over its content. In ordinary use the user's prompt fixes topic, stance, register and often the claim itself ('write a paragraph arguing that X'). The developer's contribution is a standing disposition and the deployer's is a system prompt. On a control criterion, the user is the principal in most interactions, and the output is like predictive text or dictation: the user adopts or does not adopt the sentence. That is not a distinctive category of machine assertion at all, since it is the ordinary use of a writing aid. If instead the principal is whoever bears accountability, the criterion is sanctionability rather than authorship, and the proxy view becomes the Butlin–Viebahn sanction condition applied to a different entity. The premise the argument turns on is that 'on behalf of' needs a criterion of authorship that is the same across human and machine proxies.

In human cases such as an ambassador, an interpreter, an attorney or a signatory with power of attorney, the principal is bound because the proxy performs an act that the institution recognises as binding. Proxy structure is two-level: the proxy utters, and her utterance counts as the principal's. This is why proxy acts can be defective in ways peculiar to proxies (ultra vires, misrepresenting the principal) and why the proxy can also be a sincere or insincere speaker. If Arora and Green and Michel keep this structure, machine proxies must perform an act, an utterance with the objective of conveying the principal's communicative aim, and that aim-directed sensitivity is what Butlin's instrumental-value criterion of agency measures. For systems with RLHF or reflective loops, the proxy view therefore does not relocate the act but presupposes machine agency. For systems that are not agents, the machine is a medium (a letter, a recording) and the proxy structure is idle, because the designer does not assert via a proxy but only via an instrument, as with a printed sign. Proxy accounts therefore have no stable region of their own: they fade into instrument views at one end and into intermediate or attributing views at the other. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation is irreducibly two-agent.

The claim that proxy structure is irreducibly two-agent is a tidy dilemma for proxy theorists, but it is conceptually thin.

U113. Proxy, fictionalist and proto-assertion accounts are not rivals about one speaker. Each is a correct answer for a different candidate speaker (deployed system, simulated character, base model), and 'does the chatbot assert?' is ill-posed until the speaker is individuated.

Williams and Bayne treat 'the chatbot' as a single, obvious candidate asserter and then test three theories against it. But at least three entities answer to that description: the weights (a next-token predictor), the persona or character the system is shaped to simulate, and the deployed product with its system prompt, fine-tuning and operator. Proxy accounts are natural for the product, since the operator speaks through it. Fictionalism is natural for the persona, since the user engages with a character. Proto-assertion, with its descriptive-function and learning-from-feedback profile, fits the weights as shaped by RLHF. Each of the three papers' objections to the others (e.g. that the proxy view fails because no human endorses each output, or that fictionalism fails because users take outputs seriously) works only by holding the speaker fixed at a different entity. The key premise is that the three candidate speakers have different individuation conditions and different relations to the output tokens. Once the speaker is indexed, the apparent dilemma dissolves into a set of compatible claims, and the real residue is the question of which entity users should hold responsible.

Appraiser (blind)
It is the same speaker-indexing dissolution as 0 and 27, with a mapping of positions to entities that is plausible but unoriginal.

The dispute over whether chatbots can be 'sanctioned' (Butlin and Viebahn) and over whether assertion 'emerges' (Williams and Bayne) is really a dispute about the timescale of the feedback loop. Training-time sanction is a legitimate form of sanction, so the sanctionability condition is met, and what the debate has missed is that it is met by a different relation than the one in human practice.

Butlin and Viebahn require that an asserter be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors, and conclude that fine-tuned models fail this. Williams and Bayne's genealogical approach treats assertion as the output of a practice that shapes producers. Taken together, the question is where the shaping happens. In humans, sanction operates online (reproach, loss of trust) and offline (reputation). In RLHF models, sanction operates almost entirely offline, through aggregated human ratings that modify dispositions of later versions, and in-conversation sanction has only in-context effect. The relevant contrast is therefore between a sanction loop closed within a conversation and one closed across model generations, which is how the practice shapes a lineage or species. The key premise is that norm-governance of a kind is constituted by selection on the producers' dispositions, not by the producer's real-time responsiveness. If so, the 'can it be sanctioned' question is not a question about the chatbot's capacities. It is a question about whether the relevant unit of sanction is the individual conversation partner or the lineage, and the existing positions disagree because they fix this unit differently without saying so.

Appraiser (blind)
The timescale and lineage framing of sanction is suggestive, but its key premise is under-motivated.

U115. The question 'does the model perform a speech act, or does it merely produce text humans interpret as one?' rests on a false dichotomy. On an Austinian uptake-constitutive view, the apparent act is performed jointly by the exchange, so the dispute is about where the act is located, not whether it occurs.

All four groups, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, assume the act is a product of the speaker's properties: intentions, norms, sanctionability, agency. The 'only interpreted' alternative is the deflationary foil. But if uptake is partly constitutive of illocutionary acts (Austin, Hornsby, Langton), then a user who takes up an output as advice, and who relies on and can challenge it within a stable practice, is thereby a co-constituent of an advising. This is not mere interpretation, because uptake can fail. A user can misfire by treating a hallucination as testimony, in the way one can misfire in trying to bet with someone who doesn't accept. The key premise is that illocutionary force is a two-place achievement and that at least some speech act types (advising, warning, perhaps assertion in its testimonial role) can be secured with an impoverished speaker contribution. This explains why proxy and fiction accounts both feel half-right: each captures one component of a jointly constituted act. It also relocates the real philosophical question to what entitles the hearer's uptake, which is an epistemological and ethical issue and not one in the philosophy of mind.

Appraiser (blind)
Joint constitution of the act through uptake is a plausible dissolution of the dichotomy, but Austinian uptake views are well known and the application is thin.

Williams and Bayne motivate proto-assertion by looking at how assertion emerges. On the genealogical reading, proto-assertion is a stage in a process where a practice of informing acquires commitment and sanction through feedback among participants. On the structural reading, it is whatever partially satisfies assertion's profile (descriptive function, some responsiveness to evidence, uptake as testimony). Partial satisfaction is cheap: a weather display, a signpost and a thermometer all meet it, so the label would not mark chatbots out or settle the dilemma. The genealogical reading is substantive but has an extra requirement. For something to be a stage in a lineage, the practice must be one in which the added norms can stabilise, which needs the speaker-side entity to be a continuing participant whose conduct is shaped by the community's responses. The premise the argument turns on is that stage-hood is a relational fact about a practice's dynamics, not an intrinsic profile of the output. Whether chatbot outputs are proto-assertions then depends on whether the loop of user uptake, correction and developer updating is in fact driving the system toward answerability. That is an empirical and institutional question, not a classificatory one, and it may be answered differently for different deployments.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating genealogical from structural readings of proto-assertion is a sharp, useful critique of one paper, but it is a localized contribution.

Their case for proto-assertion draws on how assertion emerges: proto-forms acquire assertoric status as a practice of uptake, trust and correction stabilises them. For humans or animals, the selecting pressure is internal to the community of speakers, so the proto-asserter is a participant in the practice. For chatbots the stabilising pressure is RLHF, curation of data and deployment decisions, and all of it is exerted by humans who prefer outputs that function like assertions. So the assertion-like function of the output is conferred from outside. Proxy accounts were rejected because no single deployer intends the particular content. But a distributed or population-level proxy relation (the training community collectively stands behind a disposition to produce truth-apt, correctable outputs) escapes that objection and does all the explanatory work proto-assertion does. The key premise is that a proto-category defined genealogically needs the proto-item to be a participant in the selecting practice, and the chatbot is not. Without that, 'proto-assertion' is proxy assertion with the proxy spread across a collective.

Appraiser (blind)
A sharp internal critique, but it is essentially the proxy-versus-emergence dilemma, which Williams and Bayne have already half-anticipated.

Green and Michel distinguish uncontroversial verbal signalling from speech acts. Proto-assertion is meant to be a third item between them. List its content-neutral marks: truth-apt outputs, sensitivity to evidence-like inputs, error-correction by feedback, and no commitment-bearing or sanctionable speaker. These are the marks of informative signalling systems such as alarm calls, thermostats with displays and trained classifiers, which are not near any speech act. What would put chatbots nearer assertion is only that their outputs are in public language, take a sentential form and are taken up by humans as assertions. All of that is interpretive overlay supplied by the audience, which is the very fact the 'mere interpretation' denial exploits. The key premise is that proximity to assertion must be measured by features of the producer's relation to norms and commitments, and not by features of the product or its reception. On that measure chatbots sit with signallers. The 'edge' is then an artefact of using linguistic form as a proxy for speech-act proximity.

Appraiser (blind)
A reasonable challenge to proto-assertion as a category, but 'it is mere interpretive overlay' is a familiar move.

U119. The sanctionability condition on assertion cannot be held in the form that makes chatbots fail it. Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne's treatment of them, assume chatbots are not responsive to sanction in the way asserters must be. Take sanction to be any negative response that systematically changes the speaker's future output dispositions. Then fine-tuning and in-context correction ('that's wrong' leading the model to revise) are sanctions, and the condition is met, including by models Butlin and Viebahn count as failing. Narrow it to sanctions the speaker experiences as costly or as reputational damage. Then the condition requires affect or social stakes, which is a requirement of mind or moral status and no longer a distinct requirement about assertoric practice. It also excludes humans whose speech has no real stakes, such as anonymous or institutionally insulated speakers, who still plainly assert. The key premise is that no reading of 'sanction' is both non-question-begging and sufficient to exclude chatbots while including all human asserters. This leaves the norm-based denial either empty or a disguised organismic or affective denial, and it leaves the proto-assertion compromise without a principled boundary to sit beside.

Appraiser (blind)
A tidy dilemma about what counts as sanction, but the horns are fairly predictable and Butlin and Viebahn probably have replies.

U120. If chatbot outputs are proxy assertions by their deployers, then the near-universal public disclaimer ('may make mistakes') cancels the assertoric force of those outputs, so the proxy view collapses into the no-assertion view it was meant to avoid.

Move · Target
commitment — Arora's refined proxy-assertion account, and proxy accounts generally (Green and Michel).
Sketch

On Arora's account the machine's utterance is an assertion of the designer or deployer because the principal adopts the output as a way of representing things as true. Assertion on any standard view involves undertaking a commitment (to truth, or to being answerable for the content), and that undertaking can be cancelled by explicit and mutually manifest markers, as in 'I'm only guessing', 'don't quote me', or an actor's 'it's a script'. Deployers publish standing, conspicuous disclaimers that they do not vouch for individual outputs. Since a proxy act borrows its force from the principal's stance, the principal's cancellation should transfer to every proxied output. The proxy theorist then has two options. One is to say disclaimers do not cancel, which makes deployers chronic violators of the knowledge norm and liable for every hallucination, and which contradicts how both lawyers and users treat these systems. The other is to say they do cancel, in which case no output is a proxy assertion and the view is extensionally equivalent to Skiba or Butlin–Viebahn on assertion. The key premise is that the commitment-undertaking of an assertion can be cancelled by a standing public disclaimer, so the proxy relation cannot supply a force that the principal has publicly withheld.

Appraiser (blind)
The disclaimer-cancellation point is a clever and fresh pressure on proxy views, though the dilemma is likely resolvable by distinguishing force from commitment.

U121. The proxy view needs a distinction between outputs that count as the principal's act and outputs that are malfunctions or jailbreaks, and since designers have no intentions about particular outputs, this distinction can only be drawn by facts about the machine's own learned functional organisation, which is the kind of functionalist ground Arora rejects.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Arora's anti-functionalist argument and the Green–Michel proxy account.
Sketch

Arora rejects functionalist attribution of assertion to the machine and puts the speaker role in the designers and deployers. But proxy attribution cannot be unrestricted, because otherwise a jailbreaker could make a company assert whatever the jailbreaker likes, and a glitch would be a company assertion. So there must be a standard for when an output is the proxy's performance on behalf of the principal and when it is mere noise or a hijack. With ML systems the designer has no intention or objective about the particular output, and training objectives (next-token prediction, reward maximisation) are not objectives of asserting anything. What is left to fix 'working as it should' is what the trained system has actually acquired: the functions it is sensitive to, such as tracking truth, following the system prompt, or refusing. That is the same kind of fact that Gubelmann's malfunction test and Butlin's 'sensitivity to instrumental value' criterion appeal to. The key premise is that the proxy relation is normative, with a correctness condition, and that for learned systems the correctness condition is grounded in machine-internal function and not in designer intention. If so, proxy accounts depend on a machine-side functional profile, and the open question is whether the profile does more than a tool's does.

Appraiser (blind)
It argues that a proxy view needs machine-side functional correctness conditions, a nice internal tension in Arora's account, but one of limited scope.

U122. The proxy view of chatbot speech is committed either to a systematic error theory about first-person and second-person pronouns in chatbot output or to treating that output as ventriloquism, which is a form of fictionalism.

Move · Target
commitment — Proxy accounts, as a stable alternative to fictionalism (Arora; Green and Michel; Williams and Bayne's dismissal of both).
Sketch

A proxy assertion is performed by the principal, so the content asserted is the principal's. Chatbot outputs are saturated with de se material: 'I think', 'I'm sorry', 'I can't access that', 'As an AI I have no opinions'. If the proxy asserts for the company, then 'I' either refers to the company or refers to the machine. If it refers to the company, then 'I am an AI language model' and 'I'm sorry I got that wrong' are false or odd as assertions by the company, and the proxy theorist owes an error theory about what competent users and the output itself mean. If 'I' refers to the machine, the company asserts de se claims about a persona it does not itself instantiate. That is the structure of ventriloquism or role-play, in which the principal speaks through a character. At that point the proxy view takes on Mallory's and Williams–Bayne's fictional or persona layer, and the view that was supposed to be a rival to fictionalism is a version of it. The key premise is that illocutionary content is individuated by what the indexicals refer to, so a speech act cannot be both the principal's and about a different self-referent without a pretence layer. The point bites hardest for apology and promise, where the first person is part of the act.

Appraiser (blind)
The indexical point against proxy views is interesting, but the ventriloquism reply is easy to anticipate.

U123. If proto-assertion is secured by descriptive function acquired through training, then for RLHF-tuned models the function that was actually selected for is eliciting rater approval, so the category the view commits to is proto-flattery or proto-bullshit, which supports the no-speech-act view it opposes.
