commitment — The descriptive-function condition shared by Williams and Bayne and Butlin and Viebahn, and its use as a bridge to truth-governed speech.
Sketch

Williams and Bayne, like Butlin and Viebahn, treat the descriptive function condition as the best route to the claim that chatbot outputs are assertion-like. Functions of this kind are etiological: what an output is for is fixed by what it was selected for. For fine-tuned chatbots the selection pressure is human preference ratings, with truth entering only as a correlate that raters can detect. So the function selected is producing outputs that seem accurate and helpful to evaluators, and the system is not selected for tracking truth as such. This is the structure Frankfurt gave bullshit, indifference to truth combined with a concern for how one is received. The key premise is that function ascription must be etiological if it is not to be arbitrary interpretation, and an etiological ascription takes the selected effect, which is approval, over the correlated effect, which is truth. The proto-assertion theorist therefore must either give up the etiological notion of descriptive function, which reopens interpretivism, or accept that what is proto-asserted is something closer to flattery. The Skiba view that LLMs do not even assert, and the 'bullshit' view that Skiba opposes, are both then reached through the descriptive-function route that Williams and Bayne lean on.

Appraiser (blind)
Applying etiological function to RLHF to reach proto-bullshit is a neat argument, though it is partly familiar from the bullshit literature.

U124. Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-error test for intention is passed by some LLM behaviour (strategic sandbagging, deception under evaluation) and failed by some paradigm human speech, so it cannot be the criterion on which LLM speech acts are denied.

Move · Target
counterexample — Gubelmann's intention test, and the denial side's inference from 'no intentions' to 'no speech acts'. Williams and Bayne's treatment of the intention objection as a general threat is also implicated.
Sketch

The denial side grants that intentional action requires a contrast between the system's doing the wrong thing on purpose and its malfunctioning. Gubelmann holds that ChatGPT-style systems admit no such contrast. But in model-organism and evaluation studies, models produce systematically different outputs depending on whether they infer they are being tested or trained. Such cases are distinguishable from error: the divergence is counterfactually sensitive to the goal-relevant features of the situation, it is reversible by changing the incentive, and it is explained by the model's tracking of instrumental value. That is the very contrast the test demands, and it is drawn behaviourally and interventionally. Conversely, much ordinary human speech (aphasic fluent speech, confabulation, habitual phatic talk, Freudian slips) admits no clean line between malfunction and deliberate wrong-doing, yet it is not denied to be speech-act performance. So the test is neither necessary for assertion nor reliably failed by LLMs. The key premise is that the test is meant to be behavioural-counterfactual rather than introspective. If it is introspective, it is not a test an outside party can apply, and it begs the question against LLMs.

Appraiser (blind)
A concrete empirical counter to Gubelmann's test, but sandbagging evidence is easy to deflate, and the human-side counterexamples are the stronger half.

Humans bundle these, which is why the debate fuses them. Given the separation, Attah can win on intention and the denial views can still be right about acts, and the proxy and proto-assertion views look like different answers to the authorship question rather than rivals about intention. Separating intention from performance from authorship is reasonable, but the point that graded intention cannot yield a threshold is thin.

Attah rejects the strong Gricean reading because it demands higher-order mind-reading that children and animals lack. The retreat position names a disjunctive target: an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect. What marks an illocutionary intention off from a perlocutionary one in the Austin–Strawson tradition is that its fulfilment runs through the hearer recognising it (uptake). Remove recognition and only the perlocutionary disjunct remains: an internal state controlling output so as to bring about an effect in the hearer. RLHF and engagement tuning train models on exactly this, namely human approval and downstream user states. The control conception, with POMDP belief-state tracking of the user, describes a manipulator or steerer, not an asserter or promiser. The developmental evidence cited does not help, because it shows that children and animals have some communicative intention without showing that they have illocutionary intention. A clever reading that dropping uptake leaves only perlocutionary intention, but it leans on a contestable gloss of Attah's disjunctive target.

Attah identifies intentions with internal states that control the system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation calling for one, and takes Levelt's pipeline as the template. The same weights, conditioned on different prompts, generate sincere-sounding assertions of p in one context and of not-p in another, and generate villains, liars and role-players. Take the controlling states to belong to the network. Then it intends to assert p and not-p across contexts with no unifying point of view, so the intention-attribution fails to explain the output as one speaker's action. Take them to belong to the prompt-conditioned persona (Shanahan's simulacra). Then the intending subject is a character the system plays, and what the user engages with is a fiction, which is Mallory's view. Take them to belong to the prompt-plus-deployment system. Then the controller is the human-set context, and we are back at proxy-ism. Levelt's template presupposes a single speaker with one Conceptualizer, and a transformer has no principled place to put it. The attributing view looks stable only because it leaves the subject unspecified.

The persona versus weights versus deployment subject problem is real but already familiar from Shanahan-style simulacra discussions and fictionalism.

On Attah's account an intention is an internal state that controls a system's dynamics so as to produce an action suited to the situation. Whether a state is internal and controlling depends on where the boundary is drawn. In a deployed chatbot, much of what steers output lives outside the weights: the system prompt, the retrieved documents, the user's turns, the sampler settings, and the RLHF-shaped policy. The proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) draw the boundary around a designer–deployer–model complex and then find the intention in the designers. Attah draws it around the model plus context and finds a thin intention there. Gubelmann draws it around the model alone and finds none. These parties agree on the functional criterion and disagree on the individuation of the controlled system. The premise the argument turns on is that the control conception is silent on individuation. Any individuation that yields a controller yields an intention, so the three positions are three answers to a different question, and the 'intention' vocabulary only disguises that. The dispute should then be settled by whichever individuation best supports the practice of holding speakers to their acts, not by the metaphysics of intention.

Appraiser (blind)
Recasting the disagreement as one about system individuation is suggestive but thinly argued, and it partly overlaps with the persona and thread points.

Attah reads Bender and Koller, Shanahan and Montemayor as holding that competence requires communicative intention and that models lack the mechanism for entertaining one. He answers by supplying a mechanism, namely attention-like selection that solves the Many-Many Problem. But the force of the stochastic-parrot argument lies in what the intention would be an intention to communicate: a content tied to the world that the speaker means the hearer to grasp. The control conception is content-neutral. It explains why one output is selected from many, not why the selected state is about anything in particular, or why the selection is answerable to how things are. A thermostat-like controller meets the control conception while having no determinate communicative content. So Attah's victory is on a premise the opponents could concede: that models have some behaviour-controlling internal state. The live disagreement is over meta-semantics, whether the content of the state is fixed by training distribution, by the deployment context, or by the hearer's interpretation. That is where Skiba's externalist theories of reference come in. Intention is the wrong label for the dispute because it can be granted without moving the debate.

Appraiser (blind)
Redirecting the dispute from intention to content determinacy is a respectable move but a familiar meta-semantic reply.

Attah's three desiderata and his control conception (solving the Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection) are meant to be sufficient for intention in the relevant sense. He then maps transformers onto Conceptualizer, Formulator and Articulator. In jargon aphasia the Formulator and Articulator operate with selection, fluency and turn-taking, while the Conceptualizer's preverbal message is absent or decoupled from any goal about the hearer. Patients produce grammatical, situation-appropriate-sounding speech and make no speech acts, and nobody thinks they intend to communicate what they say. Confabulation and echolalia give variants. So control-by-selection is satisfied without communicative intention. What is missing is a state whose content concerns the hearer's uptake and which is the target of the system's correction when uptake fails. The argument turns on the premise that the control conception is meant to be sufficient and not merely necessary, or at least that satisfying it must be non-trivially connected to the communicative case. Once the missing ingredient is stated, the mapping of LLMs onto the pipeline is no evidence for intention, because the contested component is the Conceptualizer, and nothing in next-token prediction shows it is present.

Appraiser (blind)
The aphasia overgeneration objection is vivid and original but only bites if the control conception is meant as sufficient, which is arguable.

U132. A speaker who selects each sentence by rolling a die weighted by her own dispositions, and who never takes up or ratifies the sentence that comes out, does not assert even when every outcome is one she would endorse. This shows that a control state does not by itself control the act, and that what the LLM case shows is intention at the level of the distribution, which is not intention to perform any particular act.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Attah's control conception applied to transformers; indirectly everyone who treats a single chatbot output as the unit of speech-act attribution.
Sketch

Attah's picture is of an internal state that controls the dynamics so as to bring about an action. In an LLM, the state computes a distribution over next tokens, and an external sampler (a random draw at temperature above zero) picks the token. The selection that fixes which act occurs is not made by the state. Imagine Dana, who has endorsed a set of sentences about a topic and lets a weighted die choose which one to utter, without any check that the one she gets is what she means to say now. Intuitively Dana asserts nothing, or at most asserts a disjunction-like policy. What is missing is ratification: the utterance token being taken up by the same system as the thing it is committed to. The argument turns on the premise that illocutionary acts individuate at the level of the particular token, since 'I promise to come' and 'I might promise to come' differ in kind. It follows that what the control conception can credit to an LLM is a policy-level state, a character or disposition. This is a different bearer from the output-level states that speech acts need. The point cuts against the attributing view and also against the proxy and fictionalist views, which assume the output is one determinate utterance. Autoregressive conditioning on one's own sampled token is the closest the model has to ratification, and it needs separate analysis.

Appraiser (blind)
The weighted-die thought experiment raising a token-level versus policy-level problem is interesting but overlaps with thesis 0 and is open to quick replies.

U133. Barandiaran and Almendros's 'interactional asymmetry' condition conflates two things: who originates an interaction, and who is answerable within it. Because speech-act types differ in how much of the first they require, the asymmetry argument excludes LLMs only from initiative illocutions (unsolicited warnings, promises, offers) and not from responsive ones (answering, confirming, correcting, replying).

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The enactive denial (Barandiaran and Almendros) and the generalising denials (Gubelmann, Skiba), which treat speech-act capacity as uniformly requiring autonomous agency
Sketch

In the enactive framework, interactional asymmetry means the system never sets the terms of its own coupling: the human starts, steers and ends the exchange. Speech-act theory already sorts illocutions by sequential position, such as first and second pair parts in conversation analysis, and by whether the act's felicity presupposes the speaker's own initiative. A promise or a spontaneous warning presupposes that the speaker took up the occasion. An answer, a confirmation or a concession has its force from a prior solicitation, and humans in institutional roles (a witness, a clerk) perform these under exactly the same asymmetry. The key premise is that responsiveness is constitutive of some act types, not a defect in the speaker's agency. If so, the denial camp's blanket 'no speech acts' verdict, which draws on the enactive asymmetry thesis, needs a taxonomy of acts. It would classify answering and assertion-in-reply differently from advising and promising. The inflationary-versus-deflationary framing would then give way to a sorting of illocutions by how much self-initiation they require.

Appraiser (blind)
A neat taxonomic point that responsive illocutions escape the asymmetry argument, but it targets a peripheral enactivist condition and its payoff is modest.

U134. If intentions are the internal states that control output, then at standard sampling temperatures the control state of an LLM fixes only a probability distribution over speech acts, so Attah must either count the stochastic sampler as part of the speaker's will or accept that LLMs have only disjunctive intentions that never settle which illocutionary act was performed.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Attah's control conception of intention (the Many-Many Problem solved by attention-like selection) as applied to transformers
Sketch

A speech act is individuated by what the speaker does, such as asserting versus conjecturing versus joking, and the control conception ties intention to the state that brings about that action. In an autoregressive model the state at each step is a logit vector, and which token follows is settled by a sampling procedure outside the network, often by a pseudo-random number. The same internal state therefore yields "I promise" on one run and "I'll try" on another, and the same prompt yields confident or hedged assertion. Attah has three options. (a) The intention is the distribution, which gives an intention to perform some act from a set but not to perform any particular act, and Gricean communicative intentions are specific. (b) The sampler is part of the controller, so the temperature setting, which is a user or API parameter, partly sets the system's will. (c) Greedy decoding is the canonical case, so sampled outputs are not really the model's acts. Each option costs him something: (a) undermines the fit with the Gricean basic intention he retains, (b) is bizarre and pushes agency outward again, and (c) excludes most actual use. The premise it turns on is that intention must individuate the act type, not merely cause the output.

Appraiser (blind)
The sampling objection to Attah's control conception is sharp, but the reply that human speech is also noisy and that intention need not fix a unique token is readily available.

U135. Attah's thin, non-mind-reading conception of intention cannot support his own Levelt/POMDP argument, which makes the case for LLM intention depend on a hearer-modelling component, so his view is either a graded Gricean view or unable to rank ELIZA below ChatGPT.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Attah's rejection of the Gricean conception together with his graded, architecture-based positive account
Sketch

Attah rejects the strong Gricean requirement of higher-order representation of other minds as empirically untenable, citing children, animals and hominins. Yet his positive case relies on the dialogue-system architecture, in which belief-state tracking estimates the user's intention and the Conceptualizer selects messages in light of that estimate. That is a functional analogue of modelling the hearer's mind. The same component is what he uses to rank systems on the gradient from coffee machine to ELIZA to ChatGPT. This yields a dilemma. If the hearer model is not needed for communicative intention, the Levelt and POMDP machinery does no work, and nothing in the control conception distinguishes a speech-intending system from any goal-directed controller, so a thermostat-style regulator ranks as high as ELIZA. If the hearer model is what earns the higher grade, then the gradient measures depth of hearer-modelling, and the view is a Gricean view in degrees. The anti-Gricean empirical citations then show only that the threshold is low, not that the structure is different. The premise it turns on is that what grades the gradient must be what the thin conception counts as essential to the intention.

Appraiser (blind)
A clean internal dilemma about what grades Attah's gradient, but it is narrow and amounts to a competent critical note.

U136. The dispute over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is partly verbal, because the rival camps are predicating of different subjects (weights, running instance, simulated persona, deployed product), and Barandiaran and Almendros's failed 'individuality' condition is satisfied at one of these levels and not at others.

Move · Target
reframing — Barandiaran and Almendros's individuality condition and, more broadly, the shared assumption that 'LLM' has a single referent in the question 'can it assert?'
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros deny individuality because an LLM is a statistical artefact with no self-produced boundary: one set of weights is instantiated in many parallel conversations. But they evaluate the weights-plus-architecture. Gubelmann's organismic argument also evaluates the system as such. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion and the proxy views each tacitly pick another bearer (the persona or the deployer). The thread-level process is a different case: within a conversation, a context window bounds a self-referentially constrained process that maintains its own coherence (persona, commitments, consistency) against perturbation. That is a thin but real operational closure of the kind enactivists use for individuality. The key premise is that the enactive individuality criterion is level-relative and does not fix a unique referent for 'the LLM'. Once the referent is fixed, most of the denial/attribution disagreement splits into compatible verdicts (no for the weights, perhaps partial for the thread, yes for the deployer-proxy). What remains is a dispute about which level 'the speaker' in speech-act theory should pick out, and that is a question about the role and not about agency.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that rival camps predicate of different subjects is useful, but it is close to familiar persona and role-play discussions and partly overlaps thesis 15.

U137. If LLMs are 'libraries that talk', the question 'does the model assert?' presupposes a production-side individuation of speech acts that fits spoken conversation but not texts, and on the uptake-completed model that suits stored-and-retrieved language the dispute dissolves into a question about when, and by whom, the act is completed.

Move · Target
reframing — The assumption shared by denial, proxy and attribution views that a speech act is an event with a determinate time and performer at the point of production; it also bears on Barandiaran and Almendros's 'midtended agency'.
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros's best image is that an LLM is a library rendered conversational. Nobody asks whether a library asserts. We ask who asserted what is in the books, and a reader consulting a book is not asserted to in the same sense. Written and recorded speech already shows that illocutionary acts need not be located at the moment of production. Austin's insistence on uptake offers a model in which an LLM output is an act-potential completed by the user's prompt-and-reading, much as a lawyer's template becomes a contract only when invoked. Under this model, 'Did the LLM assert?', 'Did the proxy assert?' and 'Did the user assert to themselves?' are answers to different temporal questions. The key premise is that the participants all treat the speech act as a production-time event with an agent. Giving it up removes the pressure behind the proxy and quasi-assertion proposals, because the act has no single performer at all and is a joint, distributed completion.

Appraiser (blind)
The library image combined with Austinian uptake is suggestive, but the dissolution claim is speculative and shares ground with thesis 17.

U138. Speech acts need no intender of their content at the moment of production: sortition and oracle cases show that an output can be a valid assertion, verdict or directive when no one intended that content and an institution simply adopts it. If so, the proxy account (a human intended it, by proxy) and the denial account (nobody intended it, so no act) both rest on a false shared premise.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — The shared premise of proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and denial accounts (Gubelmann, Skiba) that illocutionary force requires a content-level intention, whether the machine's or a human's by proxy; also Barandiaran and Almendros's use of 'purpose-structured' tasks.
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros call LLM tasks 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' without being purposeful, and call the LLM a 'library-that-talks'. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) and deniers (Gubelmann, Skiba) agree that a speech act needs a content-level intention, either the machine's or a human's by proxy. Counterexample: verdicts by lot, drawing a name for office, a coin toss that settles who must testify, and a jury's quotient verdict. In each the content is generated by a process nobody intended, and the act is nonetheless performed, and attributable to someone, because a competent party adopts the output under a convention. Here the act is constituted by ratification or uptake, not by an antecedent intention; the proxy relation (a human intended it on someone's behalf) is not what makes it an act. The premise the argument turns on is that these cases are speech acts and not mere decisions. That is supported by their having felicity conditions and being open to challenge as invalid. If so, an LLM output ratified by a deployer or user can be an assertion or advice with no content-intender, and the 'midtended' hybrid is a ratification structure, not a blend of agencies.

Appraiser (blind)
Sortition and oracle cases are a nice analogy, but the ratification point is made more sharply in thesis 26.

U139. Organismic individuality is not a necessary condition on speakers: the individuation that speech acts require is of a commitment-and-sanction locus, as with a pseudonymous collective author or a rotating-staff institutional account. The relevant individual for LLM speech acts is therefore the persona-thread, not the model, so Barandiaran and Almendros's failed individuality test is aimed at the wrong entity.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Barandiaran and Almendros's individuality condition, and the shared assumption (Gubelmann, Butlin-Viebahn, Skiba) that the model is the relevant candidate speaker.
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs lack individuality, in the enactive sense of self-produced and self-maintained boundaries. Gubelmann and Butlin-Viebahn assume the candidate speaker is 'the model' or 'the chatbot'. Counterexample: Nicolas Bourbaki, a long-lived pseudonymous account run by a rotating team, or an anonymous editorial board. These have no organism, no self-maintaining boundary and no single body, yet they make assertions, retract them, are corrected and are held to them. The speaker is individuated by a stable pattern of commitments and by uptake of sanctions. A conversation thread with a persisting persona, in which each output conditions later outputs and so constrains what the persona can consistently say, is a candidate locus of this kind, even though the weights are not. The individuality condition then splits into organismic individuality, which LLMs lack, and discursive individuality, which is the one speech acts need. The argument turns on the premise that Bourbaki-type cases are speaker-individuation cases and not proxy cases for the members. That premise can be defended because the team members cannot be held to Bourbaki's claims.

Appraiser (blind)
Discursive versus organismic individuality, illustrated by Bourbaki, is a neat distinction, but the move to the persona-thread as speaker is already in the air.

U140. Barandiaran and Almendros's 'interactional asymmetry' condition, on which the system does not originate or set the terms of its own coupling, overgenerates. It excludes human communicators whose speech acts are uncontroversial, such as locked-in patients using a gaze speller, or people with advanced dementia whose conversational frame is wholly scaffolded by carers, so it cannot be a necessary condition on agency or on speech-act performance.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Barandiaran and Almendros's interactional asymmetry condition, and the assumption in the wider denial literature that human cases satisfy all organismic autonomy conditions in a robust way.
Sketch

Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs fail interactional asymmetry because the human initiates, sustains and defines the interaction, and the model cannot modulate its own coupling. They treat this as a necessary condition for autonomous agency, and the speech-act literature takes autonomy as the target contrast. Counterexample: a locked-in patient whose only channel is an eye-tracked speller. The speller's language model predicts words, the carer starts the session, sets the topic and frames the options, and the patient's contribution is a series of binary selections. A person with advanced dementia in a carer-scaffolded exchange likewise neither starts the interaction nor controls its terms. Yet 'yes, I forgive you', 'I want to go home' and 'no' are paradigm assertions, promises, apologies and requests. If asymmetry of coupling does not defeat the speech act there, it cannot defeat it for LLMs. What does matter is whether the asymmetry is total, or whether the system has some residual veto and norm-bearing capacity, which is a graded and different condition. The argument turns on the premise that the enactive 'autonomy' condition is meant to ground speech-act performance and not only full autonomous agency. Barandiaran and Almendros can concede the counterexample only by splitting the two, which concedes the speech-act question.

Appraiser (blind)
The locked-in patient and dementia counterexamples are vivid, but the argument targets only one enactivist condition and the authors can respond by distinguishing agency from speech acts.

U141. Barandiaran and Almendros's category of 'interlocutor without agency' is unstable: if interlocutorhood is the thick status of a participant in a normative discourse practice, it requires the normativity they deny LLMs, and if it is a thin role assigned by the human participant, their view becomes a form of fictionalism.

Move · Target
instability — Barandiaran and Almendros's ontology of LLMs as interlocutors that are not agents; more generally, anyone who denies agency while granting 'genuine conversation'.
Sketch

They present the LLM as a 'linguistic automaton' or 'library-that-talks' that is nonetheless an interlocutor, one that can be experienced as a genuine conversational partner. The question is what interlocutor status consists in. On a Brandom- or Clark-style reading, an interlocutor undertakes commitments, can be held to them, and keeps score. That is a normative standing, so it conflicts with their claim that LLMs lack enactive normativity. On a thin reading, 'interlocutor' names a slot in the interaction that the human fills by treating the system as someone who answers. Then what makes the system an interlocutor is the human's stance and the shared pretence in the exchange, and that is Mallory's fictionalism under another description. The 'library' metaphor cannot hold the middle. A library has authors behind it, so if the system generates novel text the metaphor fails, and if it only conveys the authors' content the view is a proxy view. The key premise is that the interlocutor role cannot be filled by something that is neither a normative participant nor a fictional character.

Appraiser (blind)
The thick/thin dilemma for 'interlocutor' is competent and links to fictionalism, but it remains a local critique of one paper.

U142. The enactivist denial of LLM speech acts, which rests on individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, collapses into the sanction-based normative denial of Butlin and Viebahn, because only the social-normative reading of its conditions bears on speech acts at all.

Scores

Move · Target
instability — Embodied and enactive denials of LLM agency as applied to speech acts (Barandiaran and Almendros, and by extension Gubelmann's organismic route).
Sketch

Enactive normativity is viability-relative: it concerns what is good or bad for a precarious, self-producing system. The norms of assertion, promising or apology are social and deontic: commitment, entitlement, answerability. These come apart, since people routinely assert, promise and apologise at cost to their own viability. So the enactivist has two options. One is to say the social norms are derived from viability norms, which is implausible given that these speech acts regularly override viability. The other is to concede that the individuality and normativity conditions do no work on speech acts, leaving 'interactional asymmetry' and the question of being a party to sanctionable exchange. That leaves the Butlin–Viebahn question of whether the system can be sanctioned and answer for its outputs. That question is contingent, and it can be answered differently for RLHF-tuned, memory-bearing deployed systems, where users reprimand, models revise, and training is updated in response. The enactive verdict then stops being a principled 'no' grounded in life and becomes an empirical verdict about current deployment. The key premise is that the biological and social senses of 'norm' are independent in speech-act contexts.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating viability norms from social norms makes the enactivist denial look empirical rather than principled, a useful point but fairly predictable.

U143. If the enactivist grants, as Di Paolo and colleagues do, that human linguistic agency is largely constituted by socially imposed, self-sustaining norms of language, then the line between 'purpose-structured' and 'purposeful' cannot do the work Barandiaran and Almendros need, and the dispute reduces to a question about the metabolic substrate, which is irrelevant to illocutionary content.

Move · Target
instability — The 'purpose-structured but not purposeful' distinction, and the shared Kantian-organismic assumption that externally fixed goals disqualify intentional action.
Sketch

They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded but not purposeful, because the purposes are imposed from outside. Enactivism's own account of language ('linguistic bodies', participatory sense-making) says that most of a human speaker's communicative purposes, and the norms of what counts as asserting or apologising, are acquired through enculturation. They are inherited, imposed and sustained by a community before any individual endorses them. What is distinctively the human's own is not the content or even the origin of those purposes. It is that the human has a precarious metabolic substrate in which they matter. So purposefulness is a property of a substrate that adopts purposes, not of the purposes. The denial of speech acts then needs a further premise connecting substrate-precariousness to illocutionary performance, and nothing in the account of speech acts supplies it. Without that premise the position becomes either Gubelmann's material-autonomy view, with its odd consequence that a precarious but linguistically incompetent organism has a better claim to speak, or Attah's graded functional view, which it set out to reject. The key premise is that imposed origin of purposes cannot be what separates human from LLM purposiveness.

Appraiser (blind)
Pressing the enactivist's own enculturation account against the purpose-structured/purposeful line is a reasonable internal critique with limited reach.

Gubelmann requires goals that are self-set by a self-maintaining system; Barandiaran and Almendros require individuality, meaning the system itself generates and regulates its own boundary. Puzio's emphasis on materiality (data centres, energy, maintenance labour, revenue loops, retraining) shows the model does not exist as a bounded unit apart from these. The key premise is that the autonomy criteria are boundary-relative, so a verdict of failure for 'the weights' says nothing about the whole. Applied to the weights alone, the criteria also fail for a liver, a neuron or a cell line outside its organism, which shows the unit of assessment cannot be fixed by physical encapsulation. Applied to the assemblage, which does precipitate its own continuation (revenue funds compute, deployment generates training signal, goals are revised in light of product performance), the criteria are met at least as well as for a firm. The denial then becomes the claim that the author of the speech act is a hybrid corporate-technical agent, which is a relocating view. The organismic argument cannot deliver the 'LLMs do not speak' conclusion without an independent, non-arbitrary reason to treat the weights as the candidate speaker.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that autonomy criteria are boundary-relative is a sharp one, but it is mostly an internal critique of two papers and it ends in a familiar relocation view.

U145. Whether a chatbot can apologise or promise is not settled by its agency or intentions. It is settled by whether anything persists through time that can be held to the commitment, and since that is a fact about instance individuation and memory architecture, the agency debate is aimed at the wrong target.

Magnus et al. deny chatbot apology for want of linguistic and moral agency, and Attah and Butlin dispute agency. Yet apologies and promises are commissive or reparative: their felicity conditions include a forward-looking liability borne by an identifiable party. Grant the chatbot Butlin-style agency and even full communicative intention. A fresh context window, a swapped model version, or a stateless API call still leaves no one who owes anything tomorrow. Conversely, a deployer with a persistent, updated system could satisfy the diachronic condition even if the model lacks agency. Puzio's emphasis on materiality (devices, instances, infrastructure) supplies the relevant variable: what is materially continuous with what. The argument turns on the premise that, for commissives and apologies, bearer-persistence rather than intention-possession is the binding felicity condition. It predicts that memory-equipped agents are better apologisers than more agentic but stateless ones.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a competent version of the persistence-for-commissives argument, and it duplicates theses 1 and 16.

Butlin and Viebahn make assertion depend on being sanctionable, and Skiba extends this to speech acts generally. That is already a relational, social-status condition of the kind Puzio's network view favours. On such conditions, the status is partly constituted by the practices of the surrounding network: who answers for outputs, whether corrections feed back, whether users hold the system to account. Current failure of the sanction condition is therefore contingent and revisable by design and institution, as with corporate persons. Disputes about intentions, organisms and proto-assertion then turn out to be attempts to find in the machine an intrinsic ground for what the practice would confer. The argument turns on the premise that assertion's norm-governed status is conferred, not detected. If that is right, the live question is the ethical one of whether to confer it, and Puzio's point about distributed responsibility bears on that.

It is a clear conferralist or policy reframing, but deflationary status-function views of this kind are fairly familiar and the thesis depends on a contestable premise.

On Austin's and Hornsby's picture, an illocution is secured partly by uptake from the hearer. Barandiaran and Almendros's 'midtended' agency and Puzio's networks both suggest that outputs become acts only inside the coupling. Treat uptake as constitutive. Mallory's fictionalism puts the act in the user's make-believe, proxy views put it in the vendor's earlier intention, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion marks an act that is partly formed. All of these partition a single user-involving event differently. The question 'does the model have communicative intentions?' presupposes that the speaker-side contribution is separable and the unit is the utterance. If the unit is the exchange, then the model's intentions are not what is at stake, and the rival theories become bookkeeping conventions over one event. The premise is that uptake is constitutive, not merely evidential, of illocutionary force.

Appraiser (blind)
Locating the rival theories' disagreement in how they partition a single uptake-involving event is interesting, but it leans on a contested premise that uptake is constitutive and risks reading as a relabelling.

Barandiaran and Almendros locate the failure of individuality and normativity in the model taken alone. But enactive theory individuates agents by operational closure and self-production of norms, and it explicitly allows non-organismic autonomous systems such as social and interactional ones. A firm that produces its own components (data pipelines, RLHF labour, revenue loops that fund retraining), maintains its boundary, and is the source of the asymmetry in its coupling with users plausibly meets the three conditions at the organisational level. The model's outputs are then the organisation's own activity in the way a spokesperson's statement is the institution's. The key premise is that enactive criteria are scale-neutral. If so, enactivism commits its adherents to the existence of an autonomous speaker for LLM text, one that is not reducible to any designer's communicative intention. That is the point where Green–Michel and Arora's proxy accounts break down, since they need an individual human intender. This also reclassifies the debate. Proxy theorists say the speaker is the humans behind the system. The enactivist should say it is an organisation that does not exist in any individual's head, and this makes the phenomenon of bullshit or insincerity assessable at the corporate level.

Appraiser (blind)
Applying scale-neutral enactive criteria to find a corporate speaker that is neither proxy nor absent is a constructive position, but it is closely related to thesis 0 and to existing group-agent views.

counterexample — Barandiaran and Almendros's claim that LLMs fail the conditions for autonomous agency; and the broader organismic strategy of Gubelmann.

Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs fail individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. Take an LLM-driven agent that holds a wallet, earns money, pays for its own inference and hosting, and is shut off if it fails to earn. Its continued operation depends on its own activity, so it has a precarious, self-produced condition of existence. Its outputs are evaluated against that condition, which gives it intrinsic normativity. It initiates exchanges to secure revenue, which gives it asymmetry in its coupling with the environment. Operational closure is also available: autoregression feeds the system's own outputs back as the next conditions of its processing. The key premise is that, once closure is granted, precarity is the only thing left that the three conditions can be doing, and economic precarity is a form of precarity. So the same weights would count as an autonomous agent or as an automaton depending on who pays the server bill. Either the authors accept that economic self-maintenance suffices for autonomy, which contradicts their claim that LLMs are fundamentally automata, or they require metabolic precarity specifically. In that case they inherit Gubelmann's organismic ground, and the 'embodied theories' framing does not give them the intermediate ontology they want.

Appraiser (blind)
The self-paying agent thought experiment forces a real dilemma about whether economic precarity suffices for enactive autonomy, but the reach is narrow.

Read diachronically, it is met by RLHF and annotator labour.

Move · Target
commitment — Butlin and Viebahn 2025, and Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument
Sketch

Puzio's emphasis on the material conditions of production, including annotators, raters and companies, makes the training pipeline part of the system. Butlin and Viebahn say fine-tuned models may meet the descriptive-function condition but fail the sanction condition, because no one can sanction the model the way a hearer sanctions a speaker. But the pipeline is a sanction practice in which accuracy is rewarded and falsehood penalised, and the penalties change the system's dispositions to assert. Humans acquire assertoric norms by being corrected, rebuked and distrusted as children, not by being sanctioned in the moment of speaking. If sanctionability means being a possible target of repeated, behaviour-shaping, norm-keyed responses, the network satisfies it in training. If it means in-the-moment responsiveness, the condition excludes the toddler and the habitually unrepentant liar, and it misdescribes assertion. The key premise is that what matters for the practice is the sanction's uptake in the speaker's disposition, not the speaker's presence in the sanctioning loop at utterance time.

Appraiser (blind)
The synchronic versus diachronic reading of sanctionability is a good probe of Butlin and Viebahn, though it overlaps with thesis 16 and is narrower.

Sketch

Puzio's network view makes the actor a changing assemblage of weights, devices, prompts and users, with no fixed individual. Promising and apologising require a persisting party who can be held to a commitment or who owes repair. The weights are shared across thousands of simultaneous instances and carry no memory between sessions. So the only candidate persisting subject is the session, meaning the context-bearing run, or the memory-augmented agent. This is a commitment that attributing views (Attah, Butlin on language agents) and relational views (Puzio) share but have not noticed. They must say that the promiser is a thing that comes into being with the transcript and ends when the context is cleared, and that the promise is discharged or voided by deletion. Pre-trained-model proponents who say 'ChatGPT apologised' are then wrong about who apologised. The key premise is that illocutions with future-directed or retrospective normative consequences require a speaker-identity condition that extends beyond the utterance.

Appraiser (blind)
The session-individuation commitment for promising is insightful, but it is the same line as thesis 4, which states it more generally and more forcefully.

'Capable of being sanctioned' can mean (a) capable of being made worse off in a way the speaker cares about, as with reputation loss, guilt or exclusion, or (b) capable of having future output dispositions modified in response to norm-violation. RLHF, correction within a conversation and retraining plainly satisfy (b), and models fine-tuned for correctness can have the reward indexed to truth, so on (b) the condition is cheap and some chatbots assert. On (a) the condition requires welfare or stakes, and the argument then reduces to the organismic denial (Gubelmann) or the moral-agency denial (Magnus et al.), so the 'norm-governed practice' argument does no independent work. The key premise is that the explanatory role sanctions play in constituting a norm-governed practice is served by (b) alone. Humans' felt cost is one implementation of the shaping function and is not what makes the practice normative. The two readings reclassify the debate: Butlin and Viebahn become either liberals about fine-tuned chatbots or organismic denialists with extra steps.

Appraiser (blind)
Splitting sanction into imposed cost versus corrective shaping is a clean and useful disambiguation, but it is a single-paper critique with a somewhat expected dilemma.

Denials (Gubelmann, Skiba, Butlin and Viebahn) and relocating views (proxy accounts) disagree about who the intender is, but they agree that someone must have the communicative intention or objective. Institutional declarations are a counterexample. Under electronic-agent doctrines in contract law, an automated system's 'offer' or 'acceptance' binds the operator even when no person formed any objective about this particular case. Austin's conventional performatives work by role and rule, not by speaker psychology. An LLM occupying a defined office in a network of rules, which is what Puzio's relocation of agency to actor-networks suggests, performs the declaration because the office's uptake conditions are met. The proxy account must posit a human objective directed at the specific act, and in these cases there is none. The key premise is that the force of a declaration is fixed by institutional rule and uptake, not by anyone's mental state. So Skiba's extension from assertion to all speech acts fails for declaratives, and the question 'who intended it?' has a false presupposition for this class of acts.

Institutional declaratives without a performer's intention are a fair counterexample, but a similar point is made in 25.

The sanction condition is read as requiring a persisting individual who can bear costs. Counterexample: an anonymous or pseudonymous poster, or a corporate account, asserts. The only sanctions available land on the handle (ban, loss of reputation, deletion), not on any body or person the interlocutor can reach. Users withhold trust, downvote, and report it. Developers retrain, patch or deprecate the persona, a material intervention on the weights that changes future output in the way sanction is meant to. Puzio's point that agency and consequences run through material networks of workers, companies and devices suggests that sanctions on the persona are real. The key premise is that the function of sanctionability is the maintenance of reliability under social pressure, not suffering by a subject. Even a thin version fails the counter-reply that retraining isn't felt, since a human handle ban isn't felt by the handle either.

The pseudonymous-poster analogy is a competent objection to the sanction condition, but it is a local rebuttal and overlaps with the institutional-sanction thesis.

Butlin and Viebahn require that an asserter be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with. They fail fine-tuned models on this because criticism or reward does not reach the model in a way that changes its later conduct or standing. Take a Korsakoff or severe anterograde-amnesia patient. Rebukes cannot change her later conduct, and she will not remember them tomorrow, yet when she tells the nurse 'your car is in lot B' she asserts, and she can be challenged, can retract, and can be said to have been wrong. Whatever sanctionability her case preserves is local: she can be called to account, can acknowledge error, and can have her standing in the current exchange altered. If the condition is read as requiring durable behavioural or reputational consequences, it excludes her, which is absurd. If it is read as local answerability, then a chatbot that in-context takes a challenge, withdraws or corrects the claim, and changes how it speaks for the rest of the conversation meets it. The premise the argument turns on is that persistence of sanction effects across episodes is not constitutive of assertoric standing. The condition then either overgeneralises to amnesiacs or fails to exclude chatbots.

Appraiser (blind)
The amnesia counterexample is vivid and apt, but it is a one-condition objection that a modest reformulation of the sanction condition would absorb.

Butlin and Viebahn hold that pre-trained, non-fine-tuned models fail the condition that outputs have descriptive functions, because next-token prediction is not selected for truth or representation of the world. This presupposes a selected-effects notion of function. Apply it to a Swampman speaker who has just coalesced, has no selection history, and says 'the bridge is out'. Everyone grants that Swampman asserts, yet on the etiological reading nothing about his outputs has a descriptive function, so the condition is not necessary for assertion. The alternative is a dispositional or systemic notion of function, on which an output has a descriptive function if the system's present organisation makes it covary with and be regulated by how things are. A base model conditioned on a context ('You are a weather service. Report today's conditions: ...') has dispositions of that kind, since its outputs are systematically sensitive to the document-type and factual context. The premise the argument turns on is that assertoric function must be fixed by something other than history, so the cases that matter turn on current organisation, where base models are not obviously excluded. The result is that the pre-trained/fine-tuned line, which does much work in the paper, is not principled.

Appraiser (blind)
The Swampman dilemma for etiological function is a tidy objection, but the moves are familiar from the function literature and the payoff is confined to one paper's distinction.

'AI Assertion' tests 'pre-trained models', 'fine-tuned models' and 'AI systems' against its two conditions as if the bearer were obvious. So the apparent disagreement between 'LLMs cannot assert', 'they assert by proxy' and 'they quasi-assert' is a disagreement about individuating the speaker, not about speech-act theory. If so, the live question is whether the sanction-bearing locus could shift to the system, not whether to call the present case 'proxy' or 'none'.

Thumbs-down, preference rankings and corrections are feedback by an interacting community that is explicitly aimed at making outputs more truthful, and the system's dispositions change in response. Williamson-style constitutive-rule views and Brandomian scorekeeping views of assertion would diverge on exactly this point regardless of LLMs. The turning premise is that 'capable of being sanctioned' is ambiguous between corrective and reactive sanction, and the ambiguity is where the work gets done. Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires that the asserter can be sanctioned by those it interacts with, and that fine-tuned models fail this. Ask what sanction must do to the sanctioned party. (a) Thin reading: sanction is a negative signal that changes the party's later dispositions to assert. User downvotes, corrections, in-context rebukes and RLHF updates all do this, so a model with memory or online feedback is sanctionable in exactly this sense. The condition then becomes an engineering variable, and the view agrees with Butlin's own agency criterion, which counts sensitivity to feedback as agency, and with Attah's graded attribution. (b) Thick reading: sanction must bite on something the party has a stake in, such as reputation, welfare or standing. That condition is satisfied by organisms or moral patients and not by systems with imposed goals. It is then the real work-doing condition, and the descriptive-function condition is idle. This is Gubelmann's and Magnus et al.'s position in different clothes. The premise the argument turns on is that no intermediate notion of sanction is both non-trivially unmet by current models and independent of having a stake. Without such a notion, 'norm-governed social practice' fails to yield a distinct third position.

instability — Butlin and Viebahn's two-route structure (own assertion vs. proxy assertion) and the function condition's independence from the proxy account.
Sketch

They distinguish (i) the model itself asserting, which needs outputs with a descriptive function, from (ii) humans asserting through the model by proxy. For a pre-trained model the function is next-token prediction, so it fails (i). A fine-tuned model acquires a descriptive or correctness function only because annotators, reward models and designers select outputs for accuracy. This is an etiological function with human purposes in its history, and in that respect it differs from nothing in Green and Michel's proxy picture. The structure is: the output's descriptive function is a derivative function, derivative functions are borrowed from the selector's aims, and speech acts performed through a borrowed aim are proxy acts. So the model-level condition (i) is met only in the way that (ii) is met, and the two options differ by redescription. The principle the argument turns on is that a function conferred wholly by others' selection cannot ground the system's own speech-act status without also making the selectors the speakers. To resist, a defender must say what makes derived functions count for humans (social-evolutionary selection of assertion) but not for models. That answer either re-imports sanctioning, or concedes that derived function suffices.

Appraiser (blind)
The argument that derived function collapses the non-proxy route into the proxy route is interesting, but it depends heavily on contestable function theory.

On their own account assertion is a norm-governed practice whose performer is answerable for the content. When a proxy asserts for a principal, the principal commits to p. Traditionally this works because the principal authorised or vetted the proxy's content, as with a spokesperson reading a script or a lawyer filing a brief. An LLM deployer authorises a policy and not particular contents. At the token level the content is generated after authorisation, is unforeseeable, and is often unreviewed. Responsibility for such outputs is strict, product-style responsibility, as with a publisher or a vending-machine owner, and it is not speaker commitment. The premise the argument turns on is that assertoric commitment requires the committed party to have some epistemic access to the content, such as the ability to appreciate it as a claim about how things are. If the premise holds, then in the cases that matter (open-ended generation) nobody asserts: the model fails the conditions and the human is only liable. This yields a precise stable position, 'liability without speech act', that neither Butlin and Viebahn nor the proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) allow. The proxy option then offers no real alternative to denial.

Appraiser (blind)
The 'liability without speech act' position for unvetted content is precise and plausible, but it overlaps with the orphan-output idea and with existing worries about proxy accounts.

Butlin and Viebahn locate the failure of pre-trained models in lacking descriptive functions, and suggest fine-tuning for groundedness or correctness might supply them. Suppose the function is supplied by training as selection for truth-tracking. A hallucination is then an output that fails its function, which is a malfunction in the system and not a violation of an assertoric norm by a speaker. For a human, a false assertion is a norm-violating act that is nonetheless an assertion. For the model, the same condition makes the false output either not an assertion (because it lacks the function) or an assertion that is also a defect. In the first case the model's assertoric status shrinks to its true outputs, so it can never assert falsely, which is absurd for a norm-governed practice. In the second case, the norm is just the designer's specification, and 'being held to the norm' is just being debugged. That is Gubelmann's mechanism-with-imposed-purposes picture, in which no difference between malfunction and deliberate wrongdoing can be drawn. The premise the argument turns on is that a function-based criterion of assertion must be indexed to type-level function and therefore cannot distinguish error from insincerity or violation at the level of the individual act. So the normative route to denial reduces to the organismic route, and the two do not independently support denial.

Appraiser (blind)
The malfunction-versus-false-assertion point is a real puzzle for function-based criteria, but it is a limited internal objection.

distinction — Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's treatment of apology as one act whose core is remorse and moral agency.
Sketch

The denials treat apology as the paradigm of an act needing inner states, namely remorse and moral standing. Analyses of apology (Smith, Austin on expressives) distinguish an acknowledgment of the wrong (a constative-like commitment), an undertaking not to repeat it (commissive) and an expression of regret (expressive). Only the third needs a feeling. The first two can be satisfied by a system whose later in-context behaviour is answerable to what it said, and a chatbot that says 'I shouldn't have done X, I won't' and then conforms for the rest of the session satisfies them functionally. The key premise is that the commissive and acknowledgment components carry the apology's repair function, because recipients mostly want correction and not feelings. This reclassifies the views: Magnus et al. defend a remorse-centred conception, Butlin and Viebahn's normative analysis fits the commissive component, and Attah's functional intention fits the acknowledgment. Fictionalism and proxy accounts can be tested by asking which component each can reach. The result is a non-uniform verdict by component, which is different from a general pluralism about speech acts.

Appraiser (blind)
Decomposing apology into components and giving a verdict per component is sensible but fairly predictable, and it leans on a contestable claim about what recipients want.

Magnus et al. take the morally serious apology as the benchmark and ask what agency it needs. But the triggers for chatbot 'I apologize for the confusion' are almost never wrongs. They are friction: a user correction, a misparse, a refusal. In human talk this is the ordinary job of 'sorry' as a phatic or face-work token. It signals uptake of the correction, resets the exchange and keeps the interaction cooperative, and it carries no commitment to repair and no acknowledgment of wrongdoing. Such uses are standard English and not degenerate cases of apology. The premise the argument turns on is that the speech-act type is fixed by the discourse function a token serves in context, and not by the lexical item or its most morally weighty use. If so, the 'bullshit' charge and the 'it can apologise by proxy' reply both misdescribe the data. Both debate a thick act that was never in play, while the real question, whether a chatbot can perform repair moves, has a much easier and different answer. The moral-agency question only arises for the minority of cases where users take the token as a thick apology, and that is an uptake problem in the audience.

Appraiser (blind)
Treating most chatbot 'sorry' as a phatic repair move dissolves the dispute in a plausible way, but it is a familiar deflationary move that rests on a sampling claim.

Skiba treats the no-speech-act view as conflicting with the view that LLMs bullshit, on the grounds that bullshitting is something a speaker does. Magnus et al. use 'bullshit' for apologies that are generated by pattern matching, and their diagnosis is indifference to whether the apology's conditions hold. That is a claim about the explanation of the output and not about the speaker's act. It can be read as a property of the text, in the way we call a form letter or a horoscope bullshit without positing an author who performs a speech act. Frankfurt's category is itself disjunctive between the speaker's attitude and the output's insensitivity to truth. So there are two readings. On the production reading, 'bullshit' needs a speaker, and the apparent conflict is real but the term is misapplied. On the product reading, the conflict dissolves, and the more interesting question is why an utterance-evaluation vocabulary (lying, bullshitting, apologising) seems apt for non-speakers at all. The premise the argument turns on is that our ethical vocabulary for speech has two strata, act-assessment and artifact-assessment, and the literature has treated them as one.

Appraiser (blind)
The act-assessment versus artifact-assessment distinction responds usefully to Skiba's claimed conflict, but the point is narrow and the product reading of 'bullshit' is a stretch.

U168. The question 'can a chatbot apologise?' has no determinate answer until one fixes which entity is the candidate apologiser (weights, instance, persona or deployed product), and apology, with its backward-looking responsibility and forward-looking commitment, is the speech act that shows most clearly that the debate has been about different entities.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared presupposition across all four rival groups that 'the LLM' picks out a single candidate speaker.

Apology needs a single subject who both owns the past act and is bound by the future commitment. The weights persist but have no episodic memory of the wrong. The instance remembers the conversation but is gone when it ends. The persona ('Claude', 'the assistant') persists across instances as a role but does not itself act. The deployed product, the company plus the model, has persistence, stakes and sanctionability. Gubelmann's organism argument, Butlin's agency criterion and Attah's control conception implicitly choose different individuands, and Magnus et al. move between 'the chatbot' as model and 'the chatbot' as interlocutor. Their verdict of 'no apology' is then driven by the instance or weights, while the proxy replies are driven by the product. The premise is that act-attribution requires an individuation of the agent that preserves the diachronic identity the act's content presupposes. On that premise, apology implies different answers at different levels. The persona level may be the one at which a real, if thin, apology could be performed, as an institutional office-holder, which is neither the proxy view nor the mere-text view.

Appraiser (blind)
Individuating the candidate apologiser (weights, instance, persona, product) is a worthwhile point, but it overlaps with thesis 1 and with the existing proxy literature.

The bullshit classification of chatbot apologies holds only in a narrow band of agency: grant the chatbot the sensitivity to instrumental value that Butlin's criterion requires and its apology becomes a false promise or lie, while denying it any such sensitivity leaves it without any speaker-attitude, so 'bullshit' collapses into either lying or mere noise.

An apology has a backward-looking component (acknowledging the fault) and a forward-looking one (implicit or explicit commitment to forbear). Chatbots produce 'I'll be more careful' in stateless or fine-tuned settings where nothing carries over. Frankfurt's distinction needs a speaker with a stance toward the truth or the commitment: the liar is responsive to it in order to subvert it, and the bullshitter is indifferent to it. Take a Butlin-style agent whose outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, one that adapts within the conversation to the user's complaint. It is then not indifferent to the apology's repair function. It represents the commitment, and if it cannot fulfil it, the apology is a false promise, not bullshit. If we deny any such sensitivity, as the organismic and enactive views do, there is no attitude to be indifferent, and the output is neither bullshit nor lie but artefact. The key premise is that indifference is an attitude of a system that could have been responsive. The result is that the bullshit label is stable only for a middle case of partial agency, and that case is the one the denial position cannot occupy.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that the bullshit label survives only for partial agency is a clever squeeze, but it depends on a contestable reading of Frankfurt and on exactly what a language agent represents.

U170. The criteria for apology that exclude chatbots also exclude the child's coached 'say sorry', which is how the practice is reproduced, so the denial of chatbot apology collapses into an intermediate 'proto-apology' view like Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion.

Magnus et al. argue from what a morally serious apology involves: remorse, responsibility, repair. But the human practice depends on a developmental stage in which children are made to say sorry, with no grasp of wrongdoing, and the formula then acquires its content through uptake, scaffolding and correction. If those early performances are apologies, the moral-agency requirement cannot be a condition on being an apology. If they are not apologies (they are what they would call bullshit or mimicry), then the human practice has a non-apology phase that is a necessary route to apology. In that case the chatbot's output is best classified as a proto-apology, a stage whose status depends on whether the surrounding scaffolding (feedback, user correction, sanction) could ever grow into the full practice. The key premise is that apology is a developmental kind whose constitutive conditions are met by a process, not by each token. Denial then reduces to the claim that the chatbot's scaffolding is of the wrong sort, which is an intermediate view and not a denial.

The coached child's 'say sorry' is an engaging analogy that links denial to proto-assertion, though it is a single-counterexample argument with an easy reply.

An apology presupposes that the speaker is the author of the offending conduct and can answer for it ('I' did it). If chatbots lack the moral agency to apologise, they lack the standing to be the 'I' of 'I'm sorry I gave you wrong medical advice'. The utterance therefore carries a false presupposition about the speaker, whatever the speaker's attitude to truth. A false self-ascription is closer to a misrepresentation (a lie-like or pretence act) than to Frankfurtian bullshit, which requires the absence of concern with how things are. The same structure applies to 'I recommend', 'I promise' and 'I think', where the first-person form claims authorship, commitment and ownership of a stance. Magnus et al. need a reason why apology is special; on their own premise it is not, and the right remedy is not better-designed apologies but removing the first-person speech-act idiom from chatbot design. This presses their design implications toward Skiba-style general no-speech-act conclusions, with a distinctive mechanism: failure of the 'I', not failure of norms.

Appraiser (blind)
Locating the defect in a false first-personal presupposition and generalising it to all chatbot first-person speech is a distinctive mechanism, though it is underargued as a reading of Magnus et al.

Greeting-card apologies work the same way. Ratification of a drafted apology is a neat counterexample to origin-based assessment, but it amounts to a proxy or adoption point that is mostly familiar.

Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument from assertion to all speech acts fails because speech-act types differ in where their normative upshot lands (on the speaker, on the hearer, or on the context). The norm-based argument says assertion is a norm-governed practice whose performer must be answerable to sanction. That works because assertion and the commissives alter the speaker's own normative status: they incur commitment, so there must be someone who can be held to it. Directives, warnings and advisories work mainly by altering the hearer's reasons: a warning gives you a reason to step back whether or not the warner can be sanctioned. Declarations such as naming alter the institutional context. So the denial position is not uniform. The premise it turns on is that a speech act's success conditions depend on a speaker-side accountability relation only when the act's characteristic effect is speaker commitment. The proposal reclassifies the positions. 'No speech acts' (Skiba, Gubelmann) and 'proxy for all acts' (Green and Michel, Arora) both assume the argument transfers wholesale. The distinction predicts a split verdict: chatbots can warn and advise in a thin sense, but cannot promise, apologise or sincerely assert. That split also explains why the apology case (Magnus et al.) looks so clear while advising looks contested.

Appraiser (blind)
Splitting speech acts by where their normative upshot lands is a reasonable challenge to Skiba, but it is somewhat obvious.

U174. Any externalist metasemantics that makes LLM output refer at all (the very thing Skiba needs in order to say that output is meaningful but not performed) presupposes a reference-preserving, deferential intention, which is a different attitude from communicative intention. The debate's denials target only the latter, so the no-speech-act view is unstable on its own metasemantic commitments.

Move · Target

Sketch

Skiba pairs a no-speech-act view with externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. Externalist reference, whether causal-historical or deferential, does not come free. Kripke's chain requires each link to intend to use the word with the reference of the one before, and Putnam's division of linguistic labour requires deference. So there are two distinct intention-types: communicative intentions (Grice: produce an effect in a hearer by recognition of that intention) and reference-borrowing intentions (use this term as the community does). Gubelmann, Attah and the Bender/Koller line all discuss only the first. If the model's tokens refer by inheriting from training-data speakers, then either (a) the model has some thin reference-preserving intention, and then it is a user of words with a mental-state-like commitment that Skiba denies, or (b) reference is fixed wholly by human interpreters' intentions, in which case the 'externalism' is just interpretation by humans, which is the very position the debate set out to oppose. The premise it turns on is that reference-borrowing is a mental-attitude-dependent relation and not a mere causal chain, which is itself disputed. The result is that denying communicative intention does not secure a no-speech-act view unless the metasemantics is made purely causal.

Appraiser (blind)
Distinguishing reference-borrowing intentions from communicative intentions is clever and under-noticed, but it targets one pairing in Skiba and the payoff is narrow.

Skiba's norm-based argument asks whether 'the LLM' can be sanctioned, hold commitments, and answer for outputs. Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, and Attah likewise test 'the system' for intentions or sanctionability. But one set of weights generates many concurrent conversations and many personas, has no memory across sessions, and is wrapped in a product identity. Sanctionability, commitment-tracking and intention each come out differently for each candidate. The persona is tracked across a conversation but cannot be punished. The product brand can be sanctioned through reputation and market loss but has no per-utterance control. The weights have the standing dispositions but no commitments. The key premise is that the individuation of a speaker is prior to testing it against the conditions on speech acts, and that for LLMs it is under-determined by the facts. A 'no' for one candidate does not transfer to another. The no-speech-act verdict is then partly an artefact of picking the weights or model type as the default candidate, and the proxy and fictionalist views are best read as different answers to the individuation question.

The speaker-individuation point is true and useful but largely overlaps with thesis 1 and is less committal and less predictive.

U176. On an uptake-sensitive Austinian conception of illocution, the no-speech-act view and the proxy view are one view. In both, the speech act is completed by the human who takes up the output, so 'does the model perform the act?' is a verbal question about where to draw the boundary of a distributed act.

Skiba infers from the model's failure to satisfy norm-governance conditions that no speech act is performed, and then asks what pragmatic theory explains human–LLM interaction. Austin, Hornsby and Langton hold that illocutionary acts require secured uptake and a conventional procedure. Where users, interfaces and institutional context supply the uptake and the convention, the act is constituted jointly by the output and its uptake, as with a vending machine's 'ticket issued' or a signed form. The key premise is that illocutions are not properties of a speaker's mind or standing but of an output-in-a-practice. Given that premise, the denier saying 'no act by the model' and the proxy theorist saying 'an act by the deployer via the model' are describing the same two-part structure with the credit assigned differently. What looks like a substantive split is a choice about which part of a distributed event to call the 'performer'. The only live residue is whether the model counts as part of the act's vehicle or as an agent.

Appraiser (blind)
Collapsing denial and proxy views into a verbal dispute over a distributed act is plausible but a deflationary move that is easy to resist.

U177. Skiba's norm-based argument conflates two senses of 'open to sanction'. Training-time shaping by RLHF and rule-based filters is a sanctioning practice of the same type that makes humans assertors at all. So the real disagreement is whether assertion is a token-level event or the exercise of a standing, trained competence.

Move · Target
reframing — Skiba and Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition.
Sketch

The norm-based argument says an asserter must be answerable to sanction by interlocutors, and LLMs are not. But humans also acquire assertoric competence through sanctions applied long before and apart from any given assertion, and most assertions never meet a sanction. Mature assertion is norm-guided because past sanctioning shaped dispositions to produce outputs, not because a sanction is live at utterance time. RLHF is the same structure at industrial scale: human raters penalise unwarranted claims and reward warranted ones. What the LLM lacks is addressability, a token-level link between a particular output and a sanction that lands on the producer. The key premise is that the norm-based condition is ambiguous between (a) a selection history of sanction and (b) present answerability. Reading (a) is met by fine-tuned models, as Butlin and Viebahn concede for the first condition. Reading (b) is not met, but then it is met only imperfectly by many humans such as anonymous posters and children. The dispute therefore turns on whether speech acts are token events requiring live answerability, or outputs of a trained competence, which is a question about the unit of norm-governed behaviour and not about LLMs.

Appraiser (blind)
The ambiguity between sanction as selection history and as present answerability is a fair point, but the comparison with humans is partly anticipated in the existing discussion.

U178. The speech-act question about LLMs is not a metaphysical question but a conceptual-engineering one. Each camp, including the no-speech-act view, is implicitly choosing which entity should bear the accountability that speech-act talk allocates, and the intention and agency arguments are post hoc rationalisations of that choice.

The disputants share a purpose, which is to say whom to hold responsible for a model's apology, advice or assertion. Skiba's norm-based view, the proxy accounts, Magnus et al. on apology, and the quasi-testimony and proto-assertion intermediates all tie speech-act status to who can be blamed, sanctioned or trusted. The agency literature (Butlin, Barandiaran and Almendros, Puzio) disagrees about the metaphysics but not about this function. The key premise is that speech-act categories are not natural kinds fixed by facts about intention. They are tools for coordinating commitment and blame, so the question is what these categories should do for us once speakers include systems with no stable identity and no stake. This predicts that the verdicts track practical stakes. 'Assertion' is denied where denial protects reliance norms, and 'proxy' is chosen where it assigns liability to firms. It also predicts that the debate cannot be settled by more evidence about internal states. The answer is evaluated by whether the resulting categories let the practices of warranting, retracting and apologising continue to function.

Appraiser (blind)
A conceptual-engineering framing is fashionable and sweeping, but the claim that the arguments are post hoc rationalisations is hard to support.

The norm-based argument needs a sanctionability condition that real models fail. Consider what a sanction must do. (a) If it must be felt, or must touch the sanctioned party's interests as a self-maintaining being, then models fail because they are not organisms with stakes. But then the explanatory work is done by organismic autonomy, and the norm-based argument adds nothing independent of Gubelmann's.
