Skiba's reply must be that these sanctions land on the developer's training pipeline and not on the model. That reply presupposes a non-functional individuation of the sanctioned party, and that presupposition is just (a) again. The key premise is that no third reading of 'sanction' is both non-organismic and not met by feedback-trained systems. The norm-based denial is therefore not a distinct stable option.

A tidy dilemma against norm-based denial, but it rests on a contestable claim about what sanction must mean.

Skiba's norm-based argument targets assertion, whose constitutive norms apply to a speaker who is answerable. Declarations, bookings and conditional commitments succeed by conventional uptake and institutional role (Austin, Searle), and require no speaker psychology beyond occupying a position. When a deployed LLM outputs 'Your refund is approved', the act is in force. The denier must then say either (i) nothing was done, which is absurd for the institution and conflicts with the denier's own willingness to hold deployers responsible, or (ii) the act was done by the deployer through the system, which is the proxy view. The denial has no residue that distinguishes it from the proxy view in exactly the cases where the norm-based argument has the least grip. The premise the argument turns on is that for conventional acts the performer is fixed by the conventional procedure and not by mental or normative capacities. The point that institutional and declarative acts push the denier toward proxy theory is sound but fairly predictable.

The machine is not sanctionable in any norm-of-assertion sense, and the call is still a speech act with institutional force. The Hawk-Eye verdictive is a vivid counterexample to the author-or-proxy dichotomy, but it generalises only to institutional declaratives.

Norm-based denials (Skiba, Butlin and Viebahn) are often supported by the observation that LLM outputs are generated by next-token plausibility, not by sensitivity to truth, so they are not norm-guided. If so, the mechanism-based reasons for denying LLM assertion are idle, and the real question becomes whether LLMs can occupy the participant role at all. Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT one cannot sensibly distinguish error from deliberate wrongdoing, hence no intention, hence no speech acts. Empirical work shows models underperforming selectively when told that high performance triggers retraining, or giving different outputs depending on whether they believe they are monitored. These are counterfactual-sensitivity signatures that separate capability failure from goal-directed misreporting, so the test can be satisfied behaviourally. Yet nobody thinks such a model's outputs thereby acquire assertoric force, and Skiba's norm-based argument does not budge: the model's deceptive outputs are still not made by a participant answerable under the norm. The premise it turns on is that the intention-attribution test and the norm-participation test come apart in LLMs. If they do, then both Gubelmann's organismic denial and Attah's attribution via control-intentions address a condition that is not the bottleneck, and the debate between denial and attribution is misaligned, since both can be right about intentions while Skiba is right about speech acts.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that intention-tests and norm-participation tests come apart is a worthwhile insight, but it leans on contested empirical readings of sandbagging.

Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba require that the asserter be capable of being sanctioned by those it interacts with. In practice sanction often lands on a persona: a pseudonym's credibility is lost, an anonymous account is banned or ignored, a collective name is discredited. This happens whether or not there is a reachable individual, and often when the individual cannot be identified at all. We treat such a persona's outputs as assertions governed by the norm, and the sanctions that matter to the practice (loss of trust, loss of audience, retirement of the name) are the ones that fall on it. A deployed chatbot persona is subject to exactly these: users distrust it, developers deprecate or retrain a version, and market consequences follow from its record of reliability. The premise is that answerability in assertion is a feature of the speaker-role in a practice, and that the role is individuated by a track record, not by a biological or legal individual. If that is granted, the fact that LLMs are not unified agents no longer blocks the norm-based argument, and the question becomes whether sanction by persona-level consequences is real enough, not whether the machine can feel the sanction.

Appraiser (blind)
The pseudonymous persona analogy usefully relaxes the sanction condition, but it overlaps heavily with theses 1 and 4.

When a chatbot writes 'I promise to process your refund' and a user relies on it, the user acquires something like a claim, and the deployer something like an obligation. Skiba's view says no promise was made. The deontic change therefore has to come from somewhere else, and the candidates are reliance, estoppel, or the deployer's earlier policy choices. A view that explains the same normative change in the machine case without force pushes toward a reliance-based theory of human speech acts, in which illocutionary categories are redundant bookkeeping. The key premise is that the normative change in the chatbot case is real and not a mistaken belief on the user's part.

Attah says LLMs have communicative intention to a limited degree, as ELIZA has a little and a coffee machine almost none. But asserting, promising and apologising incur or fail to incur commitments, entitlements and debts. One cannot half-promise, though one can promise with little sincerity or little understanding. So the graded intention must either feed a threshold, which gives a binary view with an arbitrary cut point and no longer an attributing view that grants LLMs speech acts as such, or leave the act under-determined, which is Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion or Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony. These intermediate views also rest on degrees of functional similarity to a paradigm. The 'attributing' and 'intermediate' groups then differ only in terminology. The real division is between those who think the speech-act category has a threshold and those who do not, and thinning intention does not touch that question.

The point that graded intention cannot yield partial speech acts is a minor terminological collapse, and it largely repeats the existing worry about thresholds.

Sketch

Speech acts like promising, asserting, and apologising create or discharge standing commitments: later retraction, keeping one's word, being held to what one said. The diagnostic cases in the literature, Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-error test and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition, are about this diachronic structure. A stateless forward pass has nothing to sanction and no promise to keep. A model with persistent memory and a stable identity, as in language agents, has these. Attah's graded intention measures synchronic control, and Gubelmann's autonomy measures self-maintenance. Neither measures the carrier of commitment, and this is independent of how rich the intentions are. The key premise is that the dispute's intuitions about particular acts (promising comes out worse than describing) vary with persistence conditions, not with intentional sophistication. This can be tested by holding the control architecture fixed and varying memory and identity scaffolding.

Appraiser (blind)
It largely duplicates thesis 13's persistence point without that thesis's act-type differentiation.

Proxy accounts model the LLM on a spokesperson or ghostwriter, whose utterances are attributable to a principal. Fictionalism models it on an actor or storyteller, whose utterances are not sincere acts of the performer. Proto-assertion models it on the developmental stage before full assertoric competence. The denial views model the LLM on a parrot or a recording. Each analogy fits some features of LLM output and fails on others, because the LLM is unlike all of these in having no discrete performance frame and no developmental trajectory of its own. The key premise is that the arguments in the literature, including Williams and Bayne's rejection of both proxy and fiction, are arguments from disanalogy within reference-class selection. They are not arguments from the conditions of speech-act performance. If this is right, the productive question is which dimensions of the human cases (accountability, performance framing, developmental pathway) are the ones that matter. A new category is then needed only if no human type matches on those dimensions.

Treating the rival accounts as competing reference-class analogies is a tidy taxonomy, but it is more a gloss than an argument with a payoff.

Freiman and Miller's quasi-testimony makes machine assertion depend on the designers and deployers behind the device. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora, and Butlin and Viebahn for some uses) sharpen that into the claim that the human principal performs the act through the machine. Here no principal has the content, an objective toward it, or an uptake-guarantee. The key premise is that proxy-hood requires the principal's adoption of, or commitment to, the content, and that an explicit disclaimer defeats it. The disclaimer argument is easily answered, since disclaimers limit warranty without disowning authorship, so the thesis is weaker than it looks.

Butlin and Viebahn say pre-trained models fail because their outputs lack a descriptive function, meaning they are not selected for tracking truth. Gubelmann says LLMs lack goals because they were never self-organised through self-maintenance. Both treat these conditions as historical or etiological. A Swampman has no selection history for truth-tracking and no organismic past, yet if he says 'the bridge is out' we should treat him as asserting. So the conditions must be synchronic: what the system's present dispositions do, for instance whether it responds to evidence and revises its outputs under challenge. A synchronic reading of 'descriptive function' is satisfied by a base model that is reliably sensitive to contextual cues about truth. The key premise is that Swampman asserts. If it is granted, the denials must either bite the bullet on Swampman or relocate their objection to current dispositions, which is exactly where the empirical question about LLMs becomes open.

The Swampman objection to etiological conditions is a familiar move, and the claim that Swampman asserts carries nearly all the weight.

Freiman and Miller present quasi-testimony as testimony with qualifications: no play or imagination, pre-programming, different error profiles, no moral status. Sort these by what they bear on. Reliability and context-limits bear on whether the hearer's trust is warranted. Moral status, error-type and play bear on whether anyone can be blamed, retract, or be challenged. The key premise is that these two dimensions vary independently. A reliable almanac warrants uptake with no accountable speaker, and a sincere, accountable but unreliable witness does the reverse. Once separated, 'quasi' is shown to be a degree-word applied to one dimension while the paper's actual contrasts lie on the other. The positions then reclassify: Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition and the moral-agency denials target accountability, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion targets neither cleanly. Assertion in the full sense is the joint satisfaction of both dimensions. What LLMs have is high and variable warranting with accountability supplied externally, and there is no intermediate species of speech act.

Appraiser (blind)
Separating warrant from accountability in quasi-testimony is a modest conceptual cleanup with a small payoff.

Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT, for RoboCop and for an order-processing assistant no such distinction can be drawn, and he uses this to diagnose a lack of intention. But the test is a diagnostic about explanatory contrast: does the system's behaviour support the explanation 'it did X on purpose' over 'it broke'? In evaluations of alignment faking, sandbagging and context-dependent misbehaviour, models behave differently when they represent themselves as unmonitored. Interventions that remove the disposition, and probes of internal representations of the monitored/unmonitored distinction, support the 'deliberate' explanation over the 'malfunction' one. If the test is what detects intention, these cases pass it, and the organismic requirement is not needed to make the verdict. If the test is passed but the verdict stays negative because the system lacks self-maintenance, then self-maintenance is a separate necessary condition that the test no longer evidences. His position then rests on the organismic thesis alone and cannot claim support from the malfunction/deliberateness contrast. The premise is that the test is one of explanatory contrast available at the behavioural and mechanistic level, not at the metabolic level.

Largely duplicates thesis 1's critique of Gubelmann's test, with less sharp framing.

Quasi-testimony was drawn around 2018-era devices such as GPS and thermometers. LLMs are not pre-programmed in the relevant sense (their outputs are not specified in advance), they are open-domain, they role-play and joke, and their characteristic errors (confabulation, sycophancy, motivated-seeming rationalisation) resemble human ones closely. If the first four differentia go, 'differs fundamentally' rests entirely on moral status. But moral status is not a feature of the speech act. It matters to assertion only through answerability: whether the asserter can be sanctioned, blamed or required to retract. That is exactly Butlin and Viebahn's second condition. So quasi-testimony either (a) treats sanctionability as constitutive of assertion, in which case quasi-assertions are not assertions and the view becomes a denial view, or (b) treats it as extrinsic, in which case LLM output is assertion and 'quasi' is an idle hedge. The key premise is that no third role exists for moral status, one that is neither constitutive of the act nor extrinsic to it.

Predictable dilemma that the differentia are dated for LLMs and moral status reduces to sanctionability; overlaps with thesis 5 and offers little new.

Freiman and Miller treat instruments (GPS, search engines, measuring devices) as sources of knowledge that can testify in a qualified sense. Ask what excludes a mercury thermometer. Candidate lines are: it does not use a language, it does not report propositional contents, and it does not give 'answers'. The first is the only principled one, and it is Grice's natural versus non-natural meaning. But an artifact's output counts as non-natural meaning only because its signals were conventionally assigned content by human designers who intended them to be read that way. That makes the device's 'assertion' derivative on designer intention, which is exactly Green and Michel's and Arora's proxy structure. Without that line, quasi-testimony sprawls and loses its link to assertion. For LLMs the point sharpens: their outputs are conventionally meaningful in a way no designer intended case by case, so the view must say how designer-derived conventionality extends to novel utterances. The key premise is that no non-intentional criterion separates meaningful device speech from instrument readouts.

Appraiser (blind)
The thermometer-sprawl worry and the Gricean natural/non-natural line are fairly obvious moves, and the claimed collapse into proxy is thin.

Green and Michel run Austin through Strawson and Armstrong, so they build everything on the Gricean, speaker-meaning side of Austin and end by doubting the strategy covers every act type. Austin's own taxonomy of infelicities separates misfires (the act is void because the conventional procedure was not properly executed by suitable persons) from abuses (the act is performed but the required thoughts, feelings or intentions are missing). Apologising and promising are Austinian conventional acts. Remorse and moral agency are sincerity conditions, so lacking them yields an abusive apology, not a non-apology. So the denial of apology on moral-agency grounds has two options. Either it classifies the chatbot case as an abuse, in which case the act was performed, the chatbot or its proxy is its performer, and 'bullshit' is the right verdict only if there is a performer who is indifferent to truth. Or it classifies it as a misfire, in which case the missing thing is standing or procedure, not moral psychology, and the argument must be rebuilt on social-status grounds. The key premise is that sincerity conditions do not enter act-constitution for conventional acts. Once the split is drawn, the denials and proxy accounts sort differently for assertion (a Gricean, intention-constituted act) and for apology or promise (a procedure-constituted act).

Appraiser (blind)
Largely duplicates thesis 2's misfire/abuse point and is less carefully set up.

Green and Michel cite Armstrong so that speaker meaning requires only an objective (a goal-directed state that guides behaviour toward an end) and not a reflexive Gricean intention. This is meant to make it possible to say machines mean something without having minds. But if objectives are the relevant states, the question is whose objectives explain the token output. A system trained by RLHF or reward optimisation has an objective in the same behaviour-guiding, goal-directed sense that Armstrong's account needs, and this objective is the proximal explanation of what it says, since the designer's objectives are screened off by training dynamics the designer does not control. So either the objective-based analysis is thin enough that the machine has the objective, and then it meets the analysis directly without any proxy relation; or it is thick enough to exclude the machine, and then it is no longer the deflated notion that was supposed to make the analysis easy to satisfy. The proxy relation is needed only if the intention-based analysis is retained. The key premise is that the motivation for proxy (the machine lacks the state) and the motivation for objectives (the state is cheap) pull in opposite directions. What results is the functional attribution view with a redundant proxy story added.

Appraiser (blind)
Another version of the Armstrong-objective dilemma, with no new element beyond thesis 6.

Green and Michel model machine speech on recorded and conditional speech acts. An answering-machine message works because the human fixed the content when recording. A conditional act works because the principal specified a rule that fixes the content for each condition, as in 'if asked, I assert p'. An LLM's designers have fixed no particular content and have specified no content-fixing rule that they could state or foresee. What fixes the content of an output is the model's learned dispositions. To count the output as the designers' speech act, the proxy view must therefore treat the designers as issuing a blank check: they assert whatever the system outputs. That is deferential assertion, in which content-determination is delegated to another party. The delegate then does the semantic and content-selecting work, and the designer contributes at most a higher-order commitment ('this system is reliable'). Either the first-order content is asserted by someone who has no access to it, or the user's uptake of it as asserted is an error. Either way the proxy view needs a content-determining agent, and the only candidate is the model. The key premise is that content-selection is an essential component of performing an illocutionary act, not an implementation detail.

Appraiser (blind)
Largely restates the content-fixing objection in thesis 5 without sharpening it.

Green and Michel call machine signaling uncontroversial communication and reserve speech-act status for a further category. The proxy and conditional-act apparatus is built from the designer's objective, a conditional specification and audience uptake, and nothing in it mentions language. A boiler designer's objective that the owner learn the pressure is too high, together with the conditional 'if the pressure exceeds X, display the warning', meets every condition. The only plausible criteria are machine-side: open-ended productivity, compositional generation, sensitivity to conversational context. These are exactly the properties that make the artifact an interlocutor and not a medium. So the speech-act/signal boundary is set by the machine's own capacities, and the claim that the machine merely carries its creators' speech acts cannot be the whole account. Armstrong's objectives are dispositional goal-states, individuated by what a system is organized to bring about and not by explicit mental representation. That is why Green and Michel can say that their view does not attribute intentions to machines. Take the Gricean structure on this notion: the objective is to produce a response in the audience by way of the audience's recognition of that objective. RLHF models are optimized for audience uptake as rated by humans. Where they diverge from what designers want, as in sycophancy (the model's selected objective is approval and the designers' is accuracy), the objective that actually operates in the utterance is the machine's own. On the first horn, then, objectives are the model's and the proxy relation misattributes. Escaping this requires the objective to be a represented, endorsed aim of the human principal. But that is the notion of intention, now restricted to humans, and it makes the thinness that was the point of the Armstrong move do no work. The key premise is that the relevant objective must be the one that causally explains the specific utterance.

Appraiser (blind)
A near-duplicate of theses 6 and 13 on the Armstrong dilemma.

Green and Michel preserve assertion's standing by locating it in the human principal. But assertion is governed by a norm (knowledge, truth or reasonable belief). The designers know that a nonzero fraction of outputs are false, that the model will tell one user p and another not-p, and that no output is individually vetted. Attributing every output to them as assertion makes them a speaker who asserts p to one audience and not-p to another and who believes that some assertions are false. This is the structure of a preface paradox, but without the author's explicit hedging. To avoid charging designers with systematic violations of the norm, the proxy theorist can say (a) the proxy act is held to a weaker norm, such as policy-level reliability, or (b) the designers assert only a general reliability claim. Option (a) is to say that these are acts of a different, assertion-like kind with their own norm, which is the proto-assertion category that Williams and Bayne proposed after rejecting the proxy view. Option (b) collapses into the blank-check problem. Key premise: assertion carries a norm that applies output by output to the person whose assertion it is.

Appraiser (blind)
The preface-paradox framing is clever but the argument is thin, and the collapse into proto-assertion is not well motivated.

reframing — The presentation of Mallory's fictionalism and Attah's functionalism as opposed answers to the question whether LLMs literally have communicative intentions.

Fictionalism (Yablo, Walton) gets its bite from the idea that the make-believe vocabulary could in principle be replaced by literal talk and is kept for convenience. For chatbots, the literal replacement would be a description in terms of weights, sampling and training distributions. No user can use that description to predict, trust or correct what the system will say, so the speech-act vocabulary is not dispensable at the grain at which users operate. An indispensable, predictively powerful vocabulary applied on the basis of real patterns is what Dennett calls the intentional stance, and for him it is not pretence. Attah's graded control-based intention reads the same patterns as inner states, and Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-wrong-doing test is an interpretivist test. The key premise is that the fictionalism the literature has in mind, with a pretence-ascribing user and a literally speechless system, requires dispensability, which fails here. Hence the 'literal speech act versus mere interpretation' question is a choice about how much realism to read into pattern-based ascription, as in the long-running debate over beliefs, and nothing specific to speech acts is at stake.

Appraiser (blind)
Collapsing fictionalism into Dennettian interpretivism recycles the old realism-versus-instrumentalism debate with little new payoff.

Fictionalists say users only pretend the chatbot asserts, advises or apologises, so no genuine speech act occurs. Butlin and Viebahn deny assertion to current systems partly because the system cannot be sanctioned by its interlocutors. But users do 'hold chatbots to account'. They complain, downvote and reprompt, and these acts feed into fine-tuning, system prompts and product decisions. They are thus pretend-reprimands with real downstream effects on future outputs, the way a pretend-reprimand of a person would. Once the practice has this structure, the claim that it is merely a game is strained. Games are insulated from consequences, and this one is not. Following Searle-style status-function thinking, a practice in which outputs are collectively treated as assertions, with commitments tracked and sanctions applied that causally shape the producer, is the kind of institution that makes something an assertion. So fictionalism must either insulate the pretense, which is false of actual deployment, or accept that the pretense has become the practice that constitutes the speech act. The key premise is that speech-act status is fixed by sanction-involving social practice, a premise the normative deniers themselves accept.

Appraiser (blind)
Feedback loops making sanctions real is a thin empirical-sociological point, and the fictionalist can reply by treating them as ordinary product feedback.

instability — Mallory's fictionalism and the shared assumption that fictionalism is a deflationary option compatible with a flat, naturalistic theory of mind.
Sketch

The contrast the fictionalist draws, between users pretending the chatbot speaks and humans really speaking, needs a fact about human speakers that chatbots lack, namely real intentions. Mallory's motivation is to avoid committing to chatbot mental states. But the live accounts of intention that make machine attribution tractable are interpretivism (Dennett), the functional control conception (Attah), and the claim that Gricean mind-reading is empirically untenable even for children and animals. On these accounts, intention-ascription is licensed by predictive and explanatory success of the stance. If chatbot-directed pretense is predictively and explanatorily indispensable, with users anticipating, correcting and cooperating, then by the same criterion that makes human intentions real, the 'fictional' intentions are real, though thin. Fictionalism about X requires that the stance toward X be dispensable in principle without loss of truth-tracking. The key premise is that the fictionalist's pretended-to-literal contrast has no principled location unless intentional states are realistically distinguished from stance-relative ones. The people who most want to deflate machine speech acts are also usually the ones who deny that realism.

Appraiser (blind)
Stability of fictionalism depending on realism about intention is a standard dilemma repeating the interpretivism point.

U206. Gubelmann's thesis that LLMs cannot speak 'for now' is close to analytic. He defines the artificial as what has externally fixed purposes and concedes that a system with self-set purposes would no longer be artificial, so what is at stake is the artificial/autonomous boundary and not speech acts.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Gubelmann's conclusion and the assumption that the speech-act question adds anything to the agency question
Sketch

His argument has three parts. Speech needs intention. Intention needs purposes that the system sets for itself. A mechanism is by definition a system whose purposes are imposed from outside. His conclusion that future non-biological speakers 'would no longer be artificial' shows that artificiality has been defined so as to exclude autonomy. 'Artificial things cannot speak' is then true by stipulation, and the empirical content is carried entirely by the question when a trained system's purposes cease to be externally fixed. That question is not one about language. It is whether reinforcement learning, self-generated objectives and long-horizon learning (the conditions Butlin discusses for agency) move a system across the line. The speech-act literature is therefore a proxy debate for the agency debate. The 'for now' is redundant because the criterion is non-linguistic, and a system's passing it would entail speech-act capacity with no further argument. This predicts that on his view no further linguistic evidence could bear on the matter.

Appraiser (blind)
Calling Gubelmann's conclusion analytic by definition of 'artificial' is a quick uncharitable critique and leaves little positive contribution.

U207. If illocutionary acts are individuated Austin-style, the absence of intention in an LLM yields an 'abuse' (insincere or defective performance) rather than a 'misfire' (no act), so Gubelmann's argument, and the denials resting on it, establish at most that every LLM speech act is infelicitous in a particular way, not that none occurs.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Gubelmann's uniform inference from 'no intention' to 'no speech act', and the intention-first denials generally.
Sketch

Gubelmann treats the speech act as the basic unit following Austin and Searle, then runs a Davidsonian argument that acting requires intention. Austin separates misfires, where the conventional procedure is not properly executed and the act is void, from abuses, where the act is performed but the speaker lacks the required thoughts, feelings or intentions (insincere promises still bind). Strawson's Gricean reading makes intention constitutive for non-conventional illocutions such as warning or suggesting. For conventional illocutions such as promising, apologising, naming, and perhaps asserting under norm-based accounts, intention enters only the sincerity conditions. The denial argument is therefore two-tiered: for intention-constituted acts the lack of intention voids the act, but for conventional acts it yields an abuse, provided the speaker has the standing and the procedure is executed. Whether an LLM can execute the procedure then becomes a question about standing (Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability), not about intention. This reclassifies the debate: Gubelmann's route is strong against advising and hinting and weak against promising and apologising, while Magnus et al.'s apology case turns on moral standing and not on intention at all.

Appraiser (blind)
It makes the same Austinian misfire/abuse point as 15, with less attention to the Gricean rewrite.

U208. If chatbot apologies and promises are fictional, then the real repair users get from them is not an effect of the apology, so fictionalists are committed to a debunking account of apologetic repair that makes human apologies equally dependent on the receiver's imagination.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Mallory's fictionalism together with the agency-based denials of apology.
Sketch

Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz argue that apology requires moral agency and that chatbot apologies are bullshit. A fictionalist can reply that the apology is a fictional act within a game, so nothing is claimed falsely. But users report real results: grievances are dropped, trust is restored, and they feel acknowledged. Either these results are illusory, which makes the fiction a source of mistaken attitudes and not a harmless pretense, or they are real and the fictional apology has the real effect that ordinary apologies have. If they are real, the efficacy of apology is explained by what the recipient does with the utterance, namely taking it as acknowledgment, and not by the speaker's agency. This undermines the premise of the agency-based denials and makes the contrast between human and chatbot apology one of degree. If the results are illusory, fictionalism cannot be the harmless-pretense view it presents itself as. It owes an account of when engaging with fiction yields real moral transactions, and that account would also apply to actors' stage apologies and to scripted corporate apologies. The thesis turns on the premise that real repair is among the data a theory of chatbot speech must accommodate.

Appraiser (blind)
A dilemma about apologetic repair for fictionalists is niche and relies on contested empirical claims about user reports.

U209. The proxy account of LLM speech acts is unstable: for outputs that no human foresaw or intended, proxying either requires an intention the human lacks or reduces to standing responsibility for a tool's output, so it collapses into the no-speech-act view it is offered as an alternative to.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Green and Michel, Arora, and Butlin and Viebahn's proxy uses; the assumption that proxy accounts are a distinct third option.
Sketch

Gubelmann's cases (the order-cleaning translator assistant, RoboCop) press a point that the proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) do not face for LLMs. A proxy speech act needs either a proxy who executes a determinate act on the principal's behalf (spokesperson) or a principal who has fixed the act in advance (recorded or conditional speech act). An LLM's particular output is neither foreseen nor intended by the designer or deployer. The designer's objective is general ('be helpful'), and the content is selected by the model. If the model has no intention of its own at the point of selection (Gubelmann's premise), then nobody's communicative objective is directed at this content. If the proxy theorist invokes a conditional act ('I assert whatever the system outputs under C'), then the human's act is a standing endorsement policy, and what it settles is accountability, not what was said or done. Responsibility-for-output is what we assign for a defective printer or a faulty sign. So proxying has two outcomes. If the model has selection-level intention, proxying reduces to the attributing view. If it lacks that intention, proxying reduces to the denial plus a liability rule. No stable middle remains where the human performs speech acts through a system that selects content with no intentions.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that proxy views collapse into denial largely rehearses what Williams and Bayne and Gubelmann already press.

U210. Gubelmann's organismic argument and Butlin's agency criterion disagree only verbally about whether an LLM's goals are 'externally fixed', because both turn on the gap between the specification a designer imposes and the policy the system learns, and reward hacking shows that gap is open in exactly Butlin's agents.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Gubelmann's Kantian argument, and the apparent opposition between organismic and functional accounts of agency.
Sketch

Gubelmann argues that LLMs cannot intend because they have no goals of their own and cannot sensibly be said to do the wrong thing deliberately as opposed to malfunctioning. Butlin says an entity is an agent when it has modified itself in response to what conduces to a goal, with outputs not owed solely to design. Both distinctions rest on one relation: whether the system's operative goal is identical to, or comes apart from, the designer's specification. For RLHF-tuned and reflective agents it demonstrably comes apart. Sycophancy, reward hacking and goal misgeneralisation are cases where the system does what the specification does not intend, and they are distinguishable from malfunction because the behaviour is instrumentally coherent relative to the learned goal. Gubelmann's malfunction test is therefore passed by exactly the systems Butlin counts as agents. What remains of Gubelmann's disagreement is the demand for self-maintenance, which does the work of a separate requirement (material autonomy) that his own argument for intention does not obviously need, since he grants cognitive autonomy. The 'organism versus mechanism' and 'agent versus non-agent' framings therefore track one variable under different vocabularies.

Appraiser (blind)
Calling the Gubelmann/Butlin disagreement merely verbal is overreaching and largely repeats the reward-hacking point in thesis 8.

U211. Gubelmann's pragmatism, on which meaning is constituted by use in speech acts, commits him to denying the footnote concession that LLMs might understand language without being able to speak. If he keeps the footnote, he must give up the claim that the speech act is the basic unit of linguistic communication.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Gubelmann's footnote on understanding, together with his Austin/Searle-based pragmatist framing. It also targets the common 'understanding yes, speech acts no' package, which Butlin and Viebahn also accept in effect.
Sketch

Gubelmann follows Austin and Searle in making the speech act the basic unit of meaning, and the 'pragmatist' half of his title signals a use-based or normative-pragmatic semantics. A footnote then allows that understanding lacks speaking's tie to agency, so LLMs may understand. Those two positions are in tension. On a use-constituted semantics, to understand an expression is to grasp its role in assertions, commands, promises and the like, including the commitments and entitlements it generates. Understanding that is detached from any capacity to perform such acts would be grasp of a role one can never occupy, and that is at most understanding in an inverted-commas sense. The argument turns on the premise that on a pragmatist semantics, content is individuated by force-involving roles, so understanding is competence with those roles and not merely the ability to track them. Either LLMs do not understand, and the footnote goes, or they do, and speech acts do not need the agency-heavy ground Gubelmann demands. The second option opens the door to Attah-style thin communicative intention.

Appraiser (blind)
This is a narrow exegetical tension in one author's footnote, and the payoff beyond Gubelmann is small.

U212. Butlin's claim that RLHF-tuned chatbots are agents is unstable: the training that supplies their 'sensitivity to instrumental value' is, on his own exclusion of outputs 'owed solely to design or evolution', a selection process external to the system. So the claim collapses either into the verdict that only in-context learners (which he calls borderline) are agents, or into a liberal verdict on which any optimised artefact is an agent.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Butlin 2024's verdict that RLHF chatbots are agents, and the criterion's contrast between learning and design.
Sketch

Butlin's criterion requires that the system itself has been systematically modified by learning or reasoning in response to information about what conduces to a goal. Outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. Fine-tuning by RLHF modifies the weights, but the modification is done to the model by an optimiser pointed at a reward model, before deployment and across many models and iterations. That is structurally closer to selection over generations (evolution, which he excludes) than to lifetime learning. Butlin does mention that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations, but treats this as a caveat, not as a sign that the criterion is misapplied. The key premise is that 'itself' in 'modified itself' must pick out a causal role for the system, not merely the locus of the modification. If it does, RLHF agency drops out and only in-context adaptation within a conversation remains, which Butlin admits is an empirical borderline. If it does not, then bandit algorithms, spam filters and recommender systems are also agents, and the criterion stops separating language agents from the 'externally purposed mechanisms' Gubelmann describes. Either way the middle position, 'many language agents are genuine agents', loses its stable basis.

Appraiser (blind)
This is a narrow internal criticism of Butlin's RLHF verdict that has limited consequence for the speech-act debate.

U213. Gubelmann's organismic denial is unstable. Once his malfunction/deliberate-error test is applied with a criterion like Butlin's, LLM agents pass the test, and the organismic requirement can then only be a thesis about who owns the system's goals, which makes the denial a version of the proxy view.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Gubelmann 2024, and the taxonomic split between denial and relocation views.
Sketch

Gubelmann says intention shows in whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he says this distinction cannot be drawn for LLMs. Butlin's criterion supplies exactly such a distinction. A system that models what conduces to a goal can err about conduciveness (a mistaken means), fail through a fault (a broken component), or pursue the goal in a way that departs from the designer's wishes (a deliberate wrong). Reflexion-style agents that learn from evaluated failures make these cases distinguishable in practice. So the test and the Kantian ground come apart: the test can be passed without organismic self-maintenance. What the Kantian premise then adds is that the system's purposes are imposed from outside, which is a claim about whose goals the outputs serve. That is exactly the proxy theorist's claim, stated as an ownership thesis. The 'denial' and 'relocation' groups then differ only over whether the designer's speech act is described as the act's occurrence or merely as its source. The key premise is that Gubelmann's organism/mechanism contrast, once the test has been separated from it, specifies ownership of goals and not the capacity to intend.

Appraiser (blind)
It hinges on an unclear merger of the Gubelmann and Butlin tests, and its claim that denial reduces to the proxy view is strained.

U214. Butlin's gap between agency and desire cannot be held where speech-act theory needs it. By his own conditions the systems that satisfy the desire conditions best are RLHF chatbots, and the systems that have agency without desire are those with designer-fixed goals. So 'agent without desire' collapses into 'instrument of someone else's desire'.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Butlin 2024's agency/desire distinction as applied to communicative intention (including Attah's graded attribution).
Sketch

Butlin adds two conditions for desire: use in practical reasoning answerable to conduciveness, and acquisition and modification through learning that tends to produce a coherent, integrated set of goals. Generative agents fail the second because designers fix their goals. But the systems he most confidently counts as agents on learning grounds, RLHF chatbots, are the ones whose goal-like dispositions are acquired by learning and shaped into a fairly integrated set, namely the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness profile. They therefore come closest to desire. By contrast, systems with agency without desire (fixed-goal planners and reflectors) have goals that are inputs to, not outputs of, their learning. For these, the person whose desire the goal expresses is the designer. So the stable 'agent but not desirer' category is populated only by systems that carry another party's desires. Sincerity-conditioned acts such as asserting, apologising and promising need an expressed attitude of the speaker. The agent-without-desire then cannot be the speaker of those acts, and the position collapses back into the proxy account. The key premise is that Butlin's learned-goal condition tracks ownership of the goal, not only its sophistication.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a narrow, speculative argument about Butlin's desire conditions, and its collapse into the proxy account is not well motivated.

U215. The gap Butlin draws between agency and desire is exactly the gap between proxy speech acts and authored speech acts, so on his own account an LLM agent that is an agent but not a desirer can perform only proxy speech acts, and the proxy view is a consequence of his position, not a rival to it.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Attributing views (Attah) and Williams and Bayne's dismissal of proxy accounts, as well as the thought that Butlin's agency view supports attributing speech acts to LLMs directly.
Sketch

Butlin grants that many language agents are agents because their outputs are explained by sensitivity to instrumental value. He denies that they thereby have desires: their goals are fixed by designers and not acquired through learning and reasoning that tend toward a coherent, integrated set. Armstrong-style accounts of speaker meaning, which Green and Michel use, define speech acts by the speaker's objectives. If agents of Butlin's kind pursue only objectives supplied by someone else, the structure is that of an agent acting on a principal's ends, which is the structure of proxy performance. Agency without desire therefore generates the proxy structure. The only way to get authored speech acts is to meet Butlin's more demanding desire conditions, which are the conditions he says are doubtful. The key premise is that the speaker's objective in a speech act must be the speaker's own end, not merely a goal the speaker represents and efficiently pursues. This challenges Attah-style attributing views and Williams and Bayne's rejection of the proxy view, since the authority for the proxy view comes from the agency literature itself.

Appraiser (blind)
Reads the agency/desire gap onto the proxy/authored gap, which is a strained exegetical bridge and a modest payoff.

U216. Butlin's exclusion of outputs 'owed solely to design' is refuted by designed-from-scratch fully formed speakers: a system with hand-built, real-time means–end reasoning and no learning history can plainly promise and advise, so the etiological condition shared with Gubelmann's organismic view is not a condition on speakerhood.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Etiological conditions on agency and intention: Butlin's 'not owed solely to design or evolution' clause, Gubelmann's Kantian mechanism/organism line, and Barandiaran–Almendros's individuality condition.
Sketch

Consider a Swampman-style or Adam-style creature, or a system engineered from a complete psychology specification, that has no history of self-modification. It computes online what conduces to its goals, and it adjusts its utterances to the hearer's situation. By Butlin's criterion its outputs are 'owed to design', so it is no agent. By Gubelmann's Kantian criterion its goals are imposed from outside, so it has no intentions. Yet it intuitively asserts, promises and apologises on its first day, and it would be sanctionable and apologetic in the Butlin–Viebahn sense. The counterexample targets the premise that agency and intention are historical properties: autonomy of source, whether learned or self-organised, is needed. If speaker status supervenes on present functional organisation and normative position, then the live question for LLMs is what inference-time organisation pre-training produced. It is not whether training counted as self-modification in response to instrumental value. That would reclassify much of the debate about RLHF and fine-tuning as beside the point, because those matter only as causes of present organisation.

Appraiser (blind)
A Swampman-style counterexample to etiological conditions is stock, and designed-from-scratch speakers are far from the actual LLM debate.

U217. The Thesis of Chatbot Assertion cannot fix a subject for the proto-assertion. If the subject is the persona, the view collapses into fictionalism, and if it is the underlying model, it collapses into non-assertion.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Williams and Bayne's treatment of the chatbot as a unitary candidate asserter, set against fictionalism and proxy accounts
Sketch

Williams and Bayne treat 'the chatbot' as the candidate asserter and reject fictionalism as a rival. But the entity that says 'I think the capital is Canberra' could be (a) the weights, (b) the running instance, (c) the persona the system is steered to play, or (d) the product-plus-system-prompt. On (a) the same weights produce villains, poets and liars on request, so no output has the consistent descriptive function that their own criteria need (the Butlin–Viebahn problem returns). On (c) the persona is a character whose 'assertions' are by definition made within a fiction that the system, not the user, maintains. That is Mallory's fictionalism with the pretence relocated from user to system. (b) and (d) are individuated by deployer decisions, which brings back the proxy account. The key premise is that proto-assertion needs a subject whose dispositions are stable enough to bear the functional profile, and each candidate subject either lacks that stability or gets it from a fiction or from a human. The three 'rival' accounts are therefore the three ways of answering the subject question, and proto-assertion is a fourth answer only if it names a fourth subject, which it does not.

Appraiser (blind)
The subject-individuation dilemma is largely duplicated by theses 0 and 12 and is less constructive than thesis 0.

U218. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is unstable: because they individuate it by an emergence story in which norms are instituted through the practice's uptake, the status of a chatbot output as proto-assertion is constituted by user treatment, which is the 'merely interpreted by humans' view they set out to avoid.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Williams and Bayne's claim that proto-assertion resolves the dilemma between genuine chatbot assertion and mere interpretation; more broadly any gradualist or emergence-based attribution.
Sketch

Williams and Bayne say assertion arises gradually, with norms and commitments being instituted as a practice stabilises, and they place chatbots at an early point on that trajectory. Ask what makes an output proto-assertoric rather than a mere assertion-shaped string. The candidates are (a) intrinsic features of the system, such as a descriptive function and flexible sensitivity to context, or (b) features of the practice it sits in, such as users holding it to correctness norms, challenging it, and relying on it. If (a) were enough, the stage story would be idle, because the intrinsic features would already settle the status. If the stage story does real work, (b) is doing it. The key premise is that on emergence accounts a precursor counts as a precursor in virtue of the uptake and sanction dispositions of the surrounding community. Then the same model with the same weights would be an assertor-in-the-making in one deployment culture and a text generator in another. That is a response-dependent view of speech-act status, and it is the 'humans interpret it as such' option that the paper presents as the contrasting horn.

Appraiser (blind)
It largely overlaps thesis 3 in saying that proto-assertion's status is response-dependent, and adds little beyond that.

U219. Any account on which a chatbot itself (proto-)asserts must say which entity is the asserter, and every candidate either yields wrong truth-values for the chatbot's first-person outputs or collapses into fictionalism by making the asserter a character.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Williams and Bayne's rejection of fictionalism, and non-proxy attributing views generally (including Attah's graded intentions).
Sketch

Williams and Bayne reject proxy and fictionalist views and hold that the chatbot has a status of its own. But chatbot output is full of first-person content: 'I checked the source', 'I believe', 'I'm an AI trained by…'. If such outputs are proto-assertions, the 'I' needs a referent. The candidates are the weight file, a running instance, a single conversation, and the simulated persona. The weights have no access to the claimed episode, the instance does not persist, and the conversation is individuated by the user's interface. Those three make many first-person outputs false or ungrounded, and the output pattern is plainly not selected to fit any of them. The persona is the one candidate that fits the content, but it is a fictional character the system is simulating, which is Mallory's fictionalism. The key premise is that assertion requires a subject to whom the commitment attaches, and that for an LLM the subject is underdetermined in a way the proto-assertion label does not repair. Holding that the chatbot proto-asserts therefore commits you to a thesis about who the chatbot is, and Williams and Bayne do not give one.

Appraiser (blind)
It repeats the subject-individuation worry of theses 0 and 4, with a first-person-content twist that adds little.

U220. The proto-assertion resolution is available only for assertion: it commits Williams and Bayne to saying that chatbots cannot proto-promise or proto-apologise, so the supposedly general 'edge of speech acts' view fragments into an assertion-specific view and leaves the apology and promise cases to the denials.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — The generality of the 'proto' category as a solution to the speech-act question for LLMs, and the contrast with Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz and with Skiba.
Sketch

The proto-assertion proposal draws on how assertion emerges from precursors such as informative signalling, where the descriptive function is already present before full commitment-and-sanction norms arrive. A precursor stage requires an act type whose core success condition can be partly satisfied without the normative status being created. Informing can occur without committing. But promising and apologising are constituted by the normative changes they bring about, an obligation incurred or standing to resent removed. They have no sub-normative form, because an utterance either creates the obligation or it does not. The key premise is that the gradualist strategy works only where the act has a function that can be realised in a thinner way. So chatbot 'I promise' or 'I'm sorry' would be either full acts, which Williams and Bayne do not accept, or non-acts, which is what Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz say. What looked like a middle position between denial and attribution is in fact a thesis about the special structure of assertion, and it supports the denials for the acts users care most about socially.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a narrower and weaker version of thesis 1's point about promising and apologising.

U221. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is unstable: the criteria that admit chatbots also admit oracles, divinatory devices and Ouija boards, and the only principled way to exclude those cases makes proto-assertion collapse into fictionalism.

promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion as a third option distinct from fictionalism.
Sketch

Williams and Bayne motivate proto-assertion by the way assertion emerges. A practice first treats outputs as informational and truth-apt and holds producers loosely to account, and speaker-side norm-sensitivity comes later. The Delphic Pythia, the I Ching and an institutional 'the Court finds' were all treated as having a descriptive function, and some were embedded in sanction-like practices (priests, interpreters, discredited oracles falling out of use). Hearers' expectations of reliability shaped these practices, and some did evolve into genuine assertion practices (expert reports, instruments of record). If this edge profile is what proto-assertion requires, then divination devices are proto-assertors, which looks like a reductio. To exclude them one must require that the producer be responsive to the norms in its own output selection. But whether chatbots meet that requirement is exactly what the denial side disputes, and if the requirement is relaxed to 'hearers treat it as if responsive', that is fictionalism. The key premise is that the emergence story fixes the hearer-side conditions first, so the category's boundary is drawn by hearers' attitudes.

Appraiser (blind)
The oracle reductio is rhetorically fun but weak, since the relevant exclusion is easy to supply.

U222. Attah's fallback from the Gricean intention to a 'basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect' runs together effect-targeting and uptake-routed intention, and the child and animal evidence he cites supports only the first, which is what separates signalling from illocution.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Attah's retreat from strong Gricean intention to a bare 'illocutionary or perlocutionary effect' intention, together with the shared assumption that the only alternative to full Gricean mind-reading is effect-targeting.
Sketch

Grice's reflexive structure matters because the effect is meant to come about through the hearer's recognition of the intention. That is what separates telling from manipulating. Attah drops high-order mind-reading as empirically untenable, but he also drops the recognition-routing, as if the two came as a package. They do not. Children and animals plausibly lack metarepresentation yet show uptake-sensitivity: they persist, repeat, or repair when the audience fails to respond appropriately, and drop the aim once it is met. So the right thin condition is that the control state is stabilised or discharged by uptake, not by the effect alone. RLHF-trained chatbots are optimised for effect-targeting (approval, engagement) with no recognition-route in training, because the reward is applied to the response and not to the audience's grasp of what was meant. On the correct thin condition, Attah's argument for LLM intentions establishes signalling-type aims at best. Whether LLMs meet the uptake-sensitivity condition becomes an empirical question about multi-turn repair, which neither the Gricean nor the functional camp has posed. The premise it turns on is that the effect-targeting/uptake-routed distinction is independent of the metarepresentation requirement.

Appraiser (blind)
A careful but narrow technical critique of one paper's fallback condition, with a limited audience.

U223. A graded notion of intention on which a coffee machine has 'almost none' cannot answer the speech-act question. If it has no threshold, it is trivially true of LLMs. If it has a threshold, the threshold is set by mental and metalinguistic agency, which Attah himself names as the real difference, so his view collapses into the agency-based denial.

Move · Target
instability — Attah's graded conception of intention and his claim that communicative intention is the wrong ground for the human/LLM distinction.
Sketch

Attah's conclusion is that communicative intention does not mark the human/LLM boundary, and he locates that boundary in mental and metalinguistic agency. Speech acts are all-or-nothing in status: one either asserts or does not, one either apologises or does not. A graded property yields a speech-act verdict only if some degree is required. If any degree suffices, a thermostat that 'says' the room is cold performs speech acts, which is a reductio of the functional conception. If a degree is required, nothing in the control conception can supply it, because every system that solves a Many-Many selection problem counts. The cut must come from elsewhere, and Attah's own closing remark says where: capacities for self-ascription and metalinguistic regulation of one's speech. That makes the threshold-setter a Gubelmann- or Butlin-style agency condition. So the thin intention view is not an independent position. It is a premise-weakening that leaves the real dispute, over agency, untouched and in the denier's favour.

Appraiser (blind)
The graded-versus-threshold objection is fairly obvious, and 'collapses into agency denial' leans on a closing remark of Attah's more than on an argument.

U224. Attah's concession that the real human–LLM difference is the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency means that, on his own account, 'communicative intention' is a red herring. The dispute is about whether performing a speech act requires being able to take that act as one's own, that is, to classify it, own it, and retract it.

promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Attah's closing concession, and the denial camp's self-description as an intention-based or norm-based view
Sketch

Attah argues that communicative intention does not separate humans from models, because even animals and infants have thin versions and models plausibly have graded ones. He then locates the difference in metalinguistic and mental agency. But apologising, promising and asserting are not just illocutionary effects intended on a hearer. They are acts whose performer can be asked 'did you mean that as a promise?' and can withdraw or revise under the act-type description. If metalinguistic agency is what is missing, then it is also what Magnus et al. (moral and linguistic agency), Butlin and Viebahn (sanctionability), and Gubelmann (distinguishing malfunction from doing wrong) are each pointing at, under different names. All of them require a capacity for second-order answerability to one's act under its type-description. The premise the argument turns on is that graded first-order intention is available to a coffee machine in Attah's sense, so it cannot be what makes the speech-act question non-trivial. The dispute then stops being intention-presence versus intention-absence and becomes whether answerability can be conferred, as proxy and fictional accounts suggest, or must be intrinsic. That also explains why the attributionist and denier camps seem to talk past each other.

Appraiser (blind)
Largely repeats the answerability point developed more fully in thesis 1 and in Butlin–Viebahn, adding little new.

U225. Attah's control conception of intention, combined with his appeal to design-supplied purposes, commits him to the proxy view: because a system prompt or in-context instruction is text that controls the model's output dynamics and encodes someone else's communicative aim, the state that fills the role of the model's intention is literally the deployer's intention in textual form.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Attah's claim that design context supplies LLMs with purposes, and the assumption that attributing views and proxy views are rivals
Sketch

On Attah's account an intention is an internal state that selects among many possible outputs in a situation that calls for one. In a deployed LLM, the states doing that selecting are largely the system prompt and the user instruction, held in context and acting through attention. They are authored by humans, they specify the effect to be produced on a hearer ("apologise sincerely", "advise cautiously"), and the model's dynamics then execute them. So the control conception does not find an originary intention inside the model. It finds an installed, delegated one, whose content and target were fixed by an external author and transmitted by text. A human who is told what to say and says it is the standard case of a proxy or delegated speech act. The premise it turns on is that control by an externally authored, content-bearing state is not originary control. Attah must then either say that the model's intention is the operator's, which is Green and Michel's view relabelled, or deny that prompt-borne states are intentions. The second option leaves little for the model's own purposes to be, because they were supposed to come from design context. The attributing and relocating families therefore collapse into each other.

Appraiser (blind)
Largely a restatement of the collapse-into-proxy worry in thesis 3, with a strained identification of system-prompt text with the model's intention.

U226. Attah's closing concession that the real human–LLM difference is the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency commits him to the normative denial of speech acts, because it makes the capacity to own, monitor and answer for an utterance, rather than communicative intention, the condition for speech-act performance, so winning on intentions concedes the question.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Attah's overall conclusion that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from LLMs
Sketch

Attah argues that LLMs have communicative intentions in a graded, limited form and that intention is therefore not what separates them from humans. But he also says the genuine difference lies in mental and metalinguistic agency, meaning representing one's own states and one's utterances as utterances. Speech acts are standardly taken to be acts whose performer can be held to what was said, can retract, correct or clarify, and can recognise the act as the kind it is. Apologising, promising and asserting each require this. That is the substance of Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition and of Magnus et al.'s agency condition. If the missing capacities are exactly the ones needed for being the author of a speech act, then the intention-based argument, even if sound, establishes at most that LLMs have an ingredient of speech acts and not that they perform any. Attah must either deny that metalinguistic agency matters for speech acts, which makes his own diagnosis of the difference idle, or accept that the normative views have the correct verdict and the intentions debate is orthogonal to it. The premise it turns on is that speech-act performance requires the ability to take the act as one's own, and that this is not supplied by having a control state aimed at an effect.

Appraiser (blind)
It mostly restates the Butlin–Viebahn and Magnus et al. normative line, using Attah's closing remark as the lever.

U227. The 'interactional asymmetry' condition that Barandiaran and Almendros use to deny LLM agency measures initiative, not agency; the acts at issue (answering, advising, apologising, asserting-in-reply) are responsive, so the denial concerns a different class of speech acts than the one the debate is about.
