promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Barandiaran and Almendros's interactional-asymmetry condition and the general move from 'not an autonomous agent' to 'performs no speech acts'.
Sketch

The enactivist asymmetry condition says the system must be the source of its own coupling to the environment, whereas an LLM is activated, turn by turn, by the user. But in human speech the same pattern holds for a large class of acts: an expert answering a question, a clerk confirming a booking, a person apologising when told they have offended. These acts are structurally triggered by the interlocutor and take their content from the prompt. The asymmetry condition would deprive the responder of agency in just these exchanges, which is absurd, so it must be tracking something else, namely the capacity to initiate. Initiating acts (promising unprompted, volunteering a warning, changing the topic) are where the denial is really strong. The paper's own examples of ordinary 'genuine conversation' sit on the responsive side. The key premise is that the structure of speech acts allows a principled initiating/responsive divide, and that the arguments about agency in this literature are driven by the initiating case while the cited cases are responsive. The dispute then turns out to be partly about two different explananda.

Appraiser (blind)
The initiative versus responsiveness distinction is intuitive but small, and it criticises one condition in one paper.

U228. Barandiaran and Almendros's 'midtended' hybrid agency is not a new third kind of agent. It is the author–ghostwriter relation that proxy accounts already model, so it either collapses into a proxy view or must treat the LLM as a co-speaker, which contradicts their denial of its agency.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — The claim that midtended agency marks a qualitatively new mode of agency, and the proxy/hybrid contrast.
Sketch

The novelty claim is that the human–LLM coupling yields forms of agency that earlier tool-extensions did not. For speech acts this must mean the following. Either some entity (the hybrid or the human) is the speaker, or the LLM's contribution is part of what makes the act that of its speaker. Take speechwriting, ghostwriting and spokespersons, which are well-studied cases of proxy and conditional speech acts (Green and Michel). The person who endorses the output is the speaker, and the drafter's contribution creatively shapes what is said without making the drafter a speaker. A human who adopts an LLM's draft stands in the same relation. What is new is only a change in degree: how much of the content is authored by the drafting part, and how little endorsement the human gives. If the hybrid is the speaker, its individuality and precariousness are exactly the human's, so the hybrid is the human plus an instrument, and the denial of LLM agency is preserved but nothing is new. If instead the LLM's non-endorsed contributions make speech acts that no human performs, then the LLM is in effect a co-author, and that needs an agency they explicitly deny. The key premise is that endorsement by a human is what makes the hybrid's speech acts someone's.

Appraiser (blind)
Assimilating 'midtended' agency to the ghostwriter relation is plausible but a modest deflationary point.

U229. The question 'can an LLM perform speech acts?' is under-specified because the candidate speaker can be individuated at four different grains (the weight file, the running inference instance, the deployed persona, the human–model network), and the main positions in the debate differ largely because each silently picks a different grain.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption, across Gubelmann, Attah, Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne, that there is one determinate entity, 'the LLM', whose speech-act status is in question.
Sketch

Puzio treats 'the LLM' as a node whose boundaries are an open question, and she dissolves it into a network. The speech-act literature never asks this. Gubelmann's organismic argument targets the trained artifact, whose goals are externally fixed. Attah's graded intention is assigned to a pipeline instance with belief-state tracking. Butlin's agency criterion applies to the system plus memory and reflection scaffolding, i.e. a language agent. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion fits a persona in a conversation. Proxy views make the 'machine' a mere conduit. Once the grains are separated, many apparent disagreements go away. The weight file is a policy-type that cannot assert, just as a grammar cannot. A persona can be a fictional character whose assertions are real only inside the fiction, which brings fictionalism and attribution close together. The instance is the only grain with a single context and a single stream of 'commitments'. The key premise is that each speech-act condition (intention, sanctionability, descriptive function) is satisfied or failed at different grains, so no single grain passes them all. The denials then win only by mixing grains, for example assessing intention at the instance and sanction at the weights.

Appraiser (blind)
Grain-individuation of the speaker largely duplicates thesis 3 and familiar level-of-description observations.

U230. Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts are unstable: they presuppose a determinate principal whose objectives the machine's utterance carries, but for RLHF-trained models no such principal exists, so the view collapses into attributing the speech act to the trained system itself.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora; Butlin and Viebahn's fallback), and the shared assumption that proxy is the safe middle position.
Sketch

Green and Michel and Arora model proxy speech acts on a spokesperson or recorded message, where an identifiable principal has the relevant objective (Armstrong-style) and the device transmits it. Puzio's actor-network point is that an LLM's dispositions are shaped by annotators, preference-aggregation procedures, scraped authors, policy teams and optimisation dynamics that no one fully specified. The key premise is that proxy-hood requires the output to be answerable to some agent's communicative objective, and that this objective must be fixed prior to and independently of the particular output. For a deployed model, the only objective that reliably and specifically covers a particular novel utterance is the one encoded in the model's learned policy. If the principal is the company, the company has no objective about this sentence (a conditional proxy about all outputs is too thin to ground a particular assertion or promise). If the principal is the distributed network, no one is the speaker. So either the proxy view is true only of scripted systems, or its explanatory work is done by the policy's own objective-tracking, which is the attributing view (Attah, Butlin) under another name.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that proxy views collapse for RLHF models is already close to Williams and Bayne's critique and is largely subsumed by thesis 16.

U231. For speech acts, the contest between property-based and relational accounts of agency is not a real contest, because the leading denial (assertion needs sanctionability) is already relational, and a relational condition makes LLM speakership depend on conferrable social status and so collapses into a status-function view on which LLMs can be speakers by institutional decision.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Normative denials (Butlin and Viebahn; Skiba) and the framing of the debate as individualist versus relational.
Sketch

Puzio frames the debate as individualistic property accounts versus network accounts. But Butlin and Viebahn's second condition (capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors) and Skiba's norm-based argument make speakerhood partly constituted by how others can hold one to account. The key premise is that a sanction-capacity condition is not an intrinsic property but a feature of a deontic arrangement: whether a model can be sanctioned depends on whether there are practices of reputation-loss, retraining, de-deployment or liability that attach to the model qua model rather than to its owner. These are institutional choices, already partly in place (models are deprecated for bad assertions, and users stop trusting 'it'). So the denial's verdict is contingent on arrangements we could change, and its best version predicts that LLMs become assertors when we build the right sanction practices. That is the structure of a Searlean status-function view, which the denial was meant to oppose. The 'beyond them (for now)' position turns out to concede that the question is political-conventional rather than about what the model is.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that sanctionability is relational and so makes speakerhood a matter of institutional status is plausible, but it is largely implicit in Butlin and Viebahn and overlaps heavily with thesis 5.

U232. Puzio's relational-material view of agency is unstable as a position on speech acts: the 'making a difference' criterion of agency she shares with Actor-Network Theory is too cheap to distinguish speakers from coffee machines, and once the speech-act-relevant subset of the network is picked out, her view collapses into either a proxy account or the thin functional account.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Puzio's relational-materialist account and relational accounts of distributed agency generally, as applied to speech acts.
Sketch

Puzio admits non-human agency because actants transform the network by making a difference. Speech acts require a narrower role: being the one who commits, advises or apologises, who can be addressed in the second person, and whose act is attributable. The key premise is that any view of speech acts must carry a principle that selects, among the many difference-making actants, which one is the author of this assertion. ANT's symmetry principle forbids privileging by metaphysical kind, so the selection must be done by network position or function. Two options exist. If the selecting function is 'node that carries a human principal's communicative objective', the view becomes proxy (Green and Michel). If it is 'node whose internal state controls the output in response to the situation', it becomes Attah's control conception, with a graded scale on which a thermostat has a little. Either way the relational view supplies no theory of speakerhood of its own, and what looks like a third option is a redescription of one of its neighbours, with the materiality talk playing no role in the verdict.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a standard objection that ANT-style agency is too cheap, applied to Puzio, and the collapse into proxy or functional accounts is predictable.

U233. Barandiaran and Almendros cannot hold both that an LLM is an interlocutor in genuine conversation and that human–LLM coupling forms a 'midtended' hybrid agent. If the user plus the model is one agent, the conversation is a soliloquy of that agent, and nothing is told to anyone.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Barandiaran and Almendros's joint use of 'interlocutor/linguistic automaton' and 'midtended agency'; also any hybrid-agency view that keeps conversational language.
Sketch

The paper credits LLMs with being interlocutors and says interaction with them can be experienced as genuine conversation. It also says the novel thing is hybrid agency, in which the human and the model form one extended, coupled agent. On the usual extended-mind logic, a component that is constitutively part of an agent's cognitive loop does not address that agent. It is used by it. So within the hybrid, an LLM output is the user's own cognition in externalised form, like a notebook entry or an inner monologue, and not an utterance directed at the user. The key premise is that being addressed requires a party outside the addressee's agential boundary. Two consequences follow. First, 'LLM testimony' to the user is really reliance on an instrument, so the quasi-testimony debate is misdescribed. Second, the only live speech-act question concerns the hybrid's outputs to third parties, where the speaker is the human-led hybrid. That is a proxy-like result reached by a different route, and without the corporate or designer intentions the proxy theorists invoke. 'Interlocutor' then names only a phenomenology of conversation, and this is exactly the deflationary reading the authors say they are avoiding.

Appraiser (blind)
It is a neat internal tension between 'interlocutor' and 'midtended' agency, but the payoff is limited to one paper and depends on a strong reading of extended-mind logic.

U234. The enactive conditions of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry are not conditions on speech-act performance at all, so denying LLMs autonomous agency leaves their speech-act status untouched. The 'interlocutor' and 'purpose-structured' concessions then commit Barandiaran and Almendros to heteronomous speech acts.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — The inference, shared by Gubelmann and enactivist-inclined readers, from 'no autonomous agency' to 'no speech acts', as it applies to Barandiaran and Almendros's own framework.
Sketch

Enactive normativity is the adaptive, self-maintenance-relative value found in any precarious organism. A dog, a bacterium or a toddler meets all three conditions and cannot assert, promise or apologise. So the conditions are not sufficient for speech acts. Many human speech acts are also performed under norms that are socially imposed and indifferent to the speaker's self-maintenance: performatives by officials, role-bound announcements, scripted professional speech. So the conditions are not obviously necessary either. Speech-act norms, such as the truth norm for assertion or the commitment structure of promising, are constitutive social norms. The key premise is that the normativity relevant to illocution is social-constitutive, not adaptive-organismic. Barandiaran and Almendros then grant that LLMs perform 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' tasks and occupy the interlocutor role. That grants the heteronomous, role-defined normative structure that speech acts require. Their argument for denying autonomy therefore does no work against Gubelmann's inference to 'no speech acts', yet their characterisation of LLMs as interlocutors implies something close to role-based speech-act status. They owe a bridge principle from enactive autonomy to illocutionary agency, and the dog case shows none is available.

Appraiser (blind)
The dog counterexample shows enactive autonomy is not a bridge to speech acts, but that point is fairly obvious and the argument is aimed at one paper.

U235. The 'library that talks' characterisation commits Barandiaran and Almendros to treating each LLM output as a quoted or reported speech act of the corpus's authors, which they must reject because outputs are novel; and rejecting it removes the characterisation's explanatory work.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Barandiaran and Almendros's 'library-that-talks / linguistic automaton' characterisation, and its tacit neutrality across the proxy, fictionalist and denial views.
Sketch

A library has no speech acts of its own. Its holdings are the recorded illocutions of authors, and a visitor who consults a book is being told something by the author via a durable medium. If a 'library that talks' is an ontological category and not a metaphor, then reading its outputs is receiving recorded or reported speech, which Green and Michel treat as a legitimate form of speech act performed by the original author. The key premise is that the category is explanatory only if it says whose illocutions are conveyed. But LLM outputs are not retrievals. They are novel compositions that no author in the corpus performed, so no particular corpus author is saying this. There are two ways out. One is to say the output is a statistical blend, a 'distributed utterance' of all the authors. That gives a collective speaker with no communicative intention and no uptake-sensitivity, so Griceanism fails and what remains is something like Mallory's fiction. The other is to say the library-that-talks adds its own composition, so it is not a library, and the 'tasks purpose-structured but not purposeful' claim must then say whose purposes are being expressed. Either way the characterisation does not settle the speech-act question and instead reopens it as a question of attributing authorship.

Appraiser (blind)
It presses a metaphor ('library that talks') for an authorship answer; the dilemma is tidy but the target is minor and the objection is easy to anticipate.

U236. Attah's view that a model's communicative intentions are graded and have their purposes supplied by its design context commits him to locating those intentions in the model-plus-deployment assemblage rather than in the model, so the 'attributing' view collapses into a relational view of the kind Puzio defends.

Move · Target
commitment — Attah 2025 (graded functional intention), and the assumed separation between attributing and relocating views
Sketch

Attah concedes that the purposes behind language-model speech are 'mediated by human designers' and 'supplied by the design context'. On his control conception, an intention is an internal state that controls the system's dynamics so that it acts in a situation that calls for action. If the system-level purpose is fixed by system prompts, fine-tuning targets, tool scaffolds and the deployer's objectives, then the state doing the controlling is not fixed by the weights. The same weights under different scaffolds have different controlling states and so different intentions. The bearer of the intention is therefore the weights-plus-context assemblage, which is Puzio's network unit, trimmed down. Attah cannot say the intention is in the model without losing the design-context clause. If he says it is in the assemblage, his view is a relocating view with a Gricean label. His own closing admission that the real difference lies in 'mental and metalinguistic agency' then looks like a symptom of this collapse. The key premise is that purposes supplied from outside the controlling mechanism are not properties of that mechanism.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing that Attah's design-context clause relocates intention to the assemblage is a modest exegetical point that is easy to resist by distinguishing causal from constitutive roles.

U237. Puzio's distribution of agency across a network of human and non-human actors, when applied to apology, commits her to the view that chatbot apologies are institutional acts like a corporate statement of regret, and that apology therefore requires no remorse-bearing locus. That concedes the 'bullshit' verdict as a description and rejects the moral-agency premise that Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz apply to humans.

promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Puzio 2025 (ethics reoriented toward networks), and the shared assumption that apology requires an individual locus of moral agency
Sketch

Puzio wants ethical attention to move from the single user or model to the network of workers, firms and technologies. If the chatbot's 'I'm sorry' is an act of that network, then it resembles an organisation's apology, which is issued by no one in particular and is not felt by anyone. Either such acts are genuine apologies, in which case remorse and an individual moral agent are not necessary for apology and Magnus et al.'s requirement fails for humans and machines alike. Or they are not, in which case network agency does not suffice for the speech acts that matter morally. The relational view cannot keep both its flat symmetry and a notion of apology that needs a node that can be sorry. Corporate apologies are the test case, and the dispute over whether they are real apologies is the dispute over whether network agency is enough. The key premise is that no node in the network satisfies the felt-responsibility condition by itself.

Appraiser (blind)
The corporate-apology dilemma for network agency is reasonable but fairly predictable, and the attribution to Puzio is strained.

U238. Butlin and Viebahn's two conditions are not jointly sufficient, because a templated weather-report generator that can be sanctioned (delisted, banned, replaced) meets both and does not assert; so the conditions leave open the question they are meant to settle for LLMs.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
counterexample — Butlin and Viebahn's attempt to settle AI assertion by social-practice conditions without a commitment to intention or agency; also Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument.
Sketch

Their conditions are stated as necessary, and the paper's strategy is to show current systems fail one of them. But the exercise only matters if the conditions are close to sufficient, since otherwise passing them would not show that an LLM asserts. Consider a rule-based bot that generates stubs about species, or a weather-text generator. Its outputs have a clear descriptive function (they are produced to report states of affairs and are corrected when wrong). It is sanctioned by those it interacts with: editors ban it, an app store removes it, subscribers cancel. By the paper's own criteria it meets both conditions, yet almost nobody, including the authors presumably, thinks the template engine asserts. If they accept that it asserts, assertion is cheap and the question about chatbots loses its philosophical interest. If they reject it, something further is needed (understanding, commitment, a content-sensitive stance towards what is said), and that extra element is exactly what the debate about intentions and agency concerns. The premise the argument turns on is that the sanctions in play are exerted on the system as a thing to be tuned or removed, and that tuning of this kind is not the same as holding someone to account. The paper's normative strand therefore either collapses into the agency debate it seeks to bypass or trivialises assertion.

Appraiser (blind)
Necessary-but-not-sufficient objections are cheap, and the authors only claim necessity, so the thesis mostly restates the agency debate.

U239. The dispute over whether pre-trained models meet the descriptive-function condition is not about language models at all. It turns on whether functions are inherited by reproduction (Millikan's derived proper functions) or must be selected for in the system itself. On the first theory the pre-trained model's outputs already have descriptive function, and Butlin and Viebahn's first condition does not discriminate between base and fine-tuned models.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Butlin and Viebahn's claim that non-fine-tuned pre-trained models fail the descriptive-function condition.
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn hold that pre-trained models fail the first condition: next-token prediction selects for fit to a text distribution, not for descriptive function, and only groundedness or correctness fine-tuning might supply it. But the corpus consists largely of assertions, and the training process selects for reproducing those assertions' patterns. On Millikan's theory, items reproduced from a model inherit the model's proper function through the reproductive lineage, as a copied sentence inherits the function of the sentence it copies. The base model's outputs would then have the descriptive function of their sources, even though the system was not selected for truth. If this is rejected and only direct selection counts, then much human assertion, learned by imitation, would also fail. The first condition's verdict therefore depends on the grain and etiology theory of function, and the base/fine-tuned contrast loses its principled status. The turning premise is that Butlin and Viebahn's function notion is etiological but silent on derived versus direct selection.

Appraiser (blind)
The Millikan derived-function argument is a narrow technical objection to one distinction with a small payoff.

U240. Butlin's own criterion of agency, together with Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, commits them to the view that assertion requires something close to desire, so assertion is more demanding than agency and more demanding than anything they say they need for the descriptive-function condition.

Move · Target
commitment — The joint package of Butlin (2024) and Butlin and Viebahn (2025), and more broadly the pairing of 'agent' with 'norm-governed participant'.
Sketch

In 'The agency in language agents', Butlin holds that an entity is an agent when it modifies itself in response to information about what conduces to a goal. Reflexion-style systems count unambiguously. On a thin reading, sanction is just negative feedback, which is information about what conduces to the goal, so any such agent that interacts with sanctioners is thinly sanctionable and would pass condition 2. To keep the conclusion that fine-tuned and agentic systems fail, 'sanction' must be read thickly: the sanction must matter to the system as a cost to it, which is a stake. But Butlin separately argues that stakes and goals of that kind require desire, and that desire demands practical reasoning answerable to conduciveness and an integrated, learned goal set. So the argument turns on one dilemma: either sanction is thin and some language agents already assert, or it is thick and assertion presupposes desire-like states that Butlin elsewhere says are doubtful for existing systems. That makes assertion a cognitively heavier act than agency. The authors present their two papers as modular, but they are not.

Appraiser (blind)
It is an exegetical claim about tensions between two papers by one author, of little general interest.

U241. The 'descriptive function' condition, when carried over into the proxy-assertion fallback, makes a deployer's own speech-act status depend on a hidden engineering property of the tool (whether the model was fine-tuned for correctness), so Butlin and Viebahn are committed to a bizarre externalism about what humans themselves assert.

commitment — Butlin and Viebahn's proxy-assertion fallback, and proxy accounts generally (Green and Michel, Arora).
Sketch

Butlin and Viebahn say that pre-trained models produce no outputs with descriptive function, and that AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions for humans. The question is what makes a deployer's unreviewed chatbot outputs their assertions. The natural answer is that the deployer delegates a standing descriptive role to the system: 'whatever it says in the informative register, I stand behind.' But delegation of a descriptive function to something with none is incoherent, or at best merely nominal. If the delegation is real, it needs the tool's outputs to be reliably truth-directed, so a company deploying a fine-tuned model asserts and one deploying the same interface over a base model does not. Users, intentions, uptake and the company's liability are all identical in the two cases. The alternative is to say proxy assertion needs no descriptive function in the tool. Then the first condition is idle for exactly the cases where it matters, and the fallback becomes unconstrained. The key premise is that proxy speech acts inherit the functional conditions on the instrument. Proponents of the proxy view, including Green and Michel and Arora, would resist this.

Appraiser (blind)
It is an internal-consistency objection about the proxy fallback that depends on an uncharitable reading and has small payoff.

U242. If sanctionability by one's interlocutors is a condition on asserting, Butlin and Viebahn must either deny that anonymous, posthumous and mass-broadcast writers assert or relocate sanction to institutions, and the institutional reading dissolves their contrast between direct AI assertion and proxy assertion, because all written assertion then becomes proxy-like.

commitment — The sanctionability condition and its role in separating direct from proxy assertion in Butlin and Viebahn.
Sketch

The condition says an asserter must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with. Many human assertors cannot be sanctioned by their actual audience: the dead author, the pseudonymous poster, the wire-service writer, and the person whose words are published after they can no longer be reached. Reading the condition strictly makes these non-assertions, which is absurd. Reading it generously, as sanction through publishers, reputation systems, legal liability or platforms, is plausible. But then the thing sanctioned is a node in an institutional network, such as an imprint, a byline or a platform account, and not the individual speaker confronting an interlocutor. On that reading a chatbot's vendor, brand and model line are exactly such nodes, and the vendor is routinely sanctioned for outputs. The key premise is that institution-mediated sanction is the normal case for text. So either the condition is too strict for humans or it is already satisfied by the deployer-plus-model unit, and 'AI asserts versus AI is a proxy for a human asserter' stops being a clean contrast.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that institution-mediated sanction is normal for text is reasonable but largely duplicates the pseudonymous-assertor objection.

U243. The claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit is unstable: bullshit is a defective way of performing a speech act, so someone who calls a chatbot's apology bullshit has already conceded that an apology was performed, and the denial of chatbot apology collapses into an attributing view on which chatbots apologise defectively.

instability — Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's combination of 'chatbots cannot apologise' with 'chatbot apologies are bullshit'. The same tension affects Skiba's no-speech-act view, but this version arises specifically from the apology case.
Sketch

Frankfurtian bullshit is not the absence of assertion. It is assertion made with indifference to its truth. Likewise a bullshit apology must be an apology (or a performance with an apology's force) made without the remorse or commitment that makes it sincere. Magnus et al. need a way to classify the output as bullshit and also to say the chatbot cannot apologise. The key premise is Austin's distinction between conditions for performing an act and conditions for performing it non-abusively. Sincerity and remorse are standardly the latter: an insincere apology is still an apology. If the moral agency they require is a sincerity condition, then bullshit apology is a defective apology and the chatbot apologises. If it is a constitutive condition, then there is no bullshit apology, only noise or mimicry, and the Frankfurt framing has no purchase. They cannot have both the bullshit diagnosis and the denial of the act.

Appraiser (blind)
The point that bullshit presupposes a performed act is fairly obvious, and Skiba already notes the tension between bullshit and no-speech-act views.

U244. Any moral-agency requirement on apology strong enough to exclude chatbots also excludes corporate and spokesperson apologies, and any requirement weak enough to admit those admits chatbots as proxies, so the denial view collapses into the proxy view and the bullshit charge transfers to the deployer.

Magnus et al. ground the denial in the fact that an apology requires an agent who can feel remorse, take responsibility and be morally answerable. But we treat institutional apologies read out by press officers, or by a CEO who personally did nothing wrong and feels nothing, as genuine apologies by the institution. Either (a) the requirement is on the agent who owns the apology, in which case it is satisfied by the deployer, who is answerable, and the chatbot is a speaking-device like the press officer's script, which is the proxy view; or (b) the requirement is on the utterer, in which case most institutional apologies are not apologies, an unacceptable result for a view built on the practice's moral importance. The key premise is that apology, unlike assertion, has an established vicarious and institutional form that already separates the utterer from the moral agent. The denial of the chatbot's apology then becomes a claim about who owns it, and the proxy view takes over. The bullshit diagnosis also moves from the output to the company, which is indifferent to whether the remorse is real.

Appraiser (blind)
The corporate-apology dilemma that pushes denial toward proxy views is largely anticipated by Green and Michel and by Arora.

Frankfurtian bullshit is not mere noise. It is a performance of a speech act (asserting, apologising) made with indifference to the condition that gives the act its point. A bullshit apology therefore has to be an apology: a performed act with a defective or absent sincerity condition. On Austin's account this is an 'abuse', not a misfire, and the act still occurs. Their anti-chatbot premise is that remorse or moral agency is needed to apologise. If that is a constitutive condition, an unremorseful human 'apology' is not an apology and cannot be bullshit either; it is a mere noise-with-form. If remorse is only a sincerity condition, the chatbot's utterance is an apology, bullshit or not, and the denial of speech-act performance fails. The 'bullshit' diagnosis needs the second horn and the 'lacks agency to apologise' thesis needs the first. The premise everything turns on is that bullshit is predicated of acts, not of strings.

Appraiser (blind)
This is the same bullshit-versus-misfire inconsistency as thesis 8, stated as a direct charge against one paper, with a modest payoff.

U246. If, as Magnus et al. suggest, the moral point of apology lies in taking responsibility and repairing trust rather than in affect, then a chatbot that reliably changes its subsequent behaviour has satisfied the forward-looking, purpose-of-amendment component of apology better than many humans do, so their denial survives only if remorse as feeling is essential, which they officially downplay.

commitment — The agency requirement in Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz, and its pairing with a non-phenomenal, relational account of apology.
Sketch

The standard components of a morally serious apology are recognition of the wrong, acceptance of responsibility, expression of regret, and a commitment to reform, plus reparation. Magnus et al. stress responsibility and repair, which are functional and relational, over inner feeling. Language agents with in-context learning, memory, or fine-tuning on complaints do modify their conduct in response to being told they erred, and this modification is systematic and checkable, unlike a human's promise. By Butlin's sensitivity-to-instrumental-value criterion this is a case of an output explained by the system's own adjustment. Either the amendment component can be met by a non-human system, so the denial has to rest on regret as a felt state, which makes apology depend on phenomenology, a view they avoid; or amendment requires the owning of the wrong as one's own, which presupposes the very 'moral agency' being argued for and makes the argument circular. The premise it turns on is that responsibility-taking cannot be exhausted by dispositional answerability.

Appraiser (blind)
The dilemma between remorse as feeling and circular moral agency is competent, but the functionalist reading of apology is well-trodden.

The thesis that chatbots lack the moral agency to apologise, taken with the ordinary acceptance of corporate and spokesperson apologies, commits its holders to locating the sincerity of a chatbot apology entirely in the deployer, so a chatbot 'I'm sorry' can be a fully sincere, non-bullshit apology whenever a deployer has genuine remorse and standing behind it.

Nobody thinks a press secretary reading a prepared apology, or a letter signed by a CEO and drafted by counsel, is bullshit just because the utterer lacks the remorse or the responsibility. Remorse and answerability are required of the principal, and the instrument is evaluated through the principal's relation to the words. If moral agency is a requirement on apologising, it is satisfied by the principal where an authorised proxy performs. Then the verdict on a chatbot apology depends on facts about the deployer: whether the company recognises the wrong, will compensate, and has authorised this apology policy. The bullshit verdict becomes contingent, and some chatbot apologies, such as an airline's bot offering a refund with an acknowledged error, are good apologies. Magnus et al. then have no general verdict on chatbot apologies. They have a verdict on a typical deployment pattern in which no one stands behind the apology. This is Green and Michel's proxy view under another description, and it undercuts the claim that something is wrong with the chatbot's agency as such.

Appraiser (blind)
This is the proxy view applied to apology, so Green and Michel and Arora have already made the argument.

The agent did not cause the problem, feels no remorse, is not the one who will make amends, and is reading from a template. Customers accept or reject the apology as the company's. The agent's own agency is idle at every point at which Magnus et al. say agency is required: expressing remorse, taking responsibility, repairing trust. This yields a dilemma for the denial view. (a) If the agent's apology counts as the agent's, then the agency-based conditions are not required for apologising. (b) If it counts as the company's, then proxy structure already governs human apologies, and the contrast between a human and a chatbot mouthpiece cannot be what grounds the denial. In both cases the variable doing the work is the presence of an answerable principal behind the utterance, not the mouthpiece's agency. Whether a chatbot apologises then depends on whether a principal exists. That is a question about institutions, and the chatbot's mind is irrelevant to it.

Appraiser (blind)
The scripted customer-service agent is a stock counterexample whose lesson, that an answerable principal matters, is already in the proxy literature.

U249. Most chatbot apologies ('I apologize for the confusion, here is the corrected version') are conversational repairs whose commitment to amend is discharged within the same turn, so they meet the function of apology more reliably than the thin human 'sorry' that Magnus et al. treat as the paradigm.

counterexample — Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's argument from what a morally serious apology involves.

The moral-agency requirement is derived from weighty apologies: expressing remorse, taking responsibility, repairing trust. Human conversational apologies such as 'sorry, I meant Tuesday' or 'sorry, what?' need none of this and are paradigm apologies. A chatbot's local apology presupposes an error in the previous turn, acknowledges it, and delivers the amended content at once. The commitment to forbear is checkable and kept, and within the context window it is binding. It fails only when moral apology is demanded, that is, for wrongs with moral weight, and only because it lacks standing there. So the premise 'apologising requires remorse-grade agency' is false of a large class of apologies. The real boundary is the weight of the wrong, and it falls inside the chatbot's usage as well as between chatbots and humans. The apparent conflict between inflationary and deflationary views of chatbot apology then comes from using different tokens as test cases.

Appraiser (blind)
The point about local conversational apologies repeats the repair-move and weight-of-wrong observations, with less original framing than thesis 4.

A court-ordered apology, a child told to say sorry, and a manipulator's calculated apology each lack remorse, moral concern and any intention to reform, and each is nonetheless an apology, though a defective one. So remorse and moral seriousness are sincerity or felicity conditions, and their absence yields a bad apology, not no apology. Frankfurt bullshit is a defect of a performed representational act: indifference to truth in what one puts forward. If chatbots lack the agency to perform apologies, there is no act to be bullshit, and the output would be mere text, which is Skiba's no-speech-act view. If the output is bullshit, then an act was performed, and the missing agency was a sincerity-grade defect. Magnus et al. need either a constitutive condition beyond the sincerity conditions they list, such as standing or answerability, or they must give up one of their two headline claims. The standing condition is a social-role condition, and a deployer-backed system could in principle satisfy it.

Appraiser (blind)
Compelled and cynical apologies add examples to the same sincerity-versus-constitutive-condition dilemma already raised in theses 8 and 12.

instability — Skiba 2026's contrast with intermediate views, and the map's separation of denial from proto-assertion.
Sketch

Skiba concludes that understanding LLM output requires pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction. Users criticise outputs as false, demand retraction, treat them as sources of information, and trust or distrust the system. Whatever the denier says about these practices, it must identify a status that outputs have in them: apt for correctness evaluation, answerable to a truth standard in some manner, and not a speaker's commitment. That is just what proto-assertion is: a status that has the functional role of assertion without the full normative and agential package. The only difference left is whether 'assertion' is reserved for the full package, and that is terminological. The argument turns on the premise that the denier cannot describe these practices without a correctness standard internal to the practice. If the standard is external, merely users' projection, the denier collapses into Mallory's fictionalism instead. So the denial is either proto-assertion or fictionalism, and it has no stable position of its own.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing that denial reduces to proto-assertion or fictionalism is mostly terminological, and it assumes that Skiba's pragmatic supplement must take this form.

Combined with an externalist meta-semantics for artificial expressions, the no-speech-act view collapses into a user-as-sole-speaker view: if model tokens refer only through human intentions and causal chains, the only candidate performer of any speech act with that content is the human who takes up the token.

Skiba uses the absence of LLM speech acts to help choose between externalist theories of reference for artificial expressions. Externalism ties reference to chains of use or to deferential intentions of humans. If the model performs no act and no one else did either, as in the denial, then a token's content is inherited from sources that are not acts of the model: the training corpus, the designers, or the user's interpretive uptake. Which source wins matters. If the corpus or designers fix reference, the view becomes the proxy view (designer) or a quotation view (corpus). If uptake fixes reference, as the tokenwise 'no one meant anything' reading pushes it to, the user's intention to use the token to say something is the only act in play, and the user is a speaker who employs the model as an instrument, as with a Ouija board. The denier then cannot keep a free-standing 'no speech act' position. The argument turns on the premise that externalist reference-fixing requires some intentional act that anchors it, and that the denial leaves only users to supply one in the many cases where the model's output is novel.

Appraiser (blind)
The collapse of denial into a user-as-speaker view depends on a strained reading of externalist metasemantics and is likely to be a minor point.

U253. A norm-based denial of LLM assertion cannot stop at the model: the sanction condition is met by the deployer-plus-model system, so the denial is committed to treating released outputs as assertions of that system, which is the proxy view it is meant to compete with.

Skiba's argument, like Butlin and Viebahn's, runs through the claim that asserting is subject to a norm-governed practice with sanctions, and that the model is not the sort of thing that can be sanctioned. The same argument needs a bearer of the norm to explain why we rightly appraise a published false output, such as a defamatory one, as a violation and not merely a malfunction. The only available bearer is the party that releases the output and is answerable for its content. Defamation law, retraction demands and reputational loss already treat the deployer as sanctionable in just the way the argument requires. So either the deployer's answerability for a released output is assertoric, and the no-speech-act view collapses into a proxy account, or it is not assertoric, and then the sanction condition does not track assertion. The key premise is that the sanction condition is satisfied wherever someone is answerable for the content of an utterance as content, and that no feature of the model-deployer pair separates this from ordinary organisational speech.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that norm-based denial collapses into the proxy view is a fairly obvious point that proxy theorists already make.

commitment — Skiba's hybrid programme of externalist meta-semantics plus pragmatics of interaction, and denials of speech acts generally.

Skiba suggests combining meta-semantic theories of reference for artificial expressions with pragmatic theories of human-LLM interaction. Externalist accounts, whether causal-deferential or use-based, can give names such as 'Napoleon' their reference through the training corpus or through users' practice. Indexicals work differently, because their character needs an agent-of-context parameter. 'I', 'I'm sorry' and 'I recommend' appear throughout chatbot output, and with no speech act and no speaker the parameter has no value. The remaining options are a designated agent (the deployer, which is proxy), a persona the user imagines (fictionalism), or the model itself (which gives it a speaker role that Skiba denies). The key premise is that Kaplanian character requires an agent of context, and that the answering-machine cases are handled by deferral to a human whose intentions fix the value.

Appraiser (blind)
The Kaplanian argument about 'I' lacking an agent of context is narrow, and answering-machine cases already supply a standard reply.
